RF01: Imaging and Novel Technologies

RF001: MRI-derived spinal muscle metrics as predictors of physical frailty and functional impairment in degenerative spine patients

Ali Guven 1 , Erika Chiapparelli 1 , Kyle Finos 1 , Marco Burkhard 1 , Bruno Verna 1 , Charlotte Jones 1 , Anna-Maria Mielke 1 , Isaac Nathoo 1 , Artine Arzani 1 , Jennifer Shue 1 , Federico Girardi 1 , Andrew Sama 1 , Frank Cammisa 1 , Alexander Hughes 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Physical frailty is common among older spine surgery patients and is associated with worse outcomes. While imaging biomarkers such as the psoas muscle index (PMI) are used to estimate sarcopenia, they may not accurately capture frailty in spine-specific populations. Given its key stabilizing role and susceptibility to localized degeneration, the multifidus muscle may serve as a more relevant biomarker. This study aimed to evaluate whether MRI-derived quality metrics of the paraspinal muscles better predict physical frailty and poor physical performance than traditional psoas-based measures. Material and Methods: Patients who underwent lumbar spinal fusion surgery from July 2022 to October 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. Physical performance was measured using the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), which evaluates balance, gait speed, and chair stands, each scoring up to 4 points for a total score range of 0-12. Poor physical performance was defined as SPPB ≤ 8 as per guidelines. Patients were classified as not frail (0-2 components), or frail (3 or more) based on the Fried Frailty Phenotype, assessing frailty through five criteria: unintentional weight loss, grip strength, exhaustion, low activity, and slowness. Psoas, erector spinae, and multifidus muscles were segmented at the L4 upper endplate on axial T2-weighted MRI. Fat and lean areas were quantified using signal intensity thresholding. Fatty infiltration (FI) and functional cross-sectional area (fCSA) were calculated, with fCSA adjusted for height squared. Psoas fCSA was reported as the psoas muscle index (PMI). A CSF region of interest was set at the same axial level or the closest possible level if stenosis was present. The PMQ score was calculated as the ratio of lean muscle to CSF intensity (range: 0-1). Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of frailty (FFP ≥ 3) and poor performance (SPPB ≤ 8), with ROC analysis evaluating the discriminatory performance of muscle parameters in patients aged ≥ 60. Results: A total of 163 patients with a mean age of 61 ± 14 years (49.7% female) were included, of which, 19.6% were found to have low physical performance (SPPB ≤ 8) and 11.7% were frail (FFP ≥ 3). Multifidus PMQ and FI were the only muscle metrics significantly associated with both frailty (Odds ratio [OR] 1.06 per 0.01 PMQ score increase, p=0.004; OR 1.07 per 1% FI increase, p = 0.008) and poor physical performance (OR 1.03, p = 0.026; OR 1.05, p = 0.001, respectively). Erector spinae PMQ score also significantly predicted frailty (p = 0.031). PMI and fCSA of erector spinae and multifidus were not predictive. Multifidus PMQ had the highest area under the curve for frailty prediction (0.753) among all muscle metrics. Conclusion: Multifidus PMQ and fatty infiltration were significantly associated with frailty and poor physical performance in degenerative spine patients, outperforming traditional psoas-based measures such as PMI. These findings suggest that MRI-derived paraspinal muscle quality metrics, particularly those of multifidus, may serve as more specific imaging biomarkers of physiologic reserve in spine surgery candidates. Incorporating such measures into preoperative assessment may improve the evaluation of baseline functional status and guide clinical decision-making in adults with degenerative spine disease.

ID: AGS26/211

RF002: Comparative long term radiographic and clinical outcomes following isolated anterior versus transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion at the L5-S1 level

Arpitha Pamula 1 , Jason Salvato 1 , Alex Tang 2 , Tan Chen 3

1 Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine, Scranton, United States,

2 Geisinger Northeast Orthopaedic Residency, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, United States,

3 Geisinger Musculoskeletal institute, Division of Orthopaedic Spine Surgery, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, United States

Introduction: Anterior (ALIF) and transforaminal (TLIF) lumbar interbody fusions are two common techniques for addressing degenerative lumbosacral pathology, each with its own advantages and disadvantages. Differences in long-term radiographic and clinical outcomes remain unclear. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the differences between ALIF and TLIF techniques (1) in terms of radiographic parameters in the preoperative, immediate post-operative, and latest follow-up phase, and (2) in terms of patient reported outcome measures. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed between 2019-2024 identifying patients who underwent isolated elective ALIF or TLIF at the L5-S1 level. Data collected included patient demographics, perioperative data, complications, and revisions. Clinical outcomes were assessed with the Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores collected longitudinally. Delta (Δ) PROMIS and ΔODI was calculated as the difference between the 1 year follow up score from the preoperative score. A minimally clinically important difference (MCID) of 8 for ΔPROMIS and 10 for ΔODI was assumed based on previous literature. The rate of recovery was measured by finding the maximal medical improvement (MMI), the time at which 90% of the patients achieved MCID. The following parameters were used to analyze radiographic outcomes preoperatively (preop), intraoperatively (introp), and postoperatively (postop): anterior (ADH) and posterior disc height (PDH), and segmental lordosis (SL). Intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) between two observers ranged from 0.832-0.991, ensuring reliability. Descriptive and inferential statistics were utilized. Results: A total of 67 patients (TLIF, n = 38; ALIF, n = 29) were included. Demographic analysis revealed that the ALIF group had a lower BMI (27.6 ± 4.9 vs 31.4 ± 6.8, p = 0.026) and more alcohol use (55% vs 20%, p = 0.017). There was no other significant difference found with demographic data. Both the ALIF and TLIF cohort demonstrated similar preoperative L5/S1 parameters for ADH (10.6 mm vs 11.2 mm, p = 0.593), PDH (3.3 mm vs 4.3 mm, p = 0.067), SL (7.9 eg vs 7.0 deg, p = 0.311). The ALIF cohort had a significant change in ADH compared to the TLIF cohort intraoperatively (+10.3 mm vs +4.0 mm, p < 0.01) and was maintained at long term follow up (+8.2 mm vs +5.1 mm, p < 0.01). Similarly, the ALIF cohort had a significant change in SL compared to the TLIF cohort intraoperatively (+8.3 deg vs +2.5 deg, p < 0.01) and was maintained at long term follow up (+4.9 deg vs +2.3 deg, p < 0.01). Conversely, the ALIF cohort had a similar change in PDH compared to the TLIF cohort intraoperatively (+4.4 mm vs +3.4 mm, p > 0.05), but developed significant settling at long term follow up (+2.5 mm vs +3.7 mm, p < 0.01). Both cohorts clinically improved similarly, with no significant differences in PROMIS Global Overall, PROMIS Global Physical, ODI scores at preop, 6 week, 12 week, 6 month, 1 year follow up. There was no significant difference in the rate of recovery or MMI. Conclusion: The ALIF technique achieves greater correction of anterior disc height and segmental lordosis compared to the TLIF technique at the lumbosacral junction. The TLIF technique provides better long-term correction and maintenance of posterior disc height, and by association foraminal height. Similar long term clinical improvement and trajectory was observed between groups in terms of PROMIS and ODI scores. Our results suggest tailoring interbody techniques to address patient specific pathology at the L5/S1 level, whether the goals of surgery are to maximize segmental lordosis or for sustained neuroforaminal decompression

ID: AGS26/456

RF003: A machine learning algorithm to predict change in the decision-making for thoracolumbar fractures without neurological deficit after MRI: a multicenter study

Mohamed Ali 1

1 Prince Mohamed Ben AbdelAziz Hospital, Riyadh second Cluster, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Introduction: There are no clear guidelines on when to obtain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for neurologically intact patients with traumatic thoracolumbar fractures (TLFs). The aim of this study is to train a Classification and Regression Tree (CART) to predict when MRI may change the decision-making for TLFs without neurological deficit. Material and Methods: Three trauma centers recruited 619 neurologically intact patients with thoracic and lumbar fractures with available computed tomography (CT) and MRI studies within 10 days of presentation. Only AO Spine A-fractures according to CT were included, while B-type and C-type fractures, osteoporotic, and pathological fractures were excluded. CT findings indicating posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) injury were defined as: facet malalignment, horizontal laminar fracture, spinous process fracture, and interspinous widening ≥ 4 mm. The Presence of a single positive CT finding indicates an M1 modifier. The primary outcome was any change in thoracolumbar AO Spine injury severity score (TLAOSIS) treatment recommendation among the three groups: ≤ 3 (conservative), 4-5 (grey zone), and ≥ 5 (surgical) after evaluation of the MRI. Derivation and validation sets utilized 80% and 20% of the sample, respectively. A decision tree classifier with balanced class weighting was trained using the Gini impurity criterion with a maximum depth of 4. Discrimination was quantified with the area under the receiver-operating curve (AUC). Results: TLAOSIS-based management reclassification after evaluation of the MRI occurred in 82 cases (13.2%). The model used three variables: M1 modifier, A subtype (A1-A4), and spine level (importance = 0.914, 0.055, and 0.031, respectively). The decision tree achieved an AUC of 0.93, sensitivity of 87.5%, specificity of 96.3%, and mean accuracy of 92.9% (±12.0%) on cross-validation. Conclusion: Our model based on spine level, modifier M1, and A fracture subtype could accurately predict the change in TLASOSIS recommendation after MRI. This may help reduce unnecessary MRIs in neurologically intact patients with A-type injury.

RF004: Imaging biomarkers from an artificial intelligence (AI) facilitated semi-automated pipeline may improve prognostication of patients undergoing surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy

Mohammed Ali Alvi 1 , Mouad Elganga 2 , Raman Abbaspour 2 , Karlo Pedro 1 , Michael Fehlings 1

1 University Health Network, University of Toronto, Toronto Western Hospital, Toronto, Canada,

2 University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults. Conventional MRI assessment provides limited prognostic information, often relying on qualitative interpretation. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning have enabled extraction of high-dimensional imaging biomarkers from routine MRI images in a feasible way. We developed a semi-automated AI-facilitated pipeline to quantify radiomic features from baseline axial T2-weighted MRI and hypothesized that integrating these features would enhance predictive model performance for 1-year postoperative outcomes. Methods: We sourced the data from two clinical trials, the cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM) international study (CSM-I) and the CSM North America (CSM-NA) study. We excluded patients without baseline MRI imaging as well as cases where the MRI images were not in the DICOM format or were of insufficient quality. Segmentation of the spinal cord was performed using the SpinalCordToolbox (SCT v6.5). Next, we cropped each segmented MRI at the most compressed level, and the most normal/non-compressed level. Next, each set of images was processed through the PyRadiomics pipeline to extract radiomic features. The data was then split to training (70%) and validation (30%) datasets. We applied a two-stage feature truncation process: model-based selection for outcome, yielding a target-specific reduced radiomics set and 2) applying principle component analysis (PCA) on target-specific features. We then combined radiomic features with clinical features and LightGBM and XGBoost models were independently trained and tuned using the training set. The model achieving the highest mean cross-validation performance for the relevant metric (ROC-AUC for classification, negative MAE for regression) was selected as the final model for that outcome. Results: A total of 220 patients were included in the final analysis. On the held-out test set, AUCs were reported for seven outcomes across seven feature sets- a) clinical-features alone; b) all Radiomics; c) clinical-features & all Radiomics; d) Radiomics from compressed region (CR); e) clinical features & Radiomics from CR; f) Radiomics from non-compressed region (NCR) and g) clinical & NCR Radiomics. For minimum-clinically-important-difference (MCID) in NDI at 6-months, the highest AUC was 0.771 with clinical & NCR Radiomics while for 1 year NDI, the highest AUC (0.646) was obtained with clinical-features and CR Radiomics. For MCID in mJOA at 1-year, the model with clinical-features and all Radiomics reached 0.716. Next SHAP analysis revealed measures of grey-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) such as Informational Measure of Correlation 1 & 2, and maximum correlation coefficient to be among the top 3 most important metrics. The impairment in these textural features indicate structured, repetitive textures, such as fibrosis or calcifications in compressed tissue, and heterogeneous or disorganized tissue often linked to malignancy or degeneration. Conclusion: Combining radiomic features from compressed and non-compressed levels on baseline T2-weighted MRI via an AI-facilitated pipeline improved prognostic model performance for DCM surgical outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of imaging biomarkers to augment clinical decision-making, enabling more personalized risk stratification and optimizing patient counseling before surgical intervention.

ID: AGS26/1478

RF005: A generative model to synthesize spine-only image from low-dose radiographs for reliable spinal assessment

Qingzhi Xiang 1,2 , Yan Yu 1,2 , Liming Cheng 1,2

1 Division of Spine, Department of Orthopaedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China,

2 Key Laboratory of Spine and Spinal Cord Injury Repair and Regeneration (Tongji University), Ministry of Education, Shanghai, China

Introduction: Long-term monitoring of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) necessitates frequent radiographic imaging, leading to significant cumulative radiation exposure. Conventional low-dose acquisitions degrade bone contrast and obscure vertebral landmarks, compromising reliable alignment measurement. Recent advances in generative models offer a promising solution by learning anatomical priors to synthesize high-fidelity images from degraded inputs.

This study aims to develop a generative model that can synthesize precise skeleton-only (or spine-only) image from whole spine radiographs, enabling accurate spinal assessment while minimizing radiation exposure. Materials and Methods: The spine extraction net (SEN) was proposed, trained following two stage using 12,539 CT volumes: (1) a diffusion U-Net backbone was pretrained on skeleton-only (or spine-only) digitally reconstructured radiographs (DRRs) to learn the skeletal or spine manifold; (2) ControlNet conditioning blocks initialized from the pretrained backbone were attached to the network and trained with original DRRs as control inputs and skeleton-only DRRs as targets, while the backbone weights were kept frozen. At inference, the model generates skeleton-only images from low-dose radiographs, which can be fused with the original image to enhance bone contrast. Downstream modules included (i) a heatmap-based vertebral keypoints detection network for automated Cobb angle measurement and (ii) a vertebral body segmentation model. Two baselines were implemented as benchmark: a U-Net and a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework trained on paired DRRs. Evaluation included subjective image quality (three radiologists, Likert and visual grading), objective image quality (SNR, CNR), robustness to simulated dose reduction and artifacts, and downstream performance (keypoint detection: PCK@5 mm, mean error; segmentation: Dice, precision, recall, HD95; Cobb angle: MAE). Paired statistical tests were used with p < 0.05. Results: On the clinical low-dose test set (n = 266), the proposed pipeline consistently outperformed baselines. Subjective quality: mean radiologist Likert score 4.2 ± 0.6 (proposed) vs. 2.9 ± 0.7 (U-Net) and 3.2 ± 1.1 (GAN), with improved vertebral margin delineation (p < 0.01). Objective quality: SNR increased by 35.2% and CNR by 40.5%. Segmentation: mean Dice = 0.89 ± 0.07 (proposed) vs. 0.76 ± 0.14 (U-Net) and 0.80 ± 0.10 (GAN); HD95 decreased 25-30%; precision/recall improved 6-9 percentage points. Keypoints: PCK@3mm = 0.92 (proposed) vs. 0.86 (U-Net) and 0.87 (GAN); mean localization error = 2.3 ± 1.1 mm vs. 3.9 ± 1.5 mm and 3.6 ± 1.8 mm (p < 0.01). Cobb angle: MAE = 3.1 ± 1.4° vs. 4.6 ± 2.0° (U-Net) and 4.8 ± 1.8° (GAN). Stable skeleton-only reconstructions were maintained even at one-sixth of the original dose (mSv), with performance preserved under simulated dose reduction and common artifacts; hallucinations were rare due to structural conditioning. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that SEN can reliably synthesize skeleton-only (or spine-only) images from low-dose radiographs, enabling accurate scoliosis assessment at substantially reduced radiation exposure. The model maintained robustness under dose reduction minimizing risks of hallucinated structures compared with conventional U-Net and GAN approaches. SEN provide a clinically feasible strategy to preserve diagnostic reliability in long-term scoliosis follow-up to address the critical need for radiation safety.

RF006: Development of a spinal autonomous radiological Cobb-assessment AI system

Germán Casabó-Vallés 1 , Rodrigo Aldecoa 2 , Gisselle Pérez-Machado 1 , Rosa M Egea-Gámez 3 , Judith Sánchez-Raya 4 , Imma Vilalta Vidal 5 , Pedro Rubio 6 , María Gallán 3 , Judith Salat-Batlle 4 , Carles Fabrés Martín 5 , Carmen Martínez-González 3 , Joan Bagó 4 , Marta Gómez Chiari 5 , Miquel Bovea 6 , Rafael González-Díaz 3 , Rocio Garcia 5 , Judit Garcia-Guallarte 1 , Eva García-López 1 , José Luis García-Giménez 7 , Teresa Bas 6 , Salvador Mena-Mollá 7

1 EpiDisease S.L., Paterna, Spain,

2 Plaia Technologies SL, Alboraia, Spain,

3 Hospital Infantil Universitario Niño Jesús, Madrid, Spain,

4 Hospital Universitari Vall d’Hebron. Vall D’Hebron Research Institute (VHIR)., Barcelona, Spain,

5 Hospital Sant Joan de Déu, Barcelona, Spain,

6 Hospital Universitari i Politècnic La Fe. Instituto de Investigación Sanitaria IIS La Fe., València, Spain,

7 Departamento de Fisiología, Facultad de Medicina y Odontología, Universitat de València, INCLIVA Biomedical Research Institute, Center for Biomedical Network Research on Rare Diseases (CIBERER), Carlos III Health Institute, València, Spain

Introduction: Manual measurement of the Cobb angle on full-spine radiographs remains the gold standard for diagnosing Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS). However, this approach is subject to variability due to the subjective identification of vertebral endplates, leading to diagnostic uncertainty and reduced reproducibility. In this context, our objective was to develop and validate an autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of estimating Cobb angles automatically, reproducibly, and without human intervention. Material and Methods: We conducted a multicenter study involving four tertiary hospitals, collecting AP/PA full-spine radiographs from AIS patients with curves ranging from mild to severe. Each image was independently evaluated by three experienced clinicians (first round measurements). When disagreements were observed, a second review was performed, and a curated consensus dataset was generated to serve as the reference standard. We designed a deep learning pipeline composed of two specialized AI models: one dedicated to spine segmentation, and the other for individual vertebrae identification and automatic Cobb angle estimation of all detected curves. Results: A total of 484 radiographs were analyzed, resulting in a consensus of 1,054 curves. In the first manual evaluation, clinicians identified 86.4% of curves, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.41° ± 3.24° compared with the consensus, and an error range spanning from -41.3° to 40.7°. In contrast, our SPinal Autonomous Radiological Cobb-assessment (SPARC) system detected 94.0% of curves and achieved a MAE of 3.01° ± 2.71°, remaining within the clinically acceptable threshold (≤ 6°). Importantly, SPARC presented a narrower error distribution, with values between -14.6° and 20.3°. Conclusion: We introduce SPARC, a fully autonomous AI-based system for Cobb angle measurement in AP/PA spine radiographs. Compared with first manual assessments by specialists, SPARC demonstrated superior curve detection (94.0% vs. 86.4%) and markedly reduced error variability (±20.3° vs. ±41.3°). In conclusion, SPARC delivers results comparable to the average assessment of three specialists with over a decade of experience, but without intra- or inter-observer variability and operating fully autonomously. SPARC has the potential to become a reliable clinical support tool across all stages of AIS management, assisting both experienced surgeons and less specialized practitioners, and improving diagnostic confidence and efficiency in routine care.

ID: AGS26/836

RF007: Cervical pedicle inlet screws: a novel trajectory for navigated sub-axial cervical screw placement with improved biomechanical characteristics compared to lateral mass screws

Christopher Martin 1 , Deb Bhowmick 2 , Vincent Rossi 3 , Domagoj Coric 3 , Martin Pham 4 , Amber Pulido 5 , Daniel Woods 5 , Jeremy Rawlinson 5

1 University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States,

2 Duke University, Durham, United States,

3 Carolina Neurosurgery & Spine, Charlotte, United States,

4 University of California San Diego, San Diego, United States,

5 Medtronic Spine, Memphis, United States

Introduction: To investigate the biomechanical characteristics of a new screw trajectory, which we have deemed the “pedicle inlet” trajectory. Materials and Methods: Four surgeons familiar with standard and image-guided cervical pedicle screw fixation techniques placed 3.5 mm diameter cervical fixation screws randomized at each sub-axial level to one of three fixation techniques: cervical pedicle, pedicle inlet, and lateral mass screw. A total of 180 screws were placed from C3 to C7 in 18 cadaveric spine samples. Maximal insertional torque was measured during the final seating of the screws. After confirmation of accuracy of screws with post-procedural CT-imaging, individual screws in the cadaveric samples were biomechanically tested for pull-out strength. Results: All screws were placed without breach into neurovascular spaces. The final insertional torque was equivalent (ANOVA, p > 0.05, 3.6 ± 1.7 Nm) across cervical pedicle screws, pedicle inlet, and lateral mass screws. Maximal pullout strength was observed for cervical pedicle screws (814.6 ± 387.3 N). Pedicle inlet screws had a 51% higher pullout strength as compared to lateral mass screws (593.2 ± 289.9 N v 392.4 ± 284.0 N, p < 0.01). All differences were statistically distinct from each other (ANOVA, p < 0.01). Conclusions: Use of image-guidance allows for safe placement along the pedicle inlet trajectory, with no recorded screw malposition, and a 51% improvement in pull out strength as compared to lateral mass screws. The pedicle inlet trajectory offers an alternative to traditional lateral mass screws with better fixation quality and may have particular application in percutaneous or minimally invasive posterior fusions.

RF008: Vascular window in the surgical corridor for ALIF L5-S1: a simplified classification proposal

Juan Cárdenas 1 , Cristiano Menezes 2 , Alexandry Carvalho 3 , Alfredo Guiroy 4 , Alberto Gotfryd 5 , Jerônimo Milano 6 , Gabriel Lacerda 7 , Cristian Correa Valencia 8 , Facundo Van Isseldyk 9 , Matias Pereira Duarte 10 , Martin Gagliardi 11 , Jefferson Soares Leal 1

1 Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG), Columna Institute, Belo Horizonte, Brazil,

2 Federal University of Minas Gerais, Columna Institute, Belo Horizonte, Brazil,

3 Clínica Ortomed, Teresina - Piauí, Brazil,

4 Clínica de Cuyo, Mendoza, Argentina,

5 Santa Casa de São Paulo, Medical School and Hospitals, São Paulo, Brazil,

6 Neurological Institute of Curitiba, Curitiba, Brazil,

7 Hospital Felicio Rocho, Belo Horizonte, Brazil,

8 Clinica Las Condes, Santiago, Chile,

9 Hospital Privado de Rosario, Rosario, Argentina,

10 Clínica La Pequeña Familia, Junin, Argentina,

11 Northern Ontario School of Medicine University, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada

Introduction: Anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) has gained popularity for its effectiveness in correcting spinopelvic parameters and achieving indirect decompression, most commonly at L5-S1. The retroperitoneal approach provides direct access to the lumbar spine while minimizing peritoneal manipulation; however, improper handling during exposure of the disc space may cause vascular injuries, particularly lacerations of the left common iliac vein. A thorough understanding of retroperitoneal anatomy and its variations, together with meticulous preoperative planning, is essential to reduce these risks. Among the main anatomical factors influencing vascular injury are the height of the iliac bifurcation and its spatial relationship to the L5-S1 disc. To better anticipate technical difficulties related to the iliac veins, classifications based on vascular anatomy at L5-S1 have been proposed, such as the Berbeo-Díaz-Vargas (BVD) classification. While useful, its interpretation can be complex, limiting widespread application in daily practice. In this context, we propose a simplified, easy-to-use classification system. Its main advantage is that calibration is unnecessary, as it relies on a proportional approach expressed as a percentage of the vein-free vascular window, rather than absolute metric values. This facilitates interpretation and enhances applicability in surgical planning. Material and Methods: A multicenter retrospective observational study was conducted between January 2018 and August 2025, including adult patients (> 18 years) who underwent lumbosacral MRI. Exclusion criteria were prior lumbosacral or abdominal surgery, trauma, tumor, infection, or congenital iliac vascular malformations. All imaging studies were independently analyzed by senior spine surgeons. Each case was classified using both the BVD system and the proposed simplified classification. The vein-free vascular window was quantified with a proportional method, defined as the ratio between the intervascular distance (right to left iliac vein) and the total disc width, multiplied by 100. The new classification is based on the width of this vein-free corridor at L5-S1, complemented by a modifier indicating the presence (+) or absence (-) of an areolar fat plane, defined as the fatty tissue between vessel and disc. The disc space was divided into five equal zones: Type 0, no corridor; Type I, < 1/5 free vascular space; Type II, < 2/5; Type III, < 3/5; and Type IV, ≥ 3/5. Results: Seventy-eight patients were included, being 60,7% female, with a mean age of 57 years/old. The new classification (VFZ) showed the following distribution: 1.3% were Type 0; 5,1% Type I, 12,8% Type II, 21,8% Type III, and 59% Type IV. The BVD classification identified Type I in 12 cases, Type II in 6 cases, Type III in 18 cases, and Type IV in 42 cases. Both systems agreed in 65 cases (83.3%), with a Cohen’s kappa of 0.73, indicating substantial concordance. Conclusion: The simplified vascular window classification showed high agreement with the BVD system. Its proportional design eliminates the need for image calibration, facilitates interpretation, and represents a practical alternative for preoperative planning in ALIF at L5-S1, pending validation in larger multicenter cohorts.

RF009: Intraoperative contrast-enhanced ultrasound reveals hyperemia in central cord syndrome and perfusion loss in traumatic spinal cord injury

Roshini Ramkumar 1 , Christoph Hofstetter 1

1 University of Washington, Seattle, United States

Introduction: Cervical spinal cord injury leads to profound neurological deficits driven in part by secondary injury mechanisms such as vascular compromise and microcirculatory failure. Neurological assessment with the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) scale remains the clinical standard, yet it can be subjective and limited in the acute setting. Intraoperative contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) provides a real-time, objective assessment of spinal cord perfusion. To quantify these perfusion dynamics, we measured the Spinal Perfusion Index (SPI), defined as the ratio of contrast inflow at the injury site to that in adjacent intact segments, yielding a reproducible and quantitative measure of microvascular integrity. In this study, we aimed to evaluate whether distinct perfusion patterns could be identified between central cord syndrome (CCS) and traumatic spinal cord injury (tSCI). Purpose: To retrospectively evaluate intraoperative SPI values patients with cervical spinal cord injury and compare CCS and tSCI cohorts, and to assess SPI. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 27 patients with cervical SCI who underwent intraoperative CEUS during decompression procedures between 2021-2025. CEUS was performed following intravenous contrast administration, and SPI values were extracted from stored recordings using standardized post-processing techniques. Patients were subsequently categorized as CCS (n = 12) or TSCI (n = 15) based on neurological assessments and ASIA impairment scale scoring. Group SPI values were compared, and qualitative perfusion patterns were described. Reliability testing was performed using repeated SPI measurements by blinded raters, and intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Results: The mean SPI was 1.29 in CCS compared with 0.55 in TSCI (p < 0.05), demonstrating significantly higher perfusion in the injury center of CCS. CEUS revealed a consistent pattern of hyperemia at the injury center in CCS, possibly reflecting differences in injury mechanism or severity and the associated pathophysiological response. Reliability analysis confirmed strong reproducibility: intra-rater ICC = 0.86 [0.70-0.94] and inter-rater ICC = 0.83 [0.64-0.92]. Conclusion: This retrospective intraoperative analysis demonstrates that CEUS-derived SPI detects distinct perfusion patterns between CCS and TSCI. The hyperemia observed in CCS likely reflects a vascular response more akin to a bruise, whereas the reduced SPI in TSCI indicates frank microvascular disruption. By providing an objective and reproducible measure of perfusion, CEUS with SPI may complement neurological assessment and serve as a valuable adjunct for intraoperative evaluation and prognostication. Keywords: cervical spinal cord injury, central cord syndrome, traumatic SCI, contrast-enhanced ultrasound, spinal perfusion index, reliability

ID: AGS26/2441

RF010: Seeing the unseen: optical spectroscopy for real-time spinal tissue differentiation in spinal endoscopy

Pouyan Mehryar 1 , Davor Dasic 2 , Kabelan Karunaseelan 1 , Jonathan Jeffers 1 , Salvatore Russo 2

1 Department of Mechanical Engineering, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom,

2 Department of Neurosurgery, Imperial College Hospitals NHS Trust, London, United Kingdom

Introduction: Iatrogenic injury to neural structures is a significant risk during common spinal endoscopic procedures. Surgeons rely on visual landmarks, tactile feedback, and fluoroscopy to guide bone and soft tissue manipulation. Visibility can be reduced due to several factors including bleeding or the actual pathological target may not be within the field of view. Reflectance spectroscopy offers a potential solution for distinguishing tissues during spinal surgery in real-time. Our study aims to determine the feasibility of using a reflectance spectroscopy technique and advanced statistical analysis to accurately distinguish between vertebral bone, ligament, muscle and neural elements to enhance surgical precision and patient safety. Material and Methods: Ex vivo spectral measurements were acquired from spinal tissues harvested from five porcine models, following approval for the study from our institution's ethics committee (Imperial College Healthcare Tissue Bank). To simulate the intraoperative fluid environment of endoscopic surgery, all tissues were immersed in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) during data acquisition. A broadband light source illuminated the tissue surface. The resulting reflected light was captured and transmitted to a visible and near infrared light spectrometer for analysis. Spectra were acquired from nine key tissue classes: Nucleus Pulposus (NP), Annulus Fibrosus (AF), Nerve, Muscle, Ligament, Endplate, Cortical, Cancellous, and Articular Surface (AS). Statistical parametric mapping was performed using the non-parametric repeated measures ANOVA, followed by the Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc paired t-test to identify significantly different tissue pairs (α = 0.0014). Results: Analysis demonstrated that reflectance spectroscopy can reliably differentiate spinal tissues in a simulated intraoperative environment, with multiple significant pairwise separations. Nerve was significantly differentiated (p < 0.001) from 6 critical tissues, including NP, muscle, endplate, cancellous bone, AF and AS. The study also highlights that reflectance spectroscopy is not limited to nerve detection alone; discrimination among ligament, bone and disk tissues was also robust. This broader capability may assist intraoperative navigation and improve decision-making during endoscopic spinal surgery where distinguishing tissue boundaries is challenging. Limitations include the small sample size (n = 5), use of porcine rather than human tissues, and the conservative Bonferroni correction, which may underestimate the number of true significant differences. Conclusion: Reflectance spectroscopy distinguished nerve and other spinal tissues under saline conditions, reflecting the surgical environment. Beyond nerve safety, this technique also separated muscle, ligament, bone and disk tissues, suggesting broader use for intraoperative navigation. These findings support reflectance spectroscopy as a versatile optical tool to enhance precision and reduce risk in spinal surgery.

RF014: Assessing the reliability of large language models in interpreting the quality of cervical spine patient education videos on YouTube

James Bianchi 1 , Ara Khoylyan 1 , Matthew Parry 2 , Edward DelSole 3 , Tan Chen 4

1 Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine, Scranton, United States,

2 Geisinger Northeast Orthopaedic Residency, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, United States,

3 Keystone Spine & Pain Management Center, Wyomissing, United States,

4 Geisinger Musculoskeletal institute, Division of Orthopaedic Spine Surgery, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, United States

Introduction: Prior research investigated the potential utility of artificial intelligence (AI) models’ adherence to spine surgery practice guidelines; however, adherence to video education quality guidelines in spine surgery remains largely unexplored. Additionally, it is common for surgical patients to use the internet to research their medical condition, and YouTube is one of the most referenced platforms. Prior research has evaluated video education for anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) and cervical total disc replacement (CTDR), finding that the average video quality is generally low. Still, manual review of YouTube video content presents temporal and attentional challenges to physicians. This presents a robust opportunity to assess whether there is satisfactory concordance between human-AI and AI-AI reviewers in assessing the quality of patient education videos on YouTube for ACDF and CTDR via current large language models (LLMs) using the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) and DISCERN criteria. Material and Methods: A YouTube query for videos related to ACDF (keywords: “ACDF,” “Anterior Cervical Fusion”) and CTDR (keywords: “Cervical Disc Replacement,” “Cervical Disc Arthroplasty”) was performed; the top 40 suggested videos from each search were aggregated, with duplicates excluded. Each set of videos was reviewed by two expert human reviewers. Videos were transcribed using the closed captions available on YouTube, individually reviewed and corrected by a human for grammar and spelling, and uploaded with a standardized prompt to three AI models: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, and Claude Sonnet 4. Reliability was assessed using the JAMA criteria, and educational quality was assessed using the DISCERN instrument, both of which are well-validated, standardized assessment tools. Interquery reliability was assessed with serial identical queries using Fleiss’ Kappa. Decisions by AI models and physicians were compared via intraclass correlation coefficients with a two-way random effects model (ICC2k). Among LLMs using the DISCERN instrument, Claude achieved good agreement with the expert reviewers by 95% CI (ICC2k = 0.761, [0.616, 0.851]) for CTDR videos; however, all LLMs showed poor agreement for ACDF videos (ICC2ks: 0.158-0.621). For comparison, using the JAMA criteria, Claude demonstrated moderate agreement for ACDF by 95% CI (ICC2k = 0.64, [0.418, 0.778]) but poor agreement for CTDR videos (ICC2k = 0.302, [-0.0929, 0.559]). Conclusion: Overall, AI and deep learning models are not currently capable of replacing human reviewers in assessing the quality of online patient education materials in modern spine surgery. Currently, AI models are inconsistent with applying the DISCERN and JAMA criteria to ACDF and CTDR videos. Future research should investigate a greater quantity of ACDF and CTDR videos available on YouTube, incorporating more open-source and closed-source AI models.

RF015: Spontaneous spinal CSF leak presenting with isolated radiculopathy: a case report

Ricardo Lage1, Diogo Belo1,2, José Hipólito Rodrigues1,2, João Levy Melancia2, Joaquim Teixeira2

1 ULS Santa Maria, Lisbon, Portugal,

2 CUF Tejo, Lisbon, Portugal

Introduction: Spontaneous spinal cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) leaks are a rare clinical entity, with an incidence estimated at around 5 cases per 100.000 person-years. It is about twice as frequent in females. Patients typically present with orthostatic headache, occasionally associated with neck stiffness, hyperacusis, photophobia, and nausea. Diplopia, radiculopathy, or coma have rarely been reported. Case Report: A 41-year-old male presented with a 5-year history of right thenar eminence atrophy, as well as inability to extend his fourth and fifth right hand fingers - ulnar claw deformity (“preacher’s hand” sign). On MRI of the spine, an anterior epidural lesion with mass effect on the spinal cord was observed showing identical MRI signal characteristics to CSF. Electromyographic (EMG) findings were consistent with motor axonal injury and denervation involving C7-C8 nerve roots. CT myelogram confirmed spinal CSF leak, by proving extravasation of iodine contrast to a longitudinal anterior epidural space CSF collection, from C7-T1 to T10-T11, reaching a maximum anteroposterior thickness of approximately 6 mm at the T6-T9 level. Discussion: This case illustrates radiculopathy following a spontaneous epidural CSF spinal leak. This patient did not exhibit the classic orthostatic headache at presentation, possibly due to the long-term progression of symptoms and desensitization. The atypical presentation hindered differential diagnosis and workup. MRI of the spine and EMG studies were key to direct diagnostic efforts. CT-myelogram was pivotal to prove epidural CSF leakage and to establish a definitive diagnosis. Conclusion: Isolated radiculopathy due to a CSF spinal leak is a rare presentation of a rare condition. MRI of the suspected affected spine segment can help clarify the etiology behind nerve root damage. CT myelogram can help confirm the diagnosis and possibly identify the leak level. High clinical suspicion is required for this clinical entity, as its rarity may lead to an inability to establish a diagnosis. Early recognition is paramount, as delayed diagnosis may lead to irreversible neurological damage.

RF016: TMAP mean baseline variability: a multiple linear regression analysis

Kyle Dann 1 , Mihir Chandra 1 , Alfred-John Bayaton 2 , Othman Saleh 1 , Tristan Moskovic 1 , Luke Budil 1 , Ashish Patel 1

1 The Spine Center at Duly Health and Care, Naperville IL, United States,

2 Kettering Health Grandview Hospital Orthopedic Surgery Residency Program, Dayton OH, United States

Introduction: Transabdominal Muscle Action Potential (TMAP) neuromonitoring provides real-time assessment of intraoperative nerve injury. Our single-surgeon cohort previously implemented an event based-research protocol with an alert threshold of change > 400 mA from baseline to better identify when nerve compromise occurs. However, the reliability of this alert threshold may be diminished in cases where the mean baseline is already elevated. The factors that affect mean baseline measurements are not well understood. This study aims to better understand the variables that impact the mean baselines for TMAP. Material and Methods: Retrospective analysis was performed on 204 prone lateral lumbar interbody fusion (pLLIF) patients where TMAP was utilized in our single-surgeon cohort. Baselines at ten myotomes for each patient were established prior to incision. From these values, an average baseline was calculated. Multiple linear regression evaluated the relationship between mean baseline values (dependent variable) and the independent variables, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking status, diabetes, ASA class, diagnosis, and number of operative levels. Patients with incomplete TMAP or clinical data were excluded. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: Multiple linear regression of 204 pLLIF patients that utilized TMAP was statistically significant (F = 9.57, p < 0.001) with an R2 of 0.281. Higher BMI significantly predicted increased TMAP baseline values (β = 13.3, p < 0.001). Average baselines by BMI (kg/m2) were as follows: 570 ± 177.3 mA (15-19.9), 520 ± 177.4 mA (20-24.9), 608.7 ± 126.9 mA (25-29.9), 689.6 ± 165.7 mA (30-34.9), 709.3 ± 136.1 mA (35-39.9), and 793.2 ± 177.2 (40-44.9). Increasing the number of operative levels contributed to elevated baselines (β = 29.7, p < 0.001). Female sex was associated with significantly lower baseline values compared to males (β = -48.3, p = 0.024, males: 682 ± 162.0 mA, females: 631 ± 164.5 mA). Older age at time of surgery suggested lower TMAP baseline scores but did not meet the significance criteria (β = -2.1, p = 0.061). Diabetes status (β = -7.57, p = 0.749), smoking (β = -6.8, p = 0.850), ASA class (β = 15.9, p = 0.394), and diagnosis of adult degenerative scoliosis (β = -47.3, p = 0.161) were not significant predictors of baseline variability. Conclusion: This multiple linear regression analysis found that TMAP baseline values were most significantly influenced by BMI. The number of operative levels and sex were also found to be significant in predicting TMAP baselines, while age demonstrated a borderline association. In contrast, diabetes status, smoking, ASA class, and adult degenerative scoliosis did not significantly impact TMAP baseline values. These findings highlight the importance of considering these predictive factors, particularly BMI, when interpreting intraoperative TMAP data. Further analyses should aim to validate these findings in a multicenter cohort and whether incorporating baseline-adjusted thresholds will improve the accuracy of detecting intraoperative nerve injuries.

RF017: First report of chemical meningitis due to CSF hypercalcaemia following antibiotic calcium sulphate beads in a thoracic discectomy for giant calcified disc with intraoperative durotomy

David Gower 1 , Hasan Raza 1 , Zion Hwang 1 , Febisayo Sidiku 1 , Priyanshu Saha 1 , Maryam Kashif 1 , Jason Bernard 1 , Timothy Bishop 1 , Darren Lui 1

1 St George's Hospital London, London, United Kingdom

Introduction: Calcium sulphate beads are widely used in trauma and orthopaedic surgery as biodegradable carriers for targeted local antibiotic delivery. Although generally well-tolerated, recognised complications include sterile wound drainage and systemic hypercalcaemia. However, their potential to cause central nervous system complications remains under reported. Material and Methods: This study is based on a detailed retrospective case review of a patient with post-operative chemical meningitis following antibiotic impregnated calcium sulphate bead insertion during thoracic discectomy complicated by intraoperative durotomy. Clinical records, operative notes, imaging, and laboratory data were systematically analysed to evaluate the association with neurological symptoms. Results: A 52-year old woman presented with right-sided thoracic pain, which had gradually progressed to numbness extending from below the xiphisternum to her right lower limb. She also reported heaviness in the right leg, unsteadiness on walking, and one episode of urinary incontinence. Her past medical history included a borderline mucinous ovarian tumour in remission post excision several years prior. She reported no prior neurological or spinal conditions. MRI of the spine revealed cord compression and oedema from T4/T5 disc herniation. After failed conservative management, she underwent a right-sided posterolateral discectomy at T4/T5 with posterior instrumented fusion (T4-T6). An intraoperative ventral durotomy complication was sealed with Tisseel. Vancomycin and Gentamicin impregnated Calcium sulphate beads were placed in the wound. No intraoperative CSF leak was confirmed. She was discharged on post-op day (POD) 5. On POD 10, she re-presented with new progressive confusion culminating in a depressed conscious level, urinary retention and marked bilateral lower limb weakness. MRI showed a pseudomeningocele, T3 to T10, with no cord compression. MRI brain and CT head were unremarkable. Lumber puncture revealed elevated CSF calcium (4.11 mmol/L), raised protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and sterile cultures. Serum calcium was lower side of normal (2.1 mmol/L). Empirical antibiotics and antivirals were commenced. Antivirals were discontinued once viral causes were excluded. Her consciousness improved over several days. Repeat lumbar puncture showed normalised WCC and falling CSF calcium (2.04 mmol/L). Given her recovery and improving CSF profile, reoperation to remove the calcium sulphate beads was not pursued. At POD 21, she was alert, oriented, and mobilising with support. With sterile CSF, a temporal relationship to surgery, elevated CSF calcium, and clinical improvement as calcium levels declined, her presentation was attributed to the calcium sulphate beads. She was discharged with full resolution of symptoms. Conclusion: This case highlights a rare but significant delayed complication of antibiotic calcium sulphate beads use in a case of giant calcified thoracic discectomy with dural tear. Clinicians should consider chemical meningitis and CSF hypercalcaemia in patients experiencing unexplained depressed consciousness after spinal procedures involving local antibiotic carriers, especially with sterile cultures. Early identification facilitates appropriate conservative management obviating unnecessary surgical intervention.

1 Nanavati Max Super Speciality Hospital, Mumbai, India

Introduction: Alkaptonuria is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, leading to accumulation of homogentisic acid. RF020: The impact of ageing on locomotor recovery in preclinical models of traumatic spinal cord injury: a systematic review

Aniqah Bhatti 1 , Zhikai Li 1 , Yuhan Guo 1 , Jamie Brannigan 1 , Faheem Bhatti 1 , Natalia Jogodzinska 1 , Benjamin Davies 1 , Mark Kotter 1 , Oliver Mowforth 1

1 Division of Neurosurgery, Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, United Kingdom

Introduction: Ageing is known to influence recovery following spinal cord injury (SCI) however its specific impact on locomotor outcomes remains underexplored. Understanding these age-related differences is critical for developing targeted rehabilitation strategies and improving the translational relevance of SCI research. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effect of ageing on locomotor recovery in animal models of traumatic SCI. Material and Methods: A systematic search of MEDLINE and Embase was conducted to identify studies assessing the impact of ageing on post-SCI locomotor outcomes. Inclusion criteria encompassed preclinical studies comparing locomotor recovery between young and aged animals following SCI. Extracted data included sample characteristics, SCI model, locomotor outcome measures, timing of evaluation, and key findings. Risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE checklist. Results: Out of 3118 unique records screened, nine studies met inclusion criteria. Animal ages ranged from four weeks to 28 months. SCI models included cord contusion (6/9, 66.7%), hemisection (22.2%, 2/9), and clip compression (1/9, 11.1%). Seven (7/9, 77.8%) studies employed the Basso, Beattie, Bresnahan (BBB) locomotor score as the primary outcome measure. These findings underscore the importance of age as a biological variable in SCI and suggest that rehabilitative interventions, such as exercise, may mitigate age-related deficits. Future studies should explore mechanistic pathways underlying impaired recovery in aged models and evaluate targeted therapies that enhance neuroplasticity and functional restoration across age groups.

RF021: Impact of implant donation on time to surgery in spine trauma at a high-volume trauma center in Tanzania

Charlotte Wahle 1 , East Africa Spine Trauma Network 1

1 University of California, San Francisco, Institute for Global Orthopaedics and Traumatology, San Francisco, CA, United States

Introduction: The cost of spine surgery in lower middle-income countries (LMIC) often leads to major delays in surgery, threatening clinical outcomes. Spinal implants account for most surgical expenses. Prior research has indicated that implant donation programs may help alleviate this financial burden. However, the impact of this intervention has not been examined in the spine trauma setting. The objective of this study was to investigate the impact of spine implant donation on time to surgery as compared to historical controls. Material and Methods: All spine trauma patients presenting to a single high-volume institution in an LMIC over a 6-month period between July 2024 and January 2025 were included. All uninsured patients with surgical injuries were offered donated implants. Demographic information, injury characteristics, and the clinical course were recorded. Most patients were uninsured (42 patients, 81%). Of the 42 uninsured patients who underwent instrumentation, 30 (71%) received donated implants. The overall mean time to surgery from admission was 10.6 ± 7.6 days. This is a significant improvement when compared to historical controls at the same institution prior to implant donation, where the mean time to surgery was 27.4 ± 17.8 days (p < 0.001). Additionally, following initiation of the implant program, there were no significant differences in time to surgery based on insurance status (p = 0.10). Of note, the timing of surgery was still considered “delayed” in 46 of 54 patients. Conclusion: In the first 6 months of implant donation, we report a significant reduction in time to surgery as compared to historical controls. Additionally, there were no differences in time to surgery between insured and uninsured patients, suggesting that implant donation helped alleviate previous insurance-based disparities. Although there are still a number of remaining financial barriers, the implant donation program has demonstrated promising potential in providing broader access to critical, time-sensitive interventions, thus promoting improved clinical outcomes.

RF022: Impact of readily available no-cost spine implants on surgical delays after traumatic spinal cord injury in Tanzania

Romani R. Sabas 1,2 , Sheryne Zeitoun 3 , Elochukwu Ibekwe 2 , Chibuikem Ikwuegbuenyi 2 , Mariam Mzingi 1 , Chellandra Samuels 3 , Charlotte Wahle 3 , Halinder Mangat 2 , Hamisi Shabani 1 , David Shearer 3 , Ashraf El Naga 3 , David Gendelberg 3 , Roger Härtl 2 , African Spine Trauma Network, SIGN Spine 4

Introduction: Traumatic spinal cord injury (TSCI) is a major cause of disability worldwide, with the highest burden in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Timely surgical management is critical to optimize neurological recovery, reduce complications, and improve survival. However, in Tanzania and similar settings, patients often face substantial delays to surgery, driven largely by the high cost and limited availability of spinal implants. For uninsured patients in particular, purchasing implants out-of-pocket can result in prolonged waits or inability to receive surgery at all. To address this barrier, an implant donation initiative was launched at a major tertiary referral center in Tanzania. This study evaluates whether the provision of no-cost implants was associated with reduced surgical delays overall, and whether disparities in access to timely surgery persisted by insurance status. Cohort 2 (September 2024-August 2025) included 93 of 117 patients (79.5%) who underwent surgery during the period when implants were readily available at no cost through the donation initiative. Demographic characteristics and time from admission to surgery were recorded. Linear regression was used to assess the association between insurance status and surgical delay in each cohort. Results: In Cohort 1 (N = 104, mean age 35 years, 87% male), the mean time to surgery was 14.0 days (SD 9.6). Insured patients (18.0%) underwent surgery after 5.8 days, compared with 10.9 days for uninsured patients. Regression analysis showed that uninsured status was associated with an additional 8.4 days of delay in Cohort 1 (95% CI 3.7-13.1, p = 0.001, R2 = 0.11), compared with 5.1 days in Cohort 2 (95% CI 1.3-8.8, p = 0.01, R2 = 0.07). Conclusion: During the period when spine implants were made available at no cost through a donation initiative at MOI, overall surgical delays were substantially reduced compared with the prior period. However, uninsured patients still experienced significantly longer delays than those with health insurance. These findings highlight the importance of ensuring implants are consistently available at the time of surgery, without cost serving as a barrier, to achieve equitable access to timely care. Future research should further investigate institutional, financial, and logistical contributors to surgical delay and evaluate strategies to sustain and scale such models in other low- and middle-income settings, with MOI serving as a potential framework.

RF023: When less is more: outcomes of surgical techniques for fragility vertebral fractures in a retrospective cohort study

André Beco 1 , Sérgio Pita 1 , Carlos João 1 , Inês Dias Monteiro 1 , Patricia Paredes 1 , Catia Machado 1 , João Souto 1 , João Afonso 1 , Hugo Nogueira 1

1 Unidade Local de Saúde da Região de Aveiro, Aveiro, Portugal

Introduction: Surgical management of fragility vertebral fractures includes cement augmentation, such as kyphoplasty, and instrumented fixation, which can be performed through percutaneous or open approaches. Comparative clinical evidence remains heterogeneous. This study aimed to evaluate pain improvement, length of hospital stay (LOS), 1-year mortality rate and complications across different surgical techniques and approaches. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study at a secondary-level hospital. Consecutive adult patients aged ≥ 45 years who underwent surgery for a new low-energy vertebral fracture between June 2019 and April 2024 were included. Data were locked in May 2025 to ensure a minimum 12-month follow-up for the latest cases. Surgical interventions comprised isolated kyphoplasty, kyphoplasty plus short-segment pedicle fixation with cement augmented screws, short-segment pedicle fixation with cement augmented screws, and four-level pedicle screw fixation. Approaches were classified as percutaneous or open. The main outcomes were pain assessed by the visual analogue scale (VAS) at 1, 6, and 12 months, LOS (days), and complications (infection, refracture, death). Statistical analysis employed Kruskal-Wallis for continuous variables and χ2 or Fisher’s exact test for proportions (two-sided α = 0.05). Results: A total of 84 patients were included. Pain improved over time in all groups. No significant differences were observed in VAS at 1, 6, and 12 months (p = 0.247, 0.371, and 0.649, respectively), nor in VAS change from 1 to 12 months (p = 0.294). LOS differed by surgical technique (p < 0.001). Median LOS: 3.0 days for isolated kyphoplasty, 4.5 for kyphoplasty plus fixation, 11.0 for short pedicle fixation, and 13.0 for four-level fixation. Open approaches had longer LOS than percutaneous procedures (11.0 vs 9.0 days; p = 0.015). There was no significant difference in VAS by approach at 1, 6 and 12 months. Complication rates ranged from 0% to 15.8% across techniques and from 9.8% to 13.0% across approaches, although small cell counts precluded robust statistical inference. One-year mortality was 3.6% (3/84; 95% CI 1.2-10.0), with higher rates after open surgery (13.0%, 3/23) compared with percutaneous procedures (0.0%, 0/61; 95% CI upper bound 5.9). Conclusion: In this single-center cohort of fragility vertebral fractures, pain recovery at 12 months was similar across surgical techniques and approaches. Length of stay increased with procedural complexity and open exposure. One-year mortality was low overall, but tended to be higher after open and four-level fixation cases. Isolated kyphoplasty, when clinically appropriate, may minimize hospitalization without compromising pain outcomes or early safety. Larger multicenter studies are required to validate mortality signals and optimize patient selection.

RF024: Clinical and patient-reported outcomes of sagittal alignment status in surgically managed spine trauma patients

Dillon Stone 1 , Neset Tang 1 , Garrison Bentz 1 , Kayode Matthew 1 , John O’Malley 1 , Mark Lambrechts 1

1 Washington University in St. Louis Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: Maintaining sagittal alignment during spinal surgery optimizes spinal biomechanics and improves clinical outcomes. Previous literature has demonstrated that sagittal malalignment is associated with pain, disability, and decreased quality of life. Deformity procedures form much of the alignment evidence; however, these principles remain relevant and understudied in the trauma patient population. This study aims to evaluate clinical and patient reported outcomes of post-operative sagittal alignment status in trauma patients who underwent spinal fusion. Materials and Methods: The trauma database at a single Level I trauma center was queried for patients > 18 years-old diagnosed with a spinal fracture and underwent surgical intervention between October 2014 and October 2024 with minimum 6 month follow up. Demographics, clinical outcomes, radiographic measurements, and patient-reported outcomes measures were recorded. Analysis was conducted on two cohorts: patients ≤ 50 years old (< 50) and all patients (AP). Within those cohorts, characteristics were evaluated based on immediate post-operative sagittal alignment status (SA) determined by actual minus targeted L1 pelvic angle ≤ 3. Continuous variables were evaluated using a two-sample T-test and categorical variables using a Chi-square test with non-parametric substitutions as needed. Linear regression analysis was conducted for predictive factors of patient-reported outcome measurement information system (PROMIS) pain interference (PI) or physical function (PF) score trends. Significance was p < 0.05. Results: 197 patients were included (≤ 50: 87). In the < 50 cohort, appropriate SA status was correlated with a lower mean number of levels fused (3.74 vs 4.43, p = 0.033) but was not statistically different depending on age, BMI, gender, Glasgow coma score on arrival, injury severity score (ISS), smoking status, intensive care unit (ICU) stay, or hospital length of stay (LOS). None of those variables displayed differences in SA status within the AP cohort. Mean PROMIS PI and PF scores were not different from baseline in both cohorts based on SA status. Increasing the number of levels fused was shown to improve PROMIS PI scores at 6.11 points per additional level in the < 50 cohort (p = 0.024), this trend was not significant in the AP cohort. Linear regression did not find age, BMI, ICU stay, ISS, or LOS to be predictors of PROMIS PI or PF change in both cohorts. In < 50, progression to alignment (n = 5) or malalignment (n = 2) at 6 months post-operatively did not influence PROMIS PI or PF score changes. Changes between immediate post-operative and 6-month postoperative lumbar lordosis, pelvic incidence, T5-T12 kyphosis, and proximal junctional kyphosis were not different between those that progressed to alignment or malalignment. Conclusion: The number of levels fused in spine trauma patients is a debated topic and was shown to influence both sagittal alignment and PROMIS PI trends, though in opposing directions. Operating on more levels improves PROMIS PI scores at the detriment of SA. However, mean PROMIS PI and PF scores were not shown to be different based on SA status, possibly indicating that SA may not be as linked to patient-reported outcomes in this patient population. This study shows that operating on more levels could improve patient outcomes despite contradictory radiographic findings.

RF025: Early vs. late surgery in thoracic spine fractures: impact on clinical outcomes in polytrauma patients

Gustavo Leite 1 , Diego Oliveira 1 , Mariana Pontes 1 , Carlos Fernando Herrero 1

1 University of Sao Paulo, Ribeirao Preto, Brazil

Introduction: Thoracic spine fractures are common in polytrauma patients and are frequently associated with high-energy trauma and severe systemic injury. Although early surgical stabilization may improve clinical outcomes by reducing complications and hospital stay, the optimal timing for intervention remains controversial. Evidence is limited regarding the impact of surgical timing in patients with varying injury severity scores. The aim of the study was to investigate, in a cohort study, the relationship between surgical timing and clinical outcomes in polytrauma patients with thoracic spine fractures. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis in which the primary outcome was length of hospitalization (days). Patients were classified into time to surgery (score ≤ 7 vs ≥ 8) and further stratified by Surgical Severity Index (SSI ≤ 24 vs ≥ 25). A negative-binomial generalized linear model with a log link was fitted to account for over-dispersed count data, adjusting for neurological status (Frankel grade) and the need for peri-operative intubation. Pair-wise contrasts between severity groups were obtained with the emmeans package, and results are reported as adjusted rate ratios (RRs) with 95 % confidence intervals: two-sided p-values < 0.05 denoted statistical significance. Results: 57 patients were included in the study, with mean age of 38 years, composed 46 male and 11 female patients. The median hospitalization time of the entire cohort was 6 days. After adjustment for Frankel grade and intubation status, pair-wise contrasts from the negative-binomial model showed a consistent reduction in the outcome for the 7- group (≤ 7) versus the 8 + group (≥ 8), SSI category ≤ 24: the 7- group had a 34 % lower rate than the 8 + group (rate ratio = 0.66, SE = 0.16; z = -1.76; p = 0.078), and for the SSI category ≥ 25: the 7- group had a 52 % lower rate than the 8 + group (rate ratio = 0.48, SE = 0.18; z = -1.97; p = 0.049), achieving statistical significance. Thus, the protective effect of the 7-day threshold became significant in patients with higher SSI scores. Conclusion: This study adds valuable insight into optimal management strategies for thoracic spine fractures in polytrauma patients. Our findings suggest that early surgical intervention is associated with improved clinical outcomes, highlighting the importance of timely treatment in enhancing patient recovery.

RF026: Results of treatment for thoracolumbar fractures using a short fixation device including the fractured vertebra

Elyes Zoghlami 1 , Youssef Mallat 1 , Khaled Khlil0 1 , ayari rabie 1 , hadj mohamed slim 1 , Khalil Amri 1

1 Tunis Military Hospital, Tunis, Tunisia

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures (T11-L2) account for a large proportion of spinal injuries, with this transition zone being particularly vulnerable from a biomechanical point of view. Short posterior transpedicular instrumentation including the fractured vertebra (sandwich fixation) is the standard approach, allowing direct fixation of the injured level while preserving the adjacent segments. This technique of including the fractured vertebra ensures optimal biomechanical stabilization compared to conventional fixations. The objective was to evaluate the clinical and radiological results and the durability of short fixation including the fractured vertebra in thoracolumbar fractures. Material and Methods: This is a single-center retrospective study conducted at the main military training hospital in Tunis, including 32 patients with thoracolumbar fractures (T11-L2) treated with short posterior fixation systematically including the fractured vertebra in the assembly (January 2019-December 2024). The surgical technique involved the insertion of transpedicular screws into the fractured vertebra in addition to the levels above and below. Clinical evaluation used the VAS, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and Roland-Morris Questionnaire (RMDQ). Radiomorphometric analysis quantified the kyphosis angle (Cobb), vertebral compression index (ACRI), and relative height (RBH). Results: With a follow-up of 31.4±8.2 months, EVA improved from 84.2 ± 8.9 mm to 18.6 ± 12.4 mm (77.9% reduction, p < 0.001). The ODI changed from 78.4 ± 9.6% to 24.7 ± 11.8% (improvement of 68.5%, p < 0.001). Kyphotic correction was significant: Cobb angle from 31.7 ± 7.8° to 4.2 ± 2.1° (correction of 86.7%, p < 0.001). Loss of correction was limited to 2.8 ± 1.4° (8.8%). The inclusion of the fractured vertebra in the assembly demonstrated superior biomechanical stability with maintenance of reduction. Multivariate analysis identified age > 50 years (OR = 3.47), obesity (OR = 2.89), and comminution > 60% (OR = 4.12) as predictive factors for loss of correction. The fusion rate reached 96.9% (31/32 patients) with a revision-free survival rate of 96.9% at 5 years. Conclusion: Short transpedicular fixation including the fractured vertebra is the gold standard approach for thoracolumbar fractures, demonstrating exceptional corrective efficacy (86.7%), major clinical and functional improvement (ODI -68.5%), and remarkable biomechanical durability. The inclusion of the fractured vertebra in the assembly ensures an exemplary safety profile and optimal stabilization.

RF027: Functional outcomes between surgical and nonsurgical treatment for neurologically intact patients with thoracolumbar burst fractures as measured by the AO Spine PROST

Said Sadiqi1,2, Charlotte Dandurand3, Sander Muijs2, Richard Bransford4, Andrei Joaquim5, Ulrich Spiegl6, Alex Vaccaro7, Cumhur Oner2

1 St. Antonius Hospital, Utrecht, Netherlands, 2 University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht, Netherlands, 3 University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, 4 University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, United States, 5 State University of Campinas, Campinas-Sao Paulo, Brazil, 6 University of Leipzig, Leipzig, Germany, 7 Rothman Institute, Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: The optimal management of neurologically intact patients with thoracolumbar (TL) burst fractures remains debated. This variability reflects a lack of consensus and is compounded by inconsistent use of outcome measures. This prospective study aimed to evaluate and compare functional outcomes, as measured by the condition-specific AO Spine Patient Reported Outcome Spine Trauma (PROST), in neurologically intact patients with TL burst fractures treated operatively or nonoperatively. Materials and Methods: This investigation was part of a prospective observational international multicenter cohort study. Neurologically intact adults (18-65 years) with acute (≤ 10 days) TL burst fractures were included from various sites across the world. Provided treatment was determined by the local standard of care. The PROST was administered at multiple prospective timepoints from baseline up to 2-years post-injury. Descriptive statistics were used to analyze patient and clinical characteristics. Multivariable mixed models for repeated measures (MMRM) were used to assess differences in treatment groups and between the fracture types. Results: A total of 93 patients were included (mean age 41 years, 57% male). Most sustained high-energy trauma (73.1%) and had type A3 fractures (63.4%), with 61.3% treated nonoperatively. Both nonsurgical (34.2 to 86.0) and surgical (39.9 to 85.6), as well as fracture types (A4: 38.4 to 85.6; A3: 36.4 to 87.3) demonstrated significant improvements in PROST scores over time (p < 0.001). No statistically significant differences in PROST scores were found between treatment groups or fracture types. However, surgically treated patients showed faster recovery within the first 6 months, and nonsurgical patients had marginally higher scores beyond that point, converging by 2 years. Conclusion: Both surgical and nonsurgical treatment of neurologically intact TL burst fracture patients resulted in comparable long-term functional outcomes as measured by AO Spine PROST. A trend was observed with surgically treated patients having faster early recovery, while functional scores equalized by two years.

RF028: Integrating radiomics with clinical datafor enhanced prediction of vertebral fracture risk

Frank Hassel 1 , Babak Saravi 2 , Sébastien Couillard-Després 3 , Gernot Michael Lang 2 , Alisia Zink 1 , Elene Tabukashvilli 1 , Hamza Guzel 4

1 Loretto-Krankenhaus, Department of Spine Surgery, Freiburg, Germany, 2 Department of Orthopedics and Trauma Surgery, University of Freiburg, Freiburg, Germany, 3 Institute of Experimental Neuroregeneration, Spinal Cord Injury and Tissue Regeneration Center Salzburg (SCI-TReCS), Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg, Austria, 4 Department of Radiology, Ministry of Health, Izmir City Hospital, Izmir, Turkey

Introduction: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures are a major cause of morbidity, disability, and mortality among the elderly. Traditional methods for fracture risk assessment, such as dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), may not fully capture the complex factors contributing to fracture risk. This study aims to enhance vertebral fracture risk prediction by integrating radiomics features extracted from computed tomography (CT) scans with clinical data, utilizing advanced machine learning techniques

Material and Methods: We analyzed CT imaging data and clinical records from 124 patients, extracting a comprehensive set of radiomics features. The dataset included shape, texture, and intensity metrics from segmented vertebrae, alongside clinical variables such as age and DXA T-values. Feature selection was conducted using a Random Forest model, and the predictive performance of multiple machine learning models - Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Machines, and XGBoost - was evaluated. Results: Outcomes included the number of fractures (N_Fx), mean fracture grade, and mean fracture shape. Incorporating radiomics features with clinical data significantly improved predictive accuracy across all outcomes. The XGBoost model demonstrated superior performance, achieving an R2 of 0.7620 for N_Fx prediction in the training set and 0.7291 in the validation set. Key radiomics features such as Dependence Entropy, Total Energy, and Surface Volume Ratio showed strong correlations with fracture outcomes.Notably, Dependence Entropy, which reflects the complexity of voxel intensity arrangements, was a critical predictor of fracture severity and number. Conclusion: This study underscores the potential of radiomics as a valuable tool for enhancing fracture risk assessment beyond traditional clinical methods. The integration of radiomics features with clinical data provides a more nuanced understanding of vertebral bone health, facilitating more accurate risk stratification and personalized management in osteoporosis care. Future research should focus on standardizing radiomics methodologies and validating these findings across diverse populations.

Gaston Camino-Willhuber 1 , Charlotte Dandurand 2 , Cumhur Oner 3 , Mohammad El-Sharkawi 4 , Alex Vaccaro 5 , Eugen Cezar Popescu 6 , Richard Bransford 7 , Andrei Joaquim 8 , Harvinder Singh Chhabra 9 , Ulrich Spiegl 10 , Dimitri Hauri 11 , Klaus Schnake 12 , Sebastian Bigdon 13 , Jerome Paquet 14 , William Lavalle 15 , Miguel Hirschfeld 16 , Spyros Pneumaticos 17 , Gregory Schroeder 5 , Lorin Benneker 13

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures without neurologic deficit are challenging situations in terms of treatment decision making. We aimed to analyze the occurrence of adverse events (AE) after surgical and nonsurgical treatment and its impact on functional outcomes. Material and Methods: 198 patients from a prospective multicentric database were included. The occurrence of adverse events and treatment failure within 2 years of follow up were recorded. ODI was compared between patients with and without adverse events at six months, 1 year and 2 years follow up. Multivariable regression analysis was conducted to assess the association between post-treatment adverse events and ODI at 1-year follow-up. Results: 47 adverse events were recorded (23.7%). Treatment failure was observed in only 5 patients. Conclusion: We found association between the occurrence of AE and higher ODI at six-months and one-year follow up. Additionally, a higher Charlson comordidity index and smoking status were associated with higher likelihood to develop adverse events in our cohort.

RF030: Evaluating the influence of surgical timing and presence of concurrent long-bone surgery on hospitalization outcomes for polytraumatized patients with thoracolumbar fractures undergoing posterior spinal instrumentation: a comparative study

Nelo J. Z. Chihal Lima 1,2 , Emil Tahirzade 1 , Ahmet Karakaşlı 1

1 Dokuz Eylul University, Izmir, Turkey, 2 Salihli Private Hospital, Turkey, Manisa, Turkey

Introduction: Despite existing research on polytrauma patients with both spinal and non-spinal fractures, little focus has been placed on the outcomes when additional long-bone surgeries accompany thoracolumbar fractures in patients undergoing posterior spinal instrumentation (PSI). Our study addresses this gap by investigating the impact of additional long-bone surgeries on hospitalization outcomes in polytraumatized patients with unstable thoracic or lumbar fractures. We aim to specifically evaluate how factors such as long bone fractures, the Injury Severity Score (ISS), and the timing of surgical interventions influence hospital ward length of stay (LOS) and intensive care stay (ICU) LOS, blood transfusion requirements, and post-surgery complication rates. Material and Methods: This study was designed as a retrospective comparative study, where a 13-year dataset from the medical records of polytrauma patients with concomitant unstable thoracolumbar spine fractures was used. These patients were stratified into two groups: (1) those with posterior spine instrumented (PSI) spine fractures with concomitant operated long bone fractures (PSISF-LBF) and (2) those with PSI-operated spine fractures alone (PSISF). Key outcomes evaluated included hospital ward and ICU LOS, blood transfusion rates, and the incidence of post-surgery complications. Results: 69 polytrauma patients with spinal fractures treated via PSI, with an average ISS of 21.35, were included. Among them, 23 had additional non-spinal fractures requiring surgical intervention. Injuries predominantly affected the lumbar region (78.3%), with a notable occurrence of AO type A burst fracture patterns. The L1 vertebra was the most fractured, mainly due to falls and traffic accidents. The surgery timing (within or after 24 hours) showed a significant relationship with hospital ward LOS r [69]) = [.40], p = [ <.001], but no statistically significant relationship with either ICU LOS, blood transfusion needs, or post-surgery complication. ISS was positively correlated with hospital ward LOS with rho = 0.49 (95% CI: 2.8-6.5), and ICU LOS with rho=0.41 (95% CI: 2.2-6.1], in both groups. The type of spine construct (short vs long) of levels in the study’s cohort was correlated with ICU LOS, r (68) = .25, p = .039, but not associated with hospital ward LOS, blood transfusion, or post-surgery complication. Transfusion requirements varied insignificantly between groups. The overall complication rates between the two groups were similar, with infections being the most prevalent complication. No significant association was found between complication rates and the presence of concurrent bone fractures, ISS score, type of spine construct, pelvic ring injury, hospital ward/ICU LOS, and blood transfusion. Conclusion: Polytrauma patients with unstable fractures and long bone fractures are not statistically significantly correlated with more extended hospital ward/ICU LOS or higher blood transfusion rates compared to those without a long bone fracture. Early surgery doesn’t necessarily reduce hospital ward/ICU LOS, transfusion rates, or complications. Therefore, the timing of surgical intervention can be flexible based on patient optimization without compromising outcomes. While some patients may require delayed treatment for medical stabilization, especially in the PSISF-LBF group, unstable spinal fractures should be promptly treated whenever feasible.
