RF031: Risk factors for failure in short segment pedicle instrumentation in thoracolumbar fractures

Ana Vilela 1 , Bibiana Couto 2 , David Ferreira 1 , António Cruz 2 , Joana de Azevedo 1 , João Carvalho Pereira 1 , André Santos Moreira 1 , Nuno Oliveira 1 , Paulo Gil Ribeiro 1 , Pedro Lurdes 1 , Pedro Varanda 1,3 , Bruno Direito Santos 1,3

1 Unidade Local de Saúde de Braga, Braga, Portugal, 2 Escola de Medicina da Universidade do Minho, Braga, Portugal, 3 Life and Health Science Research Institute, Universidade do Minho, Braga, Portugal

Introduction: The management of thoracolumbar fractures with short-segment posterior fixation (SSF) remains a subject of debate in spine surgery. This study aimed to identify factors associated with SSF failure in traumatic thoracolumbar fractures, focusing on patient- and surgery-related variables such as age, bone mineral density (BMD), fracture level, posterior ligamentous complex (PLC) injury, screw length, type of screw (monoaxial or polyaxial), instrumentation of the fractured vertebra, and sagittal screw angle (SSA). Material and Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted including adult patients with thoracolumbar fractures treated with SSF. Exclusion criteria were multilevel or pathologic fractures, neurological deficits, or follow-up shorter than 12 months. Failure was defined as screw pull-out, implant breakage, loss of vertebral height ≥ 50%, or postoperative kyphosis ≥ 30°. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of failure. Results: Sixty-six patients were included, of whom 23 (35%) experienced SSF failure. Older age (> 60 years), lower BMD, and the use of monoaxial screws were independent predictors of failure, with elderly patients showing an eighteen-fold increased risk. Survival analysis confirmed earlier failure among patients with advanced age, PLC injuries, and monoaxial screw instrumentation. Other assessed variables were not statistically significant. Conclusion: SSF represents a valuable option for thoracolumbar fracture management, offering mobility preservation and reduced surgical morbidity. However, failure risk is strongly influenced by patient age, bone quality, and screw type. Careful patient selection is essential to optimize outcomes. Larger multicenter prospective studies are warranted to validate these findings and refine risk prediction models.

RF032: Surgical vs. conservative management of thoracolumbar AO Type B fractures in ankylosed spines: a retrospective study

Faizan Kareem 1,2 , Felix Corr 1 , Martin Stienen 1 , Benjamin Martens 1 , Stefan Motov 1

1 HOCH Health Ostschweiz, St. Gallen, Switzerland, 2 University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland

Introduction: Ankylosing spinal disorders (ASD), including ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH), predispose patients to highly unstable spinal fractures due to altered biomechanics and rigidity. Thoracolumbar AO Spine B3-type fractures, typically caused by hyperextension, are associated with progressive deformity, neurological decline, and high complication rates. While surgical stabilization is often recommended, advanced age, frailty, and comorbidities frequently necessitate conservative management. Comparative evidence between these approaches in ASD remains scarce. We retrospectively assessed surgical versus conservative management of thoracolumbar AO Spine B3-type fractures in ankylosed spines and examined predictors of treatment success and failure. Material and Methods: In this single-centre retrospective cohort (2015-2025) conducted at the Department of Neurosurgery & Interdisciplinary Spine Center, Kantonsspital St. Gallen, Switzerland, patients aged ≥ 18 years with ASD and acute thoracolumbar AO Spine B3-type fractures were included. Patients were allocated to either conservative or surgical treatment based on collective consensus in our center. Baseline demographics, fracture characteristics, and clinical outcomes (VAS, COMI, ASIA, MacNab) were recorded. Primary endpoints were pain, complications, opioid use, and hospital stay. Results: This preliminary analysis includes forty-four patients to date (conservative, n = 23; surgical, n = 21). Bone mineral density was significantly higher in the conservative group (174.5 ± 55.6 vs. 131.7 ± 28.7 HU; p = 0.004). Lever arm length did not differ significantly (5.4 ± 1.8 vs. 4.6 ± 1.9 vertebrae; p>0.05). Conservatively treated patients had a slightly higher number of fused segments below the fracture (2.9 ± 1.3 vs. 2.1 ± 1.4; p = 0.04). Hospital stay was longer after surgery (12.7 ± 6.7 vs. 8.3 ± 7.2 days; p = 0.03). Revision surgery was required in 2 surgical patients; no re-interventions occurred in the conservative group. Complication rates and opioid use were similar between groups (57.1% vs. 56.5%; p > 0.05). Both groups experienced significant pain reduction (surgical: 8.1 ± 1.9 to 2.3 ± 2.2; conservative: 7.2 ± 2.1 to 1.5 ± 1.7 VAS; p < 0.0001), without intergroup differences (p > 0.05). “Fair” outcomes on the MacNab scale were more frequent after conservative treatment (26.1% vs. 4.8%; p = 0.09). Patients treated conservatively had a higher comorbidity burden (CCI mean 6.1 vs. 4.4), with a non-significant trend towards higher CCI in the conservative group (Mann-Whitney U, p = 0.09). At final follow-up, all patients were classified as ASIA grade E. Conclusion: Both surgical and conservative management of thoracolumbar AO Spine B-type fractures in ankylosed spinal segments achieved substantial pain reduction and functional improvement. Surgical treatment was associated with longer hospitalization and an overall low rate of revision surgery, whereas conservative management was more common in patients with higher bone density. Conservatively treated patients appeared to carry a higher comorbidity burden in our cohort, yet this finding did not reach statistical significance in the preliminary analysis. Despite differing risk profiles, overall outcomes were comparable. Ongoing analysis of the full dataset is expected to help us identify predictors of treatment success and guide individualized decision-making in this extremely fragile population.

RF033: Beneficial effect of early balloon kyphoplasty on osteoporotic vertebral fractures in elderly patients

Thomas Repantis 1 , Ioanna Lianou 1 , Maria Papathanasiou 1 , Stamatia Chatziperi 1 , Argiris Theodoropoulos 1 , Andreas Baikousis 1

1 General Hospital “Agios Andreas”, Patras, Greece

Introduction: Prevalence of osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures is more than 30% in the elderly. The objective of this study is to review safety as well as outcomes in pain control and mortality rates in geriatric population, following early balloon kyphoplasty. Material - Methods: Balloon kyphoplasty was performed in 221 patients from 2020 to 2024. Patients with history of malignancy or previous spinal surgery were excluded. Patients aged > 80 years old with traumatic single-level fractures, treated with early balloon kyphoplasty without spinal fusion and regular follow up > 6 months were included. A total of 32 patients (19 females, 13 males) underwent kyphoplasty under sedation within one week of sustaining fracture. Results: Mean age of patients was 84,4 (80-95) years old. ASA score was 2,54 and VAS score was 8,86 at the initial diagnosis. Mean VAS score at the final follow up (six months after treatment was 2,36 and mortality rate was 18,75% (6 patients). Cement leakage with clinical repercussion was not detected. and Mean time to discharge was 1,13 days. Only one patient had to be hospitalized more than 48 hours. Patients gained full functionality and none of them had to stay in nursing homes during recovery period. Conclusion: Comparing the results of our study with known literature, early balloon kyphoplasty is a cost effective method with limited complications, which contribute to pain relief, early mobilization and greater survival in geriatric population.

RF034: Vertebral fractures in chronic kidney disease patients - A population-based cohort study from TCVGH-OPC database

Sheng-Chieh Tseng 1 , Chien-Chou Pan 1 , Kun-Hui Chen 1 , Cheng-Hung Lee 1

1 Department of Orthopedics, Taichung Veterans General Hospital, Taichung, Taiwan

Introduction: Previous study showed that patients of chronic kidney disease (CKD) had higher risk of skeletal fractures. The incidence of fractures is about 5 times higher in individuals with an eGFR < 15 versus > 60. Besides, 18% of patients with non-dialysis dependent CKD have vertebral fractures (VFs). And the presence of VF was an independent risk factor of all-cause mortality. This study aims to evaluate the prognosis of surgical interventions for VFs in patients with CKD and identify the risk factors for mortality, complications, and refractures. Material and Methods: Patients were enrolled from the Osteoporosis Prevention Center at Taichung Veterans General Hospital. Those who underwent vertebroplasty or spinal fusion for VF between 2011 and 2023 were included. All participants underwent dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) to assess bone mineral density (BMD). Patients with incomplete data or follow-up periods of less than three months were excluded. The cohort was analyzed for mortality rates, complication rates, and refracture rates. Additionally, the use of osteoporosis-related medications and the presence of comorbidities were examined. Results: From 2011 to 2023, 1,280 patients underwent vertebroplasty or spinal fusion for VFs. Of these, 1,007 (78.7%) were female, and 273 (21.3%) were male. A total of 349 patients (27.3%) were classified as having CKD based on an eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. Patients in the CKD group had lower BMD and a higher prevalence of comorbidities compared to non-CKD patients. CKD patients exhibited higher mortality rates (hazard ratio = 2.07) in the Cox regression model and a greater risk of complications (odds ratio = 1.78) in the logistic regression model following surgery. Multivariate regression analysis revealed that mortality was significantly associated with eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, older age, male gender, diabetes, and lower serum albumin levels. The risk of complications was correlated with diabetes, coronary artery disease, and lower serum calcium levels. Refracture rates were associated with rheumatoid arthritis, hypertension, and the use of calcium supplements postoperatively. Conclusion: Surgical treatment for vertebral fractures in patients with chronic kidney disease is associated with higher mortality rates and increased risks of complications. Spine surgeons should be vigilant about these risks when managing CKD patients undergoing such procedures.

Phuc Diep 1 , Hanh Nguyen 1 , Truc Vu 1 , Tuan Ha 1

1 Hopital for Traumatology and Orthopaedics, Ho Chi Minh city, Viet Nam

Materials and Methods: A retrospective review of 187 patients treated with SSPSF and TBG over 3 years was conducted, using six pedicle screws placed bilaterally into the fractured vertebra and its two adjacent levels, with autologous bone grafting at the lesion site. The mean ODI at final follow-up was 22.5%. On multivariate analysis, older age (OR = 1.12, p = 0.008) and smoking (OR = 2.45, p = 0.013) were independent predictors of nonunion. Conclusion: SSPSF with TBG is a technically feasible and time-efficient technique that provides favorable outcomes in TLBF. Despite the high fusion rates and low disability scores observed, potential hardware-related complications and risk factors for nonunion highlight the importance of careful patient selection and individualized surgical planning.

RF038: Unilateral biportal endoscopy vs. tubular microdiscectomy: a comparative analysis of perioperative and clinical outcomes for lumbar disc herniation

Atif Ali 1 , Shehzad Javed 1

1 Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital Lahore, Lahore, Pakistan

Introduction: Lumbar disc herniation (LDH) is a common spinal condition often requiring surgical intervention when conservative treatments fail. Unilateral biportal endoscopic (UBE) discectomy and tubular microscopic discectomy (TMD) are minimally invasive techniques aimed at reducing morbidity compared to traditional open surgery. This study compares perioperative parameters and clinical outcomes of UBE and TMD for single-level LDH. Materials and Methods: A retrospective comparative study was conducted on 102 patients with single-level LDH treated between 2023 and 2024 at the Department of Orthopaedics & Spine Centre, Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore. Results: UBE was associated with significantly longer operative times (mean: 85.4 ± 15.2 minutes vs. 70.3 ± 12.6 minutes for TMD, p < 0.01). EBL was comparable between groups (UBE: 45.2 ± 10.3 mL vs. TMD: 48.7 ± 11.8 mL, p = 0.12). LOS was slightly shorter for UBE (1.2 ± 0.4 days vs. 1.5 ± 0.5 days for TMD, p = 0.001). Complication rates were similar (UBE: 4.2% vs. TMD: 5.6%) with no significant differences in reoperation rates. Conclusion: UBE and TMD demonstrate comparable clinical efficacy for LDH, with significant improvements in pain and functional outcomes. UBE offers advantages in shorter hospital stays though it requires longer operative times, potentially due to a learning curve. Gaining a comprehensive understanding of their differential risks could significantly inform clinical decision-making regarding the optimal timing of elective posterior lumbar fusion in ESRD patients. Specifically, it enables spine surgeons to decide whether delaying surgery until after renal transplantation may be safer for patients. Conclusion: ESRD dialysis patients were about twice as likely to experience 90-day readmission after elective posterior lumbar fusion surgery when compared to renal transplant patients. Interdisciplinary perioperative optimization of dialysis patients should therefore be considered to mitigate preventable readmissions. This is the first study to provide comparative risk assessment to guide surgical timing in ESRD patients, potentially altering current perioperative pathways. Aaron Lerch 1,2 , Martin Wood 1 , Anthony Chau 1

1 Brisbane Clinical Neuroscience Centre, Brisbane, Australia, 2 University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia

Introduction: Minimally invasive lumbar decompression surgery, including laminectomy and foraminotomy, remains a standard option to relieve foraminal or canal stenosis whilst minimising iatrogenic tissue damage. Within a large cohort, this study examines rates and risk factors for reoperation, incorporating a breadth of assessed factors, short- and long-term timeframes, and patient outcomes, thereby addressing crucial gaps in the literature. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed all tubular decompressions performed by eight neurosurgeons at a single institution from 2011-2024. RF043: Risk factor analysis for complications following lateral lumbar interbody fusion surgery

Xiaopeng Li 1,2,3 , Feng Li 3 , Qiang Yang 1,2,3

The overall prevalence of SIJ pain diagnosis was 48.9% (47/96), 15/96 (15.6%) were assessed to have piriformis syndrome, 7/96 (7.2%) were assessed to have facet arthropathy, 5/96 (5.2%) were assessed to have S1 radiculopathy, 5/96 (5.2%) were assessed to have degenerative spondylolisthesis. Finally, 17/96 (18.7%) were assessed to have “other” pathology after appropriate testing. Conclusion: Our study highlights the significant overlap between SIJ pain and other etiologies of buttock and low back pain, emphasizing that SIJ dysfunction should not be presumed based on referral alone. With only 48.9% of referrals confirmed as true SIJ pathology, it is evident that diagnostic precision remains an issue.

RF048: Assisted full-endoscopic spine surgery: a hybrid concept bridging monoportal and biportal techniques with two-year outcomes

Yuka Yamami 1 , Koichiro Ono 2

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Honkawagoe Hospital, Nippon Medical School Hospital, Saitama, Japan,

2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Nippon Medical School Hospital, Tokyo, Japan

Introduction: Assisted Full-Endoscopic Spine Surgery (AFESS) is a recently developed hybrid technique that bridges the concepts of monoportal full-endoscopic spine surgery (FESS) and biportal endoscopic approaches. By utilizing the FESS system through two portals, AFESS enables effective bilateral decompression while simplifying camera handling and preserving posterior supporting structures. Previous studies have reported its short-term feasibility, but mid-term outcomes remain largely unknown. This study aimed to evaluate 2-year clinical and radiological outcomes of AFESS for single-level lumbar spinal canal stenosis and highlight its conceptual role in bridging monoportal and biportal endoscopy. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed six consecutive patients (mean age, 70.3 years; mean follow-up, 29.3 months) who underwent AFESS for single-level lumbar spinal canal stenosis. Clinical outcomes were assessed with visual analog scale (VAS) scores for low back and leg pain. Radiological outcomes included facet joint preservation ratio, calculated from axial MRI images, and spinal canal expansion. The reoperation rate was also documented. Results: Mean operative time was 119 minutes with minimal blood loss (5 mL). VAS for low back pain improved from 43.3 mm preoperatively to 15.0 mm at final follow-up, while leg pain decreased from 75 mm to 0 mm. The facet joint preservation rate averaged 79%, and the spinal canal area expanded from 59.8 mm2 to 155.4 mm2, confirming adequate decompression. Conclusion: AFESS demonstrated favorable 2-year outcomes, with sustained pain relief, significant canal expansion, and high preservation of facet integrity. Beyond its clinical results, AFESS represents a novel conceptual bridge between monoportal and biportal techniques, combining the endoscopic precision of FESS with the ergonomic advantages of biportal handling. This hybrid approach may lower the technical barrier of pure monoportal endoscopy while retaining minimally invasive benefits. The need for reoperation in one patient highlights the importance of careful patient selection and the continued refinement of surgical techniques. Larger studies are warranted to validate AFESS as a durable treatment option and to define further its role within the evolving landscape of endoscopic spine surgery.

RF049: Comparison of endoscopic lumbar discectomy with versus without annulus fibrosus suturing: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Rowen Lin 1 , Justin Chung 1 , Evan Dunn 2 , Grace Kim 3 , Kevin Mo 2 , William Fang 2 , Daniel Lee 2 , Don Park 4 , Sohaib Hashmi 4 , Yu-po Lee 4 , Nitin Bhatia 4 , Hao-Hua Wu 4

1 Touro University Nevada, College of Medicine, Henderson, United States, 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Valley Hospital Medical Center, Las Vegas, United States, 3 Western University of Health Science, Pomona, United States, 4 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of California, Irvine, United States

Introduction: Endoscopic lumbar discectomy is a minimally invasive surgical technique used to treat lumbar herniations, while allowing for reduced tissue trauma, incision length, blood loss, infection rate, and faster recovery times. The annulus fibrosus may be damaged during its incision of such spinal procedures, increasing risk for reherniation, necessitating a revision surgery. The aim of this study was to compare outcomes of endoscopic lumbar discectomies when simultaneously repairing the annulus fibrosus with sutures versus without. Material and Methods: This systematic review was conducted by 3 reviewers using PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases, from June 2025 to present, in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. All meta-analyses were conducted using STATA 18.0 College Station, TX. Results: 9 studies were included in the final review with a total of 1,192 patients that all received an endoscopic lumbar discectomy for lumbar herniation. Of this total, 514 (43.1%) patients underwent additional annulus fibrosus repair via sutures while 678 (56.9%) patients only received the initial discectomy, with the disc segment most performed on being the level of L4/L5 with 267 (44.5%) patients. Analysis showed patients that underwent endoscopic lumbar discectomy with additional annulus fibrosus suturing had statistically significant increase in operative time at 8.89 minutes [WMD 8.89; 95% CI 1.01-16.77; p = 0.03], 0.31 times the odds of developing a reherniation [OR 0.31; 95% CI 0.17-0.55; p = 0.00], and 0.26 times the odds of needing a revision surgery [OR 0.26; 95% CI 0.10-0.68; p = 0.01]. Intraoperative blood loss and hospital length of stay were statistically insignificant. No significant findings were found in either VAS/ODI at correlation coefficients r = 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7 and at immediate postoperative and 3 month follow-up. Conclusion: Lumbar endoscopic discectomy with annulus fibrosus saw a statistically significant increase in operative time, but also reduced the reherniation and preoperative rate. No significance was seen in hospital length of stay or blood loss. While not significant, conflicting results were seen in VAS and ODI scores with patients receiving both endoscopic lumbar discectomy with annulus fibrosus sutures generally performing better in ODI outcomes, but worse in VAS scores.

RF051: Intraoperative dynamics of inflammatory cytokines in the lumbar neuroforamen during endoscopic spine surgery: a preliminary analysis

Enrico Giordan 1 , Alessandro Trento 1 , Jacopo Del Verme 1 , Giuseppe Canova 1 , Diletta Trojan 2

1 AULSS 2 Marca Trevigiana, Treviso, Italy, 2 Treviso Tissue Bank Foundation, Treviso, Italy

Introduction: Endoscopic spinal procedures rely on continuous irrigation to ensure optimal visualization of the surgical field, as the constant flow of normal saline effectively clears blood and tissue debris. In conditions such as lumbar foraminal stenosis, local inflammation is a key pathological feature, contributing to pain and nerve root irritation. Continuous endoscopic irrigation not only maintains a clear operative field but may also facilitate the washout of inflammatory mediators, potentially modulating the local microenvironment. Inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-8 (IL-8), and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), play pivotal roles in pain signaling, tissue healing, and postoperative recovery. Monitoring their concentrations during surgery could provide valuable insight into the inflammatory response associated with endoscopic lumbar foraminotomy and the potential impact of continuous irrigation on cytokine clearance. We aim to conduct a prospective quantitative analysis to evaluate the presence and temporal variation of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-8 and TGF-β) within the lumbar neuroforamen during endoscopic surgery. This investigation seeks to elucidate how cytokine dynamics evolve intraoperatively and to explore the potential clinical implications for managing local inflammation in minimally invasive spinal procedures. Material and Methods: Consecutive adult patients undergoing transforaminal endoscopic lumbar foraminotomy at our institution between January 2025 and September 2025 were included in this study. Preoperative and postoperative pain intensity was assessed using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS). For each patient, irrigation fluid samples were collected at predefined time points (0, 10, and 20 minutes from the start of surgery) and analyzed for inflammatory cytokine concentrations, including IL-8, and TGF-β.Cytokine concentrations in the irrigation fluid were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA). For each patient, samples collected at the different time points were tested to evaluate temporal changes in cytokine levels. Absorbance readings were recorded using an appropriate optical instrument and software, and the resulting data were analyzed. Differences in mean cytokine concentrations over time were assessed by comparing group means. Results: Our preliminary analysis on 18 patients (10 females, 8 males; mean age 54.4 years) highlights distinct temporal patterns in cytokine dynamics. For IL-8 concentrations, patients exhibited, on average a -15.0% reduction from baseline to time 10, followed by a more pronounced -28.5% decrease between time 10 and 20. The overall decline from baseline to time 20 amounted to a mean -38.5% decrease across the cohort. These findings indicate a progressive downward trend in IL-8 concentration, with an initial moderate decrease in the early phase and a steeper decline in the later interval. For TGF-β1 concentrations, patients demonstrated a marked and sustained decline throughout the observation period. On average, there was a -79.8% reduction from baseline to time 10, followed by an additional -70.0% decrease between time 10 and 20. The cumulative effect resulted in a mean of 96.4% decline from baseline to time 20. Several patients reached complete suppression by time 20, whereas some retained minimal residual levels. Overall, the trend indicates a rapid and near-complete reduction, with inter-individual variability primarily in the rate of decline. Conclusion: Our study demonstrates a progressive reduction in inflammatory cytokine concentrations within the lumbar neuroforamen during endoscopic spine surgery. These preliminary findings suggest that the postoperative decrease in pain observed with endoscopic lumbar procedures may be attributed not only to the relief of mechanical compression but also to the intraoperative washout of inflammatory mediators.

RF052: How to predict the culprit segment in percutaneous transforaminal edoscopic surgery (PTES) under local anesthesia for surgical treatment of lumbar degenerative diseases: radiologic images or clinical symptoms?

YuTong Gu 1

1 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Zhongshan Hospital Fudan University, Shanghai, China, 2 Shanghai Southwest Spine Surgery Center, Shanghai, China

Introduction: Percutaneous transforaminal endoscopic surgery (PTES) is a novel minimally invasive technique that has been used in the treatment of lumbar degenerative diseases (LDDs). PTES under local anesthesia was performed to treat the culprit segment of LDDs predicted by radiologic images or clinical symptoms, and the efficacy, security and feasibility were evaluated. Material and Methods: 87 cases of LDDs with nerve root symptoms, which were not consistent with lumbar degenerative levels and degree on MRI and CT, were treated with PTES under local anesthesia in day surgery ward from Jan 2015 to Dec 2019. 42 patients, whose culprit segment was predicted by radiologic images are included in group A. The other 45 patients, whose culprit segment was predicted by clinical symptoms are included in group B. Leg pain VAS and ODI before and after PTES are recorded. The outcome is defined according to MacNab grade at 2-year follow-up. Postoperative complications are recorded. Results: In group A, 2 patients underwent PTES for 1 segment, 37 patients for 2 segments and 3 patients for 3 segments. One of 1-segment PTES had no relief of symptoms and underwent another PTES for other culprit segment 3 months after surgery. In group B 44 of 45 patients were treated using PTES for 1 segment and 1 patient for 2 segments. Group B showed significantly less operative duration, less blood loss and less fluoroscopy frequency than group A (p < 0.001). There was no statistical difference in ODI, and the excellent and good rate between two groups. No complications such as wound infection, permanent nerve injury were observed. Conclusion: It is much more accurate to predict the culprit segment according to clinical symptoms than radiologic images in PTES under local anesthesia for surgical treatment of LDDs. Keywords: lumbar degenerative disease, culprit segment, radiologic images, clinical symptoms, transforaminal endoscopic surgery, minimally invasive surgery

RF053: Full-endoscopic versus tubular-based microscopic decompression for degenerative lumbar canal stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

Amr El Mohamad 1 , Ali Msheik 1 , Sadeen Eid 2 , Ibrahim Abdelhafez 1 , Abdullah Illeyan 1 , Mohamad El Mohamad 3 , Alaaeldin Ahmed 1 , Ahmad Rachid El Mohamad 4 , Ghaya Al Rumaihi 1

1 Neurosurgery Department, Hamad Medical corporation, Doha, Qatar, 2 Faculty of Medicine, Jordan University of Science and Technology, Irbid, Jordan, 3 Biruni University, Istanbul, Turkey, 4 Neurosurgery Department, New Mazloum Hospital, Tripoli, Lebanon

Introduction: Degenerative lumbar canal stenosis is a common cause of disability in the elderly population, often necessitating surgical decompression when conservative therapy fails. Minimally invasive alternatives such as tubular-based microscopic decompression and full-endoscopic decompression have emerged as strategies to minimize collateral tissue damage while achieving effective neural decompression. However, uncertainty remains regarding their relative efficacy, safety, and long-term outcomes. We did a meta-analysis to compare the functional outcomes, perioperative parameters, and complication rates between full-endoscopic and tubular-based microscopic decompression in patients with degenerative lumbar canal stenosis. Material and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were performed according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines and Cochrane methodology. Randomized controlled trials comparing full-endoscopic (uniportal or biportal) versus tubular-based microscopic decompression were identified through searches of Medline, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane, and ScienceDirect up to August 2025. Primary outcomes included Oswestry Disability Index and Visual Analog Scale for pain at baseline, short-term, and long-term follow-up. Secondary outcomes included operative time, intraoperative blood loss, hospital stay, and complication rates. Data was pooled using fixed- or random-effects models depending on heterogeneity. Results: Five randomized controlled trials with 316 patients were included. Both techniques significantly improved disability and pain scores compared with baseline. Full-endoscopic decompression was associated with lower Oswestry Disability Index scores at six months (mean difference 2.37; p < 0.001), but no difference at two years. Visual Analog Scale scores for back and leg pain showed no significant differences at any timepoint. Full endoscopy demonstrated reduced intraoperative blood loss, shorter operative time, and shorter hospital stay, while complication rates, including dural tears and infections, were comparable between groups. Conclusion: Both full-endoscopic and tubular-based microscopic decompression are effective and safe surgical options for degenerative lumbar canal stenosis. Endoscopy offers short-term perioperative advantages without compromising safety, although long-term functional outcomes appear equivalent. Surgical approach selection should consider surgeon expertise, patient characteristics, and institutional resources.

RF054: Investigation of the effect of foramen dimension on dorsal root ganglion irritation following transforaminal endoscopic procedures

Gayani Petersingham 1 , Wentian Li 2 , Tyson Zhang 3 , Yingda Li 3 , Prashanth Rao 4

1 Brain and Spine Surgery, UNSW, Sydney, Australia, 2 Brain and Spine Surgery, Sydney, Australia, 3 USYD, Sydney, Australia, 4 Brain and Spine S urgery, UNSW, Macquarie University, Sydney, Australia

Introduction: Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) irritation is a frequent complication of transforaminal endoscopic spine surgery, causing acute postoperative dysesthetic radicular pain in up to 20% of patients. This study aimed to evaluate whether foraminal area correlates with the incidence of postoperative DRG-related pain. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 500 patients who underwent percutaneous endoscopic discectomy. Preoperative MRI scans were analysed to measure foraminal area at three levels: lower endplate of the superior vertebra, disc level, and upper endplate of the inferior vertebra. Postoperative dysesthetic pain was assessed within 48 hours using a visual analogue scale (VAS). Correlations between foraminal dimensions and pain outcomes were calculated. Results: Mean foraminal area ranged from 45-115 mm2. Patients with foraminal area < 65 mm2 experienced a significantly higher incidence of acute dysesthetic pain (p < 0.001). An inverse correlation was observed between foraminal area and VAS pain scores, indicating that smaller foramina were strongly predictive of increased DRG irritation. Conclusion: Smaller foraminal dimensions are significantly associated with postoperative dysesthetic radicular pain following transforaminal endoscopic procedures. RF055: Innovative use of an anterior transdiscal screw in the management of complex axis fracture: a case report

Rafael de Souza 1 , Wilker Oliveira 1 , Jose Otavio Donadeli Tome 1 , Gabrielle Amaral 2 , Bruno Motter 1 , Guilherme Foizer 1 , Andre Cesar 1 , Luciano Rodrigues 1

1 ABC Medical School, Santo André, Brazil, 2 University of São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Management of complex fractures of the axis remains challenging, particularly in the presence of concomitant vertebral artery injury that contraindicates posterior fixation. While posterior instrumentation is traditionally considered the gold standard for stabilization, anterior approaches may provide a viable alternative in anatomically or clinically restricted scenarios. We report the first clinical application of an anterior C2-C3 arthrodesis utilizing an oblique anterior transdiscal screw (ATAS) in the treatment of an unstable axis fracture associated with vertebral artery dissection. Case Description: A 57-year-old male sustained a high-energy fall from five meters, resulting in a fracture of the anterior arch of C1, an atypical oblique fracture of C2 consistent with Al-Mahfoudh type 2a, and left vertebral artery dissection at the V3 segment. Imaging confirmed instability of the axis and precluded posterior instrumentation due to the vascular lesion. Surgical management consisted of staged anterior procedures: anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) at C4-C5 followed by C2-C3 discectomy, autologous iliac crest graft placement, and stabilization with an oblique ATAS from C3 to C2, reinforced with anterior plating. Postoperative imaging demonstrated satisfactory alignment and implant positioning. At 4 months, radiographs confirmed graft incorporation and stability, while 12-month follow-up revealed favorable functional recovery without complications. Discussion: The anterior transdiscal screw construct provided immediate stabilization, graft compression, and restoration of sagittal alignment in a highly unstable fracture pattern. Biomechanical data support its rigidity, with performance comparable or superior to conventional anterior systems. In this context, the anterior approach mitigated the risks associated with posterior fixation in the presence of vertebral artery injury. This case provides the first clinical validation of ATAS application at C2-C3, extending prior experimental evidence and supporting its potential role in selected cases of upper cervical trauma. Conclusion: Anterior C2-C3 arthrodesis with oblique ATAS constitutes a safe and effective alternative for the management of complex axis fractures when posterior fixation is contraindicated. This report highlights the feasibility of this novel technique and underscores the need for further clinical investigations to define its indications and long-term outcomes.

RF057: AO Spine Delphi Study: acute C2 fractures in elderly patients (interim results ahead of study completion)

Richard Storey 1,2 , Grace Xiong 3 , Jake McDonnell 1 , Conor Kennedy 1 , Rohan Tewari 1 , Stacey Darwish 1 , Gregory Schroeder 4 , Joseph Butler 1

1 Mater Misericordiae University Hospital, University College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland, 2 University College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland, 3 Stanford University School of Medicine, Standford, United States, 4 Rothman Institute, Philidelphia, United States

Introduction: Acute C2 fractures (odontoid process, C2 body and posterior element fractures) in elderly patients presents a common and complex surgical challenge. These injuries and their management are the subject of persistent debate and controversy. Predictors of poor outcomes include patient demographics (age, sex), host factors (frailty, baseline function, comorbidities), injury characteristics (mechanism, timing, neurology, polytrauma) and radiographic features. Integration of these variables into a comprehensive surgical treatment guideline is hindered by the heterogeneity of the original literature.

The AO Spine Knowledge Forum (KF) presents an opportunity to leverage key opinion leaders expertise for to distill surgical management consensus and define knowledge gaps for future research. Material and Methods: Following literature review and preliminary discussion identified overarching and subcategory variables to be included in Round 1. A four round Delphi methodology was selected. Participants included attending/consultant spine surgeons from all five global territories of the AO Spine network. Round 1 included expert participant background, experience and surgical setting clarification. A 10-point Likert score (LS) was used to include or exclude subcategories with intermediate scores being voted for inclusion or exclusion by the AO Spine KF Trauma & Infection. Free text was used to gain variables not identified in preliminary discussions. Round 2 further investigated the role of each subcategory and overarching categories in surgical decision making using a range of survey question designs and free text. Results of Rounds 1 and 2 were used to develop statements regarding surgical indication and contraindications for acute C2 fractures in elderly patients and progressed using 5-point and 3-point agreement scales respectively. Results: Round 1 was completed in July 2025 and included 33 participants. Rounds 2 - 4 are planned for completion between September and November 2025. All expert panel participants are actively involved in the surgical management of C2 fractures in elderly patients with an average annual case volume of 14 (range 2 - 50 cases). Participating surgeons were capable of an appropriate range of anterior and posterior surgical techniques. An acute neurological deficit emerged out of Round 1 as the strongest consideration for surgical management (ASIA score and motor deficit, LS 9.5 and 9.3 respectively). Patient frailty (LS 8.4) was considered more important than chronological age (LS 7.8) in surgical decision making with an emerging preference of generalized frailty assessment (LS 8.9) over quantified frailty assessments (LS 7.8). Comorbidities (LS 8.3), particularly dementia (LS 8.5) and pulmonary conditions (LS 7.2), were of high importance as well as baseline ambulatory status (LS 8.6). The strongest radiological consideration was evidence of dynamic instability (LS 9.2). Many other static radiological findings had LS > 7.0 including; fracture classification, angulation, displacement, translation, obliquity, canal stenosis, cord oedema, comminution, adjacent joint and ligament involvement. Conclusion: The AO Spine KF T&I aims to complete future rounds of the Delphi method with the goal of establishing a consensus statement and framework for surgical decision making in this population.

RF059: Imaging biomarkers and early surgery are predictive of FIM recovery but not motor outcomes in acute traumatic central cord syndrome patients

A Aravin Kumar 1 , Linda Lim Huiling 1 , Shane Zaw 2 , Qingping Joseph Feng 1 , Damian Lee 1,2,3 , Dinesh Shree Kumar 2 , Lester Lee 1,2,3 , Robin Pillay 1 , Ji Min Ling 1,2

Outcomes were significant improvement in ASIA Motor Score (AMS) at 6 and 12 months, and significant improvements in and Functional Independence Measure (FIM) and modified Japanese orthopedic association score (mJOA) at 6-months. Twenty-three (19.8%) patients had ossification of posterior ligament (OPLL) and 102 (87.9%) patients had pre-existing cervical spondylosis with stenosis. Nine (7.8%) patients required assistance with their activities of daily living (ADLs) on admission and 16 (13.8%) presented with a high impact injury. The median AMS on admission was 85.0 (IQR: 25.8) with the median upper extremity motor score (UEMS) being 37.5 (IQR: 18.0) and median lower extremity motor score (LEMS) being 50.0 (IQR: 10.0). Median FIM on admission was 76.0 (IQR: 53.0) and median mJOA on admission was 10.0 (IQR: 7.8). Sixty-five (56.0%) of patients underwent operative management, with the median time to operation being 4.0 (IQR: 10.0) days. Of the patients who underwent operative management, 17 (26.2%) underwent early surgery, within 24 hours. Median AMS at 12-months was 100.0 (IQR: 10.3), with median improvement at 12-months being 93.4% (IQR: 53.8). The median FIM score at 6-months was 99.0 (IQR: 56.0) and the median FIM improvement rate was 36.0% (IQR: 74.7). The median mJOA at 6-months was 17.0 (IQR: 5.0) with a median mJOA recovery rate of 66.7% (IQR: 77.0). Univariate and multivariate analysis revealed that early surgery within 24 hours was negatively correlated (OR 0.1, 95% CI 0.0 - 0.5, p = 0.005) and spinal cord diameter at the level of stenosis on admission was positively correlated (OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.0 - 4.3, p = 0.044) with significant improvement in FIM at 6-months. Early surgery and imaging biomarkers were not significantly associated with other outcomes. Conclusion: In our local Asian population, early surgery and imaging biomarkers had moderate correlations with FIM improvement but not with other motor or functional outcomes.

RF060: Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI) as a predictor for survival in trauma patients following posterior cervical fusion (PCF)

Zayaan Tirmizi 1 , Ben Carnovale 1 , Samuel Wakelin 1 , Qazi Zeeshan 2 , Nitin Agarwal 1,2,3 , Kojo Hamilton 1,2,3

1 Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, United States, 2 Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, United States, 3 Neurological Surgery, Veterans Affairs Pittsburgh Healthcare System, Pittsburgh, United States

Introduction: Numerous studies have explored the effectiveness of perioperative and preoperative serum albumin and lymphocyte levels as predictors of complications and success in spine surgery. Importantly, ample confounders exist that could influence such laboratory values. The Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI) utilizes an integrated score, combining both metrics to provide a more robust depiction of a patient nutritional profile. Our study aims to explore whether such a score can be employed as a predictor of two important outcomes, survival and discharge disposition, in patients following posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCDF) for traumatic indications. Material and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted at a single quaternary care center from 2011 to 2023. Patients were included if they presented with cervical fracture from trauma with acute spinal cord injury and subsequently underwent PCDF. Patient demographic information, surgical characteristics, and patient outcomes were extracted. Outcomes included hardware failure, wound revision, discharge disposition, and death. PNI was calculated using the formula: Albumin level (in grams per liter) + 0.005 × Lymphocyte count per microliter. Multiple logistic regression was used to assess the effect of albumin levels, lymphocyte levels, and PNI on three-month, six-month, one-year, and two-year mortality rates, when controlled for age and sex. Additionally, separate logistic regressions were performed for each discharge disposition category (home, skilled nursing facility, rehabilitation facility, death) to evaluate the association with PNI, controlling for age and sex. Additionally, the median PNI score was calculated, and patients were split into high and low PNI groups based on comparison to the median. Kaplan Meier regression was performed to analyze differing survival rates among the high and low PNI groups. Additionally, albumin and lymphocyte levels were similarly split into high and low groups and analyzed for association with survival separately via Kaplan Meier regression. All tests were performed using R version 4.3.3 with p < 0.05 considered to be significant. Results: Logistic regression did not detect any significant association between PNI or lymphocyte and three-month, six-month, one-year, or two-year mortality when controlled for age and sex. No significant associations between PNI or lymphocyte levels and discharge dispositions were detected. The median albumin level was 3.5g/L, the median lymphocyte level was 3000/µL, and the median PNI was 38.5. Kaplan-Meier regression revealed a significant drop in survival among the low PNI group (p = 0.0023) following PCF with trauma indication. Additionally, survival was decreased in the high lymphocyte level group (p = 0.0086) and the low albumin group (p = 0.0011). Conclusion: Crucially, low PNI was observed to have a statistically significant drop in survival following trauma indicated PCF. Interestingly, despite the correlation between high lymphocyte level, likely elevated in this cohort due to the immune response following trauma, and poor survival, PNI was able to correct for this discrepancy and show that poor overall nutritional status leads to worse survival outcomes, showing promise as a predictor of survival preoperatively. Such a tool can be utilized to triage which patients are at highest risk of mortality, allowing surgeons to tailor surgical plans and postoperative care appropriately.

RF061: Treatment outcomes of anterior C1-C2 transarticular screw fixation versus posterior magerl and Goel-Harms techniques for geriatric odontoid fractures

Žiga Žigman 1 , Matjaž Zorman 1 , Cene Kopač 1 , Neža Rode 1 , Marko Jug 1

1 University Medical Centre Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia

Introduction: Odontoid fractures are the most common cervical spine fracture in patients over 65 years old. The optimal surgical management remains controversial, with debates surrounding the safety and efficacy of anterior versus posterior fixation approaches in this fragile population. This study compared the clinical, radiographic, and functional outcomes of anterior C1-C2 transarticular screw fixation against posterior fixation for Type II odontoid fractures in elderly patients, utilizing a propensity score-matched analysis to minimize selection bias. Materials and Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients aged 65 or older who underwent surgery for Type II odontoid fractures between March 2013 and August 2024. Patients were divided into two treatment cohorts: the first undergoing anterior C1-C2 transarticular screw fixation (AF), and the second undergoing posterior fixation (PF), which encompassed the Magerl and Goel-Harms techniques. To account for baseline confounders, a 1:1 propensity score matching was performed based on age, sex, and Charlson Comorbidity Index. Primary outcomes were 1-year mortality and fracture fusion rates. Key secondary outcomes included functional status, assessed by the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at final follow-up, operative time, and blood loss. Results: From an initial cohort of 33 patients, propensity score matching yielded a well-balanced cohort of 22 patients (11 AF, 11 PF). The matching process resulted in two groups that were nearly identical in age; the mean age was 77.1 years for the AF group and 77.3 years for the PF group (p > 0.9), with an overall age range of 65 to 93 years. The PF group had a significantly lower 1-year mortality rate (18.2%, n = 2/11) compared to the AF group (45.5%, n = 5/11; p = 0.04; Odds Ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.04-1.5). The PF group also achieved a higher fusion rate (81.8%, n = 9/11) versus the AF group (63.6%, n = 7/11), though this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.06). Among surviving patients, functional outcomes were comparable, with a median final mRS score of 2 in both groups (p = 0.99). The posterior approach was associated with a significantly longer mean operative time (138 vs. 88 min; p. < 0.01) and greater blood loss (255 vs. 95 mL; p < 0.01). Conclusion: In this propensity score-matched analysis of elderly patients with Type II odontoid fractures, posterior fixation was associated with significantly lower 1-year mortality compared to anterior C1-C2 transarticular screw fixation, despite being a surgically more demanding procedure. While a trend towards higher fusion rates with posterior fixation was observed, functional outcomes at final follow-up were similar between the two approaches among survivors. These findings suggest that posterior fixation may offer a survival benefit and should be strongly considered in the surgical management of this high-risk population.

1 Istanbul Goztepe Prof. Dr. Suleyman Yalcin City Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey, 2 Manisa City Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey, 3 Uskudar University, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Type II odontoid fractures are the most common cervical spine injuries in the elderly and present significant challenges in management due to instability, comorbidities, and poor bone quality. This study aimed to compare clinical and radiological outcomes of anterior and posterior surgical techniques, including C1-C2-3 transfacet fixation, in elderly patients. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31 patients (mean age 77.8 ± 8.8 years; range: 65-98; 21 females, 10 males) treated surgically for Type II odontoid fractures (2021-2024). Conclusion: Patients who underwent closed reduction within 24 hours of injury demonstrated significantly better neurological outcomes compared to those treated after 24 hours, with a statistically significant difference in recovery rates (p < 0.001). These results emphasize the critical need for prompt reduction of the dislocation to optimize neurological recovery and overall patient outcomes in the management of cervical spinal cord injuries (CSIs).

RF064: Specificity of GFAP and NFL as biomarkers of neuronal injury in spinal fracture patients without neurological deficits

Carlos Beredjiklian 1 , Lukas Grassner 1

1 Department of Neurosurgery, Christian Doppler Clinic, Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg, Austria, Institute of Molecular Regenerative Medicine, Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg, Austria, Spinal Cord Injury Center, BG Trauma Center, Murnau, Germany, Salzburg, Austria

Introduction: The reliable diagnosis of spinal cord injury (SCI) in the acute phase remains challenging, particularly in patients with concomitant trauma or sedation. Blood biomarkers such as glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and neurofilament light chain (NFL) have shown promise in reflecting neuronal damage. However, whether these biomarkers are specific to SCI, as opposed to general trauma from vertebral fractures without neurological impairment, is insufficiently understood. Material and Methods: In this prospective, non-interventional observational study, serum samples were collected from patients with spinal fractures without neurological deficits (SFX group, n = 23), patients with SCI (n = 77), and healthy controls (n = 24). Blood was drawn by venipuncture and processed according to standardized protocols. GFAP and NFL concentrations were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Descriptive statistics and group comparisons were conducted to assess biomarker specificity. Results: GFAP levels on day 1 post-injury were significantly elevated in both SCI (mean: ∼770 pg/mL) and SFX (mean: ∼670 pg/mL) patients compared to healthy controls (mean: ∼36 pg/mL). A significant difference was observed between SFX and SCI groups, though notable individual overlap existed. NFL concentrations displayed a similar pattern: mean values were higher in SCI (mean: ∼344 pg/mL) compared to SFX (mean: ∼68 pg/mL) and controls (mean: ∼32 pg/mL), again with overlapping ranges between SFX and SCI patients. Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that while GFAP and NFL levels are markedly elevated after SCI, patients with vertebral fractures without neurological deficits also exhibit increased concentrations of these biomarkers. This partial overlap suggests that GFAP and NFL are sensitive to neuroaxonal injury but may not be fully specific to overt SCI. Further analyses, including longitudinal sampling and correlation with clinical severity scores, are underway to refine their diagnostic utility and establish thresholds that better discriminate between fracture-related trauma and true spinal cord injury.

Carlos Beredjiklian 1 , Lukas Grassner 1

1 Department of Neurosurgery, Christian Doppler Clinic, Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg, Austria, Institute of Molecular Regenerative Medicine, Paracelsus Medical University, Salzburg, Austria, Spinal Cord Injury Center, BG Trauma Center, Murnau, Germany, Salzburg, Austria

1 St. George's, University Hospital of London, London, United Kingdom

The COVID-19 pandemic reconfigured exposures and pathways; road-traffic trauma fell, domestic injuries rose, ICU capacity tightened, and rehabilitation was disrupted. Whether these system-level changes altered the severity profile of fall-related spinal polytrauma, shifted mortality, or changed ICU utilisation remains unclear. ISS was analysed as continuous severity. Fall height was mapped from mechanism to low (<2m) v high (>2m). The study used descriptive and comparative statistical tests to compare injury severity and outcome proportions across eras, with regression models adjusting for age and injury severity to assess whether identified differences across eras were due to case-mix. ICU odds were lower in Covid and Post (roughly half those of Pre at similar age/ISS), and higher with greater ISS (p < 0.001). Within > 65, low-height falls became more common (Pre 38% > Post 49%) and low-fall ISS increased substantially by 9 points) yet fall height itself was not independently associated with mortality or ICU admission once age and ISS were included. Conclusion: Fall-related spinal polytrauma patients presented sicker through and after the pandemic as seen by the higher ISS, ICU was used more selectively, and risk-adjusted in-hospital survival was maintained, the excess risk appears to have shifted to the post-acute phase, with age-driven 1-year mortality rising. Likely drivers include a frailer and deconditioned demographic owing to the pandemic and rehabilitation/social-care disruption. A directed practice towards implementing a standardised, orthogeriatric-led pathway for > 65 with fall-related spinal trauma is recommended.

RF070: Outcomes following spinal cord injury in patients with pre-existing diabetes mellitus: a comparative analysis of type 1 and type 2 diabetes

Thomas Olson 1 , Joshua Wiener 1 , Trevor LLoyd 1 , Chris Hamad 1 , Carlos Maturana 1 , Carson McCann 1 , Amy Blackburn 1 , Aliyah Walker 1 , Rene Chun 1 , John Adams 1 , Nicholas Bernthal 1 , William Sheppard 1

1 UCLA, Los Angeles, United States

Background: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating condition with outcomes shaped by comorbidities. Diabetes mellitus (DM), both type 1 (T1DM) and type 2 (T2DM), is highly prevalent in this population and may exacerbate post-injury complications. SCI can predispose patients to metabolic dysfunction and incident T2DM, while pre-existing DM may independently worsen recovery trajectories. This study evaluates the effect of pre-existing T1DM and T2DM on clinical outcomes following SCI. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network, identifying adults with SCI between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2023. Patients with pre-existing DM were classified as T1DM or T2DM based on ICD-10 codes and medication profiles. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to balance demographics, comorbidities, and treatment characteristics between diabetic and non-diabetic cohorts, and between T1DM and T2DM subgroups. Outcomes assessed within one year included neurogenic bladder/bowel, pressure ulcers, thromboembolic events, autonomic dysfunction, osteoporotic fractures, respiratory complications, functional dependence, gait abnormalities, pain syndromes, and all-cause mortality. Statistical analyses included risk estimation, Cox proportional hazards modeling, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Results: Of 149,125 patients with SCI, 24,231 had pre-existing DM. Following matching, diabetic (n = 23,453) and non-diabetic (n = 23,453) cohorts were well balanced across baseline characteristics. SCI+DM patients experienced significantly higher one-year rates of neurogenic bladder/bowel (5.3% vs. 4.3%), pressure ulcers (6.3% vs. 3.5%), respiratory complications (6.6% vs. 4.4%), functional dependence (6.1% vs. 4.2%), gait abnormalities (11.6% vs. 9.0%), pain syndromes (13.8% vs. 12.5%), and mortality (9.9% vs. 8.2%) compared with non-diabetics (all p < 0.01). Subgroup analysis (n = 806 per group) demonstrated that SCI+T1DM patients had higher rates of pressure ulcers (7.0% vs. 2.4%), respiratory complications (7.5% vs. 3.7%), functional dependence (6.7% vs. 4.0%), gait abnormalities (11.8% vs. 7.6%), pain syndromes (18.7% vs. 13.2%), and mortality (13.1% vs. 4.9%; HR 2.80, 95% CI 1.94-4.05) compared with SCI+T2DM patients. Other outcomes, including thromboembolic events and autonomic dysfunction, did not differ significantly. Conclusions: Pre-existing DM significantly increases complication rates and mortality following SCI, with T1DM conferring a disproportionate burden of morbidity compared to T2DM. These findings suggest that diabetes is a critical risk modifier in SCI recovery, and that T1DM patients warrant particular attention for intensive monitoring, wound prevention, cardiopulmonary surveillance, and tailored rehabilitation. Future prospective studies should explore the role of glycemic control, disease duration, and autoimmune comorbidities in driving these differences and assess whether targeted interventions can improve outcomes in this high-risk population.

Among LL fractures, SSPI resulted in ODI (p = 0.255) and VAS (p = 0.066) scores comparable to TL fractures, suggesting minimal functional impairment. Radiologically, all groups exhibited significant improvements in SCA (p < 0.001). Conclusion: In this study, the SSPI method was found to be a safe option for the management of LLS fractures from both clinical and radiological perspectives. Conclusion: By measuring patient outcomes and tracking costs, this study outlines a practical method to assess the value of operative care for traumatic SCI in Nepal, while also providing information to guide policy, insurance, and referral systems.

RF075: Deep learning-based spinal cord MRI enables accurate screening and classification of degenerative cervical myelopathy

Ramesh Arnest 1 , Kevin Koch 2 , Matthew Budde 1 , Aditya Vedantam 1

1 Medical College of Wisconsin, Milwaukee, United States, 2 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is often difficult to diagnose early because of subtle and non-specific symptoms, combined with the high incidence of cervical cord compression on MRI in asymptomatic older adults. Determining whether spinal cord compression is clinically relevant and necessitates surgery remains challenging. Deep learning and computer vision approaches can leverage imaging data in standard imaging sequence to improve diagnostic accuracy. We evaluated convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for automated screening and classification of DCM using cervical spinal cord T2-weighted MRI. Material and Methods: T2-weighted 3-T cervical spine MRIs (3D isotropic resolution, 0.8 mm3) were obtained from 79 pre-surgical DCM patients (49 men, 30 women) and 51 healthy controls (25 men, 26 women), totaling 130 scans. The dataset was divided into a training set (n = 104, 80%) and independent testing set (n = 26, 20%). The spinal cord was automatically segmented using the Spinal Cord Toolbox (v6.5) and manually verified. Preprocessing included intensity normalization, probabilistic affine augmentation (p = 0.7) with small rotations (≈±9°; 0.234 rad about each axis) and translations (±4 mm), followed by cropping to a fixed size with partial padding. CNNs (ResNet-10, ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, and EfficientNet3D) were implemented in Medical Open Network for Artificial Intelligence (MONAI). Training used 5-fold cross-validation. Performance was evaluated on a held-out test set using accuracy, area under receiver operator curve (AUROC), F1-score, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), sensitivity, and specificity. Results: Among all tested architectures, ResNet10-based models demonstrated the best overall performance. On the independent test set, it reached accuracy = 0.8077; AUROC = 0.8875; F1-score = 0.8276; MCC = 0.6325; precision=92%; sensitivity = 75%; specificity = 90%. Other CNNs, including DenseNet-121 and EfficientNet3D, yielded lower performance, primarily due to overfitting in this relatively small dataset. mJOA-based binary classification was also performed with ResNet models using 5-fold cross-validation and class balancing by undersampling. The model achieved an average accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.10 for control vs. mild DCM, 0.75 ± 0.05 for mild vs. moderate+severe DCM, and 0.79 ± 0.05 for severe vs. mild+moderate DCM. Conclusion: Deep learning and computer vision can accurately discriminate DCM from non-DCM individuals using cervical spinal cord T2-weighted MRI, independent of clinical or demographic data. In addition, mJOA subgroup analyses demonstrated clinically meaningful performance, including 84% accuracy in the challenging control vs. mild classification. These findings highlight the promise of image-based artificial intelligence as a screening tool for DCM.

RF076: Preliminary results of the prospective SCREEN-DCM trial: analysis of the Geneva cohort

Aria Nouri 1 , Nasser Bouhalassa 1 , Francesca Brigatti 1 , Granit Molliqaj 1 , Alexandre Lavé 1 , Gianpaolo Jannelli 1 , Teresa Somma 2 , Carmen Vleggeert-Lankamp 3 , Allan Martin 4 , Enrico Tessitore 1 , Karl Schaller 1

1 Division of Neurosurgery, Geneva University Hospitals, Geneva, Switzerland, 2 Division of Neurosurgery, Department of Neurosciences, Reproductive and Odontostomatological Sciences, University of Naples Federico II, Naples, Italy, 3 Department of Neurosurgery, Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, The Netherlands, 4 Department of Neurological Surgery, University of California, Davis, California, United States

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction worldwide, yet it remains frequently underdiagnosed. Early identification is crucial to prevent irreversible disability. The SCREEN-DCM protocol proposes a simple score based on clinical signs and symptoms, with a threshold of ≥3 points recommending cervical MRI due to high suspicion of DCM. Stepwise elimination (AIC criterion) reduced the model to the five most relevant predictors to avoid overfitting. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. Results: In Geneva, 159 patients were screened: 45 (28%) screened positive (SCREEN-DCM score ≥ 3), and 114 (72%) screened negative (score < 3). Among these, 50 patients ultimately underwent MRI. The five-variable model demonstrated excellent discrimination (AUC = 0.905, 95% CI 0.811-0.998). Conclusion: We demonstrate that the SCREEN-DCM score identified patients at risk of DCM with moderate PPV and excellent NPV, effectively ruling out disease in screen-negative cases. Gait ataxia and Hoffman’s sign were the most powerful predictors. These are preliminary single-center results from Geneva, and while promising, they require confirmation in the ongoing multicenter cohort to establish clinical utility.

RF077: Transabdominal motor evoked potentials as a robust adjunct to transcranial monitoring in lumbar spine surgery: superior performance in patients with brain pathology

Lakota Stitt 1 , Sydney Rucker 1 , Jessica Barley 1 , Robert Ferdon 2 , John Glaser 1 , Robert Ravinsky 1 , Ezequiel Gleichgerrcht 3

1 Medical University of South Carolina, Charleston, United States, 2 University of South Carolina - School of Medicine, Columbia, United States, 3 Emory University, Atlanta, United States

Introduction: Transabdominal motor evoked potentials (taMEPs) are a novel intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) modality for lumbar spine procedures. Unlike transcranial motor evoked potentials (tcMEPs), which are susceptible to anesthetic-induced cortical suppression, taMEPs bypass the brain and may offer more stable and reliable lumbar plexus monitoring. We report on 100 consecutive cases with dual-modality MEP monitoring, focusing on comparative monitorability of TaMEP versus TcMEPs and the influence of pathology and patient comorbidities. This represents the first cohort study to evaluate the differential impact of neurological and systemic comorbidities on the monitorability of taMEPs versus tcMEPs in lumbar spine surgery. Materials and Methods: TaMEPs and tcMEPs were obtained from six muscle groups (iliopsoas, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, tibialis anterior, abductor hallucis) and monitored continuously throughout each procedure. Baseline monitorability was defined as: (1) binary (≥1 reliable response), and (2) continuous (mean percentage of muscle groups monitorable). Patient comorbidities were identified by ICD-10 codes and categorized into brain, cervical spine, peripheral neuropathy, cardiac/ischemic disease, pulmonary disease, and metabolic pathologies. Binary outcomes were compared using McNemar’s and Fisher’s exact tests, continuous outcomes with Wilcoxon signed-rank testing, and logistic regression was used to evaluate independent predictors of monitorability. Analyses were performed using RStudio and SPSS v29, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Monitorability of taMEP versus tcMEP was equivalent overall, with 92% vs 94% of cases demonstrating at least one reliable response present (p = 0.79) and mean percentage of monitorable muscles of 75% ± SD vs 71% ± SD (p = 0.86). Subgroup analysis revealed tcMEPs were significantly less monitorable in patients with brain pathology versus without (75% vs 97.6%; OR 0.07, p = 0.006), whereas TaMEP monitorability was unaffected (93.8% vs 91.7%; OR 1.36, p = 1.0), suggesting TcMEPs are selectively vulnerable to central nervous system comorbidities. Conversely, the presence of peripheral neuropathy significantly reduced monitorability of TaMEPs (60% vs 93.7%; OR 0.20, p = 0.036), with tcMEPs showing a similar but non-significant trend (80% vs 94.7%; OR 0.22, p = 0.27). No other comorbidities assessed showed significant impact on monitorability for either modality, though cervical and cardiac pathology demonstrated borderline associations with reduced taMEP reliability (p ≈ 0.10). No independent predictors of monitorability were found in preliminary analysis. Conclusion: TaMEPs demonstrate comparable monitorability to tcMEP for lumbar motor pathways, with particular robustness in patients with brain pathology, where the latter are frequently unreliable. While peripheral neuropathy may limit taMEP utility, these findings support its role as an adjunct or alternative to tcMEPs, especially in patients with central nervous system comorbidities.

No patients in either group experienced any adverse reactions. Conclusion: This study provides comparative evidence on PRP and corticosteroid-based facet injections in managing lumbar facet joint-related pain. The findings show that PRP injections are a safe and effective alternative option, with longer-lasting effects than corticosteroid injections.

RF079: Are we really reducing radiation exposure in spine surgery? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the past decade and what that means for the future

Kento Yamanouchi 1,2 , Kenneth Nguyen 1 , Emaad Lala 1 , Sydney Pattison 1,3 , Madison Alessi 1,3 , Aiyush Bansal 1 , Philip Louie 1

1 Virginia Mason Medical Center, Seattle, United States, 2 Keio University, Tokyo, Japan, 3 University of Washington, Seattle, United States

Introduction: In the past decade, advanced technologies such as O-arm, Airo, navigation systems, robotic-assisted platforms have been introduced in spine surgery, contributing to improved accuracy, safety, and efficiency. However, several studies have reported increasing intraoperative radiation exposure associated with these improving technologies. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate trends in reported radiation exposure metrics across the past ten years and projected potential trends for the next decade. Materials and Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, EMBASE, and Google Scholar was conducted to identify studies evaluating radiation exposure during spine surgery. Eligible studies reported quantitative intraoperative radiation exposure metrics associated with imaging modalities. Outcomes of interest included intraoperative radiation exposure dose, exposure time, length of stay (LOS), and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Data on study design, patient demographics, and surgical characteristics were extracted. Meta-analysis was performed with mean difference for continuous outcomes. Results: A total of 121 studies involving 13530 patients were included in this systematic review. Low dose protocols, such as pulsed fluoroscopy or low-dose imaging, were utilized in 21 studies (17.3 %). Meta-analysis demonstrated that radiation exposure dose with C-arm or fluoroscopy was significantly lower than O-arm or navigation (SMD = -1.06 [95% CI -1.24, -0.89]; SMD = -0.19 [95%CI -0.32, -0.05]). In contrast, radiation exposure with fluoroscopy was significantly higher than with robotic-assisted platforms (SMD = 1.35 [95% CI 1.22, 1.47]). Fluoroscopy was associated with longer exposure time compared with other modalities (SMD = 3.76 [95% CI 0.57, 6.96]; SMD = -0.73 [95% CI 0.59, 0.86]; SMD = 2.52 [95% CI 2.30, 2.74]). No significant differences were observed in LOS or ODI among all modalities. Conclusion: This systematic review summarized radiation exposure in spine surgery over the past decade. Our findings demonstrate that intraoperative radiation exposure has increased with the widespread introduction of advanced enabling technologies such as O-arm, navigation systems, and robotic-assisted platforms. While these technologies have improved accuracy, safety, and workflow efficiency, their increased utilization may inadvertently contribute to higher radiation doses. For the next decade, more effective radiation dose-reduction strategies will be essential.

RF082: National trends in the surgical management of lumbar facet cysts: a national database study

Joshua Sanchez 1 , Julian Smith Voudouris 1 , Katie Zehner 1 , Anthony Seddio 1 , Scott Halperin 1 , Sahir Jabbouri 1 , Jonathan Grauer 1 , Raj Gala 1

1 Yale School of Medicine, New Haven, United States

Introduction: Lumbar facet cysts can contribute to stenosis and radiculopathy. While non-operative management is a first line treatment of patients with such cysts, a subset of patients may be candidates for surgical intervention. This may be decompression (D) alone or decompression with fusion (D+F). However, the use of one modality versus the other remains a topic of discussion. As such, the current study utilized a large, national, 2010 to 2022 administrative database to determine yearly rates of D versus D+F utilization, independent predictors of D+F relative to D, 90-day overall costs (measured by insurer-payments), and 5-year survival to reoperation. Material and Methods: The 2010-2022 PearlDiver M170 database was queried for adult patients (> 17 years of age) who underwent D or D+F with a same-day diagnosis of a lumbar facet synovial cyst. Exclusion criteria included multilevel fusion, coded infection, trauma, or neoplasm related to the spine within 90 days prior to surgery, and database inactivity within 90 days following surgery. Calendar year incidence rates were assessed and trended with linear regression. Next, multivariable logistic regression was conducted to identify independent predictors of D+F relative to D alone. Ninety-day postoperative insurer-payments were also assessed and compared. To determine 5-year survival to subsequent lumbar reoperations, a 1:1 match controlling for age, sex, Elixhauser comorbidity index, spondylolisthesis, and preoperative smoker status was completed for the two groups. Kaplan-Meier curves were created and compared with log-rank test. Significance was defined as p < 0.00063, as per Bonferroni correction. Results: A total of 45,380 patients with surgically managed lumbar facet cysts were identified, of which D alone was performed for 33,988 (74.9%) and D+F for 11,392 (25.1%). The incidence of both procedures increased over the years of the study (p < 0.0001), with decompression with fusion rising at a greater rate such that D+F rose from 22.9% in 2010 to 29.4% in 2022 (p = 0.0006). Multivariable analysis found D+F to be independently more likely for those with older age (odds ratio [OR] = 1.13), female sex (OR = 1.26), higher ECI (OR = 1.11), spondylolisthesis (OR = 3.21), and orthopaedic surgeon (relative to neurological surgeon, OR = 1.38) (p < 0.0001 for all). Ninety-day overall insurer-payments were greater for D+F versus D (median $7,744 versus $3,731, p < 0.0001). Five-year survival to reoperation was not found to be different between the two groups. At 5 years, the D group had 91.5% without subsequent lumbar operation and the D+F group had 90.6% (p = 0.6000). Conclusion: While decompression alone was the most common surgical intervention for lumbar facet cysts in this large cohort study, the rate of decompression with fusion increased over the study period. Factors predictive of decompression with fusion were demographic (older/sicker patients), spondylolisthesis (as expected), and surgeon specialty (orthopaedic surgeons being more likely to fuse), suggesting non-clinical factors contribute to decisions. While the subsequent surgery rate was similar for the two groups, identifying patients most likely to benefit from D+F may optimize outcomes and resource utilization on a national level.

RF083: The current state of spine disease literature in Sub-Saharan Africa - A scoping review

Charlotte Wahle 1 , East Africa Spine Trauma Network 1

1 Institute for Global Orthopaedics and Traumatology, University of California, San Francisco, CA, United States

Introduction: Spine disease represents a major public health burden in sub-Saharan Africa. Despite this, literature in this area is sparse. Spine disease research can be costly and thus is more often performed in high-income areas. However, the results may not be generalizable to areas where resources are more constrained. The aim of this study was to assess the current state of the literature as it pertains to spine disease research being published in Sub-Saharan Africa. Material and Methods: A systematic review of the literature was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines. Inclusion criteria consisted of all original research investigating spine disease of any etiology that takes place in Sub-Saharan Africa that contained at least 10 patients and was published in English or French in the past 50 years. Exclusion criteria consisted of narrative reviews, commentaries, editorials, and case reports. Given that many of the included studies were published prior to the establishment of Levels of Evidence, a study quality variable was created which identified randomized studies, prospective studies, and studies that include a control group as having a higher level of scientific rigor. Statistical analysis was performed using STATA Version 18. Results: A total of 154 spine studies have been published from at least 26 countries since 1975 (some included multiple). Nearly half of the studies (74/154, 48%) involved collaboration with another site or country. The highest number of publications came out of Nigeria with 52 publications (34%), followed by 25 from Tanzania (16%) and 12 from Ethiopia (8%). The most common medical specialty was neurosurgery (35%) followed by orthopaedic surgery (19%) and then physical medicine and rehabilitation (8%). The most common type of studies (93/154, 62%) were retrospective cohort observational studies, followed by prospective cohort studies at 26%. Three of the studies (2%) included a control group. The most common study purpose was epidemiologic (103 studies, 67%), followed by therapeutic (49,32%) studies. Other less common study types included qualitative (9,6%), diagnostic (11, 7%), and economic analysis (8,5%). A total of 24 studies (16%) identified a funding source for the work. The majority of studies were from Lower Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) (118/147, 80%) as opposed to low-income (LIC) and Upper Middle-Income Countries (UMICs). Nearly half of studies involved collaborative partnerships. On univariate analysis, lower-income countries were more likely to engage in collaboration with other countries (OR 3.2, 95% CI: 1.2-9.8) and to receive external funding (OR 7.0, 95% CI: 2.3-20.4). Further, collaborative studies were found to produce higher quality academic publication (OR 2.0, 95% CI: 0.94-4.2). Conclusion: There is a relative paucity of spine literature from Sub-Saharan Africa with the majority coming from three LMICs (Nigeria, Tanzania, and Ethiopia). Higher research productivity was associated with higher income level, and research quality was associated with the presence of foreign collaboration. These results support the development of collaborative relationships that may foster higher quality and quantity of research aimed to address the burden of spine disease in Africa.

Conclusion: The prevalence of DISH was associated with BRI, VFA, insulin resistance, and selected lipid parameters. RF085: Routine or required? Reassessing cervical CT Use in elderly head trauma - A retrospective analysis from a German level I trauma center

Josina Straub 1 , Julia Elisabeth Lenz 1 , Leopold Henssler 1 , Kristina Gerhardinger 1 , Lisa Klute 1 , Borys Frankewycz 2 , Volker Alt 1 , Daniel Popp 1 , Siegmund Lang 1 , Maximilian Kerschbaum 1

1 Department for Trauma Surgery, University Hospital Regensburg, Regensburg, Germany,

2 Department of Clinical Acute and Emergency Medicine, University Hospital Regensburg, Regensburg, Germany

Introduction: Geriatric patients with head trauma have an increased risk of concurrent cervical spine injuries. Conclusion: This is the first large-scale normative study of sagittal spinopelvic profiles in the Turkish population using the Updated Roussouly framework. The Modified Roussouly Classification, incorporating the newly defined Type 3-4 AP subgroup, highlights both ethnic variability and continuity among sagittal morphotypes. Incorporating ethnic variability and transitional morphologies into surgical planning may help reduce complications and improve sagittal balance restoration.

Conclusion: This study represents the largest analysis to date of new-onset spinal fractures in patients with sickle cell hemoglobinopathies. RF089: Association Between Socioeconomic Indices and Baseline SRS-22r Scores in the General Adult Population: A Crowdsourced Evaluation
