These measures are increasingly utilized for evaluation and prediction of surgical outcomes in patients with spinal deformity. However, limited evidence exists regarding baseline data and the relationship between the SRS-22r and socioeconomic indices (SEIs) in the general adult population. In this study, we aimed to identify the association between SEIs and baseline SRS-22r scores. Understanding these relationships may provide insights into the clinical impact of socioeconomic status and in developing prediction strategies for ASD surgery. Population with higher ADIs already report lower subjective health status and quality of life. This implies that socioeconomic disparities in perceived spinal health exist prior to disease onset and may predispose these individuals to poorer outcomes once they develop spinal deformity or undergo surgical intervention. RF090: Baseline depression and anxiety are associated with increased neck disability after anterior cervical surgery

Isabel Iral 1,2 , Aiyush Bansal 1 , Chloe Keegan 1 , Grace Gannon 1,2 , Sydney Pattison 1,2 , Nicole Vivelo 1 , Philip Louie 1

1 Virginia Mason Medical Center, Seattle, United States, 2 University of Washington, Seattle, United States

While clinical outcomes such as length of stay and readmission are well studied, the impact of disparities on patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) is less understood. The effects of PHQ-8 (β = 0.207, p = 0.712) and GAD-7 (β = 0.888, p =0 .172) attenuated and were no longer significant. The overall model fit was R2 = 0.406 with overall F-test p < 0.001. RF091: Lateral mass anchor screws with suspensory titanium cable in cervical laminoplasty: a novel technique to prevent lamina re-closure

Shichang Zhao 1 , Haijun Tian 1

1 Department of Orthopaedics, Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China

Introduction: Traditional fixation methods in expansive open-door laminoplasty (EOLP), such as suture suspension, are associated with a significant risk of lamina re-closure, which can compromise long-term spinal canal decompression. While mini-plate fixation offers greater rigidity, it is associated with higher costs, increased implant profile, and potential biomechanical complications like stress-shielding and hinge-side fractures. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the clinical and radiological outcomes of a novel fixation technique using lateral mass anchor screws combined with a suspensory titanium cable, designed to create a pure lateral force vector to prevent re-closure and minimize stress on the hinge. Material and Methods: This was a single-center, retrospective case series of 42 consecutive patients (30 male, 12 female; mean age 61.2 years) with multi-level cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM) or ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL). All patients underwent EOLP with the novel fixation and had a minimum follow-up of 12 months. The surgical technique involved creating a standard open-door laminoplasty. On the hinge side of each instrumented level, a lateral mass screw was inserted. A high-strength titanium cable was then passed through the base of the spinous process on the open side and secured under tension to the head of the corresponding hinge-side screw. This construct generates a purely lateral suspensory force to maintain canal expansion. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, Neck Disability Index (NDI), and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for neck/arm pain. Radiological outcomes, including C2-7 Cobb angle, range of motion (ROM), and evidence of lamina re-closure or hinge fracture, were evaluated using plain radiographs and CT scans. Preoperative and final follow-up data were compared using paired t-tests. Results: At a mean follow-up of 13.5 months, significant clinical improvement was observed across all metrics (p < 0.001). The mean JOA score increased from 9.5 ± 1.5 to 14.8 ± 1.2, corresponding to a mean neurologic recovery rate of 70.7%. Mean NDI improved from 42.5% to 22.1%, and VAS scores for neck and arm pain decreased significantly. Radiologically, cervical lordosis was well-maintained (C2-7 Cobb angle: 15.1° pre-op vs. 13.8° post-op, p > 0.05). Critically, CT analysis at final follow-up revealed zero instances (0%) of lamina re-closure in all 42 patients. Complications included two cases (4.8%) of transient C5 nerve root palsy, which resolved completely, and one case (2.4%) of an asymptomatic, stable hinge-side fracture. No implant-related failures, such as screw loosening or cable breakage, occurred. Conclusion: Fixation with lateral mass anchor screws and a suspensory titanium cable is a safe and highly effective technique for EOLP. By providing a biomechanically superior, pure lateral suspensory force, this method reliably prevents lamina re-closure, ensuring durable spinal canal decompression. This novel technique represents a promising alternative to traditional EOLP fixation methods, offering robust stability with a low complication profile.

RF092: C2-C3 vertebral arch impingement is a key predictor of axial pain and kyphosis after posterior cervical laminoplasty: a retrospective cohort study

Shichang Zhao 1 , Haijun Tian 1

1 Department of Orthopaedics, Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China

Introduction: Persistent axial pain and progressive kyphosis are common, debilitating complications following posterior cervical laminoplasty. The etiology remains incompletely understood, and conventional theories focusing on posterior muscle injury do not fully account for their incidence. This study investigates the hypothesis that postoperative mechanical impingement between the C2 and C3 vertebral arches is a critical, yet overlooked, independent risk factor for these adverse outcomes. The purpose was to systematically determine the incidence of C2/C3 impingement after C3-C7 laminoplasty and to clarify its role as an independent predictor for severe postoperative axial pain and progressive cervical kyphosis. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 142 patients who underwent C3-C7 open-door laminoplasty for degenerative cervical myelopathy or ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, with a minimum 12-month follow-up. Based on terminal dynamic cervical radiographs or sagittal CT reconstructions, patients were stratified into two cohorts: an Impingement Group and a Non-impingement Group. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for axial pain. Radiographic assessment included the C2-C7 Cobb angle to evaluate cervical sagittal alignment. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors for poor outcomes, defined as severe axial pain (final VAS > 4) and significant kyphotic progression (C2-C7 Cobb angle loss > 5°). Results: The incidence of C2/C3 vertebral arch impingement was 30.3% (43 of 142 patients). At final follow-up, the Impingement Group demonstrated significantly greater axial pain (mean VAS: 5.1 vs. 2.3, p < 0.001) and more pronounced progression of cervical kyphosis (mean Cobb angle loss: 8.5° vs. 2.1°, p < 0.001) compared to the Non-impingement Group. There was no significant difference in neurological recovery rates between the groups (p = 0.435). After adjusting for potential confounders, multivariable analysis confirmed that C2/C3 impingement was the strongest independent predictor for both severe postoperative axial pain (Odds Ratio = 4.82, 95% CI: 2.15-10.80, p < 0.001) and significant kyphotic progression (Odds Ratio = 5.51, 95% CI: 2.52-12.06, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Radiographically confirmed C2/C3 vertebral arch impingement is a critical and independent risk factor for developing severe axial pain and progressive kyphosis following posterior cervical laminoplasty. This finding introduces a key mechanical etiology that complements traditional myogenic theories, suggesting that impingement acts as a trigger for a vicious cycle of local inflammation, muscle spasm, and subsequent biomechanical failure. Surgeons should consider this a preventable complication, and intraoperative strategies to ensure adequate clearance between C2 and C3, such as modifying the C3 laminar cut, may be crucial for improving long-term patient outcomes.

RF093: Clinical efficacy of laminoplasty for cervical ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament in patients with dynamic K-line positivity

Haijun Tian 1 , Shichang Zhao 1

1 Department of Orthopaedics, Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China

Introduction: Cervical ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) is a progressive disorder that can cause significant myelopathy. The anteroposterior diameter of the spinal canal is often assessed with the K-line, a virtual line drawn from the midpoints of the spinal canal at C2 and C7 on a neutral lateral radiograph. Patients whose OPLL mass exceeds the K-line are considered K-line negative and have been reported to respond poorly to posterior decompression. However, the K-line is position-dependent: some individuals whose OPLL is behind the K-line in the neutral position become K-line positive (i.e., the OPLL no longer crosses the line) in neck extension. This phenomenon - termed “dynamic K-line positivity” - may identify a subgroup for whom laminoplasty remains effective. The present prospective study was undertaken to evaluate the clinical and radiological outcomes of laminoplasty in patients with cervical OPLL who are dynamic K-line positive. Material and Methods: A total of 137 patients with OPLL were pre-operatively assessed using radiography or cone-beam CT (CBCT) to evaluate the K-line. Among them, 49 patients were identified as neutral K-line negative but extension K-line positive (EK-line(+)). All 49 patients in this cohort underwent laminoplasty. Pre- and post-operative clinical assessments included the Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, Neck Disability Index (NDI), and Visual Analog Scale (VAS). Radiological parameters, including spinal canal occupancy rate, cervical lordosis, and range of motion (ROM), were measured on lateral radiographs. Results: The mean spinal canal occupancy rate decreased significantly from 61.3 ± 15.3% pre-operatively to 25.3 ± 11.3% post-operatively. Cervical lordosis improved from 5.3° ± 7.2° to 10.4° ± 5.2°. However, the range of motion showed no significant change (35.6° ± 14.2° vs. 34.3° ± 11.2°). The mean JOA score increased significantly from 8.1 ± 2.7 to 13.3 ± 3.6 (p < 0.01). Significant improvements in NDI and VAS scores were also observed at the final follow-up. Conclusion: Laminoplasty is a favorable surgical option for patients with OPLL who are dynamic K-line positive, even if they are K-line negative in a neutral position. Cone-beam CT can serve as an effective tool for evaluating the dynamic K-line.

Jiawen Fong 1 , Hunyi Koh 1 , Crystel Tan 2 , Yan Ping Lim 3 , Yilun Huang 1

1 Sengkang General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore, 2 Allegro Therapy, Singapore, Singapore, 3 Physioplus, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Hirayama Disease (HD) is a self-limiting cervical myelopathy typically involving male adolescents of Asian descent. Prompt identification is crucial to prevent progression and permanent disability in the affected limbs. However, management in the paediatric group has been widely debated over the years. We aim to perform a review of the current literature to determine the outcomes of the different management strategies in the paediatric HD population (aged 18 years and less) and propose a recommendation for the suitability of the respective management types. Material and Methods: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systemic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines 2020 was used for the systemic review of the surgical treatment of HD in the paediatric population. Articles published from January 2004 - December 2024 were searched using various search-engines including PubMed, Cochrane Library and ScienceDirect. Inclusion criteria were: Insidious onset of HD in the paediatric age group (18 years and less) with HD, studies with individual patient-level data with description of clinical presentation and intervention by age 18 years, and post-operative outcomes during the last-follow-up. Exclusion criteria were: Articles that included any form of pooled data with mean age >18 years, abstract-only publications, no information on outcomes of treatment, and not published in English. Risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I V2 assessment tool. Data extraction and analysis were performed. Results: A total of 38 papers were included. 24 studies described conservative treatment, 8 studies described surgical intervention and 6 studies described failed conservative treatment which were subsequently converted to surgical treatment. Of the studies that described surgical intervention, 44 patients were included - 2 patients underwent staged anterior and posterior surgeries, and 6 patients underwent surgical intervention after failing conservative treatment. A total of 31 and 14 patients underwent surgical intervention via anterior and posterior approaches respectively. Of the studies that described conservative management, a total of 105 patients were included, with combinations of conservative treatment performed - 93 were subjected to cervical collars, 66 to pharmacological intervention, 17 to exercise therapy, 4 who did not receive any treatment and 1 with no mention of the type of treatment received. 37 patients had progression that ceased within 2 years of onset and 45 patients that ceased within 5 years of onset. 44 patients reported improvements in grip strength (8 conservative versus 36 surgical), 7 reported improvements of tremors (3 conservative versus 4 surgical), 7 reported reversal of atrophy (2 conservative versus 5 surgical), 1 reported improvement of paraesthesia (surgical), 3 reported improvement in subjective neck scorings (surgical), 7 reported improvement in imaging improvements or stability (3 conservative versus 4 surgical) and 2 reported objective improvements in grip strength (1 conservative versus 1 surgical). Conclusion: Paediatric HD patients who underwent surgical intervention tend to report better functional outcomes as compared to their counterparts treated conservatively. HD in the paediatric age group thus may benefit from early surgical intervention with good outcomes, while halting symptom progression from lack of compliance to conservative methods. Anterior approaches are more common and can be considered as an effective way for management of HD.

RF095: Value-based assessment of single-level lateral lumbar interbody fusions: a pilot study of the prone vs lateral decubitus position

Emaad Lala 1,2 , Aiyush Bansal 1 , Kenneth Nguyen 1 , Rafael Garcia de Oliveira 1 , Kento Yamanouchi 1,3 , Iyan Younus 1,4 , Venu Nemani 1 , Jean Christophe Leveque 1 , Philip Louie 1

1 Virginia Mason Medical Center, Seattle, United States, 2 University of Washington, Seattle, United States, 3 Keio University, Tokyo, Japan, 4 Vanderbilt University, Nashville, United States

Introduction: The prone prone lateral transpsoas (prone) approach has emerged as an alternative to the traditional lateral decubitus position for lumbar interbody fusion. While clinical outcomes comparing these approaches has been studied, a detailed analysis of their intraoperative costs and value-based outcomes remains lacking. The purpose of our study was to compare the primary supply cost drivers and value metrics (i.e. ICER and OVI) between the two approaches. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent primary single-level L4-5 LLIF with percutaneous posterior fixation by three spine surgeons at a single institution between January 2021 and June 2025. Total intraoperative supply costs were calculated as the product of unit cost and quantity used. Staff costs were derived using TDABC methodology with state hourly wage rates. Clinical outcomes included the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and quality-adjusted life years (QALY). The Operative Value Index (OVI) was calculated as %ODI or QALY improvement per $1,000. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) were also calculated. All intraoperative items were grouped into categories (e.g. implants, navigation, etc). Within each category, items were ranked by Impact Score (IS) - a metric incorporating item cost, quantity used, and frequency of use. Categories with the highest mean IS, based on their top five items, were identified as the primary cost drivers. Results: A total of 37 patients met inclusion criteria (20 lateral, 17 prone). Total intraoperative supply costs (30.32 RCU vs 26.71 RCU, p = 0.30) and staff costs (4.81 RCU vs 4.68 RCU, p = 0.76) were higher in the prone group compared to lateral group. The lateral group achieved significantly greater QALY gains at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months than the prone group. Similarly, QALY-based OVI was significantly higher in lateral group compared to the prone group at all time points. ICERs for lateral vs. prone were -83.6 RCUs at 6 weeks, -155.7 RCUs at 3 months, and -116.8 RCUs at 6 months. In lateral LLIF, cost drivers in descending order of IS were implant, instrument, biologic, neuromonitoring, and camera; in prone, they were implant, camera, neuromonitoring, instrument, and lighting. Conclusions: Compared to prone, the lateral approach demonstrated improved value-based outcomes and cost-effectiveness for single-level L4-5 LLIF. Our novel impact score methodology successfully identified previously overlooked cost drivers beyond implants, offering actionable targets for cost reduction and optimization.

RF096: Significant risk of surgical site infection with clindamycin prophylaxis in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis surgery: a retrospective cohort analysis of 344 patients

Giovanni Viroli 1 , Agnese Graziosi 2 , Matteo Traversari 1 , Marco Manzetti 1 , Alberto Ruffilli 1 , Cesare Faldini 1

1 Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy, 2 Università degli Studi di Milano, Milano, Italy

Introduction: Surgical site infection (SSI) remains one of the most relevant complications after posterior spinal fusion for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Antibiotic prophylaxis protocols vary across centers, particularly in the choice between cefazolin and clindamycin, with limited comparative evidence. Materials and Methods: We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study including all consecutive patients undergoing posterior spinal fusion for AIS between 2016 and 2024. Demographics, prophylactic antibiotic regimen (cefazolin vs clindamycin), number of postoperative doses, and infectious outcomes were recorded. Patients not allergic to beta-lactams received cefazolin (2 g at induction, repeated every 2 hours during surgery). Postoperatively, they were subdivided into three groups: standard prophylaxis (1 g every 4 hours for approximately 24 hours, i.e., 5-8 doses), fast prophylaxis (no postoperative doses), and long prophylaxis (1 g every 4 hours until drain removal, i.e., > 8 doses). Patients allergic to beta-lactams received clindamycin (600 mg at induction, repeated every 4 hours during surgery, with postoperative doses of 600 mg every 6 hours for 24 hours). Surgical site infections were defined according to CDC criteria. Microbiological cultures and resistance profiles were analyzed when available. Statistical analysis included incidence rates, odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and Fisher’s exact test. P

Results: A total of 344 patients were included (mean age 14.7 years, 78% female). Overall, 24 patients (7.0%) developed SSI. Among those receiving cefazolin (n = 331), 20 infections occurred (6.0%). Among patients receiving clindamycin (n = 13), 4 infections were observed (30.8%), corresponding to a significantly increased risk compared with cefazolin (OR 7.2, 95% CI 2.15 - 24.07, p = 0.0086). Within cefazolin regimens, infection rates were 9.1% (0 postoperative doses), 5.8% (5-8 doses), and 1.9% (> 8 doses), without significant differences between subgroups. Microbiological data were available in 14 cases: Staphylococcus spp. accounted for 57%, and Cutibacterium spp. for 29%. Overall, 46% of isolates showed resistance to prophylaxis, and 12.5% were resistant to clindamycin. Conclusion: Cefazolin-based prophylaxis was associated with a significantly lower rate of surgical site infection compared with clindamycin in AIS posterior spinal fusion. Extended cefazolin prophylaxis (> 8 doses) showed numerically lower infection rates, although it did not significantly differ from standard regimens, due to the low number of observations. Importantly, these results highlight the need for pathogen-oriented prophylaxis and careful antibiotic stewardship in AIS surgery. In our series, Cutibacterium spp. represented a relevant proportion of cases and this germ is characterized by a growing rate of resistance to clindamycin, making this drug unsuitable in this patient population.

Reaching MCID was associated with higher rates of patient satisfaction. These findings have important implications for patient counseling and quality of life, particularly for those presenting with preoperative functional and self-care deficits.

RF099: Prevention of surgical site infections in spine surgery: a literature review and creation of an institutional protocol

Jose Dangond 1 , Diana Lopez 2 , Maria Teresa Alvarado 2 , Juan Davidson 2 , Fernando Alvarado Gómez 3

1 Hospital Serena del Mar, Clinica Campbell, Cartagena, Colombia, 2 Hospital Serena del Mar, Cartagena, Colombia, 3 Fundacion Santa Fe de Bogota, Hospital Serena del Mar, Bogota, Colombia

Introduction: This review examines surgical site infections (SSI) in spinal surgery, highlighting their clinical and economic impact. SSI incidence varies from 2% to 20%, with risk factors like diabetes, obesity, and prolonged surgery. Staphylococcus aureus is a common pathogen. Preventive strategies, including topical Vancomycin and chlorhexidine baths, show effectiveness. An institutional protocol was proposed, leading to an SSI rate below 2% in a study of 457 patients from May 2021 to May 2025. The analysis included diverse spinal procedures, demonstrating the protocol's success. Standardized, evidence-based approaches are crucial for reducing infection rates and improving outcomes in spinal surgery. Material and Methods: This study of 457 patients from May 2021 to May 2025 analyzed SSI rates in diverse spinal surgeries, excluding neurolysis and injections. The protocol, which included antibiotic management and infection prevention measures, resulted in infection rates below 2%. The approach focused on standardized, evidence-based protocols tailored to spinal procedures. The findings highlight that implementing such strategies effectively reduces SSIs, improves patient outcomes, and curtails healthcare costs across various spinal surgeries. Results: Surgical site infection (SSI) rates were analyzed in various spinal procedures, excluding neurolysis and injections. The procedures included 8 endoscopic surgeries without instrumentation, 25 discectomies or tubular decompressions, 128 cases of lumbar degeneration with instrumentation, 65 cases of cervical degeneration with instrumentation, 6 deformity corrections, 75 tumor resections, and 28 trauma cases. A standardized, evidence-based protocol for infection prevention was implemented, with an emphasis on antibiotic management and surgical best practices. The results demonstrated an SSI rate of less than 2% across all procedures, significantly lower than global averages in spinal surgery. This indicates that the adoption of structured, protocol-based strategies effectively reduces postoperative infections, resulting in improved patient outcomes, lower healthcare costs, and increased safety. The findings support the importance of personalized, evidence-based approaches in spine surgery to minimize infection risks and optimize clinical outcomes. Conclusion: Our institutional protocol has demonstrated a low rate of surgical site infections during its implementation, as these rates are lower than those reported in the current literature. We believe these outcomes are due to the methodical implementation of evidence-based recommendations, which are also cost-effective measures that, when implemented in a systematic, standardized, and protocol-based manner, reduce the risk of this complication. Our study has the limitation of being a retrospective cohort; however, it serves as a starting point for conducting prospective studies with outpatients in our program to obtain more reliable data and conduct follow-up that allows for a detailed evaluation of the outcomes of patients operated on under our protocol. We also consider it relevant to conduct prospective studies in other centers that also have standardized protocols for preventing surgical site infections in spine surgery to generate feedback and gather new evidence on other measures not initially considered by our group.

RF100: Open versus minimally invasive surgical techniques for the treatment of spondylodiscitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Jose Otavio Donadeli Tome 1 , Rafael de Souza 1 , Wilker Oliveira 1 , Bruno Motter 1 , Guilherme Foizer 1 , Andre Cesar 1 , Luciano Rodrigues 2

1 ABC Medical School, Santo André, Brazil, 2 Paulista School of Medicine, Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP), São Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Although the initial treatment of spondylodiscitis is predominantly conservative, there are specific clinical scenarios in which surgical intervention is indicated. Currently, the most commonly employed surgical approach involves open techniques; however, with the advent of minimally invasive surgery (MIS), the applicability of these less invasive methods in such cases has become a subject of growing interest and debate. While some studies have already conducted direct comparisons between open and minimally invasive techniques, there is still ongoing controversy regarding the superiority of one approach over the other. Material and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials was performed to identify studies comparing minimally invasive (MIS) and open surgical techniques for the treatment of spondylodiscitis. The primary outcome was postoperative pain score. Secondary outcomes included wound revision rates, intraoperative blood loss, length of hospital stay, operative time, and postoperative C-reactive protein (CRP) and white blood cell (WBC) levels. Statistical analysis was conducted using Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.1.7, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Results: Eleven observational studies were included in this meta-analysis, comprising a total of 933 patients, of whom 432 (46%) underwent minimally invasive procedures for the treatment of spondylodiscitis. The analysis demonstrated the superiority of minimally invasive techniques in terms of postoperative pain scores (Standardized Mean Difference [SMD]: -1.03; 95% CI: -1.73 to -0.33; p = 0.004), as well as lower wound revision rates (Odds Ratio [OR]: 0.46; 95% CI: 0.23 to 0.89; p = 0.020). MIS also showed favorable intraoperative parameters compared to open surgery, including reduced blood loss (Mean Difference [MD]: -321.27 mL; 95% CI: -407.35 to -247.79; p < 0.0001) and shorter operative time (MD: -32.47 minutes; 95% CI: -47.12 to -17.83; p<0.0001). Regarding postoperative outcomes, minimally invasive techniques were associated with a shorter hospital stay (MD: -3.96 days; 95% CI: -5.30 to -2.62; p < 0.0001), lower postoperative C-reactive protein levels (MD: -0.40; 95% CI: -1.73 to 0.93; p=0.56), and reduced white blood cell counts (MD: -0.75; 95% CI: -0.98 to -0.52; p < 0.0001). Conclusion: Although open surgical techniques for the treatment of spondylodiscitis are widely utilized, our findings suggest that minimally invasive approaches may offer significant advantages compared to conventional methods. Therefore, minimally invasive surgery should be considered a valuable and effective option in the management of this condition.

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 2 Center of Research Excellence in Immunoregulation, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 3 Department of Immunology, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 4 Department of Orthopaedic surgery, Hatyai Hospital, Songkhla, Thailand, 5 Department of Radiology, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 6 Department of Microbiology, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 7 Department of Pathology, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 8 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery,Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 9 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Aranyaprathet Hospital, Sakaeo, Thailand

Introduction: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (TS) is a serious form of tuberculosis (TB) that requires tissue biopsy for definitive diagnosis. However, this can delay appropriate treatment, potentially resulting in long-term disability. An immunodiagnostic approach, such as interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), offers promising alternatives for TS diagnosis. In addition, recent advancements suggest a potential role of mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells as biomarkers for TB infection. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic performance of IGRA using the QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test (QFT-GIT) and MAIT cell analysis for diagnosing TS. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was performed to determine cutoff value and discriminative ability for TS diagnosis

Results: 65 patients suspected TS were prospectively enrolled, of whom 24 (37%) were categorized as confirmed TS. QFT-GIT demonstrated a sensitivity of 82.61% and specificity of 77.78%. Combining QFT-GIT and the proportion of MAIT cells in CD8+ T cells subset improved specificity to 96.9%. Conclusion: QFT-GIT and MAIT cells analysis are promising, non-invasive diagnostic tools with moderate sensitivity and specificity for differentiating TS in spondylodiscitis patients, particularly when tissue diagnosis is not feasible, to avoid delayed diagnosis and initiation of treatment.

RF104: Management strategies in pediatric spine tuberculosis - A retrospective longterm analysis of 108 children of Koch's spine

Sudhir Srivastava 1

1 K.J.Somaiya Medical College and Research Centre, Somaiya Ayurvihar, Sion ( E ), Mumbai, India

Introduction: Incidence of Tuberculosis of spine is significantly high in developing countries. It leads to significant morbidity and disability to the child and has deleterious effect on compromised socioeconomic status of the family. The affected pediatric spine behaves differently due to its cartilaginous nature, poor bone stock, implant issues and risk of developing severe deformity and deficit. The authors present their management strategies and principles of treatment in different regions of pediatric Koch’s spine. Material and Methods: In a span of 20 years we treated 108 children (3 yrs to 13 years of age.) suffering from spinal Tuberculosis. There were 48 males and 60 females.75 patients had Dorsal spine Koch, 20 cervical and 13 lumbo-sacral spine koch.80 patients had neurological deficit. All patients underwent biopsy and culture-sensitivity and were put on sensitive anti-tubercular drugs. There were 23 patients of multi-resistance Koch. 28 Patients were treated conservatively while 80 patients were operated. Indication of surgical intervention were significant neurological deficit, eccentric collapse with full body loss irrespective of deficit, progressive deformity and presence of other signs of spine at risk. There were 8 patients who were neurologically intact but showed the spine at risk signs and were operated. There were 8 patients who had minor deficit with mild concentric collapse of the column and were treated conservatively with sensitive anti-tubercular drugs and close observation. We used low profile, cost-effective, custom made implants of different generations (sublaminar wire, Hartshill rectangle, pedicular screw-rod system) as per the need. The principle of biomechanics and biology were followed. In dorsal spine we used versatile approach where both anterior decompression, reconstruction and posterior segmental fixation could be done in single position through a single curvilinear incision. There were 25 patients with severe deformity (> 50 degree). Deformity could be corrected safely with steps of sequential correction and guarded column shortening. Circumferential fusion of apex was done in all operative cases. Following the principles of biomechanics implant was put on the posterior (tensile) surface of spine and anterior reconstruction was done with strut graft (Rib, fibula, iliac crest graft). Results: All patients improved neurologically except 2 who had residual significant spasticity requiring Baclofen and later could walk with walking aid. Deformity could be corrected fully. There was no neurological deterioration. There were 4 cases of implant failure which was revised and refused. Five patients had superficial wound infection which healed with wound care and dressing. Conservatively treated patients maintained their neurology and column alignment

Conclusion: This retrospective study of 108 children of Koch’s spine highlights the importance of quality of pediatric spinal column, sensitive antitubercular drugs and selective surgery in different regions of affected spinal column with adherence to the principle of biomechanics and biology. Use of custom made, cost-effective, low profile implant in pediatric Koch spine serves its purpose of long term stability with long lasting positive outcome.

RF105: A comparative outcomes study of single-level anterior cervical corpectomy: anterior-only vs combined posterior fusion

Albert Brotgandel 1 , Eric Cohen 1 , Chloe Chose 1 , Thomas Karadimas 1 , Diego Soto Rubio 2 , Bryan Clampitt 1 , Ahmad Alkadri 1 , Dana Saleh 2 , Vito Evola BS 3 , Adrian Urdaneta 2 , Srujan Kopparapu 2 , Cesar Carballo 2 , Mohsen Rostami 2 , Puya Alikhani 2

1 USF Health Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States, 2 Department of Neurosurgery, Brain and Spine, University of South Florida, Morsani College of Medicine, Tampa, United States, 3 Nova Southeastern University Dr. Kiran C. Patel College Of Osteopathic Medicine, Tampa, United States

Introduction: Anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion (ACCF) may be supplemented with posterior fusion when increased stability is warranted. While often indicated for multilevel corpectomies, the role of posterior fusion is less well defined for single-level corpectomies. This study aims to compare postoperative outcomes between single-level ACCF performed with anterior-only fixation versus circumferential fusion. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of adult patients who underwent single-level ACCF between May 2020 and May 2025 at a tertiary academic center. A total of 60 patients met inclusion criteria. Demographic variables, operative details, and postoperative complications were collected. Statistical analysis used two-sided Fisher’s exact tests (or chi-square when cell counts permitted) to compare categorical outcomes and to assess associations between corpectomy level and complications, while continuous variables were compared using two-sided Welch’s t-tests (or Mann-Whitney U when normality was not met), with significance set at α = 0.05 (p ≤ 0.05). Results: Among the 60 patients, 45 underwent anterior-only (AO) fixation and 15 received additional posterior instrumentation (AP). Circumferential fusion was associated with significantly longer operative times compared with AO (371 ± 160 vs 220 ± 53 minutes, p = 0.001). Postoperative complications were overall similar between groups using two-sided Fisher’s exact tests: dysphagia (p = 0.376); dysarthria showed a non-significant trend favoring AO (0 vs 2; p = 0.059); C5 palsy/deltoid weakness (2 vs 1; p = 1.000); hardware failure (2 vs 0; p = 1.000); radiographic adjacent segment disease (3 vs 0; p = 0.566); and symptomatic adjacent segment disease (1 vs 0; p = 1.000). The level of corpectomy did not correlate with complication rates. We observed five durotomies/CSF leaks and two hardware failures, all within the AO group, and these differences were not statistically significant (durotomy p = 0.318; hardware failure p = 1.000). Patients with durotomy were significantly older than those without (p = 0.046). No vertebral artery injuries or reoperations occurred in either cohort during follow-up. Conclusion: The benefit of adding posterior fixation in single-level ACCF remains uncertain. While circumferential fusion may provide enhanced construct stability, it requires significantly longer operative times. Most patients undergoing single-level ACCF may not require posterior supplementation; however, its use may still be considered in select high-risk populations, such as those with osteoporosis, smoking history, or polytrauma. Larger, multicenter studies with longer follow-up are warranted to better define the role of posterior fixation in optimizing outcomes.

RF106: Selection of treatment strategies in brucella spondylitis: a retrospective clinical study

Ismail Kaya 1 , Aybike Ceren Aksoy 2 , Halil Ibrahim Koçhan 2 , Murat Atar 3

1 Uşak Training and Research Hospital, Uşak, Turkey, 2 Seyrantepe Hamidiye Etfal Training and Research Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey, 3 Antalya Neurosurgery Private Clinic, Antalya, Turkey

Introduction: Brucella spondylodiscitis is a rare but challenging spinal infection, and its optimal treatment strategy remains controversial. Although medical therapy is the cornerstone of treatment, surgical intervention is often required in selected cases. This study aimed to evaluate the role of surgery in brucella spondylodiscitis and compare the outcomes of different surgical techniques. Materials and Methods: Between February 2020 and June 2025, 195 patients diagnosed with brucella spondylitis were retrospectively reviewed and classified into three groups:

- Group A (n = 75): medical treatment only

- Group B (n = 59): posterior fixation and decompression

- Group C (n = 61): single-stage posterior debridement with interbody fusion followed by posterior fixation

Clinical and radiological outcomes-including Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR), C-Reactive Protein (CRP), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), lumbar lordosis angle, fusion time, Serum Agglutination Test (SAT) negativity, and complication rates-were assessed preoperatively, at 3 months postoperatively, and at final follow-up. Results: Both surgical groups achieved significantly better outcomes than the medical treatment group across most parameters (p < 0.05). Group C demonstrated significantly greater improvement in ESR, CRP, ODI, lumbar lordosis angle, and radiological findings compared with Groups A and B (p < 0.05). VAS scores improved significantly in both surgical groups relative to the medical group, with no significant difference between surgical techniques (p > 0.05). Seven patients required postoperative wound drainage. At final follow-up, 160 patients (82%) had complete clinical and radiological recovery. Conclusion: Surgical treatment of brucella spondylitis leads to faster recovery and superior radiological outcomes compared with medical therapy alone. Among the surgical strategies, single-stage posterior debridement with interbody fusion and pedicle fixation appears to be the most effective approach.

RF107: Analysis of factors associated with prolonged infection in pyogenic spondylitis using the AO classification

Takuya Iimura 1 , Masahiko Takahata 1 , Katsuhisa Yamada 2 , Satoshi Inami 1 , Hiroshi Moridaira 3 , Daisaku Takeuchi 1 , Haruki Ueda 1 , Hidekazu Arai 1 , Tomoya Kanto 1 , Satoshi Takada 1 , Kazuo Doi 1 , Hiroshi Taneichi 1

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Dokkyo Medical University, Mibu, Japan, 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Faculty of Medicine and Graduate School of Medicine, Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan, 3 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Nikko Medical Center, Dokkyo Medical University, Nikko, Japan

Introduction: In hematogenous pyogenic spondylitis, a six-week course of antibiotic therapy is generally recommended, yet infection control often fails, resulting in prolonged disease. Factors contributing to prolonged infection may include low detection rates of causative organisms, poor antibiotic penetration into bone and disc tissues, immunodeficiency due to comorbidities, extensive bone destruction, and epidural abscess formation. This study aimed to identify factors associated with prolonged infection using the AO classification of spondylitis. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of 114 patients with pyogenic spondylitis treated at two university hospitals, with a minimum follow-up of 18 weeks after treatment initiation. The mean age was 64 ± 15 years (range, 12-87 years), with 47 females and 67 males. AO classification parameters included: location (A: lumbar, B: thoracic, C: cervical), morphology of infection (0: extraspinal, 1: spondylitis/discitis without canal involvement, 2: epidural abscess without compression, 3: epidural abscess with compression, +: bone destruction), neurology (N0: normal to N4: complete paralysis), and modifiers (M1: severe pain with inability to mobilize, M2: medical comorbidities, M3: suspicion of atypical infection). For M2, comorbidity was further assessed by Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) and nutritional status by Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI). Treatment response was evaluated using total lymphocyte count (TLC) at one month. Outcomes were defined as sustained microbiological cure (CRP > 0.3 mg/dL) and failure of cure (subsequent surgery, continued parenteral antibiotics beyond 12 weeks, new neurological symptoms, or new positive cultures) at week 18. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed, with explanatory variables including CCI, TLC at one month, and affected region. Results: Sustained microbiological cure was observed in 27 patients (24%), and failure of cure in 32 patients (28%). The affected locations were lumbar (A) in 58, thoracic (B) in 23, and cervical (C) in 33. The morphology was type 0 in 2 patients, 1 in 24, 2 in 20, and 3 in 68 (58 with bone destruction). Neurology was N0 in 38, N1 in 18, N2 in 20, N3 in 36, and N4 in 2. Modifiers included M1 in 51, M2 in 7, and M3 in 2 patients. Univariate analyses showed that sustained microbiological cure was significantly associated with low PNI, high CCI, the presence of M1, and low TLC at one month. Failure of cure was associated with high CCI, non-thoracic lesions, and low TLC at one month. In the multivariate analysis, independent predictor of sustained microbiological cure at 18 weeks was low TLC at one month (OR 0.9, p = 0.0074), while independent predictors of failure of cure at 18 weeks were higher CCI (OR 1.5, p = 0.0004) and location (p = 0.002). Conclusion: Prolonged infection in pyogenic spondylitis was associated with poor nutritional status, comorbidities, lesion location (cervical or lumbar), and severe pain. In particular, sustained microbiological cure was associated with low TLC at one month after treatment, indicating poor treatment response or immunodeficiency. Early assessment of these factors may facilitate the development of more appropriate treatment strategies.

RF108: Evaluation of the cervical spine microbiome using culture and metagenomic sequencing

Philip Paschal 1 , Celeste Abjornson 1 , Fedan Avrumova 1 , Gregory Paschal 1 , Alexandra Satanovsky 1 , Darren R. Lebl 1 , Frank Cammisa 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Occult bacterial colonization of spinal implants may contribute to postoperative complications such as persistent pain and aseptic loosening. Routine culture techniques have limited sensitivity, often capturing only a fraction of the microbial diversity present within biofilms and may be vulnerable to contamination during growth. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) has the potential for the characterization of bacterial communities from surgical samples without culturing. Hence, minimizing error and better reflecting in vivo biodiversity. The objective of this study was to compare standard microbiology with mNGS in patients undergoing primary anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) with instrumentation. Material and Methods: This is a prospective study that enrolled 76 patients undergoing one- to three-level primary ACDFs. Intraoperative swabs were systematically collected from air control, skin, subcutaneous fat, fascia, muscle, cortical bone, disc space (pre- and post-removal), endplate, and surgical suction. Each specimen was processed in two pathways: (A) standard aerobic and anaerobic culture with incubation up to 14 days, and (B) mNGS. With mNGS, DNA was extracted with the Promega Maxwell RSC 48 system, libraries were prepared with Illumina Nextera XT, and pooled samples were sequenced on a NovaSeq X (paired-end 150bp). Reads were processed with KneadData to remove host DNA and low-quality sequences, taxonomic profiling was performed with MetaPhlAn4, and functional analysis with HUMAnN3. Patient outcomes included NDI, VAS neck pain and SF-12, as well as post-operative radiographs. Results: Within the 76 patients, cultures were identified bacterial growth was found in 28% of swabs, while mNGS detected microbial DNA in 62%. This represents more than a twofold increase in sensitivity. These two techniques agreed only moderately at the species level (κ = 0.41), while mNGS revealed a broader microbial spectrum. This includes low-burden Cutibacterium, Staphylococcus, and Anaerobic Taxa were not captured by culture. More importantly, contamination was minimized with mNGS since no in vitro growth was required, thus allowing an immediate biodiversity profile at the time of surgery. Patients with higher microbial diversity on mNGS trended towards worse 12-month NDI scores, with a mean of 24.3 vs 17.9. There was no statistical significance presented in this series. Conclusion: This study demonstrated that mNGS may have provided a far more comprehensive assessment of the implant-associated microbiome than standard culture. mNGS identified organisms not captured by culture and allowed immediate profiling without incubation. These findings may show the potential role of occult bacterial communities in cervical fusion outcomes and support mNGS as a potential diagnostic tool for evaluating implant-related microbiota.

RF109: Can we stay gold? Return-to-play after spinal surgery in athletes

Lucas Zubillaga 1 , Mitchell Hansen 2

1 John Hunter Hospital, Newcastle, Australia, 2 John Hunter Hospital, King Street Private Hospital, Newcastle University, Newcastle, Australia

Introduction: Return to sport (RTP) after spinal surgery requires alignment of surgical objectives, staged rehabilitation, and sport-specific biomechanical demands. In Australia - where collision and high axial-load sports are prevalent - these considerations are amplified. Although cervical disc arthroplasty (ACDA) is established as a safe alternative to ACDF, its role in contact athletes remains less clearly defined. We synthesized current evidence and compared it with our last 5-year outcomes, with a special focus on ACDA in athletes. Material and Methods: Retrospective review of consecutive competitive athletes or highly active individuals operated by a single surgeon between January 2019 and December 2024. Procedures included microdiscectomy, lumbar disc replacement, lumbar fusion, cervical disc replacement (ACDA), and cervical fusion (ACDF). RTP was defined as return to pre-injury level (training and competition). Readiness criteria combined symptom resolution, neurological recovery, objective strength/conditioning benchmarks, radiographic union (for fusion), implant stability (for arthroplasty), and sport type. Primary outcomes: RTP rate and time-to-RTP; secondary outcomes: complications/reoperations and predictors of delayed RTP. Results: Twenty-three patients were included; overall RTP was 90% (21/23) within time frames consistent with or faster than contemporary guideline benchmarks. Median time-to-RTP was shorter than guideline medians for microdiscectomy and ACDA, and shorter for ACDF in our pathway; circumferential fusion for spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis was equivalent to guidelines. No sport-ending complications occurred; reoperations were uncommon. Independent predictors of delayed RTP included residual weakness/proprioceptive deficit, residual pain, and participation in high axial-load or collision sports. Conclusion: Across 5 years, most athletes achieved RTP within procedure-appropriate windows with low sport-limiting complication rates. Motion-preserving procedures favored earlier RTP - particularly ACDA - while fusion enabled durable returns with the trade-off of longer recovery. In athletes, even modest acceleration of RTP can be career-defining; standardized, multidisciplinary criteria (neurological recovery, objective performance testing, and radiographic milestones for fusion) support safe, sustainable return and informed decision-making.

RF110: In adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, to what extent do bending x-rays modify the extent of the fusion?

Ian Harding 1 , Stephen Morris 1 , Priyan Landham 1 , Neil Upadhyay 1 , Daniel Oñate Martínez-Olascoaga 2

1 Southmead Hospital and Bristol Royal Hospital for Children, Bristol, United Kingdom, 2 Biziondo, Unidad de Columna, Bilbao, Spain

Introduction: Idiopathic Scoliosis is the most common cause of spinal deformity in pediatric patients, being AIS the most common type between all the age subgroups. The radiographic study for AIS surgical planning typically includes anteroposterior, lateral and bending x-rays. These bending x-rays provide information about the flexibility of the curves, theoretically helping to determine the extent of the spinal arthrodesis. We sought to confirm if the fusion level selection of every AIS curve pattern is really modified by this bending test. Material and Methods: Four fellowship-trained paediatric spine deformity surgeons reviewed the standing x-rays of 50 patients with different patterns of AIS, according to the Lenke classification. All the surgeons reviewed the four surveys, each of them comprised by the x-rays of the same 50 AIS patients: Surveys number 1 and number 3 showed PA and lateral x-rays only, while surveys number 2 and number 4 included bending x-rays too. In each round the surgeons had to decide the extent of the spinal fusion for each case. Two weeks separated each survey and the order of the cases was randomized. With this strategy intraobserver and interobserver variability, absolute agreement and the number of curves fused were analysed

Results: Lower Instrumented Vertebra (LIV) agreement was over 80% for Lenke types 1A, 1C, 4C, 5C and 6C, and over 70% in types 2A, 2B and 3C. Upper Instrumented Vertebra (UIV) agreement was over 80% for Lenke types 1C and 4C, and over 70% in types 2A, 2B and 5C. In 3.75% of the cases the number of curves to be fused changed after assessing the bending x-rays, being 1.50% for UIV and 2.25% for LIV. The rest of the changes accounted for 25.25% of the cases and were only in one or two vertebrae above or below. Conclusion: This study documented that the absolute agreement for fusion level selection between PA and bending x-rays can be strong in certain patterns of AIS curves. This may suggest that in these specific curve types LIV and/or UIV selection may not vary after assessing bending x-rays. LIV or UIV changed in one or two vertebrae above or below in approximately a quarter of the patients, with more variability for UIV than for LIV. In 3,75% of the patients there was a change in the number of curves to be included in the fusion.

RF111: Incidence and risk factors of revision surgery with acute proximal junctional failure after anterior column realignment for adult spinal deformity

Jin-Sung Park 1 , Se-Jun Park 1 , Dong-ho Kang 1 , Jae-Young Hong 2

1 Samsung Medical Center, Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea, 2 Korea University Ansan Hospital, Ansan, South Korea

Introduction: The association between anterior column realignment (ACR) technique and acute proximal junctional failure (APJF) in adult spinal deformity (ASD) has not been thoroughly evaluated, and risk factors for revision surgery following APJF remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to identify incidence and risk factors of revision surgery with APJF following ACR for ASD. Material and Methods: We included patients with severe degenerative sagittal imbalance who underwent deformity correction using ACR at one or more levels between 2020 and 2023. APJF was defined as proximal junctional failure occurring within 6 months postoperatively. Cases requiring revision surgery were classified as bony or soft tissue failures. Patient characteristics, surgical, and radiographic factors were compared to identify risk factors for revision surgery. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to determine independent risk factors. Results: The study included 114 patients (mean age 70.7 ± 5.3 years) with an average fusion length of 7.2 ± 1.9 levels. APJF occurred in 36 patients (31.6%), with 24 cases of bony failure and 12 of soft tissue failure. Revision surgery was performed in 14 patients (38.9% of APJF cases, 12.3% of the cohort) at an average of 156.6 ± 76.2 days postoperatively. Of these, 12 cases were due to bony failure and 2 to soft tissue failure. Univariate analysis identified cranial screw angle at the upper-instrumented vertebra (UIV), preoperative thoracic kyphosis (TK), postoperative TK, and proximal junctional angle (PJA) as significant risk factors. Multivariate analysis revealed independent risk factors for revision surgery: cranial screw angle at UIV (HR 21.578, p < 0.001), preoperative TK (HR 1.049, p = 0.034), and postoperative PJA (HR 1.125, p = 0.046). Conclusion: The incidence of revision surgery due to APJF following ACR for ASD was 12.3%. Key risk factors included cranial UIV screw angle, greater preoperative TK, and increased postoperative PJA.

RF112: Muscle matters: Goutallier grade as a predictor of postoperative risk in complex spine surgery at a single center

Arnav Gambhir 1 , Clifford Pierre 2 , Luke Jouppi 1 , Gautam Rao 2 , Julius Gerstmeyer 2 , Cameron Hogsett 2 , Mark Kraemer 2 , Colin Gold 2 , Nicholas Minissale 2 , Daniel Norvell 3 , Tara Heffernan 1 , Amir Abdul-Jabbar 2 , Rod Oskouian 2 , Jens Chapman 2

1 Seattle Science Foundation, Seattle, United States, 2 Swedish Neuroscience Institute, Seattle, United States, 3 Spectrum Research Incorporated, Seattle, United States

Introduction: Complex spine surgery for adult spinal deformity involving multilevel spine fusion carries a high risk of complications due to tissue disruption and biomechanical stress. Paraspinal muscle quality, measured by systems such as the Goutallier classification, may predict poor outcomes. The purpose of this study aimed to evaluate the association between Goutallier grading and reoperation rates, as well as related risk factors such as sagittal alignment, bone mineral density (BMD), and sarcopenia. Methods: A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted on patients who underwent multilevel thoracolumbar fusion for degenerative disease from 2015 to 2022. Imaging was reviewed for Goutallier grade, sagittal vertical axis (SVA), BMD, and sarcopenia. Clinical factors and reoperation rates were analyzed. Results: Of 246 screened patients, 45 met inclusion criteria. The mean follow-up was 1.9 years (range 1.8-2.7 years). Reoperations occurred in 25 patients (55%). These patients had significantly higher Goutallier grades (3.2 vs. 2.6, p < 0.04), greater rates of sarcopenia (75% vs. 15%, p < 0.001), and low BMD (78% vs. 14%, p < 0.001). They also showed increased postoperative SVA (7.5 vs. 3.5 cm, p < 0.001), higher BMI (32.7 vs. 27.4 kg/m2, p < 0.01), and higher rates of diabetes and smoking. Age and sex were not significantly different. Conclusion: Higher Goutallier grades, sarcopenia, poor alignment, and low BMD were linked to increased reoperation rates in multilevel spine fusion surgeries. Preoperative assessment of muscle quality may help identify patients who could benefit from targeted prehabilitation and optimization strategies to improve postoperative outcomes. References

RF113: Hybrid Junctional Rod (HJR™): a novel technique for preventing proximal junctional kyphosis in spinal deformity surgery - Clinical and biomechanical outcomes from a 15-patient series

Ercan Bal 1

1 Ankara City Hospital Neurosurgery Clinic, Ankara, Turkey

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) is a frequent complication after spinal deformity surgery, with incidences reported up to 35%. Current preventive strategies, including tethering, hooks, spacers, and cement augmentation, provide limited efficacy. We developed the Hybrid Junctional Rod (HJR™) system, designed to achieve controlled stiffness transition, graded load sharing, and posterior soft-tissue preservation to reduce PJK risk. Methods: A prospective clinical study was conducted on 15 patients (mean age: 22 years, range: 13-48; 7 males, 8 females) who underwent posterior long-segment instrumentation using the HJR™ system. Etiologies included Scheuermann kyphosis (n = 9), congenital kyphosis (n = 2), neuromuscular kyphosis (n = 1), degenerative kyphosis (n = 1), and syndromic kyphosis (n = 1). Preoperative radiographic parameters: thoracic kyphosis (TK) 79.1°, thoracolumbar kyphosis (TL) 28.1°, lumbar lordosis (LL) 68.1°, pelvic incidence (PI) 38°, and GAP score 5. The HJR™ system consists of three components: (1) distal titanium rod, (2) transitional rod segment with single screw connection, and (3) proximal polyethylene-terephthalate bands for graded tensioning and gradual load sharing. Surgical technique included pedicle screws at T6 and below, transitional screw at T5, monoaxial screws at T2-T4, and tether applied at T2-T4 with progressively reduced tension from T4 to T2. The posterior ligamentous complex was preserved. Biomechanical testing under static and cyclic loading up to 1100 N demonstrated improved durability and controlled load distribution. Outcome measures included kyphosis correction, PJK/PJF incidence, implant complications, and patient-reported outcomes (SRS-22, VAS). Mean follow-up: 1 year. Results: Mean kyphosis correction was 55%. No PJK or PJF was observed. No implant failures occurred, including rod breakage, band rupture, or screw pull-out. Infection rate was 0%. Patient-reported outcomes improved significantly: SRS-22 total scores increased by +1.2 points, and VAS pain scores decreased by -3.5 points. Radiographic follow-up showed stable sagittal alignment without progressive proximal junctional angulation at 1-year follow-up. Biomechanical testing confirmed superior load-sharing properties of HJR™ compared to conventional titanium rods. Conclusion: The Hybrid Junctional Rod (HJR™) provides a novel, implant-based strategy for PJK prevention by enabling controlled stiffness transition, graded load sharing, and posterior soft-tissue preservation. Early clinical and biomechanical data from this 15-patient series demonstrate that HJR™ is safe, effective, and cost-neutral without increasing surgical complexity. Multi-center studies with long-term follow-up are warranted to validate these promising results. Keywords: Spinal deformity, kyphosis, proximal junctional kyphosis, hybrid junctional rod, biomechanics, load sharing, posterior ligamentous preservation.

RF114: Role of paraspinal muscle fatty infiltration and relative cross-sectional area in predicting adjacent segment disease after lumbar spinal fusion: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Nguyen Lam Minh Tan 1,2,3 , Hsuan-Tung Lee 2,3 , Yu-Chi Hsu 2,3 , Serena Hu 4 , Jason Cheung 3,5 , Klaus Schnake 3,6 , Wongthawat Liawrungrueang 3 , Daisuke Sakai 3,7 , Takaki Yoshimizu 3,8 , Sung Huang Laurent Tsai 1,2,3 , Max Meng-Huang Wu 1,2,3

1 Taipei Medical University Hospital, Taipei Medical University, APSS AOSpine AP Fronterior Technologies Research Group, Taipei, Taiwan, 2 Taipei Medical University, Taipei, Taiwan, 3 APSS AOSpine AP Fronterior Technologies Research Study Group, Taipei, Taiwan, 4 Stanford University School of Medicine, Redwood City, CA, United States, 5 Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China, 6 Center for Spinal and Scoliosis Surgery, Malteser Waldkrankenhaus St. Marien, Erlangen, Germany, 7 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Surgical Science, Tokai University School of Medicine, 143 Shimokasuya, Isehara, Kanagawa, Japan, 8 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Seirei Hamamatsu General Hospital, Hamamatsu, Japan

Introduction: To evaluate whether preoperative fat infiltration (FI) and relative cross-sectional area (rCSA) in paraspinal muscles (PSMs), specifically the multifidus (MF) and erector spinae (ES), are reliable predictors of adjacent segment disease (ASD) after lumbar spinal fusion in adults. Material and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted by searching PubMed, Embase, and Scopus from inception to March 2025. Studies with cohort or case-control designs reporting on preoperative FI or rCSA and ASD development were. From 630 studies, 15 met eligible criteria (10 evaluated FI, and 8 evaluated rCSA) involving 1,748 patients were analyzed. Standardized mean differences were pooled using a random-effects model. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Results: Higher preoperative FI was significantly associated with ASD (standardized mean difference = 0.59; 95% CI = 0.43 to 0.75; IÇ = 42.4%). In contrast, rCSA showed no significant association. Patients in the ASD group were slightly older (mean difference = 1.51 years; 95% CI = 0.61 to 2.40). Subgroup analysis by fusion length (short vs. long) and muscle type (MF vs. PSM) revealed no significant differences in effect sizes, indicating the consistent predictive value of FI across groups. Meta- regression found that fusion length and age did not significantly affect the FI-ASD association, though age partially accounted for study variability. Conclusion: Preoperative FI in PSMs, particularly MF and ES, is a significant predictor of ASD after lumbar fusion, while rCSA is not. FI assessment should be considered an important component of preoperative evaluation for ASD risk stratification.

RF115: The large change between the sitting and standing positions in the C2 to upper instrument vertebra plumb line distance is a risk factor for proximal junctional failure and revision surgery in adult spinal deformity surgery

Go Yoshida 1 , Yu Yamato 1 , Tomohiro Banno 1 , Hideyuki Arima 1 , Shin Oe 1 , Hiroki Ushirozako 1 , Tomohiro Yamada 1 , Yukihiro Matsuyama 1

1 Hamamatsu University School of Medicine, Hamamatsu, Japan

Introduction: The factor of proximal junctional failure (PJF) after adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgeries has been reported to multifactorial including age, fusion to pelvis, preoperative sagittal malalignment, low bone mineral density, frail, postoperative thoracic kyphosis and the location of the upper instrumented vertebra (UIV). The effect of preoperative standing and natural sitting positions on postoperative mechanical complications in ASD is unclear. Previously we reported the large UIV to C2 plumb line distance was risk factor of PJF. Material and Methods: The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of our university hospital. Consecutive patients who underwent spinal surgery with aged 18 years or older in our institution from 2016 to 2022 with minimum 2 years follow up. We investigated the risk factors for proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK), proximal junctional failure (PJF) and revision surgery (RS) using prospectively collected data including radiographic parameter as well as HRQOL and clinical outcome. In this study, we measured the distance between UIV to C2/C7 plumb line in preoperative standing and sitting radiograph. Results: A total of 135 patients were e included (female patients were 121) in this study. The average age was 69.5 ± 7.3 years. The average of the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for radiographic assessment was 0.809. There are 80 patients with Non-PJK/PJF, 40 with PJK/PJF, and 15 with RS. One-way ANOVA revealed that the intergroup differences among the three groups were primarily observed in the following variables: T-score (p = 0.002), prestanding thoracic kyphosis (TK) (p = 0.031), presitting C2-upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) (p = 0.006), presitting TK (p = 0.047), presitting-standing ΔC2-UIV (p = 0.002), poststanding C2-UIV (p = 0.002), and poststanding TK (p = 0.001). A multinomial logistic regression was performed with the Non-PJK/PJF group serving as the reference category. The analysis revealed that T-score (p = 0.002), presitting C2-UIV (p = 0.035), and poststanding TK (p = 0.012) were independent risk factors for developing PJK/PJF, whereas ΔC2-UIV (p = 0.006) and poststanding C2- UIV (p = 0.032) were identified as independent risk factors for the RS group. Conclusion: This study indicates the utility for sitting spinal alignment evaluation, particularly in ASD patients with maximum effort of thoracic spine and lower extremities compensation at standing. With focusing no fused segment, large UIV to C2 plumb line distance may risk factor of PJF/RS, because of stress concentration to the border between motion and fusion segment.

RF116: Establishing the timeline for pelvic tilt stabilization after adult spinal deformity surgery

Lane McCoy 1 , Christopher Diaz 1 , Neset Tang 1 , Brian Neuman 1, 2

1 Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, St. Louis, United States, 2Barnes Jewish Hospital, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: Pelvic tilt (PT) plays a crucial role in sagittal alignment and functional outcomes after adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery. However, the timeline for PT stabilization postoperatively remains unclear. This study aims to determine the time point at which PT stabilizes and whether other sagittal alignment parameters follow similar trends, providing insight into postoperative alignment progression. Material and Methods: ASD patients who underwent a fusion from the upper thoracic region (T1-T5) to the pelvis and met their targeted L1 pelvic angle (PA) (L1PA = 0.5PI - 19 ± 2) goal immediate postoperative mark were evaluated. The changes in PT, C7 sagittal vertebral axis (SVA) and C2 SVA over these time points were assessed. Statistical significance was determined via paired t-tests. Results: 43 patients met our inclusion criteria. PT significantly increased from iPO to 6W (15.58 vs 19.65 [p = 0.0373]). There was no other significant increase between measured time intervals (6W:19.65, 6M: 19.33, 1Y: 21.03, 2Y: 19.63). Similarly, C7 SVA and C2 SVA exhibited a decrease from iPO to 6W (C7 SVA: 52.25 vs 23.85mm, p = 0.001, C2 SVA: 89.88 vs 49.23mm, p = 0.0003), after which they stabilized with no significant change occurring between time intervals. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that PT, C7 SVA, and C2 SVA stabilize at the 6-week postoperative point and remain consistent through 2 years in ASD patients aligned to L1PA criteria. This has significant implications for postoperative monitoring and long-term alignment expectations. Future studies should explore whether other early postoperative sagittal alignment changes could predict long-term clinical outcomes

RF117: Anterior column reconstruction after double corpectomy in thoracolumbar fractures, an analysis of 42 consecutive patients

Mohamed Alhashash 1 , Hany Gendy 1 , Mootaz Shousha 1

1 Zentralklinik Bad Berka, Germany, Alexandria University, Egypt, Bad Berka, Germany

Introduction: Thoracolumbar fractures are common injuries accounting for 30% to 60% of spinal injuries. Reconstruction after double corpectomy is challenging and literature dealing with this item is sparse. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis of the prospectively collected data in a single spine center revealed 185 patients undergoing double and triple thoracolumbar corpectomies between 1995 and 2024. In 174 patients double corpectomy was performed, and 11 patients underwent triple corpectomy. The indication for surgery varied between fractures, tumors and spondylodiscitis. Among these 185 patients, 42 patients were operated due to thoracolumbar fractures and represent the material of this work. Levels operated, fracture types, surgical approaches as well as pre- and postoperative data analysis were performed for a minimum follow up of six months. Results: The study included 42 consecutive patients. Pathological fractures as well as tumors and primary spondylodiscitis were excluded. There were 19 females and 23 males with a mean age of 65 years. 40 patients underwent double corpectomy and two patients underwent triple corpectomy. The indication for surgery was primary fracture in 35 patients and adjacent kyphosis due to fracture was diagnosed in seven patients. Corpectomy levels were thoracic in 23 patients, thoracolumbar (T12+L1) in 9 and lumbar in 10 patients. A thoracoscopic approach in prone position was used in 26 patients (Thoracic +L1), laparotomy in 10 (L2-5), costotransversectomy in three, open thoracotomy in two and thoraco-phreno-laparotomy in one patient. Implant used for reconstruction was a mesh Harms cage in two patients, thereafter X-Tenz expandable cage in 19 patients, and more recently Medi-Expand expandable cage with assembleable blocks and lordotic plates in the remaining 21 patients. The cages were filled with bone graft material taken from the removed vertebral bodies. There were no intraoperative complications and no cage revision was needed. Conclusions: Double corpectomy in thoracolumbar fractures with reconstruction of the defect using expandable cages is safe with low complication and revision rates. Modern cage designs allow more comfort in performing these challenging surgeries.

RF118: Single-level lumbar fusion outcomes in hypertensive patients: a propensity score-matched comparison of angiotensin receptor blockers and ACE inhibitors

Seungjun Lee 1 , Matthew Kim 2 , Jason Chang 1 , Graham Goh 2 , Tony Tannoury 2 , Chadi Tannoury 2

1 Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, United States, 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Boston University Medical Center, Boston, United States

Introduction: The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) influences bone remodeling, and its blockade through ARBs or ACEIs may impact arthrodesis and surgical outcomes. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to compare perioperative complications, revision rates, and resource utilization in hypertensive adults undergoing single-level lumbar fusion (ALIF/TLIF/PLIF) treated with ARBs versus ACEIs. We hypothesized that ARB therapy would be associated with lower pseudarthrosis and revision rates without a concomitant increase in adverse events. Outcomes included 90-day medical complications; surgical complications and resource utilization at 90 days, 6 months, and 1 year; and pseudarthrosis and revision through 2 years. Conclusion: In hypertensive patients undergoing single-level lumbar fusion, ARB therapy was associated with consistently lower pseudarthrosis and revision rates through 2 years, along with reduced early AKI, anemia, readmission, and ED utilization versus ACEIs (with a small increase in 90-day pneumonia). These findings support a potential class-specific advantage of ARBs for fusion biology and postoperative recovery and warrant prospective validation and perioperative management trials.

RF119: Region-specific effects of osteoporosis treatments and implications for patient optimization for spine surgery

Taim Aizooky 1 , Ben Carnovale 1 , Armani Manov 1 , Qazi Zeeshan 2 , Nami Safai Haeri 3,4 , Kojo Hamilton 1,2,5 , Nitin Agarwal 1,2,5

1 Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA, United States, 2 Department of Neurological Surgery, University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, PA, United States, 3 Division of Endocrinology, Department of Medicine, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, United States, 4 Division of Geriatrics, Department of Medicine, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA, United States, 5 Neurological Surgery, Veterans Affairs Pittsburgh Healthcare System, Pittsburgh, PA, United States

Introduction: Osteoporosis, characterized by decreased bone mineral density (BMD) and microarchitecture, has been shown to be a significant risk factor for suboptimal spine surgery outcomes, such as a higher rate of pseudarthrosis, screw loosening, and disc degeneration. Therefore, targeting low BMD to optimize patients prior to spine surgery may improve patient outcomes postoperatively. Bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, remain the first-line treatment for osteoporosis; more novel monoclonal antibodies, such as denosumab and romosozumab, have also been used to target low BMD. Understanding how these drugs uniquely affect BMD at specific orthopedic regions, may provide key insight to the most optimal osteoporosis treatment for patients undergoing spine surgery. Materials and Methods: An institutional search of the electronic medical record was performed to find patients who have taken (1) alendronate, (2) denosumab, or (3) romosozumab in the past 10 years. Patients were divided into three cohorts based on treatment. All cohorts were screened to find patients with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scans performed (1) prior to medication start date and (2) at least six months after starting treatment. Patients with DXA scans more than three years before or after medication start date were excluded from the study. For each patient with DXA scans before and after treatment, BMD measurements from the left hip and the lumbar spine were recorded, and percent change of BMD was calculated for each patient. For patients in each cohort, a single-sample t-test was used was used to determine whether the mean percentage change differed significantly from zero. To compare BMD changes across cohorts for each site, normality of residuals was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, and the Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test was used when normality was not satisfied, followed by post-hoc Dunn’s test using Bonferroni correction. p < 0.05 was considered to be significant. Results: Thirty-six female patients were included in the study (romosozumab n = 12, denosumab n = 10, alendronate n = 14). At the left hip, denosumab (p = 0.00595) was significantly associated with increased BMD. At the lumbar spine, alendronate (p < 0.0001) and romosozumab (p = 0.0008) were associated with increased BMD. Furthermore, romosozumab was associated with a significantly greater increase in BMD in the lumbar spine compared to denosumab (p = 0.003). Conclusion: This pilot study provides insight into region-specific effects of osteoporosis treatments. In our cohort, romosozumab and alendronate were associated with increased lumbar spine BMD, while denosumab was associated with increased left hip BMD. Furthermore, romosozumab showed greater lumbar spine BMD increases compared to denosumab. These findings infer the potential utility of romosozumab for optimizing lumbar spine BMD before spine surgery. Our interpretation is limited due to the modest sample size (n = 36), limited power for between-drug comparisons, and confounders such as age, fracture history, and concurrent medications. These observations, while preliminary, support the need for larger randomized controlled trials to confirm whether region-specific drug effects are clinically meaningful and can guide treatment selection for spine surgery optimization.

RF120: Preoperative handgrip strength predicts physical function recovery after surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis: a prospective cohort

Berkay Paker 1 , Ece Naz Argını 2 , Deniz Konya 1

1 Bahçeşehir University, Department of Neurosurgery, Istanbul, Turkey, 2 Medical Park Göztepe Hospital Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation Department, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Handgrip strength is a pragmatic biomarker of sarcopenia and global muscle function. We investigated whether preoperative handgrip strength relates to postoperative patient-reported outcomes after surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis. Material and Methods: Prospective, single-center cohort of consecutive lumbar spinal stenosis patients. Preoperative handgrip strength was measured with a hand grip dynamometer in a sitting position with the elbow flexed 90 degrees and supported. Three trials were performed, and the maximal value on the dominant hand was recorded. Patient-reported outcomes were collected preoperatively and at the latest follow-up: SF-36 Physical Functioning (primary endpoint), Oswestry Disability Index, Lower Extremity Functional Scale, and VAS back pain. Of 48 enrolled patients, 14 had complete paired outcomes and were analyzed. There were no reoperations among these 14. Median follow-up was 102 days (IQR 79 to 119). Patients were classified as low versus non-low handgrip strength using sex and age-specific cutoffs. Within-patient changes were summarized as means with percentile bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals using 20,000 resamples. Group differences in change (non-low minus low) were analyzed using permutation tests with 50,000 label shuffles and permutation 95 percent confidence intervals. Results: Within-patient improvement was considerable across outcomes. SF 36 Physical Functioning improved from 31.5 to 61.2 (delta +29.6; bootstrap 95 percent CI +20.4 to +40.0). Oswestry Disability Index improved from 63.6 to 30.3 (delta -33.3; -42.0 to -24.4). Lower Extremity Functional Scale improved from 27.1 to 41.7 (delta +14.6; +5.6 to +22.9).
