For the primary endpoint SF-36 Physical Functioning, mean improvement was +13.3 in the low group versus +34.5 in the non-low group, difference +21.2 (permutation 95 percent CI +6.7 to +35.3; p = 0.0036). For Oswestry Disability Index, low -17.3 versus non low -37.6, difference -20.3 (permutation 95 percent CI -39.1 to -0.36; p = 0.047). Lower Extremity Functional Scale and VAS differences trended in the same direction but were imprecise, given the small low grip cell size. Conclusion: In this prospectively collected cohort, surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis produced robust improvements in pain, disability, and physical function. Low preoperative handgrip strength was associated with smaller gains in physical functioning and less improvement in disability. The use of bootstrap confidence intervals and permutation tests provided valid small-sample inference without assuming normality. These hypothesis-generating findings support incorporating handgrip strength into preoperative risk stratification and rehabilitation planning and warrant confirmation in larger cohorts with postoperative handgrip reassessment.

RF124: Risk factors for poor functional outcomes after surgical treatment of thoracolumbar junction fractures

Jlidi Mohamed 1 , Raboudi Hamza 1 , mouldi lamouchi 1 , Karim Mallek 1 , Jihed Bechikh 1 , Ismail Karray 1 , Sami Mbarki 1 , Hedi Atig 1 , Walid Bouaicha 1 , Selim Daas 1

1 Orthopedics and Traumatology Department, Hospital of Mohamed Taher Maamouri, Nabeul, Tunisia

Introduction: Fractures of the thoracolumbar junction are among the most frequent spinal injuries because the transitional biomechanical properties of this region make it particularly vulnerable to trauma. The aim of this study was to identify clinical, fracture-related, and surgical factors associated with poor functional outcomes in patients operated for thoracolumbar junction fractures by a posterior approach. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of 120 consecutive patients treated surgically at our orthopedic and traumatology department between January 2010 and January 2020. Other variables including gender, diabetes, head injury, articular fractures, mixed fusion assembly, intra-canal fragments, and postoperative infection were not a risk factors for a poor functional outcomes. In multivariate study, only the higher UCLA grade at the last follow-up (p=0,001) at the last follow up was the risk factors for poor functional outcomes. Conclusion: Poor functional recovery after posterior stabilization of thoracolumbar junction fractures is multifactorial. In our cohort, advanced age, short fixation assembly, and higher UCLA grade at follow-up emerged as the most significant predictors. Obesity, luxation, nonunion, and implant failure may also contribute but require further validation. These findings emphasize the importance of individualized surgical planning, careful choice of construct length, and close radiological follow-up to optimize long-term functional outcomes.

RF125: Electrochemotherapy in aggressive hemangioma of the spine: a case-series and narrative literature review

Giuseppe Tedesco 1 , Luigi Emanuele Noli 1 , Cristiana Griffoni 1 , riccardo ghermandi 1 , Giancarlo Facchini 2 , Giuliano Peta 2 , Nicolas Papalexis 2 , Emanuela Asunis 1,3 , Stefano Pasini 1 , Alessandro Gasbarrini 1,4

1 Complex Spinal Surgery Unit, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy, 2 Diagnostic and Interventional Radiology Unit, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy, 3 Ortopedia e Traumatologia AORN Santobono Pausilipon, Naples, Italy, 4 Department of Biomedical and Neuromotor Sciences, University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: A hemangioma is a benign tumor of the vasculature that develops from the different blood vessel types. Vertebral hemangiomas (VHs) are extremely common lesions, with an incidence of 11% in the adult population. Most VHs are latent (Enneking Stage 1, st.1): they are intracompartimental lesions, with well-defined margin, that grow slowly and then stop and do not require specific treatment; only 1% of VHs become active and symptomatic. Approximately 55% of these symptomatic VH cases are associated with pain alone. Some VHs may become aggressive and extend into the spinal canal and/or the paravertebral space, leading to neurologic deficit (Enneking Stage 3, st.3). Symptomatic VHs can be treated with conservative medical therapy, percutaneous techniques, radiotherapy, surgery, or a combination of these. The common treatments of choice in VHs without neurologic manifestations are vertebroplasty, kyphoplasty, and/or selective arterial embolization (SAE), with good pain control results. Decompression surgery and stabilization are highly recommended in patients suffering from neurological deterioration and symptoms, with SAE often used preoperatively. Radiation alone or as adjuvant treatment is often used. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) consists of a combination of electric pulses, led directly in the tumor in order to improve cell membrane permeability, and infusion of chemotherapeutic drugs. Bleomycin and cisplatin have been shown to be the most effective and appropriate agents for electrochemotherapy in clinical use.This case series and literature review aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of electrochemotherapy in the management of aggressive spinal hemangiomas, presenting two distinct cases. Methods: We present two cases of spinal aggressive hemangioma refractory to conventional treatments, that underwent electrochemotherapy. Case 1 involves a 50-year-old female presented with an aggressive spinal hemangioma of L1, who previously underwent various treatments including surgery, radio-chemotherapy, and arterial embolization. Case 2 describes a 16-year-old female with a T12 vertebral hemangioma, previously treated with surgery and stabilization, who faced limitations in treatment options due to her young age and the location of the hemangioma. Results: In Case 1, electrochemotherapy with bleomycin was administered following the failure of previous treatments and resulted in the reduction of the lesion size and improvement in clinical symptoms. In Case 2, electrochemotherapy was chosen due to the risks associated with other treatments and was completed without any adverse events. Both cases demonstrated the potential of electrochemotherapy as a viable treatment option for spinal hemangiomas, especially in complex or recurrent cases. Conclusion: Electrochemotherapy with bleomycin is a promising treatment for aggressive spinal hemangiomas when conventional therapies are not feasible or have failed. Further research is needed to establish definitive protocols and long-term outcomes of electrochemotherapy in spinal hemangioma management.

Krish Sridhar 1 , Selvin Vijayan 1

1 Kauvery Hospital, Radial Road, Chennai, India

Introduction: Chondrosarcomas are malignant cartilage-forming neoplasms that commonly involve the pelvis and appendicular skeleton. Thoracic chondrosarcomas represent approximately 15% of cases and usually arise anteriorly from the sternum or costochondral junction. Origin from the costovertebral junction is exceedingly rare, with only 30 cases reported in the English literature to date. The case underscores the diagnostic challenge posed by such partly calcified paraspinal masses and highlights the importance of early recognition and radical surgical excision in achieving favorable outcomes. Given the anatomical complexity, individualized surgical approaches are required to balance oncological clearance with preservation of spinal stability and thoracic function. Long-term surveillance remains essential due to the risk of delayed recurrence. This report contributes to the limited global literature on costovertebral chondrosarcomas and reinforces the role of posterolateral extrapleural resection as a safe and effective technique for large paraspinal tumors.

Age, sex, BMI, smoking status, number of operative levels, cage material, average operative level bone density (Hounsfield units), graft length, width, and endplate length were collected. This was normalized to a value of 10 so that an increase or decrease of 1 unit corresponded to a 10% overhang or undersize, respectively. Post-operative implant subsidence at long-term follow-up was graded according to Marchi criteria by two separate spine surgeons. Results: 144 patients (218 levels) met the inclusion criteria. There was no difference in subsidence rate based on endplate length (p = 0.364) or cage length (p = 0.073); however, there was a statistically significant difference in risk of subsidence based on cage material (p = 0.028), cage width (p = 0.009), cage overhang (p = 0.049), overhang area (p = 0.023), and overhang ratio (p = 0.031). PEEK cage material (OR: 5.16, p = 0.001) and overhang ratio (OR 1.95, p = 0.008) were both associated with increased risk of subsidence on multiple logistic regression analysis. Conclusion: LLIF grafts with increased overhang ratio were associated with a higher rate of radiographic subsidence at long-term follow-up. Our results demonstrate 3D printed porous titanium is associated with less long-term radiographic subsidence. Subsidence is reduced by choosing a graft that most closely matches the endplate length, minimizing the overhang ratio.

RF129: Alignment factors associated with the need for revision extension surgery to the sacrum after previous lumbar spinal fusion

Catherine Hurley 1 , Manjot Singh 1 , Nicolas Carayannopoulos 1 , Jinseong Kim 2 , Zvipo Chisango 1 , Gabriel Gonzalez 1 , Michael Farias 1 , John Czerwein 2 , Bryce Basques 2 , Eren Kuris 2 , Bassel Diebo 2 , Alan Daniels 2

1 The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University, Providence, United States, 2 Brown University, Providence, United States

Introduction: Lumbar spinal fusions are common surgical procedures used to treat a range of spinal pathology. Overall, these procedures amass revision rates up to 25.9% within two years post-operatively. When planning a revision of lumbar fusion, surgeons may extend fusions with a lower instrumented vertebra of L5 to the sacrum to achieve decompressive, alignment or stability goals. However, such extension alters the regional biomechanics and is associated with increased risks including pseudoarthrosis, adjacent segment diseases, and proximal junctional kyphosis. Despite the frequency of these revisions, predictors of the need for sacral extension within the context of revision lumbar fusion remain poorly defined. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included adult patients who underwent primary anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) or transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) between 2017-2022 at a single academic institution, as well as those referred to the institution for sacral extension following their primary surgery. Patients were included if their index fusion spanned L1-L4 (UIV) to L5 or above (LIV) and subsequently underwent revision. Sacral extension (SE) was defined as instrumentation extending to S1 or the pelvis by 2 years postoperatively. Demographics, frailty indices, radiographic parameters, and surgical complications were collected. Qualitative review of operative notes identified surgeon-stated indications for SE. Radiographic changes and predictors of SE were assessed using t-tests, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression. Results: A total of 181 patients met inclusion criteria. 50 (27.6%) underwent SE during revision, while 131 (72.4%) remained fused between L1 and L5. Conclusion: In this cohort of 181 lumbar fusion patients, risk factors for the need to revise and extend lumbar fusions to the sacrum included inadequate caudal lumbar lordosis, greater frailty, and longer instrumentation constructs. The most common revision-specific indications included distal junctional degeneration, pseudoarthrosis, foraminal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis. These findings may support preoperative risk stratification and inform planning of surgeries in patients at higher risk for sacral extension.

RF131: Clinical and radiographic comparison between stand-alone ALIF vs ALIF 360° at L5-S1: case series with 6-month follow-up

Marco Gonzalez-Gomez 1 , Juan Rodriguez-Azcona 2

1 Hospital Clinica Nova, Hospital Universitario Uanl, Monterrey N.L., Mexico, 2 Hospital Clinica Nova, Monterrey N.L., Mexico

Introduction: The anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) is a well-established technique for the surgical treatment of degenerative intervertebral disc disease, particularly at the L5-S1 level. This approach allows for restoration of disc height, correction of segmental lordosis, and preservation of the posterior paravertebral musculature. ALIF has been associated with reduced blood loss, shorter operative time, and faster functional recovery compared to posterior approaches. ALIF can be performed as a stand-alone procedure or combined with posterior instrumentation (ALIF 360°). The latter is generally recommended in cases with greater instability, higher risk of pseudarthrosis, or the need for additional biomechanical support. While posterior instrumentation increases the stiffness of the operated segment and has been linked to higher fusion rates, it also entails longer operative time, increased blood loss, and the risk of complications inherent to the posterior approach. Currently, there is ongoing debate regarding which technique provides superior clinical and radiographic outcomes for isolated L5-S1 disc degeneration. Therefore, the present study aims to compare functional clinical outcomes (VAS and ODI) and interbody fusion rates between patients treated with stand-alone L5-S1 ALIF and ALIF 360°, with follow-up of up to six months. Material and Methods: Retrospective case series of 20 patients operated between 2021 and 2025 for L5-S1 degenerative pathology. Patients were divided into two groups: 12 underwent stand-alone ALIF and 8 underwent ALIF 360° (with posterior fixation). Pain and disability were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) one week before surgery, and at 1, 3, and 6 months postoperatively. Interbody fusion was evaluated through plain radiographs using the Bridwell classification at the same intervals. Surgical time, intraoperative blood loss, and complications were also analyzed. Results: The ALIF 360° group showed better clinical improvement, with lower VAS and ODI scores at all follow-up points. Fusion rates (Bridwell grade I-II) at six months were 75% in the ALIF 360° group and 50% in the stand-alone group. The stand-alone approach had shorter operative time (122 vs. 185 minutes) and less blood loss (157 vs. 227 mL). One complication occurred in each group. Conclusion: ALIF 360° was associated with better functional outcomes and higher fusion rates, while stand-alone ALIF offered advantages in terms of operative time and blood loss. Surgical approach should be individualized according to the patient's clinical and biomechanical profile.

RF132: Exploring the influence factors of pelvic tilt restoration after surgical treatment of lumbar degenerative diseases: value of preoperative standing-sitting radiograph

Siyu Zhou 1,2,3 , Yi Zhao 1,2,3 , Zhiqian Luo 4 , Hongbin He 4 , Zhuoran Sun 1,2,3 , Weishi Li 1,2,3

1 Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China, 2 Beijing Key Laboratory of Spinal Disease Research, Beijing, China, 3 Engineering Research Center of Bone and Joint Precision Medicine, Beijing, China, 4 Peking University Health Science Center, Beijing, China

Introduction: In lumbar degenerative diseases (LDD), pelvic retroversion is an important compensation mechanism for sagittal malalignment. Restoring such pelvic tilt (PT) increase relies on the rebuilding of lumbar lordosis (LL) in surgery, and is associated to the postoperative clinical outcome. However, the influence factors of PT restoration (rPT) remain unclear. This study aimed to identify potential factors affecting rPT in LDD surgery, and to recognize the correlation between postoperative sagittal parameters and clinical outcome. Material and Methods: 74 LDD patients undergoing posterior lumbar interbody fusion with restored LL were included. Sagittal parameters were measured in whole spine radiographs in standing and sitting. Δ indicated change of sagittal parameters from standing to sitting. The LL restoration (rLL) and rPT was calculated by postoperative parameters minus preoperative parameters. The visual analogue scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) was used to evaluate the clinical outcome. All participants accepted the whole spine radiographs in standing and sitting preoperatively, and accepted 1-year follow-up after surgery. Pearson correlation analysis was applied to explore preoperative parameters related to rPT. Parameters related to rPT was further included in linear regression models to build predictive formulas rPT. Further, the sagittal parameters affecting post-operative ODI, leg pain VAS and low back pain VAS was examined. Results: PT (r = -0.500), sacral slope (r = 0.400), L4-S1 lordosis (r = 0.296) and LL (r = 0.282) in standing and ΔPT (r = 0.256), ΔL4-S1 lordosis (r = -0.238) and Δthoracolumbar kyphosis (r = -0.257) from standing to sitting were significantly related to rPT. A predictive formula for rPT was developed as rPT = -0.233×PT- 0.173×rLL+ 0.140×ΔPT+ 2.750° (R2 = 0.365, p < 0.001). Postoperatively, VAS of low back pain is related to PT (r = 0.358, p < 0.01) and PI-LL (r = 0.246, p < 0.05), and ODI was significantly related to SVA (r = 0.253, p < 0.05). Conclusion: LL restoration, preoperative PT, and ΔPT from standing to sitting were identified as predictors of rPT. Moreover, postoperative PT and PI-LL were associated with the residual low back pain after surgery, and a smaller SVA was related to better quality of life. The present study revealed the unique clinical value of standing-sitting radiograph in surgical planning of LDD, and again stressed the importance of restoring sagittal balance in lumbar surgery.

RF133: Lateral Lumbar Interbody Fusion (LLIF) both with and without posterior pedicle screw instrumentation improves back pain in patients with degenerative disc disease early in the post-operative period

Lauren Barber 1 , Stone Sima 2 , Charmian Stewart 3 , Sindhu Sunkad 2 , Victor Chen 2 , Alisha Sial 2 , Ashish Diwan 2,4

1 Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, United States, 2 University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia, 3 Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, Dublin, Ireland, 4 University of Adelaide, Adelaide, Australia

Introduction: Lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) is a minimally invasive fusion technique that can be useful in patients with degenerative disc disease (DDD). LLIF can be performed either as a stand-alone construct or with supplemental posterior instrumentation. Stand-alone LLIF and even LLIF with unilateral posterior instrumentation may offer reduced operative time and cost, but risks biomechanical complications. The impact on patient-reported outcomes (PROs) remains unclear. As such, this study evaluates PROs of LLIF with and without posterior pedicle instrumentation (both unilateral and bilateral) early on in the post-operative period. Methods: This is an IRB-approved, retrospective study of adult patients undergoing LLIF with or without posterior instrumentation (unilateral or bilateral pedicle screws) for DDD between 2012 and 2021. PROs collected included Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and visual analog scale (VAS) scores for back and leg pain. These were collected pre-operatively as well as at 3- and 6-months post-operatively. Demographics including age, sex, and number of levels treated were recorded. Results: 60 total patients were included in the study (32 stand-alone LLIF, 14 LLIF with unilateral posterior fixation, and 14 LLIF with bilateral posterior fixation). The mean age was 68.1 ± 12.4 years. The stand-alone LLIF group underwent 1.79 ± 0.82 levels, patients with LLIF with unilateral posterior instrumentation underwent 1.93 ± 0.92 levels, and patients with LLIF with bilateral posterior instrumentation underwent 2.00 ± 1.04 levels (p = 0.77). There were no statistically significant differences in age (p = 0.45), sex (p = 0.47), number of levels (p = 0.77), or pre-operative PROs (ODI, p = 0.16; VAS back, p = 0.10; VAS leg, p = 0.08) between the groups. VAS back improved significantly at both post-operative timepoints for stand-alone LLIF (p = 0.03 and p = 0.01, respectively), LLIF with unilateral posterior instrumentation (p = 0.04 and p = 0.02, respectively), and LLIF with bilateral posterior instrumentation (p = 0.01 and p = 0.004, respectively). Notably, there were no statistical differences in VAS back between the 3- and 6-month timepoints in any group. While ODI and VAS leg improved from pre-operatively in all 3 groups to both timepoints post-operatively, they did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05). At 3- and 6-months post-operatively, there were no statistically significant differences in ODI, VAS back, or VAS leg, though LLIF with bilateral instrumentation did trend towards greater leg pain improvement. Conclusion: Stand-alone LLIF and LLIF with supplemental unilateral or bilateral posterior pedicle instrumentation significantly improved back pain early within the post-operative period. While ODI and VAS leg pain improved in all 3 groups at both timepoints, they did not reach statistical significance. There were no differences in PROs post-operatively between the groups. Therefore, stand-alone LLIF reached comparable improvements in PROs to LLIF with supplemental posterior instrumentation. As such, all 3 constructs greatly improve back pain quite early on in the post-operative period and may be reasonable options for treating patients with DDD depending on goals and surgeon preference. Further studies will be important in determining the longevity of these findings.

RF134: From hydration loss to structural change: disc signal intensity as a marker of degeneration

Lukas Schönnagel 1 , Jonathan Maaser 1 , Lea Cordes 1 , Fabian Titz 1 , Judith Schirneck 1 , Laura-Sophie Peters 1 , Bernhard Hoehl 1 , Hendrik Schmidt 1 , Matthias Pumberger 1

1 Charite Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Berlin, Germany

Introduction: Early degenerative changes of the spine are often not directly associated with pain, whereas later manifestations, such as degenerative scoliosis or spinal stenosis, frequently necessitate surgical intervention and contribute to healthcare burden. Disc desiccation is considered the beginning of the degenerative cascade, yet its characterization and clinical evaluation remain limited. This study aimed to assess the association between early disc degeneration and structural spinal changes, using vertebral endplate damage as a proxy. Methods: This sub-analysis of the Berlin Back Study included participants with unspecific chronic low back pain (cLBP) recruited from the general population. Disc hydration was assessed on sagittal T2-weighted MRI at the L4/5 level, selected as the biomechanically most compromised segment. Imaging was performed using a 3-Tesla scanner (TR: 4000 ms; TE: 112 ms; slice thickness: 3 mm). The disc was manually segmented, and the central region was automatically identified. Signal intensity was normalized to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to calculate the T2-adjusted Disc Intensity Index (T2DII). Endplate degeneration at L4/5 was scored using the Total Endplate Score (TEPS, range 2-12). Associations between T2DII and TEPS were analyzed using multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, BMI, and sex. Non-linearity was assessed via segmented regression and compared to the linear model using ANOVA. Results: A total of 510 patients were included in the analysis (median age: 42 years (IQR:33-55); 58.5% female). The median TEPS at L4/5 was 4 (IQR:2-6), and the median T2-adjusted Disc Intensity Index (T2DII) was 0.37 (IQR:0.25-0.48), corresponding to approximately one-third of the CSF signal intensity. The segmented (non-linear) regression model showed significantly stronger predictive performance than the linear model (p < 0.001), with the optimal breakpoint at 0.44. Within the significant segment, T2DII was strongly associated with endplate degeneration (β = -10.5, p < 0.001), with a moderate to high effect size (η2 = 0.10). Notably, age was not a significant predictor in this model (p = 0.16, η2 = 0.003), suggesting that the effect of age is largely mediated through disc desiccation. Discussion: We identified a strong non-linear association between the T2DII and endplate degeneration, with early disc dehydration showing limited structural impact, while more advanced stages exhibited a pronounced linear trend. Although normative values remain to be defined, our findings suggest that opportunistic, quantitative MRI assessment may aid early detection of disc degeneration. Compared to qualitative grading systems such as the Pfirrmann Grade, the T2DII is continuous and observer-independent, which may enable more nuanced assessment of early changes and longitudinal progression. Anticipating the clinical use of regenerative therapies, early detection may support more effective patient selection and resource allocation.

Jun-Young Choi 1 , Jae Jun Yang 1

1 Dongguk University Ilsan Hospital, Goyang, South Korea

Introduction: Total disc replacement in the lumbosacral spine has been compared with fusion surgeries to elucidate the effect of preserved segmental motion on adjacent segment degeneration (ASD). RF136: Incidence and risk factors of adjacent segment degeneration in lumbosacral or lumbo-iliac fusion with L2 as the uppermost instrumented vertebra

1 University of Virginia, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States

Introduction: Patients with symptomatic diffuse lumbar spondylosis or mild to moderate lumbar spinal deformity may warrant lumbosacral or lumbo-iliac fusion. However, the incidence of adjacent segment degeneration (ASD) following L2 to sacrum or ilium fusion has not been well studied. The incidence of ASD was analyzed. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to evaluate the symptomatic ASD-free survival. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression were used to assess potential risk factors, including patient-related factors, surgery-related factors, and pre- and post-operative spinopelvic parameters. RF137: Amyloid deposition in the ligamentum flavum causes spinal lumbar stenosis with specific disc height conservation

Karel Willems 1 , Loic van Oost 2

1 AZ Delta Roeselare, Roeselare, Belgium, 2 Kul, Leuven, Belgium

Introduction: Lumbar spinal stenosis is traditionally attributed to disc degeneration, facet arthropathy and hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum. 1 Henry Ford Health System, Detroit, United States,

2 Wayne State University School of Medicine, Henry Ford Health System, Detroit, United States,

3 Michigan State University College of Human Medicine, Henry Ford Health System, East Lansing, United States

Introduction: Interlaminar and sublaminar decompressions are standard surgical techniques when managing symptomatic lumbar stenosis, yet there is a lack of comparative patient-reported outcomes between the techniques. This study evaluates differences in PROMIS Pain and Physical Function (PF) scores between interlaminar and sublaminar lumbar decompression. Material and Methods: A retrospective review of 70 patients (ages 18-85) who underwent lumbar decompression without fusion at a US Level 1 trauma center between January 2022 and March 2024 was conducted. Patient-reported outcomes, including PROMIS Pain and PF scores, were collected preoperatively and at 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months postoperatively. Decompression type was categorized based on operative reports. Changes from baseline were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models, adjusting for age, BMI, number of surgical levels, and operative time. Results: The mean improvements from baseline PROMIS PF scores were greater in sublaminar compared to interlaminar decompression at 2 weeks (Difference: 9.31, SE: 2.70, p = .001), 4 weeks (Difference: 5.38, SE: 2.82, p = .060), 3 months (Difference: 9.32, SE: 3.13, p = .004), and 6 months (Difference: 5.96, SE: 3.33, p = .076). The absence of between-group differences in absolute PF and Pain aligns with prior observations that both techniques achieve adequate canal enlargement and also underscores known PROMIS limitations (ceiling/floor effects and perception lag) that can blunt detection of late differences. The results additionally indicate that a higher BMI is linked to worse pain, specifically in sublaminar patients. Prior literature has shown that elevated BMI predicts poorer postoperative pain/function, possibly due to additive biomechanical load, more challenging exposure, and corridor differences.

1 Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University, Philadelphia, United States, 2 Department of Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine, Temple University Hospital, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Recent evidence suggests elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels are associated with increased nonunion after spinal fusion. Statin use, however, has been linked to positive effects on bone metabolism, raising the possibility that prior findings may be confounded by differential statin use. This study evaluated the association between preoperative LDL-C levels and nonunion among statin-exposed patients undergoing posterior lumbar interbody fusion (PLIF) or transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF). Material and Methods: The TriNetX Research Network was queried for patients aged 18 - 89 who underwent single-level PLIF or TLIF between September 17, 2003 and September 17, 2023. Multilevel fusions were excluded. Patients with a statin prescription dispensed within six months before or after surgery were identified. In this subset, high LDL-C was defined as ≥ 140.2 mg/dL (one standard deviation above the mean) and low LDL-C as ≤ 65.8 mg/dL (one standard deviation below the mean). A secondary analysis compared patients with and without perioperative statin use. Propensity score matching was performed 1:1 based on demographics, BMI, and comorbidities. Pseudoarthrosis was assessed at six months, one year, and two years using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: The primary analysis included 849 matched pairs. Approximately 68% of patients were White and 58% were female. At six months, nonunion occurred in 10.5% of high LDL-C patients versus 10.1% of low LDL-C patients (RR 1.035, 95% CI 0.782 - 1.370, p = 0.827). At one year, rates were 13.0% vs. 11.9%, respectively (RR 1.089, 95% CI 0.846 - 1.402, p = 0.508). At two years, rates were 14.8% in the high LDL-C group vs. 12.9% in the low LDL-C group (RR 1.142, 95% CI 0.903 - 1.442, p = 0.267). LDL-C levels remained significantly different between groups at all intervals (p < 0.001). The secondary analysis included 23,087 matched pairs; approximately 73% were White and 54% were female. Within six months, nonunion occurred in 10.9% of statin-exposed patients compared with 13.1% of patients without documented statin use (RR 0.839, 95% CI 0.798 - 0.881, p < 0.001). At one year, rates in statin-exposed were 13.4% vs. 15.5% in statin unexposed (RR 0.867, 95% CI 0.827 - 0.908, p < 0.001), and at two years, 14.9% vs. 17.1% respectively (RR 0.874, 95% CI 0.837 - 0.914, p < 0.001). LDL-C differences persisted but were less pronounced than in the primary analysis. Conclusion: There is no relationship between LDL-C levels and union outcomes amongst statin-exposed patients who underwent PLIF or TLIF. However, we successfully replicated the previously described relationship between statin use and diagnosis of nonunion following PLIF/TLIF. Put together, our results suggest that previous retrospective studies that linked high LDL-C levels with increased incidence of nonunion diagnosis following spinal fusion surgery may be at least partially confounded by statin use as the pleiotropic effects of statin therapy on bone metabolism have been well established. Given these contrasting data, prospective studies are warranted to more clearly elucidate the relationship between LDL-C levels and union rates following spinal fusion procedures.

RF141: Morbi-mortality of left anterior retroperitoneal disc reconstruction surgery for 3 or 4 levels versus 1 or 2 levels: retrospective “case-control” analysis of a prospective cohort of 376 patients

Cherif Kamoun 1 , Jean-Baptiste Odent 1 , Marc Mouchantaf 1 , Esther Lambert 1 , Miladi Mehdi 1 , Philippe Cottin 1 , Thierry Bégué 1 , Jean-Charles Aurégan 1,2,3

Introduction: Discogenic lumbar disc disease is one of the leading causes of disability. The results of one and two-level disc reconstruction surgery have pushed some teams to propose multi-level surgeries. However, the reliability of the anterior retroperitoneal approach for 3 or 4-level disc reconstruction surgery has not been documented. Our objective was to compare the complications of disc replacement surgery via the anterior retroperitoneal approach at 3 or 4 levels versus 1 or 2 levels. We included patients operated on for disc replacement surgery for discogenic and/or degenerative disc disease by anterior retroperitoneal approach. Patients who previously underwent disc surgery via the anterior retroperitoneal approach were excluded. Results: 376 patients were included, of whom 322 patients in the control group with an average age of 49,9 years. The average follow-up was 3.62 years. The average intraoperative bleeding was 365 ml in group 2 compared to 161 ml in the control group (p < 0.001). One case of retrograde ejaculation in each group was noted. 52 patients reported elongation radicular pain in group 1 (16%), compared to fourteen (26%) in group 2, transient in all cases. Conclusion: Complications of the anterior retroperitoneal approach in multi-level disc reconstruction surgery seem low. Perioperative complications, particularly vascular, in patients operated on 3 or 4 levels seem comparable to those noted in the control group. Blood volume transfused was comparable between the two groups, as were postoperative complications. Thus, the anterior retroperitoneal approach for 3- or 4-level disc reconstruction surgery appears to be as safe as 1- or 2-level surgery.

Alan Daniels 1 , Manjot Singh 2 , Ashley Knebel 2 , Michael Farias 2 , Joseph Nassar 2 , Jinseong Kim 1 , Zvipo Chisango 2 , Nicolas Carayannopoulos 2 , Catherine Hurley 2 , Miki Jiang 2 , Rishubish Jain 2 , Daniela Baboun 2 , Eren Kuris 1 , Todd Stafford 1 , Bassel Diebo 1

1 Brown University, Providence, United States, 2 The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University, Providence, United States

Introduction: Preoperative planning for lumbar fusion involves careful consideration of segmental and regional spinopelvic alignment. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the ability of L5-S1 ALIF to restore regional L4-S1 and segmental L5-S1 lordosis according to preoperative plan. RF143: P-15 peptide enhanced bone graft demonstrates fusion superiority over autograft across all follow-ups in TLIF: 6-, 12-, and 24-month evidence from a multicenter RCT

Paul Arnold 1 , James Harrop 2 , John O'Toole 3

1 Department of Neurological Surgery, Loyola University Medical Center, Maywood, United States, 2 Departments of Neurological and Orthopedic Surgery, Thomas Jefferson Medical Center, Philadelphia, United States, 3 Department of Neurosurgery, Rush University Medical Center, Maywood, United States

Introduction: Successful arthrodesis aims to restore vertebral stability, alleviate pain, and improve quality of life while preventing implant loosening and hardware failure. There is thus a clinical value in achieving solid fusion early post-operatively. Autologous bone is considered the gold standard in spine fusion but is limited in availability and its regenerative capacity diminishes with age. P-15L (PearlMatrixTM P-15 Peptide Enhanced Bone Graft, Cerapedics Inc., Westminster, Colorado, USA) incorporates a 15 amino acid polypeptide (P-15) that enhances cellular attachment ultimately leading to new bone formation. P-15L has previously demonstrated superior clinical success and time-to-fusion compared to local autograft in transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) at 24 months with a comparable safety profile. This analysis builds on prior findings by evaluating fusion rate superiority of P-15L versus local autograft at the 6-, 12-, and 24-month follow-ups. Material and Methods: Skeletally mature patients, aged 22-80 years, with degenerative disc disease were enrolled at 33 sites and randomized 1:1 to either the P-15L treatment group or the local autograft control group during single-level TLIF with a PEEK cage and supplemental pedicle fixation. Fusion assessments occurred at 6-, 12-, and 24-months. Fusion was evaluated by two independent radiologists and defined as evidence of bridging trabecular bone by high resolution 1-mm thin-slice computed tomography (CT) scans. Bridging was defined as mature, bony continuity from endplate to endplate with no intervening fractures or discontinuities. Once fusion was radiographically confirmed, it was assumed fusion had occurred at all subsequent time points. A Wald z-test was conducted to compare fusion rates between P-15L and autograft at 6, 12, and 24 months, using data derived from the multiplicity-controlled Kaplan-Meier time-to-fusion superiority analysis. Results: A total of 141 (48.6%) patients received P-15L and 149 (51.3%) patients received autograft. At the time of randomization, the majority of patients, 58.9% in the P-15L group and 60.4% in the control group, presented with at least one comorbidity including obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2), nicotine use, or type 2 diabetes. One hundred thirty-nine (99%) patients in the P-15L group and 145 (97%) in the autograft control group were available for the Wald z-test. The Wald-z test demonstrated that P-15L was statistically superior to autograft for the fusion rates at 6-months (57.6% vs 26.9%, p < 0.0001), 12-months (68.8% vs 41.5%, p < 0.0001), and 24-months (81.1% vs 54.9%, p < 0.0001). Conclusion: P-15L demonstrated statistically superior 6-, 12-, and 24-month fusion rates as compared to autograft. Noteworthy, the superior fusion rate for P-15L at 6 months was more than twice as high as the fusion rate for autograft. Further strengthening the study’s findings, the analysis included patients with comorbidities and PEEK cages, both known to negatively impact fusion outcomes. In conclusion, this multicenter, randomized controlled trial demonstrates the superior bone-forming capacity of P-15L in instrumented TLIF procedures utilizing PEEK cages.

RF144: The quadratus lumborum in chronic low back pain

Leo Lemminger 1 , Lukas Schönnagel 1 , Rosa-Maria Berndt 1 , Isis Bowe 1 , Anna Berndt 1 , Lea Hühren 1 , Bernhard Hoehl 1 , Matthias Pumberger 1 , Hendrik Schmidt 1

1 Charite Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Berlin, Germany

Introduction: Chronic low back pain (cLBP) is the leading global cause of functional impairment and work disability. The quadratus lumborum muscle (QL) is considered an important stabilizer of the lateral and posterior lumbar spine. However, its structural relevance in cLBP remains insufficiently explored. This study aimed to assess morphological parameters of the QL using MRI and analyze their associations with pain, disability, spinal mobility, and lumbar degeneration. Materials and Methods: Patients with and without cLBP were prospectively enrolled from the general population, excluding patients with fractures, tumors, infections and patients that underwent previous spinal surgery. The QL was assessed in axial T2 weighted MRIs at all lumbar levels, whereas the level with the largest cross-section area (L3/4) was chosen for analysis. Height adjusted functional cross-sectional area (fCSA) and fatty infiltration (FI) of the QL were analyzed. Propensity score matching was used to evaluate differences in QL morphology between asymptomatic and patients with cLBP, matched for age, sex, BMI, physical activity and smoking status. To analyze the effect in the cLBP cohort, the association with pain intensity (von Korff Chronic pain grade), quality of life (SF-36), spinal mobility in the sagittal and frontal plane and lumbar disc degeneration (Measured by the Pfirrmann Grade) were evaluated, adjusted for the same confounders. Additionally, a sex specific analysis was conducted. Results: A total of 713 patients remained after exclusions, 222 (31.1%) without LBP and 491 (68.9%) with cLBP, with a mean age of 41.9 (SD 12.1). In the propensity score matching, 216 no LBP patients could be matched with 216 suffering from cLBP. No significant difference in FI (p = 0.377) nor fCSA (p = 0.922) of the QL could be observed. In the cLBP group, significant associations were found between QL fCSA and lumbar sagittal (β: 2.56, p < 0.001) and frontal (β: 1.92, p = 0.019) mobility as well as disc degeneration at the L4/5 and L5/S1 level (β: -0.15, p = 0.006 and β: -0.17, p = 0.009) after accounting for confounders. Sex specific subgroup analysis demonstrated a stronger association of these findings in females, as well as an association with the physical component score of the SF-36 (β: 1.93, p = 0.021). Effect sizes for the associations ranged from small to moderate (η2 = 0.014 - 0.033). Conclusion: Although QL morphology did not differ between individuals with and without chronic low back pain, it was significantly associated with spinal mobility and lumbar disc degeneration within the symptomatic group, with more pronounced effects in females. Given that these associations were of low to moderate strength, the QL likely plays a modulatory rather than causal role in cLBP. In this physically active population, functional assessments may provide added value beyond imaging, particularly as functional impairments can precede morphological changes.

RF146: Epidural spinal cord stimulation for restoration of cardiovascular and respiratory function in chronic spinal cord injury: a systematic review

Arash Ghaffari-Rafi 1 , Gabriel Urreolla 1 , Jose Castillo 1

1 University of California, Davis, Sacramento, United States

Introduction: Spinal cord injury (SCI) often results in severe autonomic and respiratory dysfunction, including orthostatic hypotension, impaired cardiac output, ventilator dependence, and ineffective cough. Conventional management options are frequently inadequate. Epidural spinal cord stimulation (ESCS) has recently emerged as a neuromodulatory intervention capable of restoring both cardiovascular and respiratory function in individuals with chronic SCI. Material and Methods: We conducted a systematic review of published studies from 1994 to 2025 encompassing 34 participants across 10 investigations. Twenty-four participants were included in studies evaluating cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes, while 10 participants were included in studies assessing respiratory outcomes. Stimulation was delivered via lumbosacral or thoracic electrode arrays, and outcomes measured included cardiovascular regulation, metabolic adaptations, ventilator independence, and cough restoration. Results: Across cardiovascular studies, ESCS consistently normalized blood pressure regulation, providing complete relief of orthostatic hypotension in all affected participants (6/6, 100%) while producing no aberrant responses in those without hypotension. Additional benefits included improved heart rate variability, stroke volume preservation, exercise tolerance, and favorable metabolic changes such as increased lower limb lean mass, elevated resting metabolic rate, and reduced body fat. Respiratory studies demonstrated that combined intercostal and diaphragm stimulation enabled up to 24 hours/day of ventilator independence in patients with high cervical SCI, while also improving speech, mobility, comfort, and quality of life. Thoracic stimulation (T9-T11) restored cough reflex, improved secretion clearance, reduced respiratory infections, and in some cases eliminated the need for suctioning. Reported side effects were generally mild and included transient autonomic dysreflexia, localized discomfort, and brief hemodynamic fluctuations. Conclusion: ESCS reliably restores cardiovascular stability, promotes ventilator independence, and improves airway clearance in individuals with chronic SCI, with additional systemic benefits. These findings highlight ESCS as a promising therapeutic modality to enhance independence, reduce secondary complications, and improve quality of life in SCI patients. Larger controlled trials are warranted to validate long-term efficacy and optimize stimulation protocols.

RF149: A signal transducing covalently bound peptide coating for titanium spine implants

Joseph Hudson 1 , Samuel Adida 1 , Andrew Legarreta 1 , Nitin Agarwal 1 , George Hussey 1 , Joseph Maroon 1 , Haito Liu 2

1 University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, United States,

2 University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, United States

RF150: A quality improvement project assessing the quality of metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) referrals from peripheral sites to the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital against NICE guidance

Shams Ali Baig 1 , Youssef Sadek 1 , Sarah Shammout 2 , Adrian Gardner 2

1 Medical School, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom, 2 The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, Birmingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) is an oncological emergency affecting up to 10% of cancer patients. Timely recognition and urgent surgical decompression in suitable patients are critical to prevent irreversible neurological damage and preserve functional outcomes. However, inadequate referrals lacking critical clinical, oncological, and radiological information often preclude surgical decision-making. This necessitates re-referral, prolonging the time to definitive treatment and thus increasing the risk of neurological decline. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in the UK recently updated its MSCC guidelines [NG234], emphasising the importance of adequate referral documentation to facilitate rapid decision-making on surgical suitability. Outcomes of interest were referral quality, defined as the inclusion of the key factors needed in an adequate referral as outlined in NG234, and referral to surgical decision time. Results: A total of 164 patients were included (pre-NG234: n = 79; post-NG234: n = 85). The most significant delays were attributable to absent or delayed CT/MRI, often linked to uncertainty over required imaging, procedural bottlenecks, and transfer inefficiencies. A standardised referral proforma has since been introduced to mandate inclusion of essential variables and imaging type. Future work will focus on educational interventions for referring centres and advocating for region-wide standardisation of referral systems to minimise delays and improve neurological outcomes.

RF152: Beyond PROMs: smartphone-derived walking tests as objective markers of recovery after spine surgery

Jani Puhakka 1 , Manuel Jung 1 , Tamas Fekete 1 , Markus Loibl 1 , Frank Kleinstuck 1 , Francois Porchet 1 , Mario Ropelato 1 , Maja Gocević 1 , Fabio Galbusera 2 , Andrea Cina 2 , Dave O'Riordan 2 , Jussi Kosola 3 , Daniel Haschtmann 1

1 Department of Spine Surgery, Spine Center, Schulthess Clinic, Zürich, Switzerland, 2 Department of Teaching, Research and Development, Schulthess Klinik, Zürich, Switzerland, Zürich, Switzerland, 3 Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, University of Helsinki, Helsinki, Finland, Helsinki, Finland

Introduction: Recovery after spine surgery is traditionally measured by patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), which reflect perceived disability but are subjective and prone to recall and observer bias. Objective assessments of functional capacity (e.g., 6-minute walk test) and performance (e.g., daily steps) provide complementary perspectives, yet usually require active testing or specialized devices. Modern smartphones continuously and automatically record mobility data in daily life. Because patients are unaware of data collection, automatically collected data can mitigate the Hawthorne effect and provide an unobtrusive and unbiased view of recovery. This study examined the feasibility, variability, and discriminative power of smartphone-derived short-interval walking tests compared with daily step counts. Material and Methods: Forty-one consecutive patients undergoing lumbar decompression or discectomy were identified at 6-week follow-up. Activity data were retrospectively exported from the iPhone Health app. A custom-designed analysis script identified the maximum distance walked in any 1-minute (1MWT) and 6-minute (6MWT) interval each day using a sliding-window approach. Daily step counts and active time were extracted in parallel. Four intervals were prespecified: (i) preoperative baseline (6 months), (ii) preoperative last 2 weeks, (iii) early postoperative (0-2 weeks), and (iv) late postoperative (2-6 weeks). Paired differences were tested for normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test. Normally distributed outcomes were compared with paired t-tests; non-normal outcomes with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. To control family-wise error, p-values were adjusted using the Simes-Hochberg procedure (significance: adjusted p < 0.05). Variability was quantified as the coefficient of variation (CV = 100 × SD/mean). Results are reported as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR, 25th-75th percentile). Results: The 1MWT declined from 98 meters (71-126) at baseline to 82 meters (68-97) preoperatively (p < 0.05), partially recovered early postoperatively (82 m; 62-114), and exceeded baseline by 2-6 weeks (105 meters; 71-145; p < 0.05 vs. preoperative). The 6MWT showed a similar course: 403 meters (309-489) at baseline, 345 meters (288-391) preoperatively, 340 meters (249-444) early postoperatively, and 407 meters (287-554) at 2-6 weeks (p < 0.05). Step counts decreased significantly from 5030 (3390-7366) to 3825 (2091-5390) preoperatively (p < 0.05), remained reduced early postoperatively (3177; 1568-5659), and rose to 5538 (2073-9047) by 2-6 weeks (p < 0.05). Variability was lowest for the 1MWT and 6MWT (CV 40-50%), compared with steps and active time (CV > 60%). Conclusion: Automatically collected smartphone data allow unbiased assessment of recovery after spine surgery by circumventing the Hawthorne effect. Short-interval walking tests (1MWT, 6MWT) derived from these data show lower variability than step counts and more reliably reflect functional capacity, while step counts capture everyday performance. This novel approach introduces a scalable, objective paradigm to complement PROMs in spine surgery outcomes research.

RF153: Semi-automated end-to-end quality control system for annotation data based on automated Cobb angle measurement

Jingxi Su 1,2,3 , Guilin Chen 1,2,3 , Jianguo Zhang 1,2,3 , Nan Wu 1,2,3

1 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Peking Union Medical College and Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Beijing, People’s Republic of China, Bejing, China, 2 Key Laboratory of Big Data for Skeletal Deformities, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Beijing, People’s Republic of China, Bejing, China, 3 Beijing Key Laboratory of Big Data Innovation and Application for Skeletal Health Medical Care, Beijing, People’s Republic of China, Bejing, China

Introduction: The advancement of AI models for automated Cobb angle measurement in scoliosis is critically limited by the scarcity of high-quality, large-scale annotated datasets. Current annotation workflows lack systematic quality control (QC), leading to substantial subjective variability, inefficiency, and high costs. To address this, we developed a Semi-Automated End-to-End QC (SAE-QC) System to ensure annotation accuracy and consistency, thereby enabling robust AI development. Material and Methods: We proposed the SAE-QC System, comprising three core modules: 1) a Data Assignment Module implementing a dual-blind annotation mechanism pairing medically-trained and lay annotators; 2) an Annotation Protocol QC Module enforcing standardized guidelines through structured validation; and 3) an Annotation QC Module performing comprehensive checks, including format validation, outlier detection, and multi-annotator consistency analysis. The system was evaluated on a dataset of 1,126 full-spine radiographs. A control group (n = 469) followed traditional annotation without systematic QC, while an experimental group (n = 657) utilized the full SAE-QC system. Annotation tasks included vertebral segmentation and Cobb angle measurement. Results: Implementation of the SAE-QC system dramatically enhanced annotation quality. The abnormality rate for Cobb angle measurement decreased from 66% to 19%, and measurement consistency improved by approximately 40%. For vertebral segmentation, the abnormality rate dropped from 27% to 2.9%, with a significant increase in overall accuracy. The system effectively minimized annotator subjectivity and improved the reliability of the annotated dataset. Conclusion: The SAE-QC system successfully combines automated QC with expert supervision to create an efficient, reliable, and end-to-end annotation framework. It demonstrates that non-specialist teams can produce high-quality annotations under a structured QC pipeline, providing a practical solution for building large-scale, reliable datasets essential for training trustworthy AI models in spinal deformity analysis.

RF154: Defining the gaps in transitional care for pediatric spine patients into adulthood

Daisy Lu 1,2 , Zhi Wang 1,2 , Marie-Frederique Letourneau 1 , Eileen Ou 2,3 , Gabrielle Boileau 1 , Monique Clar 2 , Jesse Shen 1,2

1 University of Montreal, Montreal, Canada,

2 Centre Hospitalier de l'Universite de Montreal, Montreal, Canada,

3 Sherbrooke University, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Transition from paediatric to adult care is a vulnerable period for youth with chronic conditions, yet their effectiveness in spine pathologies is understudied. Spine specialties lack structured, evidence-based standardized transition programs compared to their medical and surgical counterparts. We explore the structure and outcomes of transition programs for pediatric surgical spine patients, revealing key gaps and guiding future standardization efforts. Material and Methods: The databases MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science and CINAHL were searched from January 2000 to August 2025 without language restriction for studies that addressed transfer programs from pediatric to adult healthcare system across surgical conditions. This review was conducted in accordance with a previously published protocol. Results: The initial search strategy resulted in 9821 studies of which 17 were specific to orthopedics and 48 to neurosurgery. Primary spine diseases include achondroplasia (n = 1), lumbosacral dysraphism (n = 1), myelomeningocele (n = 1), scoliosis (n = 1), skeletal dysplasias (n = 1) and spina bifida (n = 10). Diseases that can affect the spine secondarily include Marfan syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta, multiple osteochondroma, juvenile idiopathic arthritis and malignant tumors of the musculoskeletal system. There are no standard transition programs specific to spine patients. General transition tools include TRxANSITION, Ready Steady Go Transition program, Am I ON TRAC for Adult Care Questionnaire (ON TRAC), ‘On Your Own Feet Transfer Experiences Scale’ (OYOF-TES), Successful Transition to Adulthood with Therapeutics (STARx), ADolescent Assessment of Preparation for Transition (ADAPT) and the Socio-ecological Model of Adolescent/Young Adult Readiness for Transition (SMART). The general themes of these transition programs include self-management and independence measures in terms of knowledge (health condition, medication, quality of life, threshold to seek medical help) and healthcare communication (asking questions, personal advocacy, scheduling appointments and attending appointments) with an added scale for transition satisfaction. Current recommendations include adapting these tools into transition milestones guidelines more specific to spinal conditions. Suggested transition structures include the presence of a dedicated transition coordinator, early assessment of transition readiness and independence skills; timely adult follow-up with the collaboration of pediatric and adult spine team; individualized plan with summary of diagnosis, surgeries, devices, future risks, anticipated adult outcomes and emergency plan with red flags identification. Because pediatric spine pathologies differ from adult ones, a tailored transition plan is essential to ensure seamless continuity of care with adult specialists who may be less familiar with these conditions. Long term health outcomes of pediatric spine conditions should be leveraged to establish the guidelines of appropriate care. Conclusion: Transition programs are increasingly recognized as essential to ensure continuity of care from paediatric to adult health services. The findings of this review may provide guidance for transition programs guideline development.

RF155: Role of artificial intelligence (AI) tools for clinical research in spine surgery: how accurate and reliable are these?

Riaz Mohammed 1 , Pranav Shah 2

1 Gloucestershire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Gloucester, United Kingdom, 2 Namaha Specialised Healthcare Hospital, Mumbai, India

Introduction: AI has potentially tremendous applications in medical research, with its access to vast array of clinical information resources. However, the reliability and validity of such resources has recently been under scrutiny in other clinical fields. We analysed the use of publicly available Chat Generative Pretrained Transformer (ChatGPT) artificial intelligence language model too for the accuracy and validity of clinical resources used in responding to a research query pertaining to spine surgery. Material and Methods: ChatGPT IOS version was utilised to generate a summary review for the research question: “serum calcium levels and impact on outcomes of anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF)”. A systematic search was conducted by ChatGPT following PRISMA guidelines in PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases up to July 2024. Studies that reported serum calcium measurements in relation to ACDF outcomes, bone healing, or postoperative complications were included. Two independent reviewers analysed the accuracy of the reference publications used by ChatGPT for the systematic review and graded these as non-existent, inaccurate or accurate references. Results: None of the 9 articles included for analyses were existent either in PubMed or Google Scholar searches. None of the titles of these publications were existent in the same pattern, nor did any of the list of authors exist. ChatGPT had generated PRISMA flow diagram used to document the study selection process, and also details of individual studies including sample sizes and fusion rates. Though the key findings and conclusion of this AI generated review mentioned correlation between surgical fusion and serum calcium levels, these seemed to have been derived from non-existent publications. Conclusion: ChatGPT cannot be used in its current state to support any scientific generation of clinical research based on the fictitious and fabricated research articles these are generated from. Similar to in other specialities, in spinal surgery medical information sought through artificial intelligence language tools such as ChatGPT may not be fully accurate nor dependable. Clinicians and patients must exercise due diligence when relying on scientific information obtained in this manner for clinical information and decision making.

RF156: Research on optimal temperature control in robotic autonomous laminectomy

Zhuofu Li 1 , Weishi Li 1

1 peking university third hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Traditional spinal robots have primarily been limited to assisting with pedicle screw placement, often only providing positional guidance while relying on surgeons to perform the actual operation. This significantly restricts its clinical application. Our team has developed an autonomous laminectomy robot that expands the indications for robotic surgery into the field of laminectomy while elevating the level of automation by enabling fully autonomous robotic operation. Preliminary studies have demonstrated that this robot can perform precise laminectomies according to pre-planned resection boundaries and stop immediately upon breaching the lamina to avoid neural damage. However, even if the robot does not directly contact neural tissues, excessively high temperatures generated during bone cutting may still cause indirect thermal injury to nerves. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the thermal safety of robotic laminectomy procedures by examining temperature fluctuations in the inner cortical bone layer during operation and determining the optimal cutting method to minimize the risk of thermal damage to neural structures. Material and Methods: A laminectomy robotic system was utilized to perform cutting on polyurethane artificial bone blocks and ex vivo animal spinal bones using an ultrasonic bone scalpel. The maximum temperatures on the inner surface of the polyurethane blocks were compared and analyzed across three different cutting techniques: vertical constant-speed cutting at 0.5 mm/s, vertical constant-speed cutting at 1 mm/s, and vertical reciprocating cutting. Based on the initial results, the two optimal vertical cutting methods were selected for subsequent experiments on ex vivo animal spinal bones. Ten ex vivo porcine spinal specimens were selected to assess the maximum temperature on the inner surface of the lamina under different ultrasonic bone-cutting modes. Results: When cutting the polyurethane bone blocks, the reciprocating cutting method resulted in a lower maximum temperature compared to constant-speed cutting at both 0.5 mm/s and 1 mm/s. In the ex vivo animal spinal bone experiments, the average maximum temperature for constant-speed cutting was 43.25°C with an average cutting time of 688.3 s, whereas for reciprocating cutting, the average maximum temperature was 34.20°C with an average cutting time of 713.0 s. Conclusion: Employing a reciprocating cutting strategy in robot-assisted laminectomy effectively reduces heat generation on the inner surface of the lamina while maintaining high cutting efficiency.

RF157: Randomized trial of protein supplementation and resistance training for improving spinal alignment and frailty in community-dwelling adults

Shin Oe 1 , Yu Yamato 1 , Miwako Niwa 2 , Yuki Murakami 1 , Koichiro Ide 1 , Yosuke Shibata 1 , Yusuke Murakami 1 , Tomohiko Hasegawa 1 , Go Yoshida 1 , Tomohiro Banno 1 , Hideyuki Arima 1 , Tomohiro Yamada 1 , Yukihiro Matsuyama 1

1 Hamamatsu University School of Medicine, Hamamatsu, Japan, 2 Toei Clinic, Toei, Japan

Introduction: Adult spinal deformity reduces health-related quality of life by causing sagittal imbalance. Although protein supplementation combined with resistance training is known to enhance muscle strength, its influence on spinal alignment remains uncertain. Material and Methods: In this randomized controlled trial, 90 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older were randomized to either an intervention group (n = 45) or a control group (n = 45). Participants in the intervention group performed lower-limb resistance training three times per week and consumed a protein-containing nutritional supplement (9 g, twice daily). Primary outcomes included knee extension strength, frailty status assessed by the Cardiovascular Health Study criteria, and whole-spine radiographic parameters measured at 3 and 6 months. Results: After accounting for dropouts, 44 participants in the intervention group and 42 in the control group (mean age 72 years) completed follow-up. Both groups improved in knee extension strength, but the intervention group showed greater gains (0.70 → 0.82 vs. 0.74 → 0.79 kgf/weight; p < 0.001). Frailty prevalence improved significantly in the intervention group (26 robust/18 pre-frail to 36/8) compared with controls (24/18 to 29/13; p = 0.033). The sagittal vertical axis remained stable in the control group (31 → 26 mm) but decreased significantly in the intervention group (32 → 23 mm; p = 0.001). Conclusion: Protein supplementation combined with resistance training improved muscle strength, frailty status, and sagittal alignment within 3 months. These findings indicate that such interventions may serve as a non-surgical strategy for managing adult spinal deformity.

RF158: The effect of L4 Tilt on in-brace correction in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis treated with the Rigo System Chêneau Brace

Kayra Barut 1 , Bedirhan Albayrak 2 , Altan Aksu 2 , Hüseyin Sina Coşkun 3

1 İzmir EMOT Hospital, İzmir, Turkey, 2 Samsun Training and Research Hospital, Samsun, Turkey, 3 Ondokuz Mayıs University, Samsun, Turkey

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a three-dimensional spinal deformity in which bracing is the mainstay of conservative management. In-brace correction (IBC) has been recognized as one of the strongest predictors of brace success. However, the potential role of lumbosacral alignment parameters, particularly L4 tilt, in influencing IBC remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between L4 tilt and in-brace correction in AIS patients treated with the Rigo System Chêneau (RSC) brace. Material and Methods: Following institutional review board approval, the records of AIS patients treated between January 2021 and January 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. A total of 79 patients 75.9% female, mean age 13.26 ± 1.55 years) who met the inclusion criteria were analyzed. Demographic variables, menarche status, Risser and Sanders stages, and curve patterns were recorded. Radiological parameters included Cobb angles, L4 tilt, and lumbopelvic relation (LPR). In-brace radiographs were obtained 1 month after brace application, and IBC was calculated as the percentage reduction in Cobb angle. Patients were also stratified into two groups based on L4 tilt (≤ 10° vs. > 10°). Statistical analyses were performed using Student’s t-test and Pearson’s correlation, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Results: In total, 79 patients were included, of whom 75.9% were female (n = 60) and 24.1% were male (n = 19), with a mean age of 13.26 ± 1.55 years (range, 10.2-15.9). The mean height and weight were 162.09 ± 8.96 cm (range, 135-181) and 49.17 ± 10.88 kg (range, 30-90), respectively, with a mean BMI of 18.64 ± 3.54 (range, 14.1-35.5). Menarche had occurred in 75% (n = 48) of female patients, with a mean menarcheal age of 12.96 ± 6.63 years. The mean thoracic and lumbar Cobb angles were 30.0° ± 7.4 and 29.9° ± 5.7, respectively. The mean L4 tilt was 13.05° ± 5.85, while the mean LPR was 11.82° ± 5.77. The mean lumbar IBC was 53.8% ± 21.5, and the thoracic IBC was 50.5% ± 21.0. L4 tilt demonstrated a significant negative correlation with both lumbar IBC (r = -0.299, p=0.017) and thoracic IBC (r = -0.449, p = 0.003). Similarly, LPR correlated negatively with lumbar IBC (r = -0.337, p = 0.008) and thoracic IBC (r = -0.507, p = 0.001). When stratified, patients with L4 tilt ≤ 10° achieved significantly higher lumbar IBC (66.8% vs. 50.4%, p = 0.013) and thoracic IBC (58.8% vs. 39.6%, p = 0.002) compared to those with L4 tilt > 10°. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that increased L4 tilt is significantly associated with reduced in-brace correction, independent of curve location. Along with LPR, L4 tilt emerged as a negative predictor of IBC. These findings suggest that baseline L4 tilt should be considered when evaluating brace candidates and may help refine prognostic models for bracing outcomes in AIS.

RF159: Remote supervision in microscope-assisted surgery - A clinical implementation and non-inferiority study

Chan Hee Koh 1,2,3 , Mohammed Al Habib 1,2,4 , emily purvis 1,2 , David Choi 1,2 , Thomas Doke 2 , Felix Josza 5 , Imran Haq 2 , Parag Sayal 2 , Danail Stoyanov 6 , George Prezerakos 1,2,3 , Hani Marcus 1,2

1 Department of Translational Neuroscience, UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, London, United Kingdom, 2 Victor Horsley Department of Neurosurgery, National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London, United Kingdom, 3 Neurosciences Institute, Cleveland Clinic London, london, United Kingdom, 4 Qatif Central Hospital, Qatif, Saudi Arabia, 5 National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, london, United Kingdom, 6 Department of Computer Science, UCL Hawkes Institute., london, United Kingdom

Introduction: Spinal surgery is widely performed to treat degenerative disease, relieving pain and disability but carrying risks of neurological injury and high indemnity costs. Surgical outcomes are strongly linked to surgeon experience and operative volume, underscoring the importance of effective training. Conventional face-to-face supervision remains the standard, yet limited senior availability often restricts trainee autonomy. Telementoring offers real-time video, audio and annotation and is established in laparoscopic surgery, where procedures are inherently screen-based. In contrast, microscope-assisted spinal surgery poses distinct challenges, as the microscope is bulky, equipment-intensive and not naturally screen-dependent. This study evaluated early implementation of remote supervision for microscope-assisted degenerative spine surgery, testing non-inferiority against conventional supervision. Material and Methods: A prospective consecutive cohort was conducted at a tertiary neurosurgical centre. Five attending surgeons and their fellows or residents performed anterior cervical, posterior cervical and posterior lumbar procedures; revision cases were excluded. Midway through the study, remote supervision was introduced using a secure livestream platform transmitting the microscope feed with two-way audio and annotation. All cases were analysed on an intention-to-treat basis. Outcomes were complication rates, operative time, clinical improvement, length of stay and trainee operative proportion. Bayesian non-inferiority models adjusted for surgeon, procedure type and levels treated. Continuous safety monitoring used cumulative sum analysis, and structured feedback guided refinements. Results: Fifty procedures were included with comparable demographics and case mix. Trainee participation was preserved: fellows and residents completed 42.6% of operative time with remote supervision versus 40.5% with face-to-face, with a posterior probability of non-inferiority > 99.9%. Supervisors valued communication, situational awareness and anatomical annotation, though annotation was one-way due to sterility. CUSUM monitoring detected no negative control limit breaches in remote supervision cases. Adjusted complication rates were 4.1% with remote versus 22.3% without (99.1% probability of non-inferiority). Operating time was slightly longer (142.4 vs 130.8 minutes). Patient-centred outcomes showed moderate support: clinical improvement (78.6% vs 85.5%) and length of stay (5.0 vs 4.4 days) yielded posterior probabilities of 60.8% and 62.0%, reflecting small numerical differences between groups and the early stage of implementation. Feedback highlighted advantages (stable image, audiovisual communication, annotation) and limitations (gaze shift, short annotation duration, lack of stereoscopy, connectivity instability, suboptimal audio). Suggested refinements included wireless headsets, improved microphones and sterile covers for closer screen placement. Conclusion: Early implementation of remote supervision for microscope-assisted degenerative spine surgery was feasible and safe, with high probability of non-inferior in complication rates and trainee operative volume. These findings support remote supervision as a promising adjunct to training. Future priorities include user interface optimisation, improved audiovisual capability and multicentre evaluation to refine indications and broaden adoption.

RF160: Intramedullary lesion length is a robust imaging biomarker in predicting presenting motor and functional scores amongst acute traumatic central cord syndrome patients

A Aravin Kumar 1 , Linda Lim Huiling 1 , Shane Zaw 2 , Qingping Joseph Feng 1 , Damian Lee 1,2,3 , Dinesh Shree Kumar 2 , Lester Lee 1,2,3 , Robin Pillay 1 , Ji Min Ling 1,2

1 Department of Neurosurgery, National Neuroscience Institute, Singapore, Singapore,

2 Department of Neurosurgery, Changi General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore,

3 Department of Neurosurgery, Singapore General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Acute traumatic central cord syndrome (ATCCS) has been reported to be the most common form of acute, incomplete spinal cord injury. Much has been published about ATCCS but this data is predominantly from North America, and the generalizability of these recommendations to Asian populations are still under investigation. The use of imaging biomarkers has been shown to correlate with motor recovery and has been purported to prognosticate recovery. In the literature, intramedullary lesion length has been found to be a useful imaging biomarker. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study in two tertiary specialist centers in Singapore from 2010 to 2023. We included all adult patients diagnosed with ATCCS. Exclusion criteria include the lack of outcome data on discharge or on follow-up, atraumatic causes of central cord syndrome, presence of concomitant neurological pathologies which may confound neurological findings and/or recovery, such as demyelinating polyneuropathies or cranial pathologies. Imaging biomarkers were measured on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans on admission. Multivariate linear regression was performed to ascertain the relationship of imaging biomarkers with presenting motor and functional scores. Results: One-hundred-and-sixteen patients were included in our study. The mean age was 64.7 (SD: 12.9) years, and 100 (86.2%) patients were male. Twenty-three (19.8%) patients had ossification of posterior ligament (OPLL) and 102 (87.9%) patients had pre-existing cervical spondylosis with stenosis. Nine (7.8%) patients required assistance with their activities of daily living (ADLs) on admission and 16 (13.8%) presented with a high impact injury. Sixty-five (56.0%) of patients underwent operative management, with the median time to operation being 4.0 (IQR: 10.0) days. The median American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Motor Score (AMS) on admission was 85.0 (IQR: 25.8) with the median upper extremity motor score (UEMS) being 37.5 (IQR: 18.0) and median lower extremity motor score (LEMS) being 50.0 (IQR: 10.0). Median Functional independence measure (FIM) on admission was 76.0 (IQR: 53.0) and median modified Japanese Orthopedic Association (mJOA) score on admission was 10.0 (IQR: 7.8). The mean spinal canal diameter at the level of stenosis was 6.3mm (SD 1.9) and the mean spinal cord diameter at the level of stenosis was 5.2mm (SD 1.4). The mean mid-sagittal diameter of the spinal canal on the mid-sagittal scans was 9.0mm (SD 1.1), the mean maximum canal compromise was 84.8 (SD 4.6) and the mean maximum spinal cord compression was 80.0 (SD 5.5). The mean intramedullary lesion length on MRI was 21.6mm (SD 18.3). Multivariate analysis showed that intramedullary lesion was negatively correlated (Beta -0.2, 95% CI -0.5 - 0.0, p = 0.027) with AMS on presentation, was negatively correlated (Beta -0.2, 95% CI -0.3 - 0.0, p = 0.025) with upper extremity motor score on presentation and was also negatively correlated (Beta -0.2, 95% CI -0.1 - 0.0, p = 0.017) with mJOA on presentation. No imaging biomarkers were found to correlate with FIM score on admission. Conclusion: In our local Asian population, intramedullary lesion length was found to predict the presenting motor and functional scores well, corroborating the literature about its efficacy as a prognostic tool for ATCCS patients.

RF161: The spine in high definition: continuous monitoring as the gateway to AI in spinal surgery

Grzegorz Miekisiak 1

1 Vratislavia Medica Research Institute, Wroclaw, Poland

Introduction: Progress in spinal care has been hampered by reliance on episodic, subjective patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). These tools produce sparse, low-fidelity data that block the path toward predictive analytics and artificial intelligence. Material and Methods: In a prospective pilot, ten patients undergoing transforaminal steroid injections were monitored continuously for 14 days using Nimbrace™, a novel wearable biomechanical dosimeter. The device quantifies spinal function in vivo by capturing inertial sensor signals at 100 Hz and securely transmitting them to a dedicated analytic platform. For the first time, this approach enabled clinical measurement of Panjabi's Neutral Zone under natural conditions of daily life. Results: Traditional PROMs yielded only two subjective data points per patient across two weeks. In contrast, Nimbrace delivered nearly one billion objective measurements over the same interval. The resulting dynamic “functional fingerprint” revealed subtle fluctuations of stability, recovery, and decompensation - insights invisible to static questionnaires. High patient compliance was observed, driven by the device's real-time feedback and guidance for safe movement. Conclusion: This study demonstrates the feasibility of continuous, objective spinal outcome assessment in real-world settings. Panjabi's Neutral Zone - long a theoretical construct - is now clinically measurable. The shift from episodic opinion-based reporting to continuous high-resolution data collection marks not an incremental advance, but the foundation of a new paradigm: evidence robust enough to fuel personalized therapies and unlock the era of artificial intelligence in spine medicine. This data density enables novel clinical services including predictive risk stratification, personalized rehabilitation protocols, and AI-driven decision support systems that could transform both clinical outcomes and healthcare economics in spinal care.
