RF162: Mentorship metrics: spine insights from AO Access (2022-2025)

Maria Celeste Zamora 1 , Waeel Hamouda 2

1 Hospital Médico Policial Churruca Visca, Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2 Security Forces Hospital Dammam, Dammam, Saudi Arabia

Introduction: Mentorship is recognized as a critical driver of professional development, career advancement, and inclusion within surgical education. Since 2022, the AO Access Mentoring Program has utilized the MentorCity platform to connect participants across AO’s clinical divisions. This abstract presents an analysis of participation patterns and demographics, with a focus on AO Spine, compared to the other divisions. Material and Methods: Data were extracted from MentorCity across the pilot (2022), cohort 1 (2023), and cohort 2 (2024). Variables included number of participants, completion rates of mentoring relationships, gender, age distribution, clinical division, and role (mentor/mentee). Subgroup analysis was conducted for AO Spine and compared to other divisions (AO Trauma, AO Recon, AO CMF, AO VET, AO ORP). Results: A total of 468 participants were included. AO Spine accounted for 80 participants, making it the second-largest group after AO Trauma (171). Thirteen completed Spine mentoring relationships were documented, comparable to AO Trauma (13) and AO Recon (15), and higher than AO CMF (8), AO VET (4), and AO ORP (3). Gender distribution in AO Spine remains low, aligning with the underrepresentation of women reported in the 2019 ODI survey. Age distribution demonstrated that Spine participants were broadly spread across career stages but tended to be younger on average than Trauma, suggesting greater mentorship needs earlier in their careers. Analysis of mentor/mentee roles indicated that most AO Spine participants entered as mentees, with a smaller but consistent pool of mentors. Regional data revealed wide geographic representation among Spine participants, consistent with AO’s global reach. Conclusion: The AO Access Mentoring Program demonstrates strong engagement across all AO divisions, with AO Spine emerging as a particularly active and diverse contributor. Given that AO Spine has historically been underrepresented in terms of women and especially in leadership positions, these results show that structured mentorship provides access to networks, mentors, and mentees who are usually underrepresented. Compared to other divisions, AO Spine showed high levels of participation, relationship completion, and balanced demographic representation. These findings highlight the program’s potential for fostering professional development, equity, and inclusion within AO Spine and across the AO community.

RF163: Pedicle screw distribution in Lenke type 1 adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: does it influence coronal and sagittal parameters?

Paolo Brigato 1 , Sergio De Salvatore 1,2 , Leonardo Oggiano 2 , Davide Palombi 3 , Sergio Sessa 2 , Pier Francesco Costici 2

1 University Hospital Campus Bio-Medico of Rome, Rome, Italy, 2 Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital, Palidoro, Italy, 3 Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS, Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Rome, Italy

Introduction: Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) affects approximately 3% of adolescents, with Lenke type 1 curves accounting for 40% of cases. Surgical intervention is typically recommended for curves greater than 40-45°. While low-density (LD) constructs have shown comparable radiological outcomes to high-density (HD) constructs, they offer notable benefits, including shorter surgery times, reduced blood loss, and a lower risk of neurological complications. However, there is no definitive evidence suggesting that LD constructs provide superior radiographic correction. This study aims to assess how the distribution of pedicle screws influences both short- and long-term coronal and sagittal parameters in AIS patients with Lenke type 1 curves. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study analyzed 86 AIS patients with Lenke type 1 curves (≤80°), treated between 2019 and 2022, and followed for a minimum of two years. All patients underwent posterior-only all screw (AS) surgery. Coronal and sagittal radiographic parameters, including apical vertebra translation (AVT), thoracic kyphosis (TK), lumbar lordosis (LL), and thoracic trunk shift (TTS), were assessed at discharge, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and annually thereafter. The study focused on screw distribution and its effect on curve correction. Exclusion criteria included patients with neuromuscular, syndromic, or congenital scoliosis; those younger than 10 or older than 20 years; other Lenke-type curves; a major thoracic curve > 80°; hook or hybrid constructs; patients who received preoperative traction, two-stage surgery or prior spinal surgeries. Statistical analysis was performed using RStudio, Chi-Squared, and Wilcoxon tests, with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Results: The average implant density was 1.64 screws per fused level (range: 1.1-2). The convex side of the spine was more frequently instrumented, particularly in the periapical regions (62% vs. 52% in the upper zone, 61% vs. 51% in the lower zone), as well as the apical zone (80% vs. 50%). The density of screws in the concave apical region positively influenced curve correction (p = 0.035). Screws placed in the periapical regions had the most significant effect on AVT and TK, while LL was significantly influenced by screws in the concave apical and lower periapical zones. Conclusions: This study underscores the potential advantages of screw placement on the concave side, especially at the apex of the curve, for improving curve correction in AIS patients with Lenke type 1 curves. The findings suggest that optimizing screw distribution, particularly in the apical and periapical regions, may enhance surgical outcomes and patient recovery. Future studies may further refine these strategies to improve the long-term results of spinal deformity correction.

RF164: Effect of pedicle morphology on screw placement method in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis surgery

Mehmet Oktay Gençay 1 , Murat Songur 1

1 Faculty of Medicine Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Specialization Thesis in Medicine, Zonguldak Bülent Ecevit University Zonguldak, Turkey

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is common in society and is among the major surgeries of the orthopedic department. Different techniques are used when placing pedicle screws in patients diagnosed with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Since 3D navigation techniques are expensive and the amount of radiation dose is high, and the free hand technique is based only on experience and knowledge, surgeons He feels the need for intraoperative fluoroscopy. In this study, we tried to reveal where the need for intraoperative fluoroscopy will occur according to the vertebral morphology. Materials and Methods: Our study was planned on the scoliosis surgery of patients diagnosed with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in our clinic. Preoperative computed tomography was taken for these patients and images were prepared. These images were used in the intraoperative process. During the surgery, we started with the free hand technique and fluoroscopy assistance was received if necessary. Basically, the levels that require fluoroscopy are determined. Vertebral morphologies were revealed. Results: 30 patients were included in the study. A total of 657 pedicle screws were placed in 30 patients. We found a relationship between the decrease in pedicle diameter and the need for fluoroscopy with p = 0.00 in the pedicle screws in which we used intraoperative fluoroscopy. We did not find a relationship between the increase in the amount of vertebral rotation and the need for fluoroscopy. This was also determined by intraoperative computerized analysis. We thought it was related to the use of tomography images. Conclusion: We argue that the vertebral morphology obtained by computerized tomography while placing pedicle screws in patients diagnosed with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis will facilitate the surgeon who will perform the procedure, reduce the use of fluoroscopy, improve the surgical time and reduce the amount of complications.

RF165: Risk factors for postoperative shoulder imbalance in patients with Lenke type 1 and 2 scoliosis treated using the vertebral coplanar alignment technique

Arihisa Shimura 1 , Hidetoshi Nojiri 1 , Hiroshi Moridaira 2 , Satoshi Takada 2 , Katsutaka Yamada 3 , Masaki Tomori 4 , Yusuke Murakami 5 , Junya Katayanagi 6 , Koji Akeda 7 , Takuya Nagai 8 , Eiichiro Nakamura 9 , Kazuyuki Otani 10 , Takuya Nikaido 11 , Mikito Tsushima 12 , Hiromitsu Toyoda 13 , Muneaki Ishijima 1 , Hiroshi Taneichi 2

1 Juntendo University, Tokyo, Japan, 2 Dokkyo Medical University, Tochigi, Japan, 3 Yokohama Brain and Spine Center, Kanagawa, Japan, 4 Saiseikai Kawaguchi General Hospital, Saitama, Japan, 5 Ehime University, Ehime, Japan, 6 Dokkyo Medical University Saitama Medical Center, Saitama, Japan, 7 Mie University, Mie, Japan, 8 University of Miyazaki, Miyazaki, Japan, 9 University of Occupational and Environmental Health, Fukuoka, Japan, 10 Kudanzaka Hospital, Tokyo, Japan, 11 Fukushima Medical University, Fukushima, Japan, 12 Konan Kosei Hospital, Aichi, Japan, 13 Osaka Metropolitan University, Osaka, Japan

Introduction: Postoperative shoulder imbalance (PSI) in scoliosis affects patients’ quality of life. Vertebral coplanar alignment (VCA) is a standardized scoliosis correction technique that uses pedicle screws on the convex side of the thoracic spine to align the vertebrae in a single plane and achieve thoracic kyphosis. This technique has demonstrated favorable results and clinical outcomes comparable with those of conventional concave-side correction techniques. While other correction methods have reported a high correction rate for the main thoracic curve (MTC) in relation to PSI, this correlation has not been confirmed for VCA. We investigated the incidence of PSI and its risk factors in patients with Lenke types 1 and 2 scoliosis corrected using VCA. Material and Methods: A total of 176 patients with Lenke type 1 or 2 scoliosis who underwent posterior corrective fusion using the VCA technique at 11 participating institutions were analyzed. At two-year follow-up, patients were devided into two groups according to radiographic shoulder height (RSH): PSI- (RSH < 2 cm) and PSI+ (RSH ≥ 2 cm). Comparative analyses were performed between groups, and multivariate regression was conducted on preoperative and postoperative radiographic parameters to identify independent risk factors for PSI. Results: The overall incidence of PSI two years postoperatively was 11.4% (20/176), with 9.2% (11/119) and 15.8% (9/57) in patients with Lenke types 1 and 2, respectively. Contrary to a previous study, a high MTC correction rate did not emerge as a risk factor for PSI. Instead, preoperative left shoulder elevation (p = 0.003) and low postoperative thoracic kyphosis (p = 0.005) and greater T1 tilt (p = 0.008) and high apical vertebral body-to-rib ratio (p = 0.001) were associated with PSI in patients with Lenke type 1. Preoperative left shoulder elevation (p = 0.019) and a low postoperative proximal thoracic curve (PTC) correction rate (p = 0.031) were identified as risk factors for PSI in patients with Lenke type 2. Conclusion: The incidence of PSI following VCA was lower than that reported for other corrective procedures. This study suggested that proper correction of PTC rather than compromising the correction of the MTC correction may help prevent PSI in the VCA technique. Restoration of physiologic thoracic kyphosis with minimal torsion is particularly advantageous for optimizing postoperative shoulder balance. Patients with preoperative left shoulder elevation, especially those with Lenke type 2 deformities, are at heightened risk and may benefit from targeted strategies to improve PTC correction. Further research is warranted to elucidate the relationship between PSI and sagittal alignment in Lenke type 1 and to refine approaches for maximizing PTC correction to reduce PSI in Lenke type 2.

RF166: Selective instrumentation techniques for pediatric scoliosis: a retrospective case series

Jorge Parra Lojan 1 , Patricia Estrella Monge 2 , Santiago Chaves Calderón 2 , Luis Espín Villamarín 1

1 Baca Ortiz Public Hospital, Quito, Ecuador, 2 Universidad San Francisco de Quito, Quito, Ecuador

Introduction: Scoliosis surgery in children and adolescents has progressively evolved from extensive spinal fusions toward more selective and motion-preserving strategies. Traditional long-segment instrumentation, although effective in correcting deformity, is associated with increased morbidity, higher risk of neurological complications, and loss of mobility in unfused spinal segments (Lenke et al., 2018; Newton et al., 2020). Selective instrumentation techniques -including selective thoracic and lumbar fusion, short fusion constructs, the Miladi method for level selection, bipolar instrumentation, low-density constructs, and minimally invasive approaches- have been developed to achieve optimal deformity correction while reducing the number of fused levels. Evidence from recent multicenter and cohort studies has shown that these strategies can achieve comparable radiographic correction and global balance, with decreased operative time, blood loss, and complication rates (Dobbs et al., 2019; Hresko, 2021; Miladi et al., 2022). The core principle is to tailor the surgical strategy to the type, magnitude, and etiology of the curve, thereby minimizing surgical risks, preventing neurological injury, and facilitating a faster recovery with shorter hospital stays. While international literature supports the effectiveness and safety of these techniques, there is limited systematic evidence in Latin America. This retrospective case series presents the experience of applying modern selective instrumentation techniques in pediatric scoliosis patients, contributing regional data to the growing body of evidence on motion-preserving spinal deformity surgery. Methods: This was a retrospective cross-sectional case series including seven pediatric and adolescent patients with scoliosis, each presenting with a different etiology, curve type, and magnitude. All patients were operated on by the same spine surgeon between 2023 and 2025. Surgical techniques applied included: selective thoracic instrumentation, selective lumbar instrumentation, short fusion, Miladi method, bipolar instrumentation, low-density constructs, and minimally invasive approaches. The surgical strategy was individualized according to the curve’s etiology, location, and severity, with the main objective of minimizing the number of fused levels while preserving coronal and sagittal balance.

Variables collected:

• Demographics: age, sex.

• Curve characteristics: etiology, Cobb angle, flexibility.

• Surgical details: technique used, number of fused levels, operative time, intraoperative blood loss.

• Postoperative outcomes: neurological status, perioperative complications, hospital stay.

• Radiographic outcomes: degree of curve correction (Cobb pre- vs. postoperative), coronal and sagittal balance. Analysis: Descriptive statistics were used. Continuous variables were expressed as means, medians, and ranges; categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. All data were anonymized, and the study was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Results: A total of seven pediatric and adolescent patients with scoliosis were included. Each patient presented with a different etiology, curve type, and magnitude, and all underwent selective instrumentation using various techniques (thoracic, lumbar, short fusion, Miladi method, bipolar, low-density, and minimally invasive).

The analysis demonstrated consistent benefits across cases:

• Reduced surgical time compared to conventional long fusions.

• Fewer instrumented levels and a lower number of pedicle screws utilized.

• Decreased intraoperative blood loss.

• Shorter intensive care unit stay and reduced overall hospitalization, with most patients discharged within 3-4 days postoperatively.

• Complication rate: no major neurological events were observed.

Radiographic outcomes:

• Average curve reduction of approximately 40% was achieved in all patients.

• Coronal and sagittal balance was adequately restored and maintained at follow-up.

• Shoulder and pelvic alignment were satisfactory in all cases.

Overall, these techniques allowed for effective deformity correction while minimizing surgical morbidity and optimizing recovery. Conclusions: Selective instrumentation techniques proved to be safe and effective in this series of seven pediatric and adolescent scoliosis patients. They allowed for shorter surgeries, fewer fused levels and screws, less blood loss, shorter hospital stays (3-4 days), and no major neurological complications. Radiographically, an average 40% curve correction was achieved, with adequate coronal/sagittal balance and good shoulder and pelvic alignment.

RF167: Transpedicular screw placement assisted by augmented reality surgical navigation (ARSN) in congenital scoliosis surgery

Patricia Estrella Monge 1 , Santiago Chaves Calderón 2 , Jorge Parra Lojan 3

1 Orthopedics and Traumatology Resident, R4, University San Francisco de Quito. Quito, Ecuador, 2 Orthopedics and Traumatology Resident, R3, University San Francisco de Quito. Quito, Ecuador, 3 Pediatric Spine Orthopedic Surgeon, Baca Ortiz Pediatric Hospital. Quito, Ecuador

Introduction: Transpedicular screw placement is essential for thoracolumbar fusion but carries significant risks due to the proximity of neural and vascular structures. Traditional techniques rely on anatomical landmarks or imaging methods that involve considerable radiation exposure. Augmented Reality Surgical Navigation (ARSN) enhances visualization through intraoperative 3D imaging. It allows surgeons to view an ideal trajectory superimposed in their visual field via a headset, aiming to ensure safety and reduce radiation exposure. Methods: We present a clinical case of a 6-year-old male with congenital scoliosis and a two-year evolution of thoracolumbar spinal deformity. Preoperative imaging showed an altered sagittal axis with a global thoracic kyphosis of 78° and thoracolumbar kyphosis of 72°, caused by a bony block affecting vertebral bodies from T9 to T12. The patient underwent posterior instrumentation and arthrodesis (T7, T8–L1, L2), spinal cord decompression, and Ponte-type osteotomies. ARSN guided the cantilever maneuver and crosslink placement at T12. Results: The surgical time was 240 minutes. The patient retained lower limb mobility, was observed in the ICU for 24 hours, and was discharged on the fourth postoperative day ambulating and with adequate pain tolerance. Postoperative imaging revealed sagittal axis recovery, with a reduction in global thoracic kyphosis to 54° and thoracolumbar kyphosis to 55°. Discussion: ARSN improved surgical field visualization, precision, and safety while minimizing radiation exposure and the need for continuous C-arm imaging. The system shows an overall accuracy of 93.1% in transpedicular screw placement. While the freehand technique is less costly, it carries a higher risk of medial and lateral breaches. However, ARSN's clinical adoption remains in early stages due to initial costs and a learning curve. Conclusions: ARSN demonstrated consistent accuracy in transpedicular screw placement, proving to be a safe and effective technique that improves workflow and minimizes radiation. More robust prospective studies are needed to assess its learning curve and compare it comprehensively with conventional methods. Conflicts of Interest

RF168: Can the LIV be left proximal to the neutral vertebra in Lenke Type 1-3 B/C curves?

Hayati Aygun 1

1 Bursa Medicana Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey

Background: Selection of the lowest instrumented vertebra (LIV) is critical for preventing distal adding-on (AO) and residual curve progression after scoliosis surgery. While extending fusion to the neutral vertebra (NV) is traditionally recommended, stopping proximal to the NV may help preserve motion segments. The safety of this strategy in Lenke type 1-3 B and C curves remains uncertain. Purpose: To evaluate mid-term radiographic and clinical outcomes in patients with Lenke type 1-3 B and C scoliosis when the LIV is intentionally placed proximal to the NV, and to identify intraoperative factors associated with AO or residual curve progression. Methods: A retrospective review was conducted of 34 consecutive patients (mean age: XX ± X years; 26 females, 8 males) who underwent posterior spinal fusion with the LIV proximal to the NV.

- Follow-up: Mean 43 months (range, 24-60).

- Radiographic measurements: Cobb angles, coronal balance, LIV tilt, and disc tilt between the LIV and its immediately proximal vertebra were evaluated preoperatively, postoperatively, and at final follow-up.

- Progression definition: Residual curve increase > 5° or development of distal AO.

- Statistics: Paired t-test and Fisher’s exact test, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Results: Cobb Angles:

- Preoperative: 58 ± 14°

- Postoperative: 11 ± 10°

- Final follow-up: 13 ± 11°

Significant correction was achieved (p < 0.001) with no meaningful loss at final follow-up (p = 0.42).

- Distal AO: Occurred in 3 patients (8.8%), all asymptomatic; no revision surgery was required.

- Spontaneous regression: 8 patients (23.5%) demonstrated spontaneous resolution of residual angulation.

- Stable group: Remaining 23 patients (67.6%) maintained stable residual curves < 5° throughout follow-up.

There were no significant differences in age, preoperative curve magnitude, LIV tilt, or coronal balance between patients with and without AO (p > 0.05). Conclusion: In this cohort, no AO or clinically significant progression occurred when the tilt of the NV, the vertebra proximal to the NV, and the intervening disc was corrected to < 5° intraoperatively. Residual angulations and vertebral tilts below 5° remained stable during mid-term follow-up. These findings suggest that, when horizontalization and coronal balance are precisely achieved, motion segments may be safely preserved by selecting an LIV proximal to the NV in Lenke type 1-3 B and C scoliosis. This < 5° threshold is a conservative technical target and aligns with prior literature linking postoperative LIV tilt and disc angle to AO risk. Keywords: Lenke classification, scoliosis, lowest instrumented vertebra, neutral vertebra, adding-on, coronal balance

RF169: Pioneering apical control in early onset scoliosis: innovations with the active apex correction (APC) technique

Uzair Rashid 1

1 Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan

Background: Early Onset Scoliosis (EOS) requires novel interventions to treat deformity without impairing spinal development and function. Active Apex Correction (APC) is a state-of-the-art non-fusion technique that uses the active tether of the apex of deformity and the dynamic deformity modification with a minimum impact on spinal biomechanics. This paper examines how APC can transform EOS management, its capacity to avoid facet fusion, and maximize long-term outcomes. Materials and Methods: A retrospective study analyzed 30 pediatric EOS patients who were treated using the APC technique in Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan. The patients in the age range of 3-10 years at the time of index surgery were included, and the follow-up was to be at least 18 months. The APC technique employed the use of highly flexible and sophisticated tethering apparatus to treat the apical vertebrae, which will accommodate growth without losing correction. The integrity of the facet joints, vertebral growth, apical vertebral translation (AVT), and Cobb angle repair were measured with high-resolution 3D CT. There were statistical comparisons between convex and concave sides. Results: The cohort had a mean age of 6.8 years at surgery and an average follow-up of 28.5 months (range: 18-48). A total of 150 apical vertebrae (300 facet joints) were analyzed. Facet fusion was observed in only 10% of facets (30/300), with 16 on the convex side and 14 on the concave side (p > 0.05, no significant difference). Non-fused facets maintained a mean joint distance of 1.14 mm (convex) and 1.19 mm (concave) (p > 0.05). Cobb angle correction averaged 65% (from 57° to 20°), and AVT improved by 60% (from 41 mm to 16 mm). Growth preservation was achieved in 94% of cases, with no evidence of crankshaft phenomenon. Conclusion: APC is a revolutionary development in the treatment of EOS that produces strong deformity correction with the least amount of facets fused, and spinal growth is maintained. Its dynamic tethering system, which is innovative and unique, is responsive to the dynamic growth patterns of a child, providing a paradigm shift to the traditional fusion-based systems. The results of this research indicate the possibility of APC transforming the EOS management to minimize complications and increase long-term spinal health.

RF170: Scoliosis surgery and neurophysiological alarms: a 4-year review at a high-complexity pediatric center

Francoise Descazeaux 1 , Diego Alvarez 1,2 , Karen Weissmann 3 , Carlos Huaiquilaf 2,3 , Alvaro Silva 1 , Camila Mora 4 , Ignacio Parra Morales 1,3

1 Hospital Exequiel Gonzalez Cortes, MEDS, Santiago, Chile, 2 Redsalud, Santiago, Chile, 3 MEDS, Santiago, Chile, 4 Hospital Barro Luco Trudeau, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring (IONM) in scoliosis surgery allows the detection and prevention of neurological injuries, using techniques such as motor evoked potentials (MEP) and somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP). Neurophysiological alarms may have surgical, physiological, anesthetic, or technical causes, and their timely identification has reduced the risk of permanent neurological damage. Our objective was to analyze neurophysiological alarms during pediatric scoliosis surgery. Material and Methods: A retrospective descriptive study of patients operated on for scoliosis between 2021 and 2024. Patients with neurophysiological alarms (> 50% decrease in potential amplitude) during neuromonitoring were identified. Epidemiological, radiological, surgical, and clinical variables were evaluated. Statistical analysis was performed using JASP software version 0.95 (IBM, Amsterdam, Netherlands). A descriptive analysis was applied, calculating measures of central tendency (mean and median) and dispersion (standard deviation and range). Results: Of 376 operated patients, 12 (3.19%) presented neurophysiological alarms. The mean age was 14 years (10-18 years), with a predominance of females (67%). The most frequent etiology was idiopathic scoliosis, and 25% corresponded to early-onset scoliosis. The mean Cobb angle was 60°, with a mean kyphosis of 55°. Half of the alarms occurred during instrumentation, 34% during reduction, 8.3% during osteotomy, and 8.3% due to equipment failure. With respect to the type of neurophysiological alert, in 50% of cases the alert was limited to MEPs, while the other 50% involved both MEPs and SSEPs. No cases of isolated SSEP alerts were recorded. A total of 66.7% of patients fully recovered their potentials during surgery, three showed partial recovery, and two showed no intraoperative recovery. The Stagnara Test (wake-up test) was performed in only one patient, because there was no recovery, showing no motor function deficit. Four patients show motor deficit after surgery, two showed total motor function recovery within 24 postoperative hours, and the other two within 72 postoperative hours. A second surgical intervention was required in only one patient. Conclusion: The incidence of neurophysiological alarms in scoliosis surgery was 3%. Intraoperative recovery after standardized interventions reached 66.7%, and postoperative neurological recovery was 100%. Overall, these findings support IONM as a fundamental tool to prevent neurological complications in scoliosis surgery and highlight the need for structured protocols, and systematic follow-up to optimize neurological outcomes in scoliosis surgery.

RF172: Effect of halo gravity traction on deformity angular ratio in severe rigid scoliosis: a clinical analysis with intraoperative neuromonitoring risk correlation

Ahmed Nenaa 1 , Joseph Boktor 1 , Ilijana Zisakis 1 , Morgan Jones 1

1 Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, Birmingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: The Deformity Angular Ratio (DAR) is a validated radiographic parameter used to quantify spinal curve rigidity and predict intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) signal loss in patients with severe scoliosis. Prior studies, including work by Lenke et al., have identified total DAR (T-DAR) values > 25 as predictive of neuromonitoring signal changes during spinal deformity correction. Halo gravity traction (HGT) is commonly used preoperatively to gradually reduce spinal deformity, potentially lowering the risk of neurological compromise during surgery. HGT was introduced to Brimingham children’s hospital (BCH) in the last few years. The aim of this study is to evaluate the efficacy of HGT in reducing DAR values among patients with severe rigid scoliosis and to examine the correlation between changes in DAR and intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) risk. Pre- and post-traction radiographic data were systematically analyzed to quantify changes in DAR metrics achieved through HGT and to evaluate whether these changes correspond to a reduction in predicted intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) risk. Baseline and post-traction DAR measurements - including Cobb Deformity Angular Ratio (C-DAR), Sagittal Deformity Angular Ratio (S-DAR), and Total Deformity Angular Ratio (T-DAR) - were obtained from standing and in-traction radiographs, respectively, prior to definitive posterior spinal fusion. Results: Twelve patients were identified, of whom three were excluded due to incomplete radiographic datasets, leaving nine patients for final statistical analysis. The mean age of the cohort was 14.8 years, and the median time in traction was 25 days (IQR 51). Paired t-tests were used to assess changes in DAR. Following HGT, mean C-DAR improved by 12.1%, S-DAR by 30.3%, and T-DAR by 13.7%. Only the reduction in T-DAR reached statistical significance (p = 0.016), while C-DAR (p = 0.590) and S-DAR (p = 0.379) showed nonsignificant trends. All patients had pre-traction T-DAR values > 25, a threshold linked with increased IONM signal loss. Post-traction, 3 of 9 patients had T-DAR reduced below 25, potentially decreasing their neuromonitoring risk during surgery. Conclusion: HGT was effective in significantly reducing T-DAR in patients with severe rigid scoliosis. Given the known correlation between elevated T-DAR and IONM signal changes, this reduction may lower the risk of intraoperative neurological events. These findings support the use of HGT as a valuable preparatory tool in high-risk spinal deformity cases. Further prospective studies are warranted to validate DAR-based risk stratification and its predictive value for IONM outcomes.

RF173: Behaviour of thoracic curvatures after pectus excavatum and carinatum surgery: a retrospective analysis

Selahaddin Aydemir 1 , Fatma Mutlu 2 , Eren Akin 3 , Emrah Karci 3 , Volkan Karacam 3 , Omer Akcalı 3

Natural history of spinal alignment in thorax deformities and the impact of thoracic surgery on spinal alignment remains unclear. This study retrospectively evaluates changes in upper thoracic (UT) and main thoracic (MT) curvatures following surgical correction in PE and PC patients and analyzes influencing factors. Material and Methods: Between 2008 and 2020, 433 PE and 148 PC patients who underwent surgical correction in the thoracic surgery department were assessed. Surgical correction of chest wall deformities may biomechanically affect spinal alignment through costovertebral junctions.

Joel Turtle 1 , Maisy Webb 1

Introduction: Skeletal maturity is a critical parameter in pediatric orthopedic decision-making. This practice increases cost and radiation exposure for patients and families. Traditional bone age models depend primarily on hand imaging and expert scoring. Conclusion: Chronological age can be accurately predicted from hand radiographs and reasonably estimated from spine imaging using deep learning. RF175: Evaluating the efficacy and safety of halo-femoral traction and halo-gravity traction techniques in severe kyphoscoliosis with spinal cord risk classification (SCRC) type 3 over the apex

Yuan-Shun Lo 1,2 , Erh-Ti Lin 1,2 , Yi-Hsun Huang 1,2 , Yong Qiu 3

1 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, China Medical University Beigang Hospital, China Medical University, Yunlin, Taiwan, 2 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, China Medical University Hospital, China Medical University, Taichung, Taiwan, 3 Division of Spine Surgery, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, Affiliated Hospital of Medical School, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China

The traction contributions were 57.6 ± 11.1% v.s. 52.3 ± 9.3% for major Cobb and 70.1 ± 10.5% v.s. 63.9 ± 11.1% for global kyphosis (GK), respectively. More than half of the total correction can be achieved gradually and safely through preoperative traction with patients in an awake state. RF176: Is the use of ‘shoulder rule’ for selection of upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis associated with improved shoulder parameters and outcomes?

Andrius Anuzis 1 , Sandra Bonczek 1 , Edidiong Essiet 1 , Roozbeh Shafafy 1 , Julian Leong 1 , Sean Molloy 1

1 Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital, London, United Kingdom

Introduction: The “shoulder rule” has been widely advocated for selection of the upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). However, its role in optimizing postoperative shoulder balance has recently been questioned. This study evaluates the association between application of the shoulder rule and radiographic as well as clinical outcomes in AIS, based on institutional experience at a national referral center. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed health records and radiographs of AIS patients who underwent corrective surgery at our institution between 2019 and 2020, with a minimum follow-up of 24 months. The shoulder rule was defined according to Suk et al. Patients were excluded if they were > 18 years of age, had non-idiopathic scoliosis, Lenke type 5 curves, prior scoliosis surgery, or very limited imaging. Radiographic shoulder parameters assessed included radiographic shoulder height, clavicle angle, coracoid process height difference, first rib angle, and T1 tilt. Measurements were performed preoperatively, at 6 weeks-3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 2 years, and at final follow-up. Clinical outcomes were evaluated with SRS-22 total and self-image scores at corresponding intervals. Statistical analysis was performed with SPSS 27.0; significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: A total of 115 patients met the inclusion criteria. Mean age was 14.7 years. 78.3% of the patients were females. Lenke type 1 was the most common curve pattern (50.4%). Posterior fusion was performed in 64.3% and combined anterior-posterior fusion in 35.7%. 48 (41.7%) patients were classified as rule followers (RF) and 67 (58.3%) as rule breakers (RB). Mean follow-up was 43 months, with 47 (40.9%) patients followed for ≥ 48 months. At baseline, RFs were more likely to present with Lenke type 2 (p = 0.045) and type 4 (p = 0.002) curves; otherwise, baseline characteristics did not differ significantly. Across all time points, including ≥ 48 months, no significant differences were observed between RFs and RBs in radiographic shoulder parameters, overall curve correction, or SRS-22 outcomes. In Lenke type 3 curves, RFs demonstrated significantly reduced T1 tilt at 6 months (4° vs 8.6°, p = 0.044), although this difference resolved by 2 years. At 2 years, shoulder balance was significantly more favorable among RFs in Lenke type 3 curves (p = 0.025). Conclusion: Our findings align with recent reports questioning the utility of the shoulder rule in AIS. Based on our institutional experience, application of the rule does not consistently yield superior radiographic shoulder balance or clinical outcomes. Its role may be curve-type dependent. We suggest that the shoulder rule requires refinement and validation across specific Lenke subtypes, with emphasis on mid- to long-term outcomes.

RF177: Free-hand pedicle screw placement accuracy with 3D MPR CT planning in severe scoliosis

Kadir Abul 1 , Erhan Memiş 2 , Mehmet Talmaç 3 , Mehmet Balioğlu 3

1 Başakşehir Çam and Sakura City Hospital, Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology,, Istanbul, Turkey, 2 Başakşehir Çam and Sakura City Hospital, Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Istanbul, Turkey, 2 Başakşehir Çam and Sakura City Hospital, Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Severe scoliosis (Cobb angle > 90°) poses major technical challenges for free-hand pedicle screw placement due to vertebral rotation, dysplastic pedicles, and intraspinal anomalies. Preoperative 3D multiplanar reconstruction (MPR) CT provides detailed evaluation of pedicle morphology and trajectory planning, potentially improving screw accuracy and surgical safety. This study aimed to assess the impact of 3D MPR CT analysis on free-hand pedicle screw placement accuracy and deformity correction in severe scoliosis. Materials and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 59 patients with severe scoliosis (mean preoperative Cobb 105° ± 17°, range 80°-149°) who underwent posterior fusion with free-hand pedicle screws. Preoperative CT scans were reconstructed in multiplanar views to characterize pedicle morphology (Watanabe classification) and guide trajectory planning. MRI was evaluated for apical spinal cord morphology (Sielatycki classification). A total of 1,891 pedicles were analyzed, and postoperative CT was used to grade pedicle screw accuracy (Gertzbein-Robbins). Coronal Cobb angle, apical vertebral translation (AVT), sagittal alignment, intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) events, complications, and follow-up outcomes were recorded. Results: The major curve Cobb angle improved from 105° preoperatively to 45° ± 20° postoperatively, reflecting a mean 56% correction. Mean AVT decreased from 63 ± 40 mm to 31 ± 23 mm (p < 0.05). Thoracic kyphosis and global sagittal alignment were preserved within physiological ranges. Pedicle morphology distribution showed 56% Type A, 26% Type B, 11% Type C, and 7% Type D, with high-risk Type C/D pedicles more frequent on the concavity. Of the 1,862 screws placed, 95% were accurately positioned (Grades A/B), 3% were Grade C, and 2% were Grade D/E, with no screws requiring revision or causing permanent neurologic deficit. MRI demonstrated apical spinal cord anomalies in 51% of patients (Types II-III most frequent), which correlated with higher IONM alerts (5%, all resolved without residual deficit). Overall complication rate was 22%, including 2 deep infections, 2 implant-related revisions, 1 dural tear, and 1 pleural injury, but no long-term neurological morbidity. Mean follow-up was 4.5 years, and correction was maintained. Conclusion: Preoperative 3D MPR CT analysis significantly enhanced the accuracy of free-hand pedicle screw placement in severe scoliosis, enabling high precision even in anatomically distorted pedicles. By anticipating pedicle morphology and spinal cord risks, surgeons achieved robust deformity correction (56% Cobb, 50% AVT reduction) with a 95% screw accuracy rate and no permanent neurologic deficits. This cost-effective adjunct improves surgeon confidence and outcomes, representing a practical alternative to navigation or robotics in complex scoliosis correction.

RF178: Patient-specific rods and sublaminar bands in scoliosis: analysis of thoracic kyphosis correction

Alberto Balagna 1,2 , Emmanuelle Ferrero 2 , Alice Toya 1 , Andrea Serratrice 2,3 , Marc Khalife 2 , Pierre Guigui 2

1 Università degli Studi di Torino, HEGP - Paris, Turin, Italy, 2 HEGP-Paris, Paris, France, 3 Università degli Studi di Roma, Rome, Italy

Introduction: The use of patient-specific implants in spine surgery is steadily increasing. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of customized rods in the correction of deformities, particularly sagittal alignment. Earlier investigations primarily assessed scoliosis correction using either all-screw constructs or hybrid constructs incorporating sublaminar bands. The aim of this study was to evaluate postoperative kyphosis correction using a hybrid construct with patient-specific rods. Material and Methods: A retrospective study was conducted in an adult spine surgery center, including 103 patients (mean age 27.9 ± 17.6 years, 78 females and 25 males) operated between 2022 and 2025. The inclusion criteria comprised patients with idiopathic or degenerative scoliosis, without previous spine surgery, treated with a hybrid construct combining thoracic sublaminar bands, proximal and lumbar pedicle screws, and pre-contoured titanium rods (6 mm diameter).

All patients underwent preoperative and early postoperative (0-3-6-12- 24 months) full-spine radiographs (anteroposterior and lateral views). Standard sagittal and coronal parameters were analyzed using rod planning software. Results: A total of 103 patients were included (mean age 27.9 ± 17.6 years, 78 females and 25 males). The mean Cobb angle correction was approximately 60% (p < 0.05). Idiopathic scoliosis accounted for 64% of cases (n = 66), with the remainder represented by syndromic, congenital, degenerative, or complex scoliosis (n = 37). In the AIS group (mean age 22.0 ± 12.0 years, 47 females and 19 males), the T1 slope increased significantly from 15.9 ± 10.9° preoperatively to 24.2 ± 14.7° postoperatively, in line with planning (23.2 ± 7.4°). In the non-AIS group (mean age 38.8 ± 21.0 years, 31 females and 6 males), the T1 slope changed from 29.2 ± 19.5° preoperatively to 29.0 ± 13.8° postoperatively, also consistent with planning (23.3 ± 11.4°). Cervical kyphosis also increased significantly (p = 0.01). No significant differences were observed between planning and postoperative results regarding lumbar lordosis or pelvic parameters. Global alignment parameters were comparable to planned values. No intraoperative or postoperative mechanical complications were reported. Conclusion: The combination of thoracic sublaminar bands with patient-specific rods appears to be a safe and effective option for scoliosis correction. This technique allows sagittal alignment consistent with preoperative planning without rod flattening. It may represent an alternative for kyphosis correction and could reduce the risk of junctional kyphosis as well as rod breakage. Longer-term prospective studies are required to confirm these findings and refine surgical indications, particularly in older patients.

RF179: Management of severe and rigid adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (> 120°) with modified halo pelvic traction (HPT) and single stage posterior only surgical correction

Muhammad Faheem 1

1 Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan

Introduction: The management of severe and rigid spinal deformities which result from neglected adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a great surgical challenge. There is often cardio-pulmonary compromise that accompanies such cases, which increases the challenge in treatment of these patients. This study was undertaken to evaluate the outcome, efficacy as well as the safety of a modified halo-pelvic traction (HPT) followed by posterior instrumentation only surgical correction for the management of severe and rigid curves of more than 120 degrees in children presenting with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). Material and Methods: From 2022-2025, 35 patients were included in this study who presented with severe and rigid AIS of more than 120°. The corrective loss rate of Cobb angle was only 0.67% at the last follow-up. The function of the spinal cord was stable, and there were no new or persistent neurological symptoms after correction. Conclusion: Modified Halo Pelvic Traction followed by a single stage posterior only fusion is an effective method for the management of severe and rigid AIS greater than 120° in reducing the rate of complications and achieving appropriate surgical correction.

1 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, College of Medicine, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 2 Orthopedic Department, Diriyah Hospital, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 3 Department of Surgery, Division of orthopedic surgery, King Faisal Specialist Hospital & Research Centre, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, a Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Western Ontario, London Health Sciences Center, London, ON, Canada, London, Canada

Introduction: This study aims to compare between all pedicle screws and hybrid hook-screw from the aspect of the surgical complications and the curvature correction on all planes including the coronal, sagittal and frontal. The choice between techniques should be individualized based on patient characteristics, curve patterns, and surgeon expertise, with both approaches representing safe and effective treatment options for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.

RF182: The impact of “keyhole” when discussing spine surgery - A deep dive into patient’s perception of minimally invasive spine surgery

Joel Yeh Siang Chen 1 , Adriel Seah 1 , Guna Pradeep 1 2 , Cayden Leyu 3 , Martin Loh 4 , Jacob Oh 1

1 Tan Tock Seng Hospital, Singapore, Singapore, 2 Meenakshi Mission Hospital and Research Centre, Tamil Nadu, India, 3 Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, Singapore, Singapore, 4 Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: In recent years, minimally invasive spine surgery (MISS) has gained popularity due to improved short-term outcomes and technological advances. However, clinical literature suggests long-term results are comparable to open surgery. The gold standard for spine surgery hence remains an ongoing debate amongst surgeons, heavily influencing surgical techniques offered. Yet, patients’ perspective of MISS has remained grossly underexplored despite its importance to decision-making in surgery. Misconceptions driven by buzzwords like “keyhole” surgery and limited patient education may distort their expectations of MISS, complicating decision-making. Hence, this study aims to evaluate patient’s current perceptions of spine surgery with a focus on MISS, if this perception changes with “keyhole” surgery mentioned, and its relevance to the spine surgical landscape. Material and Methods: A 5-section anonymous questionnaire was conducted from June to November 2024 in a tertiary hospital in Singapore. The questionnaire consisted of: Patient biodata, patient perspective of spine surgery, patient knowledge, perspective and demand for “keyhole” spine surgery. This study included symptomatic surgical candidates with degenerative lumbar pathologies indicated for lumbar decompression and/or fusion surgery. Cervical pathologies, or lumbar pathologies secondary to trauma, infection, inflammation or tumors were excluded. Results: A total of 50 patients participated. 100% of patients understood “keyhole” meant MISS. Of these, 92% chose “keyhole” surgery over open surgery, citing lower complication risks (67%) and better outcomes (65%) as primary reasons. Most viewed “keyhole” surgery as a minor surgery (44%) than a major surgery (18%), with 74% believing most-to-all patients are suitable candidates. As a result, more than 50% of patients were willing to wait longer, pay more, and travel further for MISS. Despite this strong demand, most (90%) were unaware of the difference between endoscopic, tubular approaches and MISS, and 100% were unaware of uniportal and biportal terminologies. Conclusion: The term “keyhole” strongly influences patient interest in spine surgery. Many who initially perceived spine surgery as high-risk view MISS as a safer alternative, associating it with fewer complications and better outcomes than open surgery. While demand for MISS is high, misconceptions about its complexity and limitations remain. Addressing these requires effective patient education to ensure expectations align with clinical realities, fostering trust and satisfaction from the preoperative stage. Furthermore, the preference for MISS underscores the importance of surgeons being proficient in both open and minimally invasive approaches, enabling adaptation to individual patient needs.

There were no clinically or statistically significant differences in all patient-reported outcomes between randomized groups at all time-points. Anti-adhesive group shows a significantly lower rate of extensive epidural fibrosis at 3 months (8.7% versus 32%; p = 0.047). There was no difference in complication rates. Conclusion: An anti-adhesive agent used in endoscopic lumbar discectomy showed significant improvements in patient-reported outcomes at 1, 3, and 6 months after the operation. However, the difference in patient-reported outcomes between anti-adhesive and methylprednisolone was not significant. An anti-adhesive agent also showed better prevention of epidural fibrosis at 3-month follow-up. Keywords: Endoscopic lumbar discectomy, epidural fibrosis, anti-adhesive agent

16 Center for Neurosciences and Spine, Virginia Mason Medical Center,, Seattle, United States,

17 Department of Orthopaedics and Traumatology, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China,

18 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, the University of California, Davis, Sacramento, United States,

19 Department of Orthopaedics, Xuanwu Hospital Capital Medical University, Beijing, China,

20 Research Department, AO Spine, AO Foundation, Davos, Switzerland,

21 Department of Orthopaedics, Emory University, Atlanta, United States

Introduction: Minimally invasive spine surgery (MISS) is well-established for treating degenerative spine diseases. No standardized classification exists to assess the invasiveness of different MISS approaches. This study aimed to identify factors that determine invasiveness and develop a standardized scale for ranking MISS procedures. Material and Methods: Members of the AO Spine Degenerative Knowledge Forum who specialize in MISS were recruited to participate in this study. The study was divided into two stages. The first stage focused on defining factors that influence the invasiveness of MISS and developing a grading scale to rank the invasiveness for each factor. The second stage involved using this scale to survey participating surgeons on the invasiveness of surgical approaches to refine the grading scale further and gain consensus. Results: The first stage was completed over the course of 8 months and 7 meetings. The proposed factors included procedure time, number of approaches, blood loss, pedicle screw placement, muscle dissection, anesthesia, number of levels, fusion technique, and whether it was a revision procedure. Each factor was graded on a scale of 0 to 2, with 0 being the least invasive and 2 being the most invasive. Using blood loss as an example, minimal (< 50 mL) loss was assigned 0 points, < 200 mL was assigned 1 point, and > 200 mL was assigned 2 points. Twenty international surgeons were recruited to complete the second stage, which occurred over 2 months and 2 meetings. The procedures consisted of endoscopic 1-level discectomy (mean = 0.79 points), tubular 1-level discectomy (mean = 1.95 points), open 1-level discectomy (mean = 2.89 points),1-level lateral lumbar interbody fusion (mean = 3.89 points), open 1-level laminectomy (mean = 4.79 points), MISS 1-level transforaminal interbody fusion (TLIF) (mean = 5.16 points), open 3-level laminectomy (mean = 6 points), 1-level anterior lumbar interbody fusion with percutaneous pedicle screw fixation (mean = 7.16 points), MISS 2-level TLIF (mean = 8 points), open 1-level TLIF (mean = 8.05 points), and thoracic to pelvis fixation with a 1-level TLIF (mean = 13.58 points). Conclusion: This study established an invasiveness classification grading scale for procedures based on 9 factors. Using the developed grading scale, an endoscopic 1-level discectomy was the least invasive procedure graded, and a thoracic to pelvis fixation the most invasive. Further validation of this classification system is needed through both clinical studies to assess its practical utility and a Delphi study to establish consensus on procedure rankings.

RF187: Complications in minimally invasive spine surgery (2013-2024): a proportional meta-analysis series for thoracic spine - Tubular, uniportal, and biportal endoscopic spine surgery

Sean Inzerillo 1 , Chibuikem Ikwuegbuenyi 1 , Eesha Gurav 1 , Noah Willett 1 , Mousa Hamad 1 , Ibrahim Hussain 1 , Alan Hernandez-Hernandez 1 , Galal Elsayed 1 , Osama Kashlan 1 , Roger Härtl 1

1 Department of Neurological Surgery, Och Spine at New York-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center, New York, United States

Introduction: MISS is increasingly used for thoracic spinal pathologies due to reduced tissue trauma and faster recovery. However, complication rates vary (0%-43%), and differences between tubular, uniportal, and biportal approaches remain unclear. The purpose of this review was to evaluate overall and approach-specific complication rates associated with thoracic minimally invasive spine surgery (MISS) using tubular, uniportal endoscopic, and biportal endoscopic techniques, as part two of a five-part proportional meta-analysis series on MISS complications. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42024594316). PubMed, Medline, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched (Jan 2013-Mar 2024) for thoracic MISS studies using tubular, uniportal, or biportal approaches. Studies reporting complication rates in adult cohorts were included. Exclusions were non-English articles, reviews, and abstracts. Quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. A random-effects model with subgroup analyses was used, and heterogeneity assessed via I2. Analyses were performed in R Studio. Results: Nine studies with 234 patients were included, all with moderate risk of bias. Mean age ranged from 49.9 to 64.0 years; 59.7% were female. The pooled overall complication rate was 6.76% (95% CI: 2.38-17.71%) with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 35.8%). The tubular approach (six studies) had the lowest rate at 3.46% (95% CI: 1.08-10.51%), followed by uniportal (two studies) at 16.28% (95% CI: 9.88-25.63%). The biportal approach showed a 42.86% rate (95% CI: 20.65-68.37%), based on a single study and requiring cautious interpretation. Common complications included neural injuries (3.01%), CSF leaks (2.64%), and dural tears (1.25%). Revisions occurred in 1.30%. Conclusions: Thoracic MISS has a low complication rate overall, with tubular showing the lowest risk. However, technique-specific comparisons remain limited by available data. Larger comparative studies are needed to define safety better and optimize outcomes.

RF188: Comparing the perioperative and postoperative outcomes of interlaminar and transforaminal endoscopic lumbar facet cyst removal: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Ian Teng 1 , You Qian Lin 1 , Keng Siang Lee 2 , Thomas Choo Heng Tan 2,3,4

1 Lee Kong Chian School of Medicine, Singapore, Singapore, 2 National Neurological Institute, Singapore, Singapore, 3 AO Spine, Davos, Switzerland, 4 Society for Minimally Invasive Spine Surgery, Illinois, United States

Introduction: Lumbar facet cysts refer to fluid-filled sacs anatomically adjacent to zygapophyseal joints of the lumbar spine. They are often seen in older adults as one of the manifestations of degenerative spine disease, presenting with radiculopathy and back pain. Endoscopic facet cyst removal is an effective alternative to open surgery (laminectomy/hemilaminectomy), given its ability to achieve better outcomes such as greater functional improvement and shorter hospital stays, while maintaining similar complication rates. Two common techniques in endoscopic facet cyst removal include the interlaminar and transforaminal approaches, but literature comparing the endoscopic approaches is limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis thus aims to examine the perioperative and postoperative outcomes of interlaminar and transforaminal approaches to endoscopic lumbar facet cyst removal. Material and Methods: This study was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and is registered on PROSPERO (CRD42025641852). A systematic search was performed on January 14, 2025 for PubMed, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, Embase, and Web of Science Core Collection. Studies that reported on endoscopic resection of facet cysts via interlaminar and/or transforaminal approaches were included, while studies that lacked primary data, outcome data or had inadequate sample size (< 2) were excluded. Meta-analysis was performed using R in the RStudio environment. Single-arm meta-analysis of proportions and pairwise meta-analysis of odds ratios were performed for dichotomous outcomes, while single-arm and pairwise meta-analysis of means were performed for continuous outcomes. Results: A total of nine studies involving 204 patients were included. Three studies utilised the interlaminar approach, two studies utilised the transforaminal approach and four studies utilised both. No statistically significant difference was found between the two techniques for operative time, dural tear, nerve injury or damage, postoperative MacNab scores, cyst recurrence, residual cyst, instability at 12 months follow-up, and length of stay. A significant decrease was observed for both groups when comparing pre- and postoperative Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores, with no significant difference between the groups. Notably, postoperative neurological deficit was less common in the interlaminar group compared to the transforaminal group (OR = 0.09, 95% CI 0.01-0.55). Conclusion: This study demonstrates that both approaches are effective, yielding significant reduction in clinical symptoms without major perioperative or postoperative complications. While both techniques were associated with transient dysesthesia, there was a greater proportion of postoperative dysesthesia with the transforaminal approach. The lower incidence observed in the interlaminar group may be attributable to better visualisation and minimal retraction and manipulation of the dorsal root ganglion during surgery. Ultimately, given the similarity in most outcomes, the choice of approach should depend on the surgeon's familiarity and preference, as well as patient factors such as the spinal level of the cyst and its position relative to the facet joint (cranial or caudal). More studies comparing the two surgical approaches are needed for greater certainty on the estimates.

RF189: C1 lateral mass-C2 body (LM-B) screw: a cadaveric anatomical study of a novel posterior trajectory

Bahadır Topal 1 , Yahya Guvenc 2

1 Department of Neurosurgery Basaksehir Cam and Sakura City Hospital, istabul, Turkey, 2 Department of Neurosurgery Marmara University, Istanbul, Turkey

Objective: To describe and anatomically evaluate a novel C1 lateral mass–C2 body (LM-B) screw trajectory as a safe alternative to conventional C1–C2 fusion techniques. The trajectory features a posterolateral entry point and advances directly into the C2 vertebral body without traversing the C2 pedicle or the vertebral artery canal. Methods: Four formalin-fixed adult cadaveric cervical spine specimens were instrumented bilaterally with LM-B screws under C-arm fluoroscopy (8 screws total). Screw entry points, trajectories, and angulations were standardized using anatomical landmarks. Post-instrumentation computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction was performed to assess cortical integrity, intrabony course, and spatial relationship to the vertebral artery canal. Medial and caudal angulations were quantified using standardized multiplanar reference planes. Results: The LM-B screw entry point was consistently identified at the junction of the C1 posterior arch, lateral mass, and transverse process in all specimens. All screws reached the C2 vertebral body without violation of the vertebral artery canal (0/8). Inline screw-axis multiplanar reconstructions confirmed that all screws followed a fully intrabony course without medial encroachment of the spinal canal or inferior breach toward the vertebral artery canal. The mean medial angulation was 33.1° ± 5.1° and the mean caudal angulation was 32.8° ± 9.7°. The feasible medial angular range extended from 25.1° to 37.8°, while the feasible caudal angular range ranged from 15.7° to 45.7°. The mean intraosseous screw length was 37.3 ± 5.5 mm. No cortical breach, spinal canal encroachment, or need for screw repositioning was observed. Conclusion: Within the anatomical conditions examined, the LM-B screw pathway demonstrated a fully intrabony posterior corridor from the C1 lateral mass to the C2 vertebral body, defining an anatomically feasible posterolateral C1–C2 screw trajectory. This technique may serve as a valuable alternative in cases where traditional methods are limited by high-riding vertebral arteries or narrow C2 pedicles. Further biomechanical and clinical studies are warranted to validate these findings.

RF190: Training platform for endoscopic spine surgery with artificial intelligence and augmented reality: innovation to overcome the learning curve

1 Santa Casa de São Paulo, Spine AI, São paulo, Brazil, 2 Envision 3D Brasil, São José dos Campos, Brazil

Introduction: Endoscopic spine surgery has undergone significant advancements in the last decade, establishing itself as a minimally invasive treatment for degenerative and traumatic conditions. Unlike Virtual Reality (VR), which immerses users in an entirely digital environment, AR overlays digital elements onto the physical world, allowing surgeons to interact with both simultaneously. In spine surgery, AR offers real-time anatomical guidance and procedural steps projected directly onto the operative field, enhancing spatial awareness without disconnecting the surgeon from reality. Material and Methods: Spine AI® was developed by a national multidisciplinary team. Results: The development process produced a functional platform capable of simulating the surgical environment immersively. It guides each procedural step using anatomical AR overlays and provides automated feedback on movement and positioning. Internal testing demonstrated system stability, projection accuracy, and strong educational potential. The platform allows uninterrupted procedural navigation and can be used beyond operating rooms or cadaver labs, reducing costs and improving accessibility to endoscopic training. Conclusion: The steep learning curve of endoscopic spine surgery remains a major barrier, with studies such as Kim et al. (2023) estimating up to 500 cases to achieve proficiency in advanced lumbar procedures. This highlights the need for tools that ensure continuous, safe, and structured training. Research by Shin et al. (2021), Maatuk et al. (2022), Zhang et al. (2023), and Yao et al. (2024) supports the educational potential of AR and AI, while Van Isseldyk et al. (2025) and Schwendner et al. (2023) demonstrated benefits in workload reduction, ergonomics, accuracy, and efficiency. Spine AI® introduces a conversational AI avatar that acts as a virtual mentor, answering questions, providing contextual guidance, and reinforcing surgical concepts. This embodies Augmented Intelligence, where technology enhances human cognitive ability rather than replacing decision-making. By amplifying perception, reasoning, and learning capacity, this human-centered approach promotes autonomy and safety in training. In summary, Spine AI® represents a breakthrough in endoscopic spine surgery education. It offers an immersive, affordable, and intelligent solution that improves access, safety, and training quality while eliminating radiation exposure and reducing the reliance on expensive cadaver labs or navigation systems.

RF191: A prompt engineered large language model assistant for spine patient history taking: a two-phase study

Begüm Aslantaş Kaplan 1 , Ali Kaplan 1 , İlker Solmaz 2 , Tolga Ege 3 , Ali Aydilek 3

1 Tokat Erbaa State Hospital, Tokat, Turkey, 2 Private Practice, Ankara, Turkey, 3 Health sciences University Gülhane Research and Training Hospital, Ankara, Turkey

Introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being investigated for clinical applications, though their potential as real-time, patient-facing interfaces remains largely unexplored. Prompt engineering, the process of designing specific inputs to guide LLM behavior, offers a method to create interactive clinical assistants without modifying the model's underlying parameters. In spine surgery, where detailed history-taking is crucial, an LLM assistant could streamline workflows and enhance consultation quality. We developed Spine-GPT, a prompt-engineered LLM-based assistant using GPT-4o, to conduct pre-consultation interviews and provide structured summaries for surgeons. This study evaluates its performance in both simulated and real-world clinical settings. Material and Methods: A two-phase study evaluated Spine-GPT's performance in simulated and clinical settings. Spine-GPT was implemented using GPT-4o through multi-layered prompt engineering incorporating expertise emulation, dual-role assignment, stepwise adaptive questioning, chain-of-thought prompting, justification prompting, reflection prompting, and directive instructions. Phase 0 involved 24 fictional clinical scenarios covering diverse spine pathologies, with one author simulating patient responses. Three board-certified spine surgeons with ≥ 15 years experience evaluated transcripts using 5-point Likert scales across seven domains: adaptive questioning, complaint comprehension, diagnostic accuracy, diagnostic justification, appropriateness of recommendations, red-flag recognition, and professional tone. Phase 1 was a prospective single-center study of 60 consecutive eligible adults over three days. The first 30 patients underwent conventional consultations (control), while the remaining 30 completed Spine-GPT interviews prior to surgeon consultation (intervention). Primary outcome was active history-taking time. Secondary outcomes included information completeness (18-item checklist), red-flag detection accuracy, surgeon/patient satisfaction, and editing burden

Results: Phase 0 demonstrated consistently high performance across all domains, with mean Likert scores ranging from 4.02 ± 0.39 to 4.87 ± 0.16 and composite score of 4.53 ± 0.28. Red-flag recognition achieved the highest score (4.87 ± 0.16), while adaptive questioning scored lowest (4.02 ± 0.39). In Phase 1, Spine-GPT significantly reduced active history-taking time from 11.47 ± 2.56 to 7.88 ± 1.74 minutes, representing a 31.3% decrease (p < 0.001). Information completeness improved by 2.10 items, equivalent to an 11.7 percentage-point increase (p < 0.001). All three red-flag cases (two vertebral metastases, one progressive neurological deficit) were correctly identified by both surgeons and Spine-GPT. Surgeon satisfaction increased from 3.20 ± 0.92 to 4.80 ± 0.40 (p < 0.001), and patient satisfaction from 3.80 ± 0.76 to 4.67 ± 0.47 (p < 0.001). Seventy percent of AI-generated summaries required no manual editing. Conclusion: Spine-GPT demonstrates significant potential for enhancing outpatient spine consultations through prompt engineering. The system achieved substantial time efficiency gains while improving information capture and maintaining safety-critical red-flag recognition. High user satisfaction and minimal editing requirements suggest favorable acceptability for clinical implementation. This study provides proof-of-concept for structured prompting approaches that enable general-purpose LLMs to emulate clinically relevant behavior, offering a modular framework for future developments in AI-assisted clinical workflows. By transforming patient narratives into structured, clinician-oriented summaries, such tools have the potential to enhance clinical efficiency and support decision-making. While this study serves as a strong proof-of-concept, the clinician's role remains central for supervision and validation. Future multi-center studies are warranted to confirm these findings and explore broader implementation.

Friedman test indicated a significant overall difference (p < 0.001). For Caudal VBH Friedman test did not indicate a significant change over time (p = 0.129), and none of the pairwise comparisons reached statistical significance. There were minimal procedural complications, with no reports of microsphere leakage or migration. Conclusion: Titanium microspheres in kyphoplasty are effective and safe for treating VCFs, providing significant pain relief and quality of life improvements. RF193: Quantifying ergonomics with dynamic motion sensors in lumbar decompression surgeries

Philip Louie 1 , Takeshi Fujii 1,2 , Kenneth Nguyen 1 , Patricia Lipson 1,3 , Rafael Garcia de Oliveira 1 , Venu Nemani 1 , Jean Christophe Leveque 1 , Farrokh Farrokhi 1 , Aiyush Bansal 1

1 Virginia Mason Medical Center, Seattle, United States, 2 Keio University, Tokyo, Japan, 3 University of Washington, Seattle, United States

Introduction: Spine surgeons are at high risk for work-related musculoskeletal disorders due to prolonged strained postures and repetitive motions during surgery. However, few studies have quantified ergonomic exposures across specific stages of spine surgery, particularly in lumbar decompression procedures. This study aims to demonstrate the feasibility of real-time, dynamic monitoring of surgeon ergonomics through: (1) quantitative assessment of high-risk postures throughout the entire procedure, (2) the identification of predominant high-risk postures maintained during critical phases of a single-level microdiscectomy, and (3) the evaluation of cumulative ergonomic loads across the entire surgery. Materials and Methods: Five cases of single-level microdiscectomy were analyzed, performed by three right-handed surgeons. A full-body inertial motion capture system with 17 inertial measurement units (IMUs) was used to track body motion throughout the surgery. The data were segmented into three operative phases: laminotomy, flavectomy, and discectomy. Each body region was assessed using ergonomic thresholds, classifying postures as low, medium, or high risk. For each phase, we calculated the mean joint angles, proportion of time spent in medium or high-risk postures; and the area under the curve (AUC) as a measure of cumulative ergonomic load for each surgeon. Results: Overall, forearm rotation, wrist abduction, and wrist flexion/extension were the predominant movements at the highest ergonomic risk. During the surgical phases, the right forearm remained supinated above 70° during laminotomy, and both wrists spent more than 60% of the time in high-risk abduction. During flavectomy, the left wrist averaged 37.4° (81% in high risk), while forearm rotation reached 84.2° on the right (88% in high risk) and 36.1° on the left (40% in medium risk). In the discectomy phase, high-risk wrist abduction and forearm supination persisted, with additional right wrist abduction at 56.8° (42% in high risk). Cumulative joint-angle exposure (AUC, deg·min) for forearm rotation was higher on the right (2196.9) than the left (1050.9), while wrist flexion/extension was similar bilaterally (right: 1140.0, left: 1122.4). Left wrist abduction had higher AUC (942.8) compared to the right (697.1). Conclusion: Forearm rotation, wrist abduction, and wrist flexion/extension were found to be the most ergonomically hazardous postures during single-level microdiscectomy, remaining in high-risk zones throughout the procedure. The laminotomy, flavectomy, and discectomy phases all involve these high-risk movements. Real-time motion capture is a valuable tool for identifying these risks and guiding targeted ergonomic interventions to reduce occupational injury risk among spine surgeons.

Xian Jun Ngoh 1 , Shawn Seah 1 , Yee Gen Lim 1 , Lei Jiang 1

1 Singapore General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: The use of ultrasonic bone cutting instruments have gained traction in open, minimally invasive spine surgery and most recently biportal endoscopic surgery due to its selective bone-cutting ability while preserving adjacent soft tissue structures unlike conventional high-speed drills. However, its application in uniportal endoscopic spine surgery remains unreported in peer-reviewed literature. The aim of this technical note it to presents a novel spine surgical technique using a novel ultrasonic osteotome surgical system (UOSS) in uniportal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion (U-ELIF), highlight the pearls and pitfalls of using the UOSS and to report preliminary results of this technique. This article introduces a novel ultrasonic osteotome device (Ultrasonic Osteotomy Surgical System (UOSS), SMTP, China) that is compatible with uniportal full-endoscopic lumbar spine surgical systems. The device consists of a handpiece, a 210mm or 300mm slim profile shaft and a blunt ultrasonic scalpel tip that oscillates at a frequency of 39kHz and an excursion of < 120µm. The long shaft allows for compatibility with uniportal endoscope systems. The high frequency beyond auditory range allows for a quiet yet precise cutting of noncompliant crystalline structures of mineralized tissue like bone, while more compliant surrounding soft tissue is theoretically not affected by the low excursion ultrasonic oscillation. The UOSS also allows for local bone to be harvested as bone chips during bone work which would otherwise be washed away as particulate matter in the continuously irrigated environment of endoscopic spine surgery if traditional high-speed drills are used. Results: Seven patients underwent U-ELIF for 10 segments with the aid of UOSS from 1 May 2025 to 15 August 2025. Three patients underwent two level U-ELIF while four patients underwent single level U-ELIF. Three patients had lumbar spondylolisthesis while the other four had lumbar spinal stenosis. The group included 2 men and 5 women. The average age of the patients was 61.7 (age range 49 - 71 years old). Total average operating time was 252min (209min for single level U-ELIF; 312min for double level U-ELIF). There were no complications directly associated with decompression laminotomy or ipsilateral total facetectomy using the ultrasonic osteotome. Specifically, there was no incidence of dura tear or neural structure injury in all seven cases. All patients experienced improvements in their lower limb radicular symptoms and were ambulating by post-operative day (POD) one. The average length of stay (LOS) was 4.5 days (LOS range 2 - 5). All patients reported early postoperative improvement in radicular symptoms. Conclusion: Ultrasonic osteotome assisted U-ELIF is feasible and safe with the UOSS in our early experience. The device enables controlled bone removal, excellent visualization under irrigation and preservation of local autograft for interbody fusion. Larger comparative studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm the benefits in clinical outcomes and fusion success.

RF199: Relationship between baseline global sagittal alignment and cervical alignment changes following lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy

Bruno Verna 1 , Thomas Caffard 1,2 , Marco Burkhard 1 , Ali Guven 1 , Anna-Maria Mielke 1,3 , Erika Chiapparelli 1 , Ranqing Lan 1 , Jennifer Shue 1 , Andrew Sama 1 , Federico Girardi 1 , Frank Cammisa 1 , Alexander Hughes 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States, 2 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, University of Ulm, Ulm, Germany, 3 Centrum für Muskuloskeletale Chirurgie, Charité, Berlin, Germany

Introduction: Changes in cervical alignment after lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) have been reported, yet the progression over time and predictors of long-term decompensation are poorly understood. This study analyzed cervical sagittal alignment changes in patients who underwent lumbar PSO and evaluated the association between preoperative global sagittal alignment (GSA) and immediate postoperative changes in cervical alignment as well as decompensation over one year. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis of 99 patients who underwent lumbar PSO was performed, evaluating changes in cervical alignment on preoperative standing lateral radiographs and those at five postoperative timepoints: (PO1: 1-30 days, PO2: 31-90 days, PO3: 91-180 days, PO4: 181 days-1 year, PO5: 1-2 years). Wilcoxon was used to evaluate immediate postoperative changes (Preop to PO1) and maintenance versus decompensation over time (PO1 to PO5). Multivariable linear regression, adjusting for age, sex and BMI, assessed if preoperative GSA parameters influenced immediate and long-term cervical alignment. To evaluate longitudinal trends across all postoperative intervals, mixed-effects models were constructed. Results: Significant immediate cervical alignment changes were observed after surgery, including decreases in C2-7 sagittal vertical axis (cSVA) (p = 0.027), T1 slope (p < 0.001), C7 slope (p < 0.001), cervical tilt (p = 0.024), and neck tilt (p < 0.001) from preoperative to PO1. Cervical lordosis (CL) significantly decreased from preoperative to PO1, PO2, PO3, and PO5 (all p < 0.050). Progressive decompensation in cSVA was observed after PO1, with 35 patients demonstrating ≥ 10 mm increase at > 1 year. In the multivariable regression model, higher preoperative global SVA was associated with greater immediate cSVA reduction (p = 0.008) and T1 slope correction (p < 0.001). BMI was also positively associated with early T1 slope correction (p = 0.023). Longer-term analysis showed that preoperative PT negatively associated with T1 slope progression (p = 0.016), whereas pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis mismatch (PI-LL) positively associated with T1 slope progression (p = 0.029). Conclusion: This study highlighted both immediate changes and progressive decompensation of cervical alignment following lumbar PSO. While previous studies have emphasized lumbar-driven cervical adaptation, our findings indicate that preoperative GSA parameters influence cervical alignment in a phase-specific manner. Higher preoperative SVA predicts immediate cervical adaptation, whereas pelvic parameters predict long-term compensatory responses. Preoperative assessment should not only consider GSA but biomechanical patient-specific factors such as muscle morphology and soft tissue integrity. Future research should focus on identifying modifiable predictors of cervical decompensation aiding in developing targeted rehabilitation strategies and optimizing surgical planning.
