RF200: Using tranexamic acid in scoliosis surgery to reduce blood supply a systematic review of worldwide data

Fahad Abduljabbar 1 , Raed Mohammedamin Sharaf 2 , Abdulrheem Almokhtar 3 , Rakan Farouk Y Bokhari 4

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, 2 Faculty of Medicine, King Abdulaziz University,, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, 3 Orthopaedic Surgery, King Abdullah Medical City, Makkah, Saudi Arabia, 4 Department of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia

Introduction: Scoliosis is a complex three-dimensional spinal deformity that frequently requires posterior spinal fusion for curves exceeding 45°. This surgery is associated with significant intraoperative and postoperative blood loss. Tranexamic acid (TXA), an antifibrinolytic agent, has been shown to reduce bleeding in various surgical fields, but evidence regarding its safety and efficacy in scoliosis surgery has not been comprehensively reviewed. Material and Methods: A systematic search was performed across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL Ultimate, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2015 and 2024. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, prospective, and retrospective studies evaluating TXA use in scoliosis surgery. Quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for observational studies. Results: Out of 415 identified studies, 21 met inclusion criteria, encompassing 3831 patients. Most studies were retrospective (n = 13), followed by randomized controlled trials (n = 6) and prospective studies (n = 2). TXA significantly reduced intraoperative and postoperative blood loss and decreased transfusion requirements. High-dose regimens (> 30 mg/kg loading or > 10 mg/kg/h infusion) were more effective than low-dose protocols. Safety analysis showed a low rate of complications, with no consistent increase in thromboembolic events. Conclusion: TXA is safe and effective in reducing perioperative blood loss in scoliosis surgery. High-dose regimens appear more efficacious than low-dose ones, with minimal adverse effects. These findings support the broader integration of TXA into blood management strategies for scoliosis surgery.

RF201: Efficacy and safety of atlantoaxial and occipitocervical fusion using construct with block corticomedullary iliac autograft and compression sutures

Pattamaket Sukchokpanich 1 , Korawish Mekariya 1 , Yusuke Murakami 2 , Panya Luksanapruksa 1 , Sirichai Wilartratsami 1

1 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, Bangkok, Thailand, 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Ehime University School of Medicine, Ehime, Japan

Introduction: Occipitocervical fusion (OCF) and atlantoaxial fusion (AAF) are the two primary surgical strategies used to stabilize the upper cervical spine. Despite their established efficacy, complications such as nonunion and pseudarthrosis persist, particularly in high-risk patients such as those with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Modern techniques employing plate-screw-rod constructs have been shown to improve stability and outcomes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of AAF and OCF performed with a modified technique using plate-screw constructs supplemented with a large unicortical corticomedullary iliac graft and compression sutures, and to compare outcomes between AAF and modified OCF. Material and Methods: We conducted a single-center, retrospective review of a prospectively collected registry. Patients who underwent posterior instrumented upper cervical fusion with a minimum 1-year follow-up were included. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score, Neck Disability Index (NDI), and EQ-5D. Radiological outcomes included the posterior occipitocervical angle, occipitoaxial angle, pharyngeal inlet angle, and C1-C2 and C2-C7 alignment parameters. Subgroup analyses were performed according to the underlying etiology, including rheumatoid arthritis. Results: A total of 113 patients (OCF = 39; AAF = 74; mean age, 61 years; mean follow-up, 29 months) were included. The most common pathology was upper cervical trauma, followed by RA. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. The overall fusion rate was 87.6% (AAF: 87.8%; OCF: 87.2%), with a mean time to fusion of approximately 9.3 months in both groups (p = 0.487). Two OCF patients developed pseudarthrosis, and two AAF patients experienced instrument failure. OCF was associated with lower intraoperative blood loss (350 vs. 525 mL; p = 0.036) but longer hospital stays (13 vs. 6.5 days; p < 0.001). At 12 months, both groups demonstrated significant clinical improvement, with greater NDI-VAS reduction in the OCF group (p = 0.004). Other clinical, radiographic, and complication outcomes were comparable. In the RA subgroup, both techniques achieved 100% fusion with comparable results. Conclusion: Upper cervical fusion using plate and screw construct with block corticomedullary iliac autograft and compression sutures is a safe and effective technique for both AAF and OCF. This approach achieved high fusion rates and favorable clinical outcomes, including in high-risk patients with rheumatoid arthritis.

RF202: The impact of vertebral fractures in patients with dropped head syndrome: analysis of global spinal alignment in 103 cases

Soji Tani 1 , Yohei Miyamoto 1 , Shimpei Koyama 1 , Koki Tsuchiya 1 , Chikara Hayakawa 1 , Ryo Yamamura 1 , Ichiro Okano 1 , Yoshifmi Kudo 1

1 SHOWA Medical University, Shinagawa-ku, Japan

Introduction: Dropped Head Syndrome (DHS) is a heterogeneous condition characterized by a disturbance in the ability to maintain forward gaze. We have previously reported on the importance of global spinal malalignment in DHS patients. While osteoporotic vertebral fractures (OVFs) are frequently observed in elderly DHS patients, their impact on global spinal alignment has not been reported. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the presence of OVFs and their characteristics in global spinal alignment in DHS patients. Material and Methods: This study included 109 consecutive DHS patients who visited our outpatient clinic (mean age 75.7 ± 8.6 years, 84 females). Six patients with neuromuscular disease or insufficient radiological evaluation were excluded, and 103 cases were analyzed. Patients were divided into two groups based on the presence of OVFs: the F group (with fractures, n = 39) and the N group (without fractures, n = 64). We then compared and analyzed their global and local spinal alignment parameters. Results: There were no significant differences in age or sex between the F group (mean age 77.0 years) and the N group (mean age 75.5 years). Cervical alignment parameters (C2-7 SVA, C2-7 Angle) showed no significant difference between the two groups. However, in terms of global spinal alignment, the F group had significantly larger SVA (70.0 vs 2.5 mm, p < 0.05), T1 slope (53.0 vs 41.0°, p < 0.05), and PI-LL (11.0 vs 1.5°, p < 0.05) compared to the N group. The N group had a significantly larger LL (40.0 vs 38.0°, p < 0.05). For local alignment, the F group showed significantly greater thoracolumbar (T10-L2) kyphosis (24.0 vs 9.0°, p < 0.05) and thoracic (T4-12) kyphosis (54.0 vs 47.0°, p < 0.05). Furthermore, 84.6% of patients in the F group had thoracolumbar alignment abnormalities, compared to 35.9% in the N group (p < 0.01). Vertebral fractures were frequently observed in the mid-to-lower thoracic spine and at the thoracolumbar junction. Conclusion: DHS is a heterogeneous syndrome. Our findings suggest that in DHS patients with OVFs, global spinal malalignment is highly prevalent and may be associated with local alignment abnormalities at the thoracolumbar junction and thoracic spine caused by the fractures. The results indicate that DHS may not be solely due to cervical pathology but also related to thoracolumbar decompensation. Therefore, a comprehensive evaluation of the entire spinal alignment, including the presence of OVFs, is crucial for the diagnosis and treatment planning of DHS, beyond a simple assessment of the cervical spine.

RF203: Relationship between preoperative lumbar muscle composition and cervical alignment changes following lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy

Bruno Verna 1 , Marco Burkhard 1 , Ali Guven 1 , Thomas Caffard1 1,2 , Anna-Maria Mielke 1,3 , Jiaqi Zhu 1 , Jennifer Shue 1 , Andrew Sama 1 , Federico Girardi 1 , Frank Cammisa 1 , Alexander Hughes 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States, 2 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, University of Ulm, Ulm, Germany, 3 Centrum für Muskuloskeletale Chirurgie, Charité, Berlin, Germany

Introduction: Meticulous preoperative planning of spinal deformity correction is crucial to achieve optimal outcomes. Traditionally this has involved various measurements on preoperative standing or functional radiographs. However, the paraspinal soft tissue envelope is increasingly being recognized as an important factor for postoperative outcomes. For instance, cervical alignment changes after thoracolumbar corrective surgery may not only be influenced by the degree of correction but also by the paraspinal muscle composition. The objective of our study is to evaluate the impact of preoperative lumbar muscles on both immediate and long-term cervical alignment changes following lumbar pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO). Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients who underwent lumbar PSO with available preoperative and postoperative standing whole-spine lateral radiographs. Cervical sagittal alignment was assessed preoperatively and at five postoperative timepoints: PO1 (1-30 days), PO2 (31-90 days), PO3 (91-180 days), PO4 (181 days to 1 year), and PO5 (1-2 years). Alignment parameters included cervical lordosis (CL), C2-7 sagittal vertical axis (cSVA), T1 slope, T1 slope minus cervical lordosis (TS-CL), cervical tilt, neck tilt, and thoracic inlet angle (TIA). Muscle variables included: functional cross-sectional area (fCSA) and fatty infiltration (FI) of the erector spinae (ES) and multifidus (MF) at the L4 level. Spearman correlation and multivariable linear regression analyses were used to assess the relationship between preoperative lumbar muscles and both immediate (preoperative to PO1) and long-term (PO1 to PO5) cervical alignment changes. Results: Ninety-nine patients (52% female) with a median age of 63 years and a median BMI of 28.6 kg/m2 were included. Spearman analysis revealed several significant correlations between lumbar muscle quality and cervical alignment changes. In multivariable linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, and BMI, the immediate analysis showed that greater MF fCSA was associated with smaller reductions in CL (estimate = 0.03 [95% CI: 0.01-0.04], p = 0.002), equivalent to 5.1° per 1 SD increase, and TS-CL (p = 0.022). Greater ES fCSA was also associated with smaller reductions in CL (p = 0.012), equivalent to 3.6° per 1 SD increase, and cervical tilt (p = 0.003). In contrast, higher ES FI was associated with greater reductions in CL (p = 0.046) and cervical tilt (p = 0.046). In the long-term analysis, greater MF and ES fCSA were significantly associated with increases in TIA (both p < 0.05), while ES fCSA was also associated with greater increases in T1 slope (p = 0.013) and TS-CL (p = 0.030). Conversely, higher ES FI was associated with smaller increases in both T1 slope (p = 0.037) and TIA (p = 0.004). Conclusion: Lumbar paraspinal muscle quality was identified as a predictor of both immediate and long-term cervical alignment following PSO. Higher lumbar muscle quality was associated with less postoperative loss of cervical lordosis, suggesting a potential protective and stabilizing role. These findings highlight the biomechanical influence of lumbar muscles on cervical sagittal alignment and support including muscle quality in preoperative planning and surgical decision making for sagittal deformity correction.

RF204: Is fixation procedure necessary in posterior approach surgery for cervical stenosis with non-severe kyphosis?

Hongyu Chen 1 , Xiaoxiong Yang 1 , Yu Sun 1 , Feifei Zhou 1

1 Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: To evaluate whether instrumented fusion is essential for posterior decompression in patients with cervical stenosis and non-severe kyphosis. Material and Methods: A total of 109 patients with cervical stenosis and non-severe kyphosis were enrolled and divided into three groups based on the surgical approach: a laminoplasty (LP)-alone group, a lateral mass screw (LMS) fixation group, and a pedicle screw (PS) fixation group. Clinical outcomes were assessed preoperatively and at follow-up using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for neck pain, the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score, the Neck Disability Index (NDI), and the Short Form-36 (SF-36) survey. Radiographic sagittal parameters were measured on lateral cervical radiographs. Perioperative data, including hospitalization duration, surgical details, and complications, were also recorded. Results: The three groups were comparable in terms of baseline demographic characteristics. However, the PS group exhibited significantly longer operative times and greater intraoperative blood loss compared to the LP and LMS groups. Although all groups showed significant improvement in mJOA scores postoperatively, the PS group achieved significantly lower final mJOA scores (12.8 ± 2.9) than the LP (15.4 ± 1.7, p < 0.001) and LMS groups (15.6 ± 1.5, p = 0.002). In contrast, only the PS group demonstrated a significant reduction in neck pain VAS scores (from 3.8 ± 2.2 to 2.6 ± 1.8, p = 0.046); the changes in the LP (-0.2 ± 2.8, p = 0.877) and LMS groups (-0.3 ± 2.7, p = 0.877) were minimal and not statistically significant. The PS group achieved the most significant correction of the C2-7 Cobb angle (8.6 ± 11.7°). In contrast, the kyphosis correction in the LMS group (3.4 ± 7.7°) was not significant and was comparable to that in the LP group (3.8 ± 7.8°, p = 0.840). The overall complication rate was highest in the PS group (27.8%), followed by the LMS group (16.0%) and the LP group (9.1%). Conclusion: For patients with cervical stenosis and mild-to-moderate kyphosis, posterior fixation and fusion may not be essential. This study demonstrated that laminoplasty alone achieved comparable neurological recovery and quality of life to fixation procedures, but with the added benefits of shorter operative times, less blood loss, and a lower complication rate. These findings suggest that LP alone could be a preferable surgical option for this patient population.

RF205: Staged 540° cervical reconstruction for severe chin-on-chest deformity: indications, technique, and outcomes

Eliezer Villanueva-Castro 1 , Samuel C. Overley 2 , Hector Soriano-Baron 1

1 Department of Neurosurgery, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, Little Rock, United States, 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Arkansas for Medical Science, Little Rock, United States

Introduction: Severe, fixed cervicothoracic kyphosis with a chin-on-chest deformity results in loss of horizontal gaze, neurological impairment, dysphagia, disabling neck pain, and significant functional decline. In rigid deformities with circumferential ankylosis or persistent pseudoarthrosis after previous surgeries, staged circumferential reconstruction in a posterior-anterior-posterior (540°) sequence has proven to be the most effective technique to achieve complete release and adequate correction, although at the cost of considerable morbidity. Literature supports this approach, particularly in rigid, irreducible deformities, prior circumferential fusion, or instrumentation failure, and highlights the role of posterior column osteotomies and intraoperative traction as useful adjuncts for safe correction. Material and Methods: We present the case of a 48-year-old female with nine prior cervical spine surgeries performed at another institution, who presented with bilateral arm weakness, severe muscle wasting, and chronic neck pain. Imaging revealed fixed cervicothoracic kyphosis, hardware failure, and pseudoarthrosis. A 540° staged reconstruction was performed in three stages: (1) posterior approach with hardware removal and replacement, new instrumentation from C2 to T4, and multiple posterior osteotomies; (2) anterior approach with hardware removal, fusion from C3 to T2, T1 corpectomy, and intraoperative traction; (3) posterior approach for final deformity correction and placement of a triple-rod construct to reinforce stability. Results: The patient demonstrated immediate postoperative improvement with recovery of upper extremity strength and significant reduction in pain. Radiographic evaluation confirmed substantial correction of cervical alignment and restoration of horizontal gaze. At six-month follow-up, the patient showed satisfactory evolution, with evidence of fusion, meaningful functional improvement, and no permanent neurological complications. Conclusion: Staged 540° circumferential reconstruction is an effective surgical strategy in patients with severe rigid cervicothoracic kyphosis and chin-on-chest deformity, particularly in cases with irreducible deformities, circumferential ankylosis, pseudoarthrosis, and failed prior instrumentation. Although the potential morbidity is considerable, when performed in specialized centers, this approach enables safe correction, significant pain relief, functional recovery, and restoration of quality of life.

RF206: Efficacy of combined anterior and posterior corrective surgery for dropped head syndrome using a unilateral anterior cage screw fixation

Ryo Yamamura 1 , Soji Tani 1 , Chikara Hayakawa 1 , Koki Tsuchiya 1 , Yohei Miyamoto 1 , Shimpei Koyama 1 , Ichiro Okano 1 , Tomoaki Toyone 1 , Yoshifmi Kudo 1

1 Showa Medical University, Shinagawa-ku, Japan

Introduction: The optimal surgical strategy for kyphotic deformity in DHS with severe degeneration remains a subject of debate. Our approach involves a combined anterior and posterior fusion, where an anterior cage is initially fixed with a unilateral screw to allow for additional posterior correction. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the multifaceted utility of this unilateral anterior cage screw fixation method. Material and Methods: This study included 27 patients who underwent combined anterior and posterior corrective fusion from the cervical to upper thoracic spine for DHS since 2015, using a screw-fixed cage for anterior fixation. After unilateral anterior cage fixation, additional correction was performed from the posterior approach. We investigated preoperative, post-anterior, and post-posterior C2-7 angles, the additional correction angle achieved by the posterior procedure, and complications (postoperative neurological symptoms, pseudoarthrosis, dysphagia, and PJK/DJK). Using pre- and postoperative CT scans, we measured and statistically compared the changes in the average vertical and horizontal diameters of the right and left intervertebral foramina at C3/4 to C6/7 levels. Results: The mean C2-7 angle significantly improved from -44.0° preoperatively to 5.8° post-anterior surgery, and further to 16.8° after additional posterior correction. An average of 11° of additional correction was achieved with the posterior procedure. CT evaluation confirmed a significant expansion of both the vertical and horizontal diameters of the intervertebral foramina on both sides at all levels from C3/4 to C6/7 compared to preoperative measurements. Postoperative C5 palsy was observed in two cases, but both were transient. There were no rod breakages. One case of dysphagia and three cases of DJK were observed. Conclusion: By using a unilateral anterior screw fixation, which maintains the mobility of the cage, this method allows for additional correction from the posterior approach and also contributes to preventing cage migration. Furthermore, the expansion of the intervertebral foramina can prevent iatrogenic foraminal stenosis after posterior correction. The significant foraminal enlargement observed at all evaluated levels suggests that this indirect decompression effect may reduce nerve root damage, contributing to the prevention or avoidance of severe iatrogenic nerve palsy. Combined anterior and posterior surgery with unilateral anterior cage screw fixation is a safe and rational treatment option for DHS, providing excellent correction while also offering the potential for indirect decompression through foraminal enlargement.

RF207: Pathology type and outcome in patients who had post-flip neuromonitoring change: impact of head holder type

Ashel Dsouza 1 , Niall Buckley 1 , Danielle Niento 1 , Lee Tan 1

1 University of California San Francisco, San Francisco, United States

Introduction: Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) changes during patient positioning, particularly after the “flip” to prone, are critical indicators of potential neural compromise in cervical spine surgery. Head immobilization devices like the Gardner-Wells tongs (GW) and Mayfield skull clamp differ in design, potentially affecting stability and IONM alert rates. This study examines the association between head holder type and IONM changes post-flip, focusing on patient characteristics and outcomes by pathology type. Materials and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 594 patients (operated in a tertiary care centre from 2018-2024) and a sub analysis was performed on 38 patients who experienced IONM changes post-flip clustered by 14 surgeons. Patient characteristics (age, BMI, sex, diabetes prevalence) were compared by head holder type (GW: n = 32; Mayfield: n = 6). Clustered logistic regression (adjusted for 14 surgeon clusters) assessed the odds of IONM changes with GW vs. Mayfield, controlling for diagnosis (kyphosis/deformity, myelopathy, trauma, tumor). Outcomes included new neurological deficits and signal recovery rates, estimated from cohort patterns and literature. Results: Patients with IONM changes had a mean age of 65.0 ± 12.9 years, BMI of 26.9 ± 6.4, 44.7% male, and 30.6% diabetes. GW users (n = 32) were slightly older (65.3 ± 13.3) with higher BMI (27.1 ± 6.7) and diabetes (32.3%) compared to Mayfield users (n = 6; 63.2 ± 11.1, 25.7 ± 4.5, 20.0%). No significant demographic differences were found (all p > 0.05). Pathology distribution estimated GW changes at 84.2% of cases, with myelopathy (30-35%) and trauma (25-30%) most common, followed by kyphosis/deformity (20-30%) and tumor (10-20%). Clustered regression showed GW associated with lower odds of IONM change (OR = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.51-0.96, p = 0.025). Signal recovery rates were 80-100% for kyphosis/deformity, 69-90% for myelopathy, 70-95% for trauma, and 60-80% for tumor; new deficit rates ranged from 5-15% by pathology. Conclusions: To the authors' knowledge, this is one of the largest cohorts specifically examining the association between head immobilization device type and IONM alert rates post-flip, with 38 change cases out of 594 patients. Gardner-Wells head holder use correlates with statistically lower IONM change rates post-flip, potentially due to adjustable traction, across diverse pathologies. High recovery rates suggest positioning adjustments mitigate risks, though deficit risks vary by pathology (e.g., higher in trauma/myelopathy). Prospective studies are needed to confirm causality and optimize device selection.

RF208: How do zero-profile devices with integrated screw fixation compare with traditional ACDF/plating? Single- and multilevel anterior cervical discectomy and fusion: a review of 369 patients across 930 levels

Burak Ozgur 1 , Kareem Khalifeh 2 , Janneinne Le 1

1 Hoag Spine Institute, Newport Beach, United States, 2 University of California, San Diego Medical Center, San Diego, United States

Introduction: While conventional anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) plate and cage (PC) constructs have demonstrated successful clinical outcomes, the anterior plating on these implants has been associated with complications including dysphagia, pseudoarthrosis, and need for reoperation. Thus, alternative surgical devices consisting of a zero-profile and integrated screw fixation (ZP-ISF) have evolved. The objective of this study is to assess clinical outcomes of ACDF using these newer implants, particularly in multilevel procedures. Material and Methods: A retrospective review was conducted on patients who underwent single- or multilevel ACDF using ZP-ISF devices over an eleven-year period. All cases were performed by the same neurosurgeon at a single institution. Outcome measures included visual analog scale (VAS) scores, complications, and readmissions. Results: 369 patients (mean age 64; 57% male) underwent ACDF between January 2014 and August 2025 (one-level, n = 54; two-level, n = 120; three-level, n = 131; four-level, n = 58; total, n = 919). Average length of stay was one day. Mean preop, 2-week, 6-week, 3-month, 6-month, and 1-year VAS scores were 4.88, 3.03, 2.24, 1.94, 1.83, and 1.59, respectively. VAS scores improved significantly between each follow-up period until 3 months (p < 0.05). The clinical sample experienced no infections. There were no cases of clinically significant pseudoarthrosis or subsidence requiring reoperation. One patient was readmitted for dysphagia which completely resolved by post-op week 6. Another patient developed mild postoperative paresthesia in bilateral lower extremities with MRI evidence of a possible hematoma and underwent reoperation. Overall, the ZP-ISF construct was associated with a 0.6% complication rate and demonstrated favorable clinical outcomes compared to traditional PC devices, which have reported complication rates as high as 16.5% for multilevel ACDF based on the existing literature. Conclusion: ZP-ISF constructs are safe and effective in both single- and multilevel ACDF. Further work distinguishing these devices from other types of zero-profile implants would be beneficial in terms of properly classifying efficacy and complication rates. Additionally, a prospective study also evaluating patient-reported-outcomes (PROs) would be helpful in the analysis.

RF209: The impact of anterior cervical spine surgery on objective fluoroscopic swallowing kinematics

Eric Klineberg 1 , Mohamed A. Aboueisha 2 , Peter Belafsky 2

1 University of Texas Health, Houston, United States, 2 University of California Davis, Sacramento, United States

Introduction: Dysphagia following anterior cervical spine (ACS) surgery is common. The effect of ACS surgery on objective video-fluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) parameters has not been prospectively evaluated. The purpose of this investigation was to prospectively evaluate the effect of ACS surgery on objective VFSS data. Methods: All persons undergoing ACS surgery at a single institution between 01/01/23 and 12/31/24 were eligible for enrollment. Patients with previous ACS surgery and those with medical comorbidity associated with swallowing impairment (e.g. neurodegenerative disease, head and neck cancer) were excluded. Surgical approach and instrumentation and patient demographics were obtained from the medical record. Patients prospectively underwent VFSS within 4 weeks before and 3 months after ACS surgery. Subjective dysphagia was evaluated pre and 3-months post-op with the 10-item Eating Assessment Tool (EAT10). All objective VFSS parameters have been previously validated and included the pharyngeal constriction ratio (PCR), penetration aspiration scale (PAS), posterior pharyngeal wall thickness (PPWT), pharyngeal area (PA), pharyngoesophageal segment (PES) opening, oral phase transit time (OPTT), and hypopharyngeal transit time (HPTT). Results: 24 patients were enrolled. The mean age of the cohort was 62 (±12) years and 54% was male. 62% (15/24) underwent anterior cervical discectomy and fusion and 37% (9/24) underwent cervical disc replacement. The mean number of levels fused was 2.2 (±0.9). Preoperative dysphagia (EAT10 > 2) was reported in 33% (8/24) of patients. The EAT10 increased from 3.9 (±6.3) preoperatively to 8.1 (±8.6) postoperatively (p = 0.01). All objective fluoroscopic parameters were worse. PPW thickness increased from 0.42 (±0.11) to 0.59 (±0.17) (p < 0.001), PA increased from 8.1 (±2.28) to 8.8 (±2.9) (p = 0.044), and PCR increased from 0.04 (±0.04) to 0.06 (±0.07) (p = 0.024). Non-significant worsening was observed in PES opening, OPTT, and HPTT. Conclusions: Patients undergoing anterior cervical spine surgery experienced notable declines in both subjective dysphagia symptoms and objective fluoroscopic swallowing parameters. The most significant deterioration in swallowing kinematics appears to be an elevated pharyngeal area and diminished pharyngeal contractility suggesting that pharyngeal dilation and weakness are common side-effects of anterior surgery. Further investigation is required to see if these findings persist beyond 3 months post-op.

Ping-Yeh Chiu 1

1 Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Taoyuan, Taiwan

Introduction: Conventional open-door laminoplasty (ODLP) effectively treats multilevel cervical myelopathy but may reduce cervical range of motion (ROM) and increase axial pain. RF211: Comparison of rigid and non-rigid interbody fusion device for cervical degenerative disc disease in adults - A randomized, prospective, multicenter clinical trial

Ting-Li Shen 1 , Pao-Chun Lin 2 , Wei-Lung Tseng 2 , Se-Yi Chen 3 , Chang-Jung Chiang 4 , Shih-Hung Yang 5 , Yuan-Shen Chen 6 , Shao-Hua Ko 7 , Huan-Chih Wang 5 , Shiu-Jau Chen 8 , Yun-Heng Li 5 , Po-Jen Shih 1 , Feng Huei Lin 1 , Fon-Yih Tsuang 5

1 National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan, 2 Fu Jen Catholic University Hospital, New Taipei, Taiwan, 3 Chung Shan Medical University Hospital, Taichung, Taiwan, 4 Shuang Ho Hospital, New Taipei, Taiwan, 5 National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan, 6 National Taiwan University Hospital, Yunlin, Taiwan, 7 Min Sheng General Hospital, Taoyuan, Taiwan, 8 MacKay Memorial Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is the standard treatment for cervical degenerative disc disease, achieving high fusion rates but also associated with complications such as pseudoarthrosis and adjacent segment degeneration (ASD). Conventional rigid cages, commonly made of titanium or PEEK, are mechanically stiffer than the native disc, resulting in stress shielding and altered biomechanics. To address these limitations, non-rigid cervical cages with dynamic design features have been developed to preserve controlled micro-motion under physiological loading. This randomized multicenter trial was designed to compare the clinical and radiological outcomes of non-rigid dynamic cages versus conventional rigid cages in ACDF. The present report summarizes the midterm enrollment progress and baseline findings. Material and Methods: This prospective randomized multicenter clinical trial is being conducted from 2020 to 2027 across 13 centers, with a planned enrollment of 180 patients requiring one- or two-level ACDF. Patients are randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive either a non-rigid titanium dynamic cage or a conventional rigid PEEK cage. Eligible patients present with symptomatic radiculopathy or myelopathy refractory to conservative management, while those with osteoporosis, multi-level (> 2) procedures, prior cervical fusion, autoimmune disease, infection, or malignancy are excluded. Clinical outcomes include the Neck Disability Index (NDI), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), SF-12 PCS/MCS, patient satisfaction, and reoperation rates. Radiological outcomes are assessed by dynamic radiographs and CT for fusion and cage subsidence. Follow-ups are scheduled at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months. Statistical analysis is planned using repeated measures ANOVA with significance set at p < 0.05. Results: As of August 2025, a total of 54 patients have been enrolled across 8 hospitals, with surgeries performed by 11 surgeons. Thirty-seven patients were randomized to the non-rigid cage group and 17 to the rigid cage group. The mean age was 56 years (range 28-80), and the mean BMI was 25.9 (range 18.6-35.1). Twenty-one patients underwent single-level ACDF, while 33 received two-level procedures. Baseline demographic and surgical characteristics, including age, sex, BMI, and surgical levels, were comparable between groups, confirming successful randomization. Clinical and radiological follow-up is ongoing, and preliminary baseline data demonstrate feasibility of multicenter enrollment and balanced group allocation. Conclusion: This is the first multicenter randomized trial directly comparing rigid and non-rigid cervical cages in ACDF. The midterm results confirm balanced enrollment and appropriate group distribution across multiple centers. Ongoing follow-up will determine whether non-rigid cage designs can reduce subsidence, improve fusion, and enhance patient-reported outcomes compared with conventional rigid cages. Final 24-month analyses are expected to provide important evidence to guide implant selection and surgical decision-making in cervical degenerative disc disease.

RF212: Evaluating the impact of single or two-level anterior cervical surgery on extensor neck muscle volume in patients presenting with degenerative pathology

Sydney Pattison 1,2 , Aiyush Bansal 1 , Madison Alessi 1,2 , Kento Yamanouchi 1,3 , Kenneth Nguyen 1 , Rakesh Kumar 1 , Jean Christophe Leveque 1 , Venu Nemani 1 , Philip Louie 1

1 Virginia Mason Medical Center, Seattle, United States, 2 University of Washington, Seattle, United States, 3 Keio University, Tokyo, Japan

Introduction: Degenerative changes in the cervical spine can cause radicular symptoms requiring surgery. Studies have shown that cervical extensor muscles (CEM) may be associated with development of cervical degenerative disorders, and muscle degeneration has been associated with worse functional and symptomatic outcomes. However, research exploring changes in CEM following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) or cervical disc replacement (CDR) is limited. This pilot study aimed to 1) assess MRI-measured CEM volume changes in patients undergoing single or two-level ACDF or CDR, 2) compare the magnitudes of these changes between ACDF and CDR surgeries, and 3) establish a preliminary effect size to guide future study sample size calculations. Materials and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed patients undergoing single- or two-level ACDF or CDR for degenerative pathology, without prior instrumentation or cervical spine surgery. Cross-sectional areas (CSA) of left and right CEMs (splenius capitis [including splenius cervicis], semispinalis capitis, and multifidus [including semispinalis cervicis]) were measured on pre- and postoperative axial T2 weighted-MRIs at the C4-C5 intervertebral disc using Philips IntelliSpace PACS. Follow-up imaging was obtained opportunistically at an average of 15.2 months postoperatively. Three personnel trained by a board-certified radiologist conducted measurements; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) ranged from 0.94 to 0.98. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to calculate intra-subject changes from pre- to postoperative measurements; Wilcoxon rank-sum tests compared differences between ACDF and CDR groups. Due to baseline age differences, 1:1 propensity score matching was performed. Power analyses were conducted for within-subjects and between-group comparisons. Results: The initial cohort included 34 patients (nACDF = 22; nCDR = 12). ACDF patients were older (62.1 vs. 46.4 years, p < 0.001), while other demographics were similar. Across the full cohort, postoperative muscle CSA decreased significantly. Right-sided CSA decreased from a median of 10.14 cm2 to 9.44 cm2 (p < 0.001) and left-sided CSA from 9.84 cm2 to 9.68 cm2 (p = 0.003), with median percent reductions of 6.47% and 6.12%, respectively. Power for paired comparisons was 85% (left) and 97% (right) achieved. After age-matching, (nACDF = 9; nCDR = 9) no significant differences in muscle CSA change were observed between ACDF and CDR. Median right-sided change was -1.21 cm2 (-8.91%) for ACDF versus -0.44 cm2 (-4.65%) for CDR (p = 0.35); median left-sided change was -0.885 cm2 (-7.47%) for ACDF versus -0.300 cm2 (-3.39%) for CDR (p = 0.48). Conclusion: This pilot study demonstrates CEM CSA decreases following an ACDF or CDR for degenerative pathology, measured approximately one year postoperatively. While muscle atrophy did not differ significantly between the two procedures, ACDF showed greater variability in muscle change. Given the pilot nature of this current work, this study was underpowered to detect a difference between surgical techniques. These findings suggest ACDF was non-inferior to CDR regarding postoperative muscle preservation, but evaluating additional patients will more accurately determine if differences in CEM morphology exist in patients undergoing fusion or motion-preserving anterior cervical operation.

RF213: Stand-alone expandable cage for anterior cervical corpectomy: long-term follow-up

Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad 1,2 , Seyed-Emadaldin Sadat 1 , Ahmed Elsaghir 1 , Hamdan Abdelrahman 1 , Ali Ezzati 1

1 Helios Hospitals Erfurt - Germany, Assiut University Hospitals - Egypt, Erfurt, Germany, 2 Assiut University Hospitals, Assiut, Egypt

Introduction: Anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion (ACCF) is indicated for various cervical conditions involving spinal canal stenosis or instability. Non-expandable vertebral body replacement cages (VBRC) require additional anterior plate fixation or posterior lateral mass fixation. Recently, the advent of expandable VBRCs with larger footprints has enabled their use as standalone implants. This is the first study to present long-term results of standalone VBRCs after ACCF. Material and Methods: Between October 2013 and January 2020, 88 patients with various cervical pathologies underwent surgery at our center using ACCF and stand-alone expandable VBRCs. Long-term complications such as pseudoarthrosis, mechanical failure, subsidence, and re-operations were documented. Results: Eighty-eight patients underwent surgery, with two lost to follow-up. The average age was 66 years. Fifty-five patients received a single-level ACCF, 31 received a double-level ACCF, and 2 underwent a triple-level ACCF. The most common pathology was degenerative, found in 75 patients, followed by trauma in 7 cases, and tumors and infections in 3 cases each. RF214: Investigating the relationship between low density lipoprotein cholesterol and cervical spinal fusion outcomes amongst statin users: a propensity-matched analysis

Kyle Stump 1 , Henry Morar 1 , Stephan Aynaszyan 2 , Dhara Patel 2 , Theresa Pazionis 2

1 Lewis Katz School of Medicine at Temple University, Philadelphia, United States, 2 Department of Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine, Temple University Hospital, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Emerging evidence suggests high low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is linked to higher rates of nonunion after spinal fusion. Conversely, statins may benefit bone metabolism, raising the question of whether prior associations between LDL-C and fusion outcomes are confounded by statin use. This study evaluated the relationship between preoperative LDL-C levels and nonunion in statin-exposed patients undergoing single-level anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). Materials and Methods: The TriNetX Research Network was queried for patients aged 18 - 89 years who underwent single-level ACDF between September 17, 2003 and September 17, 2023. Multilevel procedures were excluded. Next, patients with a statin prescription within six months before or after surgery were identified. LDL-C groups were defined as high (≥ 140.2 mg/dL, one standard deviation above the mean) and low (≤ 65.8 mg/dL, one standard deviation below the mean). A secondary analysis compared ACDF patients with versus without perioperative statin use. Propensity score matching (1:1) was applied for demographics, body mass index, and comorbidities. Diagnosis of nonunion was assessed at six months, one year, and two years using risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results: In the primary analysis, 538 matched pairs were included. Seventy percent of patients were White, and 41% were female. Within six months, nonunion occurred in 14.3% of high LDL-C patients versus 11.3% of low LDL-C patients (RR 1.262, 95% CI 0.922 - 1.728, p = 0.145). At one year, rates were 15.2% and 13.6% in the high LDL-C and low LDL-C groups, respectively (RR 1.123, 95% CI 0.839 - 1.504, p = 0.435), and at two years, 16.0% versus 14.1% (RR 1.134, 95% CI 0.864 - 1.488, p = 0.364). LDL-C levels remained significantly different between groups at all intervals (p < 0.001). In the secondary analysis, 12,446 matched pairs were included. Seventy-three percent of patients were White, and 42% were female. Nonunion was significantly lower among statin users: 14.1% versus 16.3% at six months (RR 0.867, 95% CI 0.817 - 0.919, p < 0.001), 15.2% versus 17.5% at one year (RR 0.870, 95% CI 0.822 - 0.921, p < 0.001), and 16.0% versus 18.6% at two years (RR 0.859, 95% CI 0.810 - 0.910, p < 0.001). LDL-C levels also differed significantly between groups, though the absolute differences were smaller than in the primary analysis. Conclusion: This study found no association between LDL-C levels and nonunion in statin-exposed patients undergoing ACDF. However, perioperative statin use was consistently associated with reduced nonunion risk, replicating prior findings. In conjunction with the greater LDL-C differences in the primary analysis compared with the secondary, our findings suggest that earlier retrospective reports linking elevated LDL-C to higher nonunion rates may be confounded by statin therapy, given its established pleiotropic effects on bone metabolism. These findings highlight the need for prospective studies to better delineate the independent effects of LDL-C and statins on spinal fusion outcomes.

RF215: Preoperative cervical canal narrowing as a predictor for subsequent posterior cervical decompression and fusion following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion

Sertac Kirnaz 1 , Jaewoo Park 1 , Rose Fluss 1 , Saikiran Murthy 1 , Rafael De La Garza Ramos 1 , Reza Yassari 1 , Yaroslav Gelfand 1

1 Montefiore Medical Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, United States

Introduction: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is a common surgical procedure used to address cervical spine pathology. However, some patients subsequently require additional posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCF) due to persistent or progressive spinal stenosis and neurological compromise. The purpose of this study was to determine whether patients with narrower cervical canal areas preoperatively are more likely to require a subsequent PCF following an initial ACDF. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective review of patients who underwent ACDF at our institution between 2019 and 2023. Inclusion criteria were patients who had 1- or 2-level ACDF and at least two years of postoperative follow-up. Patients with prior cervical spine surgery were excluded. Participants were divided into two groups: the control group included patients who only underwent ACDF, and the experimental group included those who required PCF within two years after their initial ACDF. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was analyzed to measure the cervical spinal canal area for each vertebral level from C3 to C7. Additional measurements included anterior encroachment, posterior encroachment, and the effectively available canal area at each corresponding disc level. Results: Fifty-three patients met inclusion criteria, with 40 in the control group and 13 in the experimental group. The mean overall canal area in the control group was significantly larger than in the experimental group (12.43 mm2 vs. 10.09 mm2; p < 0.05). When analyzed by individual vertebral levels (C3-C7), the canal area was consistently smaller in the experimental group compared to controls, with statistically significant differences observed at each level: C3 (12.52 mm2 vs. 10.58 mm2), C4 (12.24 mm2 vs. 9.99 mm2), C5 (12.14 mm2 vs. 9.83 mm2), C6 (12.68 mm2 vs. 9.85 mm2), and C7 (12.58 mm2 vs. 10.21 mm2) with p < 0.05 for all comparisons. Similarly, mean available canal area from C3 to C7 was significantly reduced in the experimental group (7.85 mm2) compared to the control group (10.57 mm2; p < 0.05). Individual levels also demonstrated significant differences in available canal area: C3 (11.19 mm2 vs. 7.88 mm2), C4 (9.97 mm2 vs. 8.43 mm2), C5 (10.34 mm2 vs. 7.46 mm2), and C6 (10.80 mm2 vs. 7.62 mm2); all p < 0.05. These findings indicate that patients requiring PCF had significantly narrower preoperative canal dimensions. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that patients who require posterior cervical decompression and fusion following initial ACDF have significantly narrower cervical canal and available canal areas preoperatively compared to those who do not require subsequent posterior surgery. These findings suggest that preoperative assessment of canal dimensions may be critical in identifying patients at higher risk for requiring additional posterior decompression. Early recognition of narrow canal anatomy could inform surgical planning and prompt consideration of combined or staged anterior-posterior approaches to optimize patient outcomes. Further prospective studies are warranted to validate these findings and to develop standardized thresholds for clinical decision-making.

RF216: Integrating RCT and cohort design - The future of large-scale spine surgery research

Nádia Simões de Souza 1 , Anne Broekema 1 , Remko Soer 1,2 , Katalin Tamasi 1,3 , Thea van Asselt 1 , Michiel Reneman 1,4 , Jos Kuijlen 1 , Marc van Dijk 1

1 Department of Neurosurgery,

2 Department of Anesthesiology, University of Groningen, Groningen, The Netherlands,

3 Department of Epidemiology,

4 Department of Rehabilitation, University Medical Center Groningen, University of Groningen, Groningen, The Netherlands

Introduction: In most randomized controlled trials (RCT), data is primarily and often only available for individuals who have agreed to be randomized, with little, if any, consideration for those who elected not to participate. This study evaluated the value of including a concurrent nationwide observational cohort of patients who declined randomization in the Foraminotomy ACDF Cost-Effectiveness Trial (FACET-RCT) but still underwent anterior or posterior cervical surgery. The goal was to determine if the FACET-RCT results could be generalized by comparing baseline characteristics and clinical outcomes between the randomized trial and observational cohort recruiting patients from routine care. Material and Methods: Demographic data was collected, and primary outcomes included treatment success, evaluated using the Odom criteria as well as reduction in arm pain, assessed with a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) at 6 weeks, and every 6 months up to 2 years postsurgery. Secondary outcomes included VAS for neck pain, neck disability, work ability, quality of life, treatment satisfaction, and need for revision surgeries. Baseline characteristics were compared between the FACET-RCT and cohort using logistic regression. Primary and secondary outcomes were analyzed for differences between study designs using mixed-model analyses adjusted for confounders. The primary noninferiority endpoint of the FACET-RCT was evaluated in both the cohort and combined data from both cohort and FACET-RCT at 2 years of follow-up. Results: Between January 2016 and May 2020, 389 patients with cervical radiculopathy were screened, and 358 were eligible. Of these, 265 (74%) were randomized in the FACET-RCT for either posterior or anterior cervical surgery, while 80 (22%) opted out of randomization and were followed in an observational cohort. Only 13 (4%) patients declined participation in both FACET-RCT and cohort. Patients in the cohort were slightly younger than those in the FACET-RCT (mean age of 48.4 versus 51.2 years; mean difference [MD], -2.5; 95% confidence interval [CI], -4.8 to -0.2; p = .04). In sub-analyses stratified by surgical approach (anterior vs posterior surgery), fewer patients in the observational cohort who underwent posterior surgery reported severe neck pain at baseline compared to their counterparts in the FACET-RCT (OR, 0.38; 95% CI: 0.14 to 0.92; p = .04). No other significant baseline differences were found. No significant differences in treatment success (OR, 1.3; 95% CI: 0.3 to 6.0; p = .75) and arm pain reduction (MD, -3.9; 95% CI: -9.2 to 1.5; p = .16) were observed between study designs. The primary noninferiority endpoint was achieved in the combined data from both the cohort and FACET-RCT, with a narrower CI compared to the FACET-RCT alone, indicating a more robust result. Secondary outcomes were comparable between groups. Conclusion: Randomization did not influence clinical outcomes for cervical surgery patients. Combining RCT with the observational cohort increased statistical power, external validity and robustness. Our findings support the value of observational methods as a complement to RCTs, especially when a large number of patients refuse RCT participation and high dropout and crossover rates are expected.

RF217: C5 nerve root palsy after posterior cervical spine surgery

Nail Demirel 1 , Oğuz Alp ÇAKIR 2 , Okan Türk 2 , İbrahim Burak Atçı 2 , Nafiye Şanlıer 2 , Taha Altunkaya 2 , Onur Açar 2

1 Fatih Sultan Mehmet Training and Research Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey, 2 Istanbul Training and Research Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: C5 nerve root palsy is a well-recognized and challenging complication following posterior cervical spine surgery. It is characterized by new-onset weakness of the deltoid and biceps muscles and may significantly affect functional recovery and quality of life. Although its reported incidence varies between 5% and 15%, the exact pathophysiology remains unclear. Proposed mechanisms include posterior spinal cord shift, nerve root traction, ischemia, and preexisting foraminal stenosis. This study aims to evaluate the incidence, clinical course, and outcomes of C5 palsy after posterior cervical decompression and to review preventive and management strategies. Materials and Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 97 patients who underwent posterior cervical decompression surgery between 2015 and 2023. Demographic characteristics, surgical techniques, and postoperative neurological outcomes were evaluated. Neurological deficits and recovery were assessed using manual muscle testing based on the Klein and Garfin grading system. The use of intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM), prophylactic foraminotomy, and postoperative management strategies was recorded. Results: Among 97 patients, C5 palsy developed in a subset consistent with rates reported in the literature (5–15%). Most patients experienced favorable neurological recovery with appropriate postoperative management. Recovery times ranged from 2 to 41 months, reflecting considerable individual variability. Axial pain persisted in only three patients during follow-up, while the majority demonstrated substantial improvement over time. The use of intraoperative neuromonitoring, including transcranial motor-evoked potentials and electromyography, facilitated early detection of nerve root compromise. Prophylactic C4–C5 foraminotomy was associated with a reduced incidence of postoperative C5 palsy, particularly in patients with preexisting foraminal stenosis. Conservative treatment, including rest and structured physical rehabilitation, resulted in satisfactory functional recovery in most cases. A small number of patients required secondary surgical intervention due to persistent deficits. Older age, male sex, preoperative neurological impairment, and foraminal stenosis were identified as potential risk factors influencing recovery time and severity. Conclusion: C5 palsy remains a multifactorial complication of posterior cervical spine surgery. Careful preoperative evaluation, individualized surgical planning, and the use of intraoperative neuromonitoring are critical for risk reduction. Prophylactic foraminotomy may be beneficial in selected high-risk patients. Most cases demonstrate gradual neurological recovery with appropriate rehabilitation; however, severe deficits may require prolonged follow-up or revision surgery. Further research is needed to better elucidate the underlying mechanisms and to standardize preventive strategies.

RF218: Preoperative anemia severity predicts complications following lumbar decompression and fusion

Melissa Romoff 1 , Michael Kim 1 , Emily Tse 1 , Courtney Spitzer 1 , Andy Ton 1 , Vivian Chen 1 , Ryan Le 1 , Abhinav Sharma 1 , Justin Chan 1 , Emily Mills 1 , Hao-Hua Wu 1 , Don Park 1 , Yu-po Lee 1 , Nitin Bhatia 1 , Sohaib Hashmi 1

1 Univeristy of California, Irvine, Orange, United States

Introduction: Preoperative anemia is a well-established risk factor for adverse surgical outcomes, with several studies in joint arthroplasty demonstrating a stepwise increase in complication risk as anemia severity worsens. These findings have led to the integration of anemia screening and optimization protocols into perioperative pathways for total hip and knee arthroplasty. However, despite similar concerns around blood loss, transfusion, and recovery in spine surgery, anemia severity has not been systematically studied in this population. In particular, lumbar decompression and fusion procedures have unique physiologic demands and may be especially sensitive to hematologic compromise. Understanding how the degree of postoperative anemia influences both short-term complications and longer-term structural outcomes is essential for tailoring perioperative care and implementing patient counseling. This study evaluates the relationship between anemia severity and postoperative outcomes in a large cohort of patients undergoing lumbar decompression and fusion, with 90-day and 1-year follow-up

Material and Methods: Using the TriNetX Research Network, adult patients who underwent lumbar decompression and fusion procedures were identified and stratified into four groups based on preoperative anemia severity: severe (< 8g/dL), moderate (8-9.9 g/dL), and mild (10-11.9g/dL), and no anemia. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed using the Charlson Comorbidity Index to control for baseline medical complexity across cohorts. Postoperative outcomes were assessed at two time points: 90-day complications (surgical site infection, transfusion, pneumonia, postoperative anemia, and venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) and 1-year outcomes (pseudoarthrosis and reoperation). Risk ratios (RR), 95% confidence intervals (CI), and p-values were calculated for each comparison. Results: Among over 149,000 patients undergoing lumbar decompression and fusion, increasing anemia severity was significantly associated with elevated rates of both 90-day complications and 1-year outcomes. Patients with severe anemia had the highest relative risk across all outcomes, including transfusion (RR; 4.83, p < 0.0001), postoperative anemia (RR: 2.86, p < 0.0001), and lumbar fracture (RR: 2.67, p < 0.0001), pseudoarthrosis (RR: 1.60, p < 0.0001), and reoperation (RR: 1.49, p < 0.0001). Moderate anemia was similarly associated with increased transfusion, postoperative anemia, lumbar fracture, pseudoarthrosis, and reoperation. Even mild anemia conferred higher rates of complications. These findings demonstrate a clear dose-dependent relationship between anemia severity and adverse postoperative outcomes following lumbar decompression and fusion. Conclusion: Preoperative anemia, particularly when moderate to severe, is an independent predictor of both early postoperative complications and 1-year reoperation. The stepwise increase in risk with worsening anemia underscores the need for anemia stratification in preoperative risk models. While anemia is not always modifiable, especially in the setting of chronic disease or malignancy, its presence should prompt heightened perioperative vigilance and transparent discussion with patients regarding surgical risk. Future prospective studies are warranted to determine whether preoperative correction of anemia can reduce complication rates and improve long-term outcomes in patients undergoing lumbar decompression and fusion.

RF219: National trends in postoperative complications following lumbar fusion with iliac crest bone graft from 2012-2022

Emily Tse 1 , Arthur Cowman 1 , Sultan Baz 1 , Makenzie Tomihiro 1 , Joshua Lee 2 , Ian Newberg 3 , Lainie Carter 1 , Yu-po Lee 1

1 University of California, Irvine, School of Medicine, Irvine, United States, 2 University of Southern California, Los Angeles, United States, 3 University of San Diego, San Diego, United States

Introduction: Lumbar spinal fusion (LSF) is a common treatment for degenerative and traumatic lumbar pathology, with graft selection contributing significantly to cost and outcomes. Iliac crest bone graft (ICBG) remains the biologic gold standard but introduces additional morbidity due to autograft surgery, leading many surgeons to favor more expensive allografts despite studies demonstrating ICBG to be more cost-effective than allograft ($21,308 per quality-adjusted life year vs. $28,153). Nonetheless, longitudinal data on ICBG complication trends are limited, and understanding these patterns is important for evaluating its continued role as a cost-effective graft option. This study aims to assess trends in postoperative complications following LSF with ICBG using a high-powered, nationally representative cohort from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP) database. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis of the ACS-NSQIP database (2012-2022) was conducted to identify patients aged > 18 who underwent LSF involving at least one level (CPT 22612). Patients were further divided into two groups based on graft type, with ICBG (CPT 20937) and allograft (CPT 20936) identified. Some patients received more than one graft type. Annual rates of procedure usage were analyzed for both graft procedures, while univariate analyses of 30-day complications were only conducted for the ICBG cohort. Results: Among 20,337 lumbar fusion patients, 4,448 (21.9%) received ICBG and 18,661 (91.8%) allograft. ICBG use rose from 19.5% in 2012 to 25.9% in 2015, then declined to 16.1% by 2022, while allograft use increased from 80.5% to 83.9%. In the ICBG cohort, transfusion rates decreased from 22.9% (2012) to 8.0% (2022, p < 0.001), and deep wound infections peaked at 2.2% (2013) before falling to 0.9% (2022, p = 0.012). No significant trends were observed for superficial or organ space infections, pneumonia, reintubation, pulmonary embolism, respiratory failure, renal failure, urinary tract infection (UTI), cardiac arrest, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), sepsis, septic shock, reoperation, or mortality. Conclusion: Despite declining use due to donor-site morbidity and nonsurgical factors, ICBG complication rates in lumbar fusion have improved over the past decade, with significant reductions in transfusion and deep wound infections and stability across other outcomes. Given its lower cost relative to allograft use, the sustained safety of ICBG supports its continued consideration as a cost-effective graft option, particularly in an era where hospitals are facing increasing financial constraints.

RF221: Determining clinically excessive blood loss in surgery for severe congenital spinal deformity

Di Liu 1 , Jianguo Zhang 1 , Nan Wu 1

1 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Peking Union Medical College and Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Beijing, People’s Republic of China, Beijing, China

Introduction: There are currently no well-established thresholds that define clinically significant excessive blood loss in patients with severe congenital spinal deformity. To determine clinically relevant thresholds for total blood loss (TBL), normalized TBL (N-TBL), estimated blood volume loss (EBVL), hidden blood loss (HBL), and normalized HBL (N-TBL), and to identify factors associated with increased blood loss. Material and Methods: Consecutive patients who underwent surgical correction for severe spinal deformity were retrospectively included. Patient’s total blood volume (BV) was estimated using Nadler’s formula. TBL was calculated based on hematocrit values, and EBVL was obtained by dividing TBL by the estimated BV. The Spine Adverse Events Severity System version 2 (SAVES-V2) was used to identify clinically important adverse events (SAVES-V2 grade ≥ 2). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was employed to determine optimal threshold for each blood loss measure. Multiple linear regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of increased blood loss. Results: A total of 79 patients were included, with a mean age of 17.4 ± 11.6 years at the time of surgery. The median TBL, EBVL, and HBL were 1601.5 mL (interquartile range [IQR], 1124.2-2234.9 mL), 59.4% (IQR, 44.1%-79.6%), and 984.6 mL (IQR, 702.7-1621.1 mL). The median HBL was. Thirty-five patients experienced perioperative adverse events graded ≥ 2 on SAVES-V2. The optimal thresholds for clinically significant blood loss were identified as follows: TBL ≥ 2424.6 mL, N-TBL ≥ 32.6 mL/kg, EBVL ≥ 55.7%, HBL ≥ 1523.8 mL, and N-HBL ≥ 32.4 mL/kg. Older age, male sex, longer operative duration, prolonged fused levels, and anterior column reconstruction were significantly associated with increased blood loss. In contrast, the use of tranexamic acid (TXA) was associated with reduced blood loss across all measures. Conclusion: In severe congenital spinal deformity surgery, clinically significant blood loss can be defined using specific thresholds. Several factors predicted greater blood loss, while TXA plays a protective role in blood loss.

RF222: Abdominal aortic calcification as a risk factor for complications and hospital readmissions in thoracolumbar spine surgery: a retrospective cohort analysis

1 Orthopedic Department, Hospital Italiano de Buenos Aires, Buenos Aires, Argentina

Additionally, we evaluated whether incorporating AAC into the modified 5-item frailty index (mFI-5) improved its predictive ability for major postoperative complications and unplanned readmissions. RF223: Assessment of lumbar spine mobility after arthrodesis

Elyes Zoghlami 1 , ayari rabie 1 , Khaled Khlil0 1 , Youssef Mallat 1 , hadj mohamed slim 1 , Khalil Amri 1

1 Tunis Military Hospital, Tunis, Tunisia

Introduction: Instrumented lumbar arthrodesis induces major biomechanical modifications of spinal kinematics through segmental rigidification, generating compensatory stress transfer to adjacent levels. These alterations represent an established risk factor for adjacent segment syndrome (ASS). The objective was to quantitatively evaluate segmental mobility modifications after lumbar arthrodesis through dynamic radiographic analysis. Material and Methods: This was a retrospective single-center study conducted at the Principal Military Teaching Hospital of Tunis, between January 2018 and December 2024, including 85 patients who underwent instrumented lumbar arthrodesis. Kinematic evaluation was based on dynamic radiographic analysis in flexion-extension with measurement of segmental Range of Motion (ROM) according to the Cobb method. Studied parameters included ROM of the fused segment, adjacent segments, and functional assessment using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Measurements were performed preoperatively and at a mean follow-up of 24 months. Results: The ROM of the fused segment decreased from 7.8 ± 2.1° to 1.1 ± 0.4°, representing an 85.9% reduction (p < 0.001). Compensatory hypermobility was observed at adjacent segments with ROM evolving from 8.5 ± 1.8° to 12.2 ± 2.4°, corresponding to a 43.5% increase (p < 0.001). Correlational analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between adjacent hypermobility and ODI functional deterioration (r = 0.68, p < 0.001). Patients with adjacent ROM > 15° presented significantly higher ODI scores (52.4 ± 12.1 vs 38.7 ± 9.8, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Instrumented lumbar arthrodesis induces major kinematic modifications characterized by complete segmental rigidification (ROM reduction of 85.9%) and compensatory hypermobility of adjacent segments (+43.5%). This hypermobility constitutes a predictive biomarker of functional deterioration and risk of adjacent segment syndrome. Dynamic radiographic evaluation represents an essential diagnostic tool for post-operative biomechanical surveillance and early detection of adjacent complications.

Abdus Salam 1 , Qudrat Ullah Khan 1

1 Ghurki Trust Teaching Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan

Introduction: Incidental durotomy is a recognized complication of spine surgery that may lead to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage, wound infection, and prolonged recovery. RF226: Paraspinal muscle endurance and morphology (PMEM) score: a new method for prediction of postoperative mechanical complications after lumbar fusion

Gengyu Han 1 , zheyu fan 1 , lihao yue 1 , Siyu Zhou 1 , Weishi Li 1

1 Peking University Third Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Although the relationships between paraspinal muscles and lumbar degenerative disorders have been acknowledged, paraspinal muscle evaluation has not been incorporated into clinical therapies. Thus, we aimed to establish a novel paraspinal muscle endurance and morphology (PMEM) score to better predict mechanical complications after lumbar fusion. Material and Methods: This is a prospective cohort study. A total of 212 patients undergoing posterior lumbar interbody fusion with at least one year of follow-up were finally included. Mechanical complications including screw loosening, pseudarthrosis and other complications like cage subsidence, and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated at last follow-up. The PMEM score comprised one functional muscular parameter (the performance time of the endurance test) and two imaging muscular parameters (relative functional cross-sectional area [rFCSA] of paraspinal extensor muscles [PEM] and psoas major [PS] on magnetic resonance imaging). The score was established based on a weighted scoring system created by rounding β regression coefficients to the nearest integer in univariate logistic regression. The diagnostic performance of the PMEM score was determined by binary logistic regression model and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve with the area under the curve (AUC). Additionally, pairwise comparisons of ROC curves were conducted to compare the diagnostic performance of the PMEM score with conventional methods based on a single muscular parameter. Moreover, differences of mechanical complications and patient-reported outcomes among the PMEM categories were analyzed using Chi-square test with Bonferroni correction. Results: The PMEM score, calculated by adding the scores for each parameter, ranges from 0 to 5 points. Patients with higher PMEM scores exhibited higher rates of mechanical complications (p < 0.001). Moreover, the AUC of the PMEM score (AUC = 0.756) was significantly greater than those of the conventional methods including the endurance test (AUC = 0.691, Z = 2.036, p < 0.05), PEM rFCSA (AUC = 0.690, Z = 2.016, p < 0.05) and PS rFCSA (AUC = 0.640, Z = 2.771, p < 0.01). In terms of the PMEM categories, a score of 0 to 1 was categorized as low-risk muscular state of mechanical complications; 2 to 3, as moderate; and 4 to 5, as high-risk state. Moving from the low-risk state to the high-risk state, there was a progressive increase in the rates of mechanical complications (13.8% vs 32.1% vs 72.7%; p < 0.001), and a decrease in the rates of clinically significant improvement of patient-reported outcomes (all p < 0.05). Conclusion: The PMEM score might comprehensively evaluate paraspinal muscle degeneration and exhibit greater ability in predicting mechanical complications than the conventional evaluations after lumbar fusion. Surgeons might develop individualized treatment strategy tailored to different muscle degeneration statuses reflected by the PMEM score for decreasing the risk of mechanical complications.

1 Univeristy of California, Irvine, Orange, United States

However, recent large-scale matched cohort studies have reported no reduction in prosthetic joint infection rates and, in some cases, an increase in complications. Despite limited evidence, the practice remains widespread, particularly among high-risk patients. In spine surgery, the efficacy of extended oral antibiotics in reducing postoperative infection, sepsis, or revision rates has not been evaluated in large, multi-institutional studies. Given the rising concerns over antibiotic resistance and microbiome disruption, this study investigates the clinical utility of extended prophylaxis following lumbar spine decompression and fusion. These findings, while accounting for potential selection bias, challenge the presumed protective benefit of extended antibiotic use in this context. In light of the increased complication rates and the broader implications for antimicrobial resistance and microbiome disruption, the routine use of extended prophylaxis warrants critical reevaluation.

RF229: Failure modes of dural repair devices: a five-year analysis of the FDA MAUDE database for dural sealants and grafts

Nathan McLaughlin 1 , Zachary Lowe 1 , Advika Srinivas 1 , Amir Fanaei 1 , Nidhi Checka 1 , Nagheli Borjas 1 , Mauricio Avila 1

1 Saint Louis University, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: Incidental durotomy is a common neurosurgical complication, requiring effective dural repair to prevent subsequent complications such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak. While adjuncts such as sealants and onlay grafts are widely used, their real-world failure modes and resultant clinical consequences remain poorly characterized. This study aims to describe and compare adverse events associated with dural sealants and grafts as reported to the FDA’s Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database. Methods: The MAUDE database was queried for all adverse event reports associated with dural sealant (NQR) and dural graft (GXQ) product codes from January 1, 2020, to December 31, 2024. Reports were reviewed to exclude duplicates, and non-event summaries. Data were extracted for patient demographics, event timing, device-specific failure modes, and resulting patient complications. Descriptive statistics were used to analyze and compare findings between the two device cohorts. Results: A total of 386 unique adverse event reports were analyzed: 90 for dural sealants (NQR) and 296 for dural grafts (GXQ), revealing markedly different failure profiles. Sealant events occurred predominantly intraoperatively (70.0%). Common device problems were application-related, including applicator malfunctions (32.2%, failure to polymerize (22.2%), and premature polymerization (20.0%), frequently causing surgical delays. Conversely, dural graft events occurred overwhelmingly postoperatively (90.8%). The predominant failure was postoperative graft leakage (43.6%), which was the primary device problem and patient complication. Sealant failures are typically mechanical, intraoperative events related to device application, while graft failures are more often clinical, postoperative events related to the device’s inability to maintain a durable seal. This analysis of real-world data highlights the importance for clinicians to recognize these differing complication patterns when selecting a dural repair adjunct to better inform intraoperative decision-making and guide postoperative management.

RF230: The impact of Body Mass Index stratification on perioperative complications in open, tubular, and endoscopic lumbar microdiscectomy

Dillon Stone 1 , Lane McCoy 1 , John O'Malley 1 , Garrison Bentz 1 , Lucas Budd 1 , Pallavi Jonnalagadda 1 , Salim Yakdan 2 , John Ogunlade 2 , Mark Lambrechts 1

Methods and Materials: Patients > 18 years-old who underwent a primary, elective single-level lumbar microdiscectomy with 3 months follow-up between June 2018 to March 2025 were included. Continuous variables were compared utilizing Kruskal-Wallis one way analysis of variance with a Dunn test for post-hoc analysis of significant findings. Categorical variables were compared utilizing Chi-Square tests. Statistical significance was p < 0.05. Results: In total, 757 patients were included (OM: 422, TM: 190, ED: 145). Patients with a higher obesity class underwent a greater proportion of ED (p = 0.038). For OM (WO: 258, CI: 97, CII: 50, CIII: 17), CI had a greater proportion of males while CII had a lower proportion (p = 0.007). For ED (WO: 79, CI: 31, CII: 20, CIII: 15), mean patient age was highest in WO and lowest in CIII (p = 0.004). In CIII patients, EBL was greater (p = 0.028) and time to revision shorter (p < 0.001) than all other classes. There were no significant differences between the classes in the other variables evaluated. Conclusions: ED was more commonly performed in patients with higher obesity classes. In the OM cohort, CII and CIII obesity was associated with increased operative time, longer LOS, and greater EBL likely related to increased surgical exposure requirements. CIII patients also had a small (< 5 mL), but significantly greater, EBL during ED procedures. CII obesity patients undergoing OM were more likely to return to the ER for surgery-related reasons, however the TM and ED cohorts did not display obesity class related complication differences. These results suggest that obesity severity does not play a significant role in the development of postoperative complications in TM or ED and that minimally invasive techniques have a lower risk of complications compared to OM. Minimally invasive techniques are shown to provide improved operative and complication outcomes, however, due to the retrospective nature of this study and limited number of CIII patients, more research is needed to fully investigate this relationship.

Despite primary studies evaluating the benefits of cement augmentation, there is a lack of consensus in the literature regarding the clinical outcomes and complications of pedicle screw cement augmentation in metastatic spine disease.

Logistic regression analysis indicated that male sex (OR = 0.8, p = 0.022) and surgical complications (OR = 0.7, p < 0.001) significantly decreased the likelihood of achieving the MOI threshold. Conversely, preoperative neurological deficits were associated with significantly increased odds of meeting this threshold (OR = 1.6, p = 0.041). Conclusion: For patients with severe spinal deformity, the MOI threshold for the SRS-22r score was determined to be 43.5% at a minimum 2-year follow-up. Male patients and those with perioperative complications demonstrated a significantly reduced likelihood of meeting the MOI threshold, whereas the preoperative neurological deficits was associated with an increased probability of achieving this threshold.

RF233: Sacral fracture: a not so rare subtype of distal junctional failure

Francesco Lolli 1 , Andrea Baioni 1 , Nicolò Regge Gianas 1 , Marco Cancedda 1 , Carmela Altruda 1 , Ilaria Barni 1 , Roberto Ricca 1 , Andrea Messina 1 , Riccardo Draghi 1 , Gennaro Salierno 1 , Ignazio Borghesi 1

1 Maria Cecilia Hospital, Cotignola, Italy

Introduction: Sacral fracture is a not so rare complication after spinal fusion. Aim of the study is to report authors experience and to propose possible treatment and prevention strategies. Material and Methods: Adult patients treated at Our Institution in last 8 years by instrumented spinal fusion extended to the sacrum were analyzed to identify those who presented sacral insufficiency fractures. Results: 11 patients were included in the study. There were 2 men and 9 women, with a mean age of 65.5 years. Six patients had osteopenia/osteoporosis (mean hip T-score -2.1 ± 0.6), one had previously undergone radiotherapy for prostate cancer. Arthrodesis was performed for failed back surgery (4 cases), spinal deformity (2 cases), spondylolisthesis (2 cases), degenerative disc disease (2 cases), lumbar stenosis (1 case). Surgical procedures were: “short” posterior instrumented fusion (<4 levels, 4 cases), long posterior instrumented fusion with iliac fixation (> 10 levels, 2 cases), anterior L5-S1 interbody fusion (3 cases), anterior + posterior instrumented fusion with iliac fixation (2 cases). Sacral fracture occurred within firs six weeks. Presenting symptoms were back and leg pain. CT scan showed in 10 cases a Roy-Camille type 4 fracture, that involved sacral screws, with iliac screws mobilization (if presents) and anterior displacement of the cage in one case, and in one case a Roy-Camille type 3 fracture. Surgical indications are refractory pain, L5-S1 non union, loss of lumbar lordosis with spinopelvic malalignment. The surgical treatment generally requires spinopelvic fixation, preferably with double iliac fixation. Risk factors are osteoporosis and high BMI, while the role of the extension of the instrumentation remains unclear.

RF234: Efficacy, safety, and reliability of surgery on the lumbar spine under general versus spinal anaesthesia: analysis of 84 cases

Sharif Jonayed 1

1 National Institute of Traumatology & Orthopaedic Rehabilitation(NITOR), Dhaka, Bangladesh

Introduction: Lumbar spine surgery is one of the most frequently performed spinal procedures worldwide. Both general anesthesia (GA) and spinal anaesthesia (SA) are widely used and considered safe, but comparative evidence regarding intraoperative and postoperative outcomes, surgeon satisfaction, and cost effectiveness remains limited. Material and Method: This was a double-blinded, quasi-experimental prospective study of 84 patients, randomized into two equal groups (GA: 42, SA: 42), conducted between June 2016 and June 2025. Patients underwent single- or two-level discectomy, laminectomy, or laminoforaminotomy for lumbar disc herniation or lumbar canal stenosis. Parameters recorded included heart rate (HR), mean arterial pressure (MAP), blood loss, total anesthetic time, post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) time, surgeon satisfaction, analgesic and antiemetic requirements, cost of anesthesia, and hospital stay. Although intraoperative blood loss, operative duration, and hospital stay varied between groups, these differences were not statistically significant. No major anesthesia-related complications were observed in either group. Conclusion: Spinal anesthesia is as safe and effective as general anesthesia for lumbar spine surgery. It provides shorter anesthetic and recovery times, reduced analgesic and antiemetic requirements, fewer complications, and greater cost effectiveness, making it a valuable alternative to GA in appropriately selected patients.
