RF235: Examining the outcomes of multilevel thoracolumbar instrumented fusion constructs with concomitant sacroiliac joint fusion using s2-alar-iliac screws: a systematic review

Amanda Moser 1 , Omkar Anaspure 1 , Ziad Hassan 1 , Julian Peregoff 1 , Nnaemeka Okorie 2 , Tensae Assefa 2 , David Casper 1,2 , Amrit Khalsa 1,2

1 Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, United States, 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA, Philadelphia, United States

Introduction: Adult spinal deformity (ASD) often leads to pain, disability, and sacroiliac joint (SIJ) degeneration, especially following long-segment fusions ending at the sacrum. As S2-alar-iliac (S2AI) screws have become preferred for pelvic fixation, concerns about SIJ integrity have prompted growing interest in combining S2AI fixation with concurrent SIJ fusion. This systematic review evaluates whether added SIJ fusion to S2AI fixation improves clinical, radiographic, and patient-reported outcomes. Material and Methods: This systematic review aims to evaluate the clinical outcomes of S2AI screw placement in adult spinal deformity surgery with concomitant pelvic fusion. We excluded case reports, nonhuman studies, technology reviews, non-operative studies or studies unrelated to SIA fusion. PubMed, SCOPUS, COCHRANE, and Web of Science were queried on March 31st, 2025. Results: Out of 1,412 studies reviewed, 6 retrospective studies met the inclusion criteria. These studies involved 332 patients (mean age 63.1 ± 6.7 years; mean follow-up 704.5 ± 286.9 days) comparing S2AI fixation (n = 118) and S2AI fixation with SIJ fusion (n = 204). Functional lumbopelvic outcomes assessed included pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis (PI-LL) mismatch, and pre- and postoperative Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores for both lower-extremity and back pain. Among 180 patients with reported SIJ outcomes (63 with SIJ fusion, 117 without), postoperative SIJ pain was significantly lower in the fusion group (1.6% vs. 32.2%). The use of dual S2AI screws and triangular titanium SIJ fusion implants was associated with improved fusion outcomes and significantly reduced rates of SI screw loosening and rod breakage compared to single S2AI screw constructs (23% vs. 65%). Conclusion: Concomitant sacroiliac joint (SIJ) fusion during S2AI screw fixation in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery is associated with significantly improved outcomes, including lower rates of postoperative SIJ pain, reduced hardware complications, and better patient-reported pain and disability scores. Dual S2AI screw constructs further enhance mechanical stability by decreasing screw loosening and rod breakage compared to single-screw configurations. Additionally, postoperative changes in pelvic incidence (PI) - traditionally considered a fixed parameter - were more pronounced in patients without SIJ fusion, suggesting that SIJ mobility contributes to PI variability and potential sagittal imbalance. These findings support the biomechanical and clinical advantages of incorporating SIJ fusion into long thoracolumbar constructs, though further prospective studies are needed to validate long-term benefits and refine patient selection.

Lijin Zhou 1 , Honghao Yang 1 , Yong Hai 1

1 Beijing Chao-Yang Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) often leads to severe thoracolumbar kyphotic deformity, requiring surgical correction. Pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) is the gold standard but carries risks of significant blood loss and neurological complications. Posterior trans-intervertebral osteotomy (PTIO) has emerged as a less invasive alternative, but its comparative efficacy and safety remain unclear. This study aimed to compare radiographic outcomes, surgical parameters, and complications between PTIO and PSO in AS-related kyphosis. RF237: Clinical and radiological outcomes of transverse process hooks versus pedicle screws at the upper instrumented vertebra in adult spinal deformity patients undergoing three-column osteotomy: a retrospective comparative study

Introduction: Junctional failure remains a major complication after long-segment fusion in adult spinal deformity (ASD). RF238: Regional contributions to thoracic flexibility: implications for proximal junctional complications lower thoracic to pelvic fusion in adult spinal deformity

Andrea Pezzi 1 , Han Jo Kim 1 , Atahan Durbas 1 , Robert Uzzo 1 , Gabrielle Dykhouse 1 , Tejas Subramanian 1 , Stephane Owusu-Sarpong 1 , Jung Kee Mok 1 , Mihir Dekhne 1 , Justin Samuel 1 , Kasra Araghi 1 , Quante Singleton 1 , Farah Musharbash 1 , Matthew Cunningham 1 , Francis Lovecchio 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Restoring sagittal alignment is a primary goal in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery, but long fusions from the lower thoracic (LT) spine to the pelvis are susceptible to proximal junctional complications, including proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and proximal junctional failure (PJF), which impact long-term outcomes. While thoracic flexibility (TF) may influence this, prior studies mostly focused on global parameters and have not examined segmental differences within the thoracic spine. The thoracolumbar junction (TLJ; T10-L2) is an anatomically distinct transition zone that may have a greater effect on postoperative complications. This study aimed to evaluate segmental TF in T10-L2 compared with thoracic kyphosis (TK; T4-T12) to explore their links to PJK and PJF after LT to pelvic fusion in ASD patients. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included ASD patients undergoing fusion from T9-T12 to the pelvis, fused ≥5 levels, excluding those with prior thoracic fusions. All patients had preoperative standing and supine radiographs and postoperative follow-up imaging. TF was assessed using two methods: the supine-to-standing Cobb angle (CA) ratio (lower indicates higher flexibility) and the standing-supine CA difference. Patients were grouped by junctional complications: PJK (PJA ≥ 10° or ΔPJA ≥ 10°) and PJF (PJA ≥ 28° or ΔPJA ≥ 22°, or proximal fusion extension). Radiographic measurements included pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), T4-T12 and T10-L2 CAs, T4-pelvic angle (T4PA), and L1-pelvic angle (L1PA). Associations were tested using t-tests, chi-square, and logistic regression. Results: The cohort included 87 ASD patients with a mean age of 65.6 ± 8.1 years and a BMI of 26.7 ± 5.5. The average follow-up duration was 1.9 ± 0.9 years. PJK and PJF occurred in 31 (35.6%) and 8 (9.2%) patients, respectively. Baseline demographics and global sagittal alignment parameters showed no differences between the complication and non-complication groups. In regional analysis, PJK patients had higher preoperative T10-L2 CA (p = 0.003) and more lordotic correction at T10-L2 postoperatively (p = 0.003). Patients with PJF had higher preoperative T4-T12 CA (p = 0.03). The absolute difference in supine-standing CA at T10-L2 was greater in the PJK group compared to those without complications (9.6° vs. 3.7°, p = 0.003). Within the PJK group, T10-L2 demonstrated greater flexibility than T4-T12 by both ratio (0.18 vs. 0.98, p < 0.001) and absolute difference (10.6° vs. 3.4°, p = 0.003). Multivariate regression analysis showed that increased T10-L2 flexibility (lower ratio) was associated with both PJK (OR 0.58, 95% CI: 0.27-0.95) and PJF (OR 3.67, 95% CI: 1.23-15.01). Higher preoperative T4-T12 CA was also associated with PJF (OR 1.16, 95% CI: 1.02-1.39). Conclusion: TF shows regional differences, with the T10-L2 segment being more flexible than T4-T12. Absolute Cobb angle differences provide effective stratification across patients, whereas supine-to-standing ratios better reflect segmental behavior and are independently predictive in multivariate models. This may predispose the TLJ to inadvertent “flattening” during LT to pelvic fusions, which could increase the risk of PJK.

RF239: Rod fracture after lateral lumbar interbody fusion in adult spinal deformity: incidence, risk factors, and prevention with a minimum 5 years of follow-up

Jung-Hee Lee 1 , Ki Young Lee 1 , Woo Jae Jang 1 , Hong-sik Park 1

1 Kyung Hee University Hospital, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Minimally invasive lateral lumbar interbody fusion (LLIF) has gained recognition for its role in sagittal realignment in adult spinal deformity (ASD), offering advantages over traditional osteotomy techniques. However, rod fracture (RF) remains a major complication, often necessitating revision surgery. The purpose of this study was to investigate the incidence, risk factors, and preventive strategies for RF after long-segment deformity correction using LLIF. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included 151 ASD patients (mean age 71.6 years) who underwent LLIF with long-segment fixation, including sacropelvic fixation. Sufficient LL correction is essential for optimizing sagittal balance and is not associated with an increased risk of RF, particularly in patients with severe baseline deformity characterized by high PI and pelvic non-responder characteristics.

RF241: Measuring spinopelvic parameters in patients with 6 lumbar vertebrae: a matched cohort comparison of asymptomatic volunteers

Chloe Cadieux 1,2 , Ruheksh Raj 1,2 , Farbod Moghaddam 3 , May Choi 3,4 , Fred Nicholls 1,2

1 Department of Orthopaedics, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada, 2 Combined Orthopedic and Neurosurgery Spine Program, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada, 3 McCaig Institute for Bone and Joint Health, Calgary, Canada, 4 Department of Medicine, Cumming School of Medicine, University of Calgary, Calgary, Canada

Introduction: Spinopelvic parameters are fundamental for evaluating sagittal alignment and guiding surgical planning. These parameters are traditionally measured using the superior endplate of S1 as a reference; however, anatomic variants such as the presence of a sixth lumbar vertebra (L6) complicate this convention. In such cases, it remains unclear whether parameters should be referenced to the L6 or S1 endplate. This study aims to assess the difference in measurements when using L6 and S1 as a reference, in comparison to matched controls. This knowledge will help standardize spinopelvic measurements in patients with a sixth lumbar vertebrae. Material and Methods: Healthy volunteers with no pre-existing hip or spine pathology were recruited for this study (n = 497). Whole-body 2D EOS scans were obtained. Cases that had a well-formed L6 vertebrae were identified (n = 29). Two independent surgeons reviewed the radiographs included in the L6 cohort and using an image segmentation software (KEOPS, by SMAIO), spinopelvic angles were calculated. Measurements included pelvic incidence (PI), pelvic tilt (PT), sacral slope (SS), L1-pelvic angle (L1PA), T4-pelvic angle (T4PA), and sagittal vertical angle (SVA) using both L6 and S1 as a reference for each patient. Segmental lordosis was also calculated. L6 cases were then matched to normative controls for comparison. Results: Cases were matched 1:1 to normative controls based on PI and SS. Nine cases measured off of S1 and eight cases measured off of L6 were matched to controls within one degree. In the cohort that used S1 as a reference, PI was found to be significantly higher in comparison to lower values when using L6 (49.6° ± 9.2° vs. 42.7° ± 4.7°, p = .038). Similar results were seen with SS, with higher values seen in the S1 reference group (43.0° ± 4.8° vs. 32.5° ± 4.6°, p < .001). Additionally, significant differences were seen between groups for segmental lower lumbar lordosis. In the S1 reference group, L5-6 lordosis was significantly higher than the L6 reference group (11.7° ± 3.4° vs. 8.4° ± 1.9°, p = .014) as was L6-S1 lordosis (14.8° ± 4.4° vs. 5.9° ± 3.5°, p < .001). No significant differences were seen between groups when measuring L1PA, T4PA, or SVA. Conclusion: This study demonstrates the difference in spinopelvic measurements when using L6 or S1 as a reference in healthy volunteers with a L6 vertebrae. It confirms that the choice of endplate reference effects spinopelvic parameters in patients with a L6 vertebrae, which can subsequently effect surgical planning and goals. When matched to normative controls, the cohort using S1 as a reference had significantly higher values in PI, SS, L5-L6 and L6-S1 lordosis compared to the cohort measured off of L6. These results suggest that using S1 as a reference may lead to more accurate spinopelvic measurements in patients with a high PI and increased lumbar lordosis. However, larger studies are needed to confirm if there are other characteristics that effect which reference vertebrae should be used.

RF243: Surgical predictors of rod fracture in adult spinal deformity: the role of anterior column manipulation

Schahin Salmanian 1 , Bryan Clampitt 1 , Kiana Yeganeh 1 , Ryan Screven 1 , Diego Soto Rubio 1 , Mohsen Rostami 1 , Jay I. Kumar 1 , Puya Alikhani 1

1 University of South Florida, Department of Neurosurgery, Brain, and Spine, Tampa, United States

Introduction: Rod fracture (RF) is a major mechanical complication following adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery, often necessitating revision and impairing long-term outcomes. While sagittal alignment has been linked to RF, the role of anterior column manipulation-through anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) or anterior column realignment (ACR)-remains under-explored. Our study evaluated the impact of anterior column procedures on rates of RF occurrence. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 140 ASD patients who underwent long-segment posterior spinal fusion (≥ 7 levels) between 2015 and 2023. Demographic, radiographic, and surgical characteristics were compared between patients with and without RF. Differences in osteotomy techniques (ACR, pedicle subtraction osteotomy [PSO], intradiscal osteotomy [IDO]) and interbody fusions (ALIF, TLIF, LLIF) were analyzed. Multivariate logistic regression incorporating spinopelvic parameters was performed to identify independent predictors of RF. Results: RF occurred in 35.7% of patients at a median of 761 days postoperatively. Baseline demographics, including age (63.4 years), sex (≈48% male), and BMI (≈30 kg/m2), were comparable across groups. Anterior column procedures were significantly overrepresented in the RF group. ACR was performed in 18.0% of RF patients compared to 6.9% without RF (p = 0.045). ALIF was performed in 37.5% of RF patients versus 12.5% of non-RF patients (p = 0.004). Unlike TLIF, LLIF, or 3CO procedures, ALIF and ACR may impose unique biomechanical demands on rods, contributing to fatigue and breakage. These findings highlight the need for surgical caution when employing anterior column techniques in ASD correction and suggest that augmented stabilization strategies, such as multi-rod constructs, may be warranted in this high-risk subgroup.

PJF requiring revision surgery was observed in 5 pts (6.3%) in UT group, 4 pts (3%) in T9G and 7 (12%) in T10G pts. SVA and T4PA improvement was greater in UT Group. RF245: Sagittal alignment showdown: SRS-Schwab vs age-adjusted vs T4-L1 hip axis - Which is superior?

Jay Kumar 1,2 , Bryan Clampitt 2 , Kiran Kittur 2 , Chloe Chose 2 , Bassel El Sayed 2 , Schahin Salmanian 2 , Mohsen Rostami 2 , Puya Alikhani 2

RF246: Distal extension risk after long fusion to lower instrumented vertebrae of L4 or L5 in adult spinal deformity: a multicenter cohort study

Tejas Subramanian 1 , Atahan Durbas 1 , Francis Lovecchio 1 , Renaud Lafage 2 , Christopher Ames 3 , Shay Bess 4 , Robert Eastlack 5 , Munish Gupta 6 , Richard Hostin 7 , Khaled Kebaish 8 , Eric Klineberg 9 , Gregory Mundis 10 , David Okonkwo 11 , Frank Schwab 2 , Christopher Shaffrey 12 , Justin Smith 13 , Virginie Lafage 2 , Han Jo Kim 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States, 2 Lenox Hill Hospital, New York, United States, 3 University of San Francisco, San Francisco, United States, 4 Denver International Spine Center, Denver, United States, 5 Scripps Clinic, La Jolla, United States, 6 Washington University in St Louis, St. Louis, United States, 7 Southwest Scoliosis Institute, Plano, United States, 8 Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, United States, 9 UTHealth McGovern Medical School, Houston, United States, 10 San Diego Spine, La Jolla, United States, 11 University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh, United States, 12 Duke University Medical Center, Durham, United States, 13 University of Virginia Health System, Charlottesville, United States

Introduction: The optimal lower instrumented vertebra (LIV) in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery remains controversial, particularly in patients with preserved lumbosacral motion segments.1 Terminating long fusions at L4 or L5 preserves motion but may increase the risk of distal degeneration and failure, often requiring revision to the pelvis.2 This study aimed to understand the incidence, risk factors, and radiographic indicators of distal extension after long fusions to S1 or the pelvis. Material and Methods: This multicenter retrospective cohort study included patients with ASD who underwent fusion at four or more levels, with LIV of L4 or L5, and a minimum two-year follow-up. Patients were categorized based on whether they required distal extension to the pelvis (extension cohort, EC) or not (non-extension cohort, NEC). Demographic data, pre- and postoperative alignment parameters, disc integrity, and patient-reported outcomes (ODI, VAS) were compared at different time points before and after surgery. For EC patients, outcomes were evaluated at the time of revision; for NEC patients, outcomes were assessed at two years. Results: A total of 65 patients (52 females and 13 males) with a mean age of 47.9 years, a mean BMI of 25.3, and an average of 8.7 fused levels were included; 41 of the fusions ended at L4, and 24 at L5. 11 patients (16.9%) required distal extension to the pelvis, with a median time of 517 days after surgery. The risk of extension did not differ between LIV of L4 and L5 (13.9% vs. 33.3%, p = 0.304). Reasons for extension included sagittal malalignment with distal kyphotic change (n = 2), sagittal malalignment without distal kyphotic change (n = 3), adjacent segment disease without sagittal malalignment (n = 4), and distal mechanical failure (screw pullout, pseudarthrosis) (n = 2). Baseline demographic and radiographic data were similar between groups. However, EC patients showed greater anterior translation at L5-S1 at 6 weeks post-op (-2.1 mm vs. -0.8 mm, p = 0.049) and increased pelvic tilt after 1 year (23.6° vs. 16.4°, p = 0.024). Early worsening of disability (ODI at 6 months: 47.3 vs. 30.3, p = 0.047) and a progressive decrease in L5-S1 anterior disc height at final follow-up (10.6 mm vs. 15.2 mm, p = 0.026) were observed in the EC group. Conclusion: Stopping long fusion at L4 or L5 is associated with an 83.1% extension-free survival rate at 2 years follow-up. The majority of failures occur early and are indicated by subtle changes in distal segment alignment and disc height. The risk for revision may be reduced by avoiding malalignment, reinforcing distal fixation, and spanning any segment with preoperative listhesis > 0.5 mm. Careful patient selection and early radiographic surveillance are warranted to optimize outcomes for constructs terminating at L4/L5

RF247: Dynamic adaptations of the thoracolumbar spine: a cross-sectional analysis of vertebral pelvic angle changes from standing to sitting

Atahan Durbas 1 , Han Jo Kim 1 , Robert Uzzo 1 , Gabrielle Dykhouse 1 , Justin Samuel 1 , Tejas Subramanian 1 , Michael Mazzucco 1 , Michael Kelly 2 , Jeffrey Hills 3 , Matthew Cunningham 1 , Francis Lovecchio 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States, 2 Rady Children's Hospital, San Diego, United States, 3 University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, San Antonio, United States

Introduction: Surgical alignment goals in adult spinal deformity (ASD) are primarily based on standing radiographs. However, patients spend substantial time in sitting characterized by lumbar flattening, pelvic retroversion, and altered thoracolumbar loading. Vertebropelvic angles (VPAs) have become increasingly recognized as a method for describing spinal shapes, yet VPAs in standing have been extensively characterized; positional changes during sitting and their modulation by patient-specific factors influence these changes remain unclear. This study aimed to examine the differences in VPAs from standing to sitting across thoracolumbar levels and to assess the impact of age, pelvic incidence (PI), body mass index (BMI), and gender on these adaptations. Material and Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional imaging study involved adults being considered for hip replacement surgery. Patients with prior spinal surgery, spondylolisthesis, coronal Cobb angle (CA) > 20°, or severe hip osteoarthritis were excluded. Lateral radiographs in both positions were reviewed, with VPAs measured from T10 to L5, the uppermost visible level. Changes in VPAs (ΔVPA) were calculated as standing minus sitting values. Age quartiles and sex groups were compared. Statistical analyses included paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, as well as multivariable linear regression, adjusting for PI, age, BMI, and gender. Results: The study population included 1,428 patients: 764 females (53.5%) and 664 males (46.5%). The mean age was 62.9 ± 11.3 years, the mean BMI was 28.9 ± 5.7 kg/m2, and the mean PI was 52.6° ± 11.9. All VPAs from T10-L5 showed significant positional changes (p < 0.001). The mean ΔVPAs increased cranially: ΔL5PA -0.24° (± 1.96), ΔL4PA -2.17° (± 2.91), ΔL3PA -4.52° (± 4.23), ΔL2PA -6.73° (± 5.27), ΔL1PA -8.78° (± 6.24), ΔT12PA -10.47° (± 7.16), ΔT11PA -11.95° (± 7.93), and ΔT10PA -13.72° (± 8.50). Findings indicate a larger posterior angular shift in the thoracic and upper lumbar spine during sitting. Age-based analysis showed progressive reductions in ΔVPAs, PT, and LL with increasing age quartile (p < 0.001). Older patients demonstrated markedly reduced thoracic adaptability. Male patients exhibited greater ΔPT (p = 0.004), larger ΔLL (p = 0.001), and increased ΔVPA at T12 (p = 0.01) and L1 (p = 0.04). Multivariable regression indicated that higher PI was significantly linked to larger ΔVPAs at L4 and L5 (both p < 0.001; β = 0.03). Older age was associated with greater ΔVPAs at all levels (all p < 0.001), with regression coefficients ranging from 0.02 at L5 to 0.35 at T10. Higher BMI was associated with larger ΔVPAs from T12 to L4 (all p < 0.001; β = 0.11 at T12, L1, and L2; β = 0.08 at L3; β = 0.06 at L4), and at T11 (p = 0.03; β = 0.09). Male gender was associated with decreased ΔT12PA (p = 0.02; β = -0.86). Conclusion: This study provides the first systematic characterization of VPA changes between standing and sitting. VPAs significantly increase in the sitting position, especially in the lower thoracic and proximal lumbar spine. These positional changes are influenced by PI, age, BMI, and gender, emphasizing the need for considering functional postures and individual modifiers when setting spinal alignment goals for surgery, especially in long-segment fusion.

RF248: Improving outcomes: seven-year retrospective trend analysis of decreasing medical complications in ASD surgery at a single institution

Atahan Durbas 1 , Francis Lovecchio 1 , Andrea Pezzi 1 , Austin Kaidi 1 , Jung Kee Mok 1 , Gregory Kazarian 1 , Tomoyuki Asada 1 , Annika Bay 1 , David Foley 1 , Alexander Upfill-Brown 1 , Chierika Coco Ukogu Clements 1 , Luis Felipe Colon 1 , Stephane Owusu-Sarpong 1 , Matthew Cunningham 1 , Han Jo Kim 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Postoperative medical complications remain a major concern in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery, reflecting both patient comorbidities and surgical invasiveness. Validated metrics such as the Adult Spinal Deformity-Surgical (ASD-S) and the Adult Spinal Deformity-Surgical and Radiographical (ASD-SR) scores incorporate procedural and radiographic factors to measure surgical invasiveness. However, it is unclear whether advances in perioperative care have influenced complication risk across different levels of invasiveness. This study aimed to analyze temporal trends in medical complication rates and identify predictors of complications in ASD surgery. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed all ASD patients who underwent instrumented fusion of five or more spinal levels, with a minimum of two years of follow-up, from 2017 to 2023 at a single tertiary center. Surgical invasiveness was measured using the ASD-SR score, and patients were stratified into low- and high-ASD-SR groups based on the median ASD-SR value. Postoperative medical complications were systematically recorded and categorized according to the ISSG-AO Spine Complications Classification. Annual complication rates were calculated for each group, and temporal trends were assessed with linear regression. Univariate logistic regression assessed the relationship between patient, surgical, and radiographic factors and the likelihood of medical complications. Variables with p < 0.3 in univariate analysis were then included in the final multivariable logistic regression model. Results: A total of 485 patients were included (Low ASD-SR: n = 244; High ASD-SR: n = 241). There were no significant differences between the groups in age, BMI, comorbidity index, number of revision cases, or overall medical complication rates and types. The high-complication group demonstrated greater baseline deformity severity, with higher ASD-S scores (44.0 ± 13.5 vs. 30.3 ± 9.7, p < 0.001) and ASD-SR radiographic scores (23.4 ± 24.5 vs. 13.7 ± 10.0, p < 0.001). Surgically, they underwent longer constructs (10.5 ± 3.9 vs. 7.3 ± 2.6 fused levels, p < 0.001), longer operations (301.4 ± 122.0 vs. 222.4 ± 94.7 mins, p < 0.001), and had greater intraoperative blood loss (1262.8 ± 1062.0 vs. 664.5 ± 507.9 mL, p < 0.001). They also experienced longer hospital stays (153.9 ± 97.2 vs. 132.8 ± 98.8 hours, p = 0.01) and included more females (69.5% vs. 56.1%, p = 0.003). The overall medical complication rate decreased by 2.46% annually (p = 0.04), with both low- and high-ASD-SR groups showing similar downward trends (p = 0.25), yet no significant difference was observed between the groups. In univariate analysis, the surgical year was the only factor associated with fewer complications (OR = 0.83 per year, p = 0.001). In the final multivariable analysis, after adjusting for ASD-SR group, gender, operation time, and length of stay, only the surgical year was found to be associated with fewer medical complications (OR = 0.82, p = 0.001). Conclusion: Medical complication rates after ASD surgery have significantly declined over the past seven years, regardless of surgical invasiveness. These findings indicate that advances in perioperative care, complication prevention strategies, and multidisciplinary approaches have effectively lowered the risk of medical complications across all ASD procedures.

RF249: Measuring the unseen: hidden blood loss in open thoracolumbar fusion

Jakub Jezek 1 , Petr Kafka 2 , Jiri Skala-Rosenbaum 1 , Jan Svec 1

1 Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, University Hospital Kralovske Vinohrady and Third Medical Faculty of Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic, 2 Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care, University Hospital Kralovske Vinohrady and Third Medical Faculty of Charles University, Prague, Czech Republic

Introduction: In major spinal surgery, perioperative blood loss is routinely estimated from suction canisters, surgical sponges, and drain output. However, these methods systematically underestimate the true extent of bleeding, as they neglect hidden blood loss (HBL) caused by hemolysis, blood extravasation into tissues, and dilutional shifts. Data on HBL in spine surgery remain limited. Objective: To quantify the proportion of HBL during open posterior thoracolumbar fusion and identify perioperative factors influencing its magnitude. Material and Methods: Twenty-three adult patients undergoing elective posterior thoracolumbar fusion with anticipated intraoperative blood loss > 1 L were prospectively enrolled. Total blood loss (TBL) was calculated using the Gross formula from perioperative hematocrit changes, corrected for transfusions. Visible blood loss (VBL) included suction and sponge loss intraoperatively plus postoperative drain output. HBL was defined as TBL - VBL. Associations between HBL, patient characteristics, and surgical parameters were analyzed. Results: Mean VBL was 1,864 ± 461 mL, mean TBL 2,721 ± 671 mL, and mean HBL 857 ± 259 mL, corresponding to 31.3 ± 4.3% of TBL. HBL correlated inversely with age (ρ = -0.492, p = 0.017), but showed no significant association with sex, BMI, ASA class, number of fused levels, or operative time. VBL correlated negatively with age (ρ = -0.430, p = 0.040) and positively with surgical duration (ρ = 0.503, p = 0.014). Conclusion: Approximately one-third of blood loss during thoracolumbar fusion is hidden and not captured by routine methods. Younger patients appear particularly vulnerable, likely reflecting higher vascular reserve and fluid dynamics. Recognition and integration of HBL into perioperative management may improve transfusion strategies and patient outcomes.

RF250: Difference in sitting sagittal balance from standing balance in scoliotic and non-scoliotic adolescents

Xavier Lavigne 1 , Emmanuelle Bélanger 1 , Marie-Lyne Nault 1 , Marjolaine Roy-Beaudry 1 , Stefan Parent 1 , Etienne Belzile 2

1 CHU Sainte‐Justine, Montreal, Canada, 2 CHU de Québec, Quebec, Canada

Introduction: Spino-pelvic (SP) morphological parameters are important determinants of hip and spine dynamics and have not been well defined in an adolescent population. This descriptive study of patients with scoliosis and a matched, asymptomatic, control group aimed to determine spinopelvic differences between the two groups and define the relative contribution of the hips to the spinopelvic balance. Our hypothesis is that sagittal spinopelvic alignment of scoliosis demonstrated greater change between the standing and deep-flexed seated position. Material and Methods: This descriptive study of sixty patients aged between 8 and 17 years old with scoliosis and a matched, asymptomatic, control group, had their spinopelvic parameters measured (lumbar lordosis, sacral slope, pelvic tilt, pelvic incidence, and pelvic-femoral angle) on lateral radiographs taken in the standing and deep-flexed seated positions. Spinopelvic movement was calculated as the change between the different positions and hip contributions was defined by calculating the hip user index. We also performed a complete physical exam focused on the hip to define hip flexion and extension. Results: Going from a standing to a deep-flexed seated position, scoliotic patients demonstrated a reduction in pelvic incidence of 3° (p < 0.001), compared to only 1° in the control group (p = 0.121). They also demonstrated 8° more hip flexion (p = 0.046), 8° less lumbar flexion (p = 0.008) and a more anterior pelvic tilt (ΔPT: -15˚ ± 12 vs -8˚ ± 12; p = 0.024) than in the control group. The patients were therefore deemed to have a higher hip user index (63% vs 58%; p ≤ 0.001). The physical exam also yielded similar results as patients had 6° more isolated hip flexion (p = 0.018) than controls. Conclusion: Scoliotic patients showed less flexibility in the lumbar spine which led to a more anterior pelvis and likely compensation in hip flexion by a similar amount. The relative contribution of the hips was thus higher in our population. Therefore, decreased mobility in the lower spine in scoliotic patients seems to be compensated by both higher hip flexion and anterior tilting of the pelvis when compared with controls. These radiographic results also seemed to be correlated to physical examination of the hip range of motion. Although these may be secondary changes to the spinal deformity, it may also play a role in scoliosis initiation and progression.

RF251: Transition rods with or without junctional tethering in the prevention of proximal junctional kyphosis in adult spinal deformities surgery

Francesco Lolli 1 , Marco Ialuna 1 , Andrea Messina 1 , Nicolò Regge Gianas 1 , Andrea Baioni 1 , Marco Cancedda 1 , Ilaria Barni 1 , Riccardo Draghi 1 , Roberto Ricca 1 , Carmela Altruda 1 , Ignazio Borghesi 1

1 Maria Cecilia Hospital, Cotignola (Ravenna), Italy

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) is one of the most problematic complications in the field of spinal deformities surgery. Aim of the study is to evaluate the effectiveness of transition rods with or without junctional tethering to prevent this complication in adult patients. Methods: 97 consecutive patients were included in the study. All patients had been treated by “long” posterior instrumented fusion (screws only construct, with or without anterior lumbar support), extended from the proximal thoracic segment (T1-T5) to the pelvis, for an adult spinal deformity in the coronal or sagittal plane. Conclusion: The use of transition rods has been shown to be effective in adult spinal deformities surgery, with a statistically significant reduction of PJK if compared to 5.5 mm rods. RF252: Comparative performance of the ESSG-ADSCI and ISSG-SII in a single-center adult spinal deformity database

Peter Passias 1 , Francesca Totis 1 , Kyriakos Chatzis 1 , Mohammad Daher 1 , Anthony Baumann 2 , Peter Tretiakov 1 , Tobi Onafowokan 1 , Max Fisher 1 , Ethan Cottrill 1

1 Duke University, Durham, United States, 2 Cleveland Clinic, Ohio, United States

Introduction: In 2018, the International Spine Study Group (ISSG) and European Spine Study Group (ESSG) developed their surgical complexity indices specific to surgical treatment of adult spinal deformity (ASD): the ISSG-Surgical Invasiveness Index (SII) and the ESSG-Adult Deformity Surgery Complexity Index (ADSCI), respectively. However, no study in the literature has compared these two indices against one another, hindering surgeon decision-making. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to directly compare the performance of the ISSG-SII versus the ESSG-ADSCI to predict outcomes in patients who had surgery for ASD within a single database. Methods: A retrospective single-center study of patients who underwent surgery for ASD with complete baseline and two-year follow-up data were assessed via the ISSG-SII and the ESSG-ADSCI. The primary outcome measures for this study were intraoperative estimated blood loss (EBL), operative time, and length of stay (LOS). Secondary outcomes included the occurrence of surgical, medical, and intraoperative complications, adverse events, reoperations, and complications. We utilized receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves while classifying outcomes into binary outcomes for use of the corresponding area under the curve (AUC) values. Results: A total of 693 patients who underwent surgery for ASD (mean age: 61 years; 77% female; BMI: 27kg/m2) met the inclusion criteria of this study. For our primary outcomes, both the ISSG-SII (mean: 90.0 ± 38.1) and ESSG-ADSCI (mean: 19.3 ± 7.5) were found to be a significant independent predictor of LOS, operative time, and EBL (p < 0.001). The ISSG-SII outperformed the ESSG-ADSCI in predicting EBL greater than 1500 mL (AUC: 0.687 versus 0.604, p < 0.001), and surgery duration over 240 minutes (AUC: 0.705 versus 0.658, p = 0.036). However, there was no significant difference between the indices in predicting LOS beyond seven days (AUC: 0.687 vs. 0.654, p = 0.103). The ISSG-SII outperformed the ESSG-ADSCI in predicting overall surgical complications (AUC: 0.645 versus 0.597, p = 0.018). A sub-analysis of patients who had surgery before 2017 reveals comparable outcomes, reinforcing the consistency of these findings. Discussion: While both the ISSG-SII and the ESSG-ADSCI demonstrated independent predictive value for numerous invasiveness outcomes, the ISSG-SII consistently outperformed the ESSG-ADSCI among patients who had surgery for ASD. Future research is needed to corroborate our findings.

RF253: Vertebral bone mineral density decrease following lumbar decompression surgery

Ali Guven 1 , Bruno Verna 1 , Ranqing Lan 1 , Marco Burkhard 1 , Erika Chiapparelli 1 , Anna-Maria Mielke 1 , Jennifer Shue 1 , Andrew Sama 1 , Federico Girardi 1 , Frank Cammisa 1 , Alexander Hughes 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Postoperative decreases in volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD) have been reported in patients undergoing posterior spinal fusion, as well as in those undergoing lateral lumbar interbody fusion without screw fixation. The underlying mechanisms of vBMD loss remain unclear and may involve both local and systemic inflammatory responses, along with postoperative factors such as pain medication use and reduced mobility. However, vBMD changes following spinal decompression without fusion remain unexplored. This study aimed to assess changes in vBMD following lumbar decompression surgery. Material and Methods: Patients without prior lumbar surgery who underwent decompression between March 2016 and October 2023 were retrospectively included. Eligibility required preoperative and postoperative lumbar CT scans obtained 6-12 months apart, with postoperative imaging acquired at least 3 months after surgery. vBMD was measured at each lumbar level using quantitative CT. Patient age, sex, body mass index (BMI), and history of epidural steroid injections were recorded. The primary outcome was the change in vBMD between timepoints. Paired t-tests were used to assess overall vBMD change. Multivariable linear regression was performed to identify predictors of vBMD change, adjusting for age, sex, BMI, preoperative vBMD, and epidural injections before and during the study period. A linear mixed-effects model was used to evaluate the effect of surgery at each spinal level, with patient ID included as a random intercept. Results: A total of 77 patients met the inclusion criteria, with a mean age of 62 ± 16 years (37.7% female) and a mean BMI of 29 ± 6 kg/m2. The median preoperative and postoperative vBMD, averaged across levels, were 107 mg/cm3 (interquartile range [IQR]: 86-143) and 100 mg/cm3 (IQR: 77-135), respectively. The median vBMD change was -6.6 mg/cm3 (IQR: -12.5 to -0.5) corresponding to a decrease of 6.5% (IQR: 12.1-0.4). Regression analysis identified preoperative vBMD as the sole significant predictor of vBMD change (estimate: -0.10, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.17 to -0.02, p = 0.014). Age, sex, BMI, and epidural steroid injections before and within the study timeframe did not significantly predict vBMD change (p > 0.05). The mixed-effects model indicated that surgical level was not a significant predictor of vBMD decrease (p = 0.845). Conclusion: This is the first study to assess vBMD changes following lumbar decompression surgery. Our findings demonstrate a global vBMD decrease in the lumbar spine following surgery, rather than a localized surgical-level effect. These results suggest that vBMD loss may be attributable to systemic factors, such as postoperative relative immobility, rather than surgical-level specific mechanisms. Prospective studies minimizing selection bias and incorporating outcome measures are needed to draw definitive clinical conclusions.

RF254: Effect of implant removal after lumbar fusion surgery on the risk of adjacent segment disease - A retrospective study

Yun Heng Li 1 , Fon-Yih Tsuang 1

1 National Taiwan University Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan

Introduction: Lumbar fusion surgery using interbody cages and fixation devices is an established treatment for lumbar degeneration disease, aiming to restore alignment and achieve solid arthrodesis. However, the increased rigidity may increase the risk of adjacent segment degeneration (ASDeg) and, in some cases, adjacent segment disease (ASDis), which can result in reoperation. Biomechanical studies demonstrate that fusion alters load distribution by raising intradiscal pressure and facet joint stress at adjacent levels, thereby accelerating degeneration. To reduce this risk, flexible or bioabsorbable implants have been introduced, though their clinical benefit remains inconclusive. Removal of fixation devices after fusion has been reported as a safe procedure, with potential advantages including improved pain control, decreased opioid use, and higher patient satisfaction. Furthermore, finite element analyses suggest that implant removal may reduce stress transfer to adjacent segments while maintaining sagittal alignment. Nevertheless, clinical evidence on its impact in preventing ASDeg or ASDis is scarce. Therefore, further investigation is necessary to clarify whether implant removal can mitigate long-term complications following lumbar fusion. Material and Methods: This retrospective study utilized database from National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) to identify patients undergoing lumbar interbody fusion between 2017 and 2021. Inclusion required ≥ 4 years follow-up and complete imaging; prior lumbar surgery, tumors, fractures, or infections were excluded. Patients were divided into an experimental group (n = 40; solid fusion at 2 years with implants removal) and a control group (n = 317; implants retained). Primary outcome was adjacent segment disease (ASDis) requiring surgery; secondary outcome was radiographic adjacent segment degeneration (ASDeg). Demographics, comorbidities, surgical details, and radiographic parameters (pelvic tilt, sacral slope, pelvic incidence, sagittal vertical axis, and segmental range of motion) were collected. Multivariable logistic regression were planned to adjust for confounders. Categorical variables will be analyzed using chi-square test or Fisher’s exact tests, and continuous variables will be assessed with independent t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests based on data distribution. Statistical significance is defined as p < 0.05. Results: A total of 357 patients were included, with a mean age of 64.8 years and 35.0% males. The mean height and weight were 157.7 cm and 65.4 kg. The most frequently treated level was L4-L5 (60.5%), followed by multilevel procedures L3-L4-L5 (14.3%) and L4-L5-S1 (7.8%). Mean follow-up duration was 7.1 years. Regarding study outcomes, the experimental group had only one case of ASDis (2.5%) and two cases of ASDeg (5.0%), whereas the control group reported 58 cases of ASDis (18.3%) and 91 cases of ASDeg (28.7%). Conclusion: This study is ongoing, and preliminary findings suggest a potential benefit of implant removal in mitigating ASDis and ASDeg. RF255: Could alteration in the vacuum phenomenon rather than its presence be a sign of spinal instability?

Murat Ekşi 1 , Emel Özcan-Ekşi 2

1 İstinye University, Istanbul, Turkey, 2 Private Practice, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: The intradiscal vacuum phenomenon (VP) has traditionally been regarded as a radiologic indicator of segmental instability. However, its direct relationship with postoperative spinal fusion outcomes and mechanical complications remains inadequately understood. This study aimed to investigate whether changes in the natural course of intradiscal and intrafacet VP influence clinical and mechanical outcomes following lumbar fusion surgery. Material and Methods: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients who underwent lumbar fusion surgery for degenerative spinal disorders at a tertiary spine center. Lumbar computed tomography scans obtained preoperatively and at the final follow-up were reviewed for the presence or absence of intradiscal and intrafacet VP. Associations between VP dynamics and mechanical complications (e.g., adjacent segment disease and pseudoarthrosis) were analyzed alongside patient-reported functional outcomes. Results: The appearance of new intrafacet VP and the resolution of pre-existing intrafacet VP at follow-up were significantly associated with increased rates of mechanical failure and adjacent segment disease. In contrast, intradiscal VP showed no significant correlation with mechanical complications. Patients with newly developed intrafacet VP also demonstrated significantly poorer outcomes in terms of achieving the minimal clinically important difference for the Oswestry Disability Index. Furthermore, the presence of interbody fusion, as opposed to posterolateral fusion alone, was more closely associated with VP alterations and functional outcomes. The resolution of intradiscal VP-presumably due to solid interbody fusion-was linked to improved quality of life, whereas similar changes in intrafacet VP were associated with poorer outcomes. These associations remained relevant when analyzed along with participants’ comorbidities. Conclusion: Postoperative changes in intrafacet VP, rather than its mere presence, may serve as a more accurate indicator of mechanical complications and functional decline following lumbar fusion. These findings challenge the conventional assumption that intradiscal VP is the primary radiologic marker of instability. The results suggest that interbody fusion may offer improved outcomes in this context, although further prospective studies are warranted. These insights may assist clinicians in preoperative planning and patient counseling regarding the risks and expected postoperative course following lumbar fusion surgery.

RF256: Perioperative morbidity and mortality following elective spinal surgery in octogenarians and beyond: a systematic review and meta-analysis

Daniel Nikitin 1 , Austin Bermudez-Hiu 2 , Frank Koziarz 3 , Fan Jiang 4 , Colby Oitment 4

1 University of Toronto, Mississauga, Canada, 2 University of Toronto, St George, Toronto, Canada, 3 McMaster University, Hamilton, Canada, 4 Scarborough General Hospital, Scarborough Health Network, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

Introduction: Elective spinal surgery is increasingly offered to elderly patients, yet outcomes at the extremes of age remain poorly characterized. With the global population living longer and the prevalence of degenerative spinal pathology rising, surgeons must balance potential benefits against perioperative risks in this vulnerable group. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated short- (30 day) and long-term (> 30 day - 1 year) survival and morbidity in patients aged ≥ 80 years undergoing elective spine surgery. Material and Methods: A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases (MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL) in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, identifying studies published between 1996 and 2024 reporting morbidity and mortality after elective spinal surgery in patients over 80 years. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included mortality at 60 days, 6 months, and 1 year, as well as 30-day morbidity. Two reviewers independently performed study screening, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Random effects meta-analysis was used to pool outcomes. Results: Twelve studies including 89,529 patients (mean age 85.4 years, range 80-99) met inclusion criteria. Pooled 30- day survival was 98% (95% CI: 94-99%), though heterogeneity was high (I2 = 98.6%). Reported early survival was high ranging from 87% to 100%. At one year, survival ranged from 75% to 94% across four studies. Complications were frequent, with pooled overall morbidity of 16% (unweighted mean 21.8%); major complications occurred in 5.2% pooled versus 10% unweighted, with smaller institutional series reporting rates as high as 60%. Conclusion: Short-term survival after elective spinal surgery in patients aged 80 and older appears excellent, although the risk of complications remains considerable. Reported outcomes are influenced by patient selection, with healthier individuals being more likely to be offered surgery. This suggests that the numbers here are best-case scenario. Despite that, substantial morbidity is reported at 30 days. Smaller institutional series suggest higher complication rates than large database studies. The discrepancy between pooled and unweighted estimates underscores substantial heterogeneity and the potential for publication bias. Elective surgery therefore can be undertaken safely in carefully chosen patients over 80, but thorough preoperative evaluation and candid patient counseling are essential.

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Tan Tock Seng Hospital, Singapore, 2 Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore, Singapore

This is in keeping with existing literature. Western alignment targets can result in overzealous correction of lordosis which can result in proximal junctional failure or adjacent segment disease. Instead, surgeons should aim to restore patient to their native segmental and global alignment.

RF261: Vertebropexy - Long-term durability of tendon-based spinal stabilization under cyclic loading

Jana Felicitas Schader 1,2,3 , Oliver Wigger 4 , Marie-Rosa Fasser 4 , Ramon Rohner 4 , Anna Katharina Calek 1,2 , Anna Schuler 1,4 , Niels Hammer 5,6,7 , Jess Snedeker 1,3 , Mazda Farshad 1,2 , Jonas Widmer 4

1 Department of Orthopedics, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, University Spine Center Zürich, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, Institute of Biomechanics, Balgrist Campus, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, 2 University Spine Center Zurich, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, 3 Institute of Biomechanics, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, 4 Spine Biomechanics, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Balgrist University Hospital, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland, 5 Division of Macroscopic and Clinical Anatomy, Gottfried Schatz Research Center, Medical University of Graz, Graz, Austria, 6 Department of Orthopedic and Trauma Surgery, University of Leipzig, Leipzig, Germany, 7 Division of Biomechatronics, Fraunhofer Institute for Machine Tools and Forming Technology, Dresden, Germany

Introduction: Similar to other sports orthopaedic techniques, vertebropexy (VPX) is a tendon-only fixation approach for the lumbar spine. It stabilizes flexion without restricting movement in other planes, potentially overcoming certain biomechanical drawbacks of both fusion and decompression procedures. Although short-term biomechanical and clinical outcomes are promising, long-term performance data are missing. It is hypothesized that tendon-based spinal stabilization (vertebropexy) demonstrates reliable long-term performance when subjected to a newly designed cyclic biomechanical testing protocol. Material and Methods: Five motion segments from three human cadaveric lumbar spines were evaluated. VPX was performed using a human peroneus longus tendon allograft, looped twice around the spinous processes and secured with a Prusik knot. Each specimen underwent load-controlled flexion-extension testing across five states: native (intact), post-decompression (deco-pre, bilateral laminorecessotomy), after vertebropexy (VPX-pre), after prolonged cyclic testing (VPX-post), and after removal of VPX (deco-post). Results: Relative to the intact condition (100%), median flexion immediately after VPX was reduced to 0.5% [25th-75th percentile: -25.8% to 13.4%]. Median absolute flexion for each condition was: native 3.7° [2.6°-4.7°], deco-pre 3.8° [2.6°-4.5°], VPX-pre 0.0° [-1.0°-0.3°], VPX-post 0.8° [0.2°-2.0°], and deco-post 4.6° [3.7°-4.7°]. After 6 months, imaging demonstrated an intact tendon construct without evidence of instability, while VAS back pain scores decreased from 4 preoperatively to 2, and ODI improved from 32 to 2. Conclusion: VPX demonstrated preserved functional stability over time. Immediately after decompression, pre-tensioning substantially limited flexion, effectively immobilizing the segment. Over the simulated 6-month daily activity period, this restriction decreased moderately, as intended, stabilizing at roughly a 40% sustained motion reduction while maintaining segmental stability. These biomechanical features may reduce long-term complications relative to conventional decompression or fusion procedures.

1 Department of Neurosurgery, Royal Preston Hospital, Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Preston, United Kingdom, 2 Melanin Medics Research Network, Luton, United Kingdom

Introduction: Moderate-to-severe pain is common after spine surgery. While opioids remain standard analgesia, their adverse effects have prompted opioid-sparing strategies. Postoperative HADS scores showed a significant reduction in anxiety and depressive symptoms compared with preoperative levels (p < 0.05). At the six-month follow-up, 71.9% of patients demonstrated improvements in HADS depression scores, and 79.74% in HADS anxiety scores. The median HADS depression score decreased by 2 points, while the anxiety score decreased by more than 3 points. Additionally, 59.38% of patients shifted from the “abnormal” to the “normal” category in the depression score, and 80.49% shifted to the “normal” category in the anxiety score. Conclusion: These findings highlight the need for comprehensive and multidisciplinary approaches to managing both the physical and psychological aspects of LSS, ultimately contributing to more effective and holistic patient care.

RF268: Segmental lumbar lordosis correction with anterior-TLIF cage: a bivariate regression analysis

However, none of these changes reached statistical significance. RF269: The intrathecal morphine analgesia for full endoscopic lumbar discectomy: a prospective dose-finding study

Lei Yue 1 , Haolin Sun 1

1 Peking University First Hospital, Beijing, China

Introduction: Anesthesia for full endoscopic lumbar discectomy (FELD), typically administered locally or regionally, often fails to provide adequate analgesia, necessitating additional analgesics or even sedation. Our previous work has shown that intrathecal morphine (ITM) administration is considered an effective adjuvant approach for managing peri-operative pain for FELD, but the adverse events (AEs) for ITM remain concerns. This study aimed to determine the effective dose of intrathecal morphine required to eliminate intraoperative pain in 90% of patients (ED90) undergoing FELD under spinal anesthesia and to evaluate the safety profile of ITM within 100 µg. Material and Methods: A prospective, double-blind, sequential allocation dose-finding study was conducted using the biased coin up-down method. Patients undergoing single-segment FELD received ITM through the same route as spinal anesthesia. The ITM dose was adjusted using a 1/9 probability of dose reduction following an effective response, or increased for the subsequent patient if the response was ineffective. Sample size for drug dose-finding studies typically ranges between 20 and 40 participants; this study included 30 participants. All patients underwent single-segment interlaminar or transforaminal FELD under spinal anesthesia. The ITM dosage range was established at 25, 50, 75, and 100 µg. An effective response was defined as an intraoperative VAS score of 0 with no need for additional analgesics. The dose was adjusted using a biased coin up-down method, with a 1/9 probability of dose reduction after an effective response. If an ineffective response occurred-defined as an intraoperative VAS score > 0 or the requirement for supplemental analgesics-the ITM dose was upgraded for the next patient. The study was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2200067060). Results: Thirty patients were enrolled and completed the study between November 2022 and August 2024. The ED90of ITM for FELD was 90.89 µg (95% CI 80.05-149.23 µg). Satisfactory analgesia (VAS = 0) was achieved in 15/16 patients at 100 µg, 11/13 patients at 75 µg, and none at 50 µg. ITM-related AEs occurred in 22/30 patients, with no significant difference in overall AE incidence between the 100 µg high-dose and lower doses. Nausea or vomiting was the most common AE during the operation and 1 h postoperatively, while pruritus was most frequent at 12 and 24 h postoperatively. More participants receiving 100 µg ITM reported pruritus compared to those receiving lower doses (7/16 vs. 1/14, p = 0.039). A total of 30% of participants required treatment for AEs, which resolved within 12 h postoperatively. No respiratory depression or motor block was observed. Conclusion: ITM provides effective intraoperative analgesia for FELD. Although decreasing the ITM dose seems to lessen the likelihood of AEs such as pruritus and may hasten the resolution of the side effects, the findings suggest that an approximate dose of 90.89 µg ITM may be optimal for achieving effective intraoperative pain control in most patients. Despite observing a correlation between ITM dose and morphine-related adverse events, more investigation is crucial to accurately establish the safest and most effective dosage.

RF271: Influence of disc space morphology and endplate concavity depth on choice of implant for cervical disc arthroplasty

Zhi Chen Kim Koh 1 , Hasjmy Mohamad 1 , Jon Yin Joseph Wan 1 , Michael Janssen 2 , Zhihong Chew 1 , Dalun Leong 1 , Andy Yeo Kuei Siong 1 , Dinesh Shree Kumar 1 , Terry Teo 3 , Gennie Yan Cen Lim 1

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Changi General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore, 2 Center for Spine and Orthopaedics, Denver, United States, 3 SportsIn Orthopaedic Clinic, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) aims to preserve spinal motion while preventing adjacent segment degeneration seen with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). However, suboptimal implant selection can lead to complications such as implant subsidence or migration. One of the key consideration of implants is the type of implant endplate anchors - spiked, or keeled. Disc morphology, particularly sagittal endplate concavity, may influence implant fit, biomechanics, and postoperative outcomes. This study aims to assess whether pre-operative endplate morphology, measured via sagittal Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), can guide implant choice in CDA and improve lordosis preservation. Material and Methods: This is a retrospective cohort study of patient who underwent cervical disc arthroplasty or hybrid (combination of CDA and ACDF) procedures in a single tertiary centre from January 2024 to March 2025. All procedures were performed by a single fellowship trained spine surgeon. The study included patients who underwent either single, double, or triple level CDA with either a domed spiked implant, or flat keeled implant. Mid-sagittal MRI was used to measure endplate concavity depth (ECD), and lateral radiographs were used to assess segmental and global cervical lordosis pre and postoperatively. The primary outcome measure of this study was ECD, which influenced the choice of keeled or spiked CDA implant, while secondary outcomes were sagittal alignment measurements and complications

Results: 30 patients, and a total of 56 cervical spine disc levels were included into this study. 33 levels were implanted with a spiked implant, and 23 were implanted with a keeled implant. It was found that disc spaces implanted with spike-based implant had a mean ECD of 2.6 mm, while disc spaces implanted with keel-based implant averaged 1.59 mm. Postoperative segmental lordosis was preserved or improved in 87.5% of operated levels and in 73% globally. No implant migrations or significant subsidence were observed in either group. It was also found that there was a decrease in ECD moving cranially to caudally from C3-4 to C6-7, with the C3-4 level receiving the highest proportion of spiked implant at 83%. Conclusion: CDA is a viable alternative compared to traditional fusion techniques at restoring cervical lordosis. Preoperative ECD measurement offers a simple, reproducible method for selecting CDA implants tailored to sagittal disc morphology. A greater ECD of an intervertebral disc space is better tailored to domed spiked implants. We propose a new classification system: domed spiked implants are suggested for Type A discs (ECD > 2 mm) while flat keeled implants are suggested for Type B discs (ECD < 2 mm). Appropriate matching of CDA prosthesis to disc spaces should be considered to improve clinical outcomes and reduce post-operative complications. Further clinical and radiographical outcome studies in this regard are required

RF272: Implant migration and dislocation in cervical disc arthroplasty: a systematic review

Amirzeb Aurangzeb 1 , Raj Kumar Sockalingam 1 , Dalun Leong 1 , Dinesh Shree Kumar 1 , Michael Janssen 2 , Terry Teo 3 , Zhihong Chew 1

1 Changi General Hospital, Singapore, Singapore, 2 Center for Spine and Ortho, Denver, Colorado, United States, Colorado, United States, 3 SportsIn Orthopaedic Clinic, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) has emerged as a motion-preserving alternative to fusion in managing degenerative cervical disc disease. Although prosthesis dislocation is uncommon, it can lead to devastating consequences. Despite the rising use of CDA, risk factors for implant migration have not been systematically consolidated, and guidance for clinical decision-making remains limited. This review provides the first comprehensive synthesis of reported cases of CDA-related implant migration, with a focus on identifying risk factors, patterns of failure, and treatment outcomes. Material and Methods: A structured search of PubMed yielded 16 eligible studies. Extracted data included study characteristics, patient demographics, implant design, timing and direction of migration, associated risk factors, revision strategies, and postoperative outcomes. Results: Forty cases of implant dislocation were identified. The majority involved anterior migration (70.0%), frequently linked to trauma, hyperlordotic alignment, or failed osseointegration. Posterior migration (17.5%) was primarily associated with polyethylene wear or osteolysis, while 12.5% were not directionally specified. Revision surgery was undertaken in 62.5% of cases, most commonly anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF, 88%). Two patients died from complications following revision procedures. Conclusion: Implant stability in CDA is influenced by both patient and surgical factors. Careful candidate selection, precise prosthesis sizing, and strict adherence to surgical technique are essential to reduce migration risk. CDA should be avoided in patients with cervical kyphosis, and constrained devices may be preferable in those with elevated risk profiles. Early diagnosis and prompt revision surgery are critical for optimizing patient outcomes.

RF273: Predictors of heterotopic ossification after cervical disc arthroplasty

Elisabetta de Rinaldis 1 , Zhaojie Chin 2,3 , Evelyn Linyi Koh2,3, Alex Quok An Teo2,3, Tan Jun Hao Tan2,3, Shuxun Lin2,3, Dennis Hey Hwee Weng2,3

1 Departmental Faculty of Medicine and Surgery, Research Unit of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Universitá Campus Bio-Medico di Roma, Rome, Italy, 2 National University Hospital, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Singapore, Singapore, 3 Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore

Introduction: Cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) has gained popularity as a suitable alternative to ACDF for treatment of anterior cervical compressive pathologies. One of the most frequently reported complications of CDA is heterotopic ossification (HO), defined as the ectopic formation of mature lamellar bone within soft tissues surrounding the prosthesis. Clinically, HO potentially compromises intended motion-preserving function of CDA, with progressive ossification leading to reduced segmental range of motion, functional ankylosis, or even outcomes resembling that of fusion - thereby negating the primary advantage of arthroplasty. The objective of this study is to analyze incidences of HO following CDA from a single-surgeon series and identify potential predictors, so as to mitigate its occurrence. Material and Methods: A retrospective review of 50 patients (122 levels) who underwent CDA with a minimum of 2-year follow up was conducted. Baseline characteristics, clinical presentation, perioperative details, and postoperative details were collected. Radiological parameters included grades and morphology of postoperative heterotopic ossification, pre and post operative osteophyte size, global cervical alignment, and segmental range of motion. Implant specific data such as height and width of implant, endplate coverage ratio, as well as inferior and superior endplate anterior uncoverage, were included. Results: Heterotopic ossification was observed up to 35 levels (28%) at 2-year follow-up. Most cases of HO were grade 3 and 4, with all morphologically appearing as claw-shaped. Statistically significant risk factors for HO included inferior and superior endplate anterior uncoverage, preoperative osteophyte size, multilevel surgery, and extent of osteophyte removal intraoperatively. Age, sex, implant height and width, and pre and postoperative FSU and C2-7 range of motion were not significantly associated with risk of HO. Expectedly, the non-HO group showed a trend of higher range of motion at any postoperative time compared to the HO group. Conclusion: Reduced implant coverage of endplates, larger preoperative osteophyte size, and greater extent of osteophyte removal intraoperatively are associated with increased risk of HO development following CDA. Using an appropriately-sized implant and minimizing intraoperative osteophyte resection, whilst encouraging neck exercises postoperatively, may help mitigate development and progression of HO.

RF274: Comparative analysis of wear particles and osteolysis in lumbar total disc replacement: biocompatibility signals of a viscoelastic monoblock disc

Kingsley Chin 1 , Erik Spayde 2 , William M. Costigan 3 , Sandra Thompson 4 , Mark Jones 5 , Ajay Yeddu 6 , Rajmani Krishnan 7 , Vito Lore 1 , Hope Estevez 1 , Suraj Yeddu 1 , Sajni Yeddu 1 , Shreyas Krishnan 8 , Sukanya Chebrolu 1 , Jason A. Seale 1 , Chukwunonso Ilogu 1 , Jacob Ryu 9

1 LESS Society, LESS Clinic, Fort Lauderdale, United States, 2 St. Charles Spine Institute, Thousand Oaks, CA, United States, 3 Congress Orthopaedic Associates, Pasadena, United States, 4 The Pain Center, Boise, Idaho, United States, 5 Pain Medicine of the Sounth, Knoxville, United States, 6 Desert Interventional Spine Consultants, Gilbert, United States, 7 Island Interventional Pain Management, Commack, NY, United States, 8 LESS Society, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, United States, 9 Midwestern University Chicago - College of Osteopathic Medicine, Chicago, United States

Introduction: Wear particle -driven osteolysis is a recognized long-term risk in lumbar total disc replacement. Submicron debris from polymer cores or mechanical articulations can trigger inflammatory bone loss and compromise fixation. A viscoelastic monoblock disc that bonds an elastic core to endplates eliminates articulating surfaces and may reduce particle burden. We compared wear characteristics and osteolysis signals across contemporary designs and evaluated whether a viscoelastic monoblock construct offers a biocompatibility advantage. Materials and Methods: We conducted a structured comparative analysis integrating bench testing, particle characterization, and targeted clinical literature review. Bench tests followed ISO-style multidirectional loading in flexion, extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation to high cycle counts. A viscoelastic monoblock disc and comparator designs representative of polymer-core or metal -polymer articulations were evaluated. Primary endpoints were gravimetric wear, particle size distribution relative to the phagocytosis threshold, and tribocorrosion. Secondary endpoints included surface integrity on profilometry and elemental composition by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Histologic response was evaluated in bone models exposed to test particles using tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase and cytokine labeling. Published reports and registries were screened for osteolysis, particle-related revisions, and long-term follow-up signals by two independent reviewers. Results: Bench testing showed minimal mass loss and preserved surface integrity for the viscoelastic monoblock disc, while articulating or polymer-core comparators exhibited greater abrasion and volumetric loss under high-motion conditions. Electron microscopy demonstrated fewer particles overall for the viscoelastic construct, with diameters predominantly > 1 µm. Comparator devices generated higher volumes of submicron (< 1 µm) debris and showed localized tribocorrosion at motion interfaces. Elemental analysis identified inert polymer and titanium constituents for viscoelastic debris without oxidation products, whereas comparators yielded metallic oxides or fragmented polymer. Histology revealed low osteoclast activation after exposure to viscoelastic particles, whereas submicron polymeric debris from comparators increased osteoclast density. In cadaveric spine models, bone mineral density adjacent to the viscoelastic implant was unchanged after simulation, while comparators demonstrated reductions of approximately 5 -8% at the superior vertebral body. Across targeted clinical sources, osteolysis has been reported with several articulating or polymer-core devices. By contrast, available long-term series for viscoelastic monoblock discs report no osteolysis cases, with follow-up beyond five years and low revision rates. In aggregated registry signals, osteolysis incidence for traditional mechanical designs reached up to 10%, whereas viscoelastic cohorts were reported at < 1%. Conclusion: Material choice and construct mechanics influence particle generation and biologic response in lumbar disc replacement. Across bench, histologic, and clinical signals synthesized here, the viscoelastic monoblock design produced larger, fewer, and more inert particles, with reduced markers of osteolysis compared with articulating or polymer-core comparators. Quantitative observations -5 -8% bone mineral density reductions with comparators after simulation and osteolysis rates < 1% for viscoelastic cohorts versus up to 10% for traditional designs with >5-year follow-up and support a biocompatibility signal for viscoelastic constructs. Prospective studies with standardized wear protocols, predefined imaging, and retrieval analysis are needed to validate durability, quantify rare events, and refine patient-specific indications.

RF277: Clinical relationship between curve location and body image, quality of life, and depression levels in patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis

Büşra Nur Özcan Erişgin 1 , Bedirhan Albayrak 2 , Altan Aksu 2 , Mennan Ece Pirzirenli 1 , Ahmet Uzun 1 , Hüseyin Sina Coşkun 1

1 Ondokuz Mayıs University, Samsun, Turkey, 2 Samsun Training and Research Hospital, Samsun, Turkey

Introduction: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is not merely a structural spinal deformity but a condition affecting orthopedics, psychology, and quality of life. While the Cobb angle is central in radiographic assessment, patients often face impairments in body image, self-esteem, and mental health during adolescence. Although the Scoliosis Research Society-22 (SRS-22) questionnaire is widely used to evaluate health-related quality of life (HRQoL), the role of curve location in psychosocial outcomes remains unclear. This study examined whether the anatomical region of spinal curvature (proximal thoracic, main thoracic, thoracolumbar/lumbar) is associated with differences in HRQoL, body image, and depression in AIS patients. Material and Methods: This cross-sectional study included 65 AIS patients (mean age 14.9 years) evaluated at a university hospital outpatient clinic. Participants completed the validated Turkish version of the SRS-22 questionnaire, assessing function/activity, pain, self-image, mental health, and satisfaction with management. Standing posteroanterior spinal radiographs were reviewed for Cobb angle, curve location, and Risser stage. Curves were categorized as proximal thoracic, main thoracic, or thoracolumbar/lumbar. Non-parametric tests were used due to non-normal SRS-22 score distributions. The Kruskal-Wallis H test compared SRS-22 scores across curve locations. Associations between curve severity and quality of life were assessed using Spearman’s correlation. Within-subject differences among SRS-22 subdomains were analyzed with the Friedman test, followed by Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons. Multiple linear regression explored the predictive effects of curve severity, age, and gender. A p-value < .05 was considered significant. Results: No statistically significant differences in total SRS-22 scores were observed among patients with proximal thoracic, main thoracic, or thoracolumbar/lumbar curves (p > .05). Subjective variables such as perceived body image, self-rated attractiveness, and resting back pain frequency also showed no significant associations with total or domain-specific scores (p > .26). However, within-subject comparisons of SRS-22 domains revealed important findings. The Friedman test indicated that body image and mental health scored significantly lower than pain, function/activity, and treatment satisfaction (χ2 = 78.18, p < .001; Kendall’s W = .30). Post-hoc Wilcoxon tests confirmed that body image scores were lower than all other domains except mental health (p < .01). These results highlight the psychosocial burden of AIS, independent of radiographic parameters. Regression analysis showed a borderline association between main thoracic curve severity and depressive mood scores (R2 = .06, p = .052). Neither age nor gender predicted HRQoL or body image outcomes (p > .40). Conclusion: Radiographic parameters such as curve location and severity did not significantly affect overall HRQoL in AIS patients. Nonetheless, SRS-22 subdomain analysis revealed significant impairments in body image and mental health. These findings emphasize that the psychosocial burden of scoliosis exists independently of anatomical deformity. Addressing emotional well-being and self-perception should therefore be integral to clinical evaluation and treatment planning. Future studies should further investigate the biopsychosocial dimensions of AIS and incorporate patient-reported outcomes into holistic management strategies.

RF278: Management of adult degenerative scoliosis in a neurosurgical department: outcomes and perspectives based on 34 cases

Ghassen Gader 1 , Aziz Bedioui 1 , Mohamed Aziz Hermassi 1 , Mouna Rkhami 1 , Mohamed Badri 1 , Kamel Bahri 1 , Ihsèn Zammel 1

1 Trauma and Burns Center, Ben Arous, Tunisia

Introduction: Adult degenerative scoliosis (ADS) is a common spinal pathology in the aging population, often associated with neurogenic symptoms and progressive spinal imbalance. While frequently addressed in orthopedic settings, neurosurgeons are increasingly involved in its management. This study aims to evaluate the outcomes of ADS surgeries performed in a neurosurgical department and to discuss related perspectives. Methods: A retrospective review was conducted of 34 patients with ADS who underwent surgical management between 2016 and 2024 in a university-affiliated neurosurgical center. The scoliosis was thoracolumbar in 73.5% of cases, lumbar in 20.6%, and thoracic in 5.9%. Curve magnitudes ranged from 15° to 48° (mean: 26.3°). All patients received decompression with or without instrumentation and deformity correction. Radiological parameters (Cobb angle, sagittal vertical axis, pelvic tilt) and clinical outcomes (ODI, VAS) were analyzed over a follow-up period of 12 to 60 months. Results: The mean patient age was 64.7 years (range: 52-78), with 61.7% being female. Preoperative symptoms included neurogenic claudication (79%), radicular pain (64%), and axial low back pain (55%). The mean postoperative Cobb angle was reduced to 12.1°, with significant improvement in sagittal alignment in 76% of cases. Complications occurred in 14.7% of patients, including 1 postoperative infection and 1 case of proximal junctional kyphosis. No intraoperative neurological deficits or perioperative mortality were observed. Clinical improvement (ODI and VAS) was noted in 85% of patients. Conclusion: The neurosurgical management of adult degenerative scoliosis is both safe and effective, particularly in thoracolumbar deformities. With proper patient selection and alignment planning, neurosurgical teams can achieve favorable outcomes comparable to orthopedic standards. Further prospective studies are needed to refine indications and optimize minimally invasive approaches.

Conclusion: Persistent MC Type 1 represent a distinct high-risk phenotype characterized by early re-herniation, higher re-revison rates and accelerated disc degeneration with superior response to IF versus MD. The 3.7-fold higher re-revision rate with MD (48.8% vs 13.0%, p < 0.01) and better functional outcomes with fusion support persistent MC Type 1 pattern as biomarker for surgical selection in ReLDH.
