RF281: Obesity may have minimal impact on operative time or early ambulationfollowing one to two level robotic spine surgery

Rowen Lin 1 , Kevin Mo 2 , Justin Chung 1 , William Fang 2 , Shanthan Challa 2 , Daniel Lee 2 , Hugh Bassewitz 2

1 Touro University Nevada, College of Medicine, Henderson, United States, 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Valley Hospital Medical Center, Las Vegas, United States

Introduction: Obesity is a well-recognized risk factor for adverse outcomes in traditional spine surgery, often leading to longer operative times, hospital stays, and delayed mobilization. With the rise of robotic-assisted techniques, it remains unclear whether elevated body mass index (BMI) will similarly influence peri-operative and postoperative metrics. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 per WHO criteria) affects operative time, length of stay (LOS), and early mobility following one- to two-level robotic lumbar fusion. Material and Methods: Adult patients undergoing one to two level robotic lumbar fusion were queried from a single surgeon's database from 2018-2022. Patients were then sub-stratified into two cohorts: 1) patients who were non-obese (BMI < 30 kg/m2), 2) patients who were obese (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2). Pre-operative, intra-operative, perioperative, 6 weeks and 6 months post-operative data were collected. A threshold-regression model was used to confirm BMI = 30 kg/m2 as the inflection point for total operative time. Bivariate analysis was then conducted using STATA 17.0 College Station, TX. Results: 97 adult patients undergoing one to two level robotic lumbar fusions were identified. Of these patients, 39 patients were obese (> 30 BMI). The average age of all patients was 55 (SD 13), 44 were female (45%), 64 patients use opiates preoperatively (66%), and 32 patients were on Workers Compensation (32%). Upon bivariate analysis, non-obese and obese patients showed no statistical significant differences in pre-operative, intra-operative, peri-operative, 6 week, or 6 month post-operative factors. This included operative time (239 ± 47 min vs 250 ± 71 min; p = 0.36), POD1 mobility (178 ± 215 m vs 195 ± 200 m; p = 0.70), hospital LOS (3.1 ± 1.4 days vs 2.7 ± 1.4 days; p = 0.22), week 6 VAS (5.2 ± 3.3 vs 6.0 ± 3.3; p = 0.23), or week 6 satisfaction (52 vs 34 patients; p = 0.71). However, bivariate analysis did show that morbidly obese patients were statistically significant for higher rate of opiate usage at 6 weeks postoperatively. Conclusion: Despite similar pre-operative characteristics, obesity or morbid obesity did not impact operative time, LOS, early ambulation, pain, or satisfaction outcomes at 6 weeks and 6 months after one to two level robotic lumbar fusion. However, morbidly obese patients were at higher risk of using opiates postoperatively at 6 weeks. These findings suggest that robotic surgery may not be impacted by high BMI. Further studies are necessary to determine whether this can be used to inform surgical decisions.

RF282: Impact of diabetes mellitus on mechanical complications and patient-report outcome measures in adult spinal deformity surgery

Tomohiro Yamada 1

1 Hamamatsu University School of Medicine, Hamamatsu, Japan

Introduction: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a common comorbidity in adult patients with spinal deformity (ASD), complicating surgical recovery and affecting functional recovery and healthcare costs. We investigated to clarify the effects of DM on mechanical complications and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) after ASD surgery. Material and Methods: This retrospective study was based on a prospective patient database of a single academic spinal surgery department. Four hundred and thirty-seven patients with ASD underwent corrective fusion surgery at a single academic center between 2010 and 2020. Primary outcome was perioperative medical and mechanical complications, pre- and postoperative sagittal alignments, and PROMs. Perioperative medical and mechanical complications included proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK), proximal junctional failure (PJF), distal junctional kyphosis (DJK), and rod fractures. Conclusion: DM may negatively affects trunk stability and musculoskeletal integrity, likely contributing to higher rates of mechanical complications and worsening postoperative alignment in ASD surgery. This study suggests that preoperative bone quality assessments and improved DM management could help mitigate these risks and ultimately enhance outcomes in patients with ASD.

RF283: The influence of patient-reported allergies on postoperative mobility, pain, and long term outcomes following lumbar interbody fusion

Jason Salvato 1 , Evan Florey 1 , Aidan Johnson 1 , Michael Pheasant 2 , Alex Tang 2 , Tan Chen 3

1 Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine, Scranton, United States, 2 Geisinger Northeast Orthopaedic Residency, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, United States, 3 Division of Orthopaedic Spine Surgery, Geisinger Musculoskeletal institute, Wilkes-Barre/Scranton, United States

Introduction: Prior studies have suggested a correlation between patient-reported allergies (PRAs) and poorer surgical outcomes, including increased psychological distress, higher postoperative pain, and reduced postoperative mobility in orthopedic populations. However, the impact of PRAs on outcomes after lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) remains unclear. The purpose of the study is to evaluate the relationship between PRAs and postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing LIF, including pain, mobility, and patient-reported functional improvement. Material and Methods: Retrospective chart review of patients undergoing elective LIF with degenerative spine pathology between November 2019 and January 2023 were included. Baseline demographics, psychiatric history, preoperative opioid use, and all reported allergies were recorded and categorized as medical (e.g., medications) or environmental (e.g., food, animals) were collected. Primary outcomes included changes in overall and mental health domains in Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) and Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) scores from baseline to one year postoperatively. Secondary outcomes included postoperative visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores and Activity Measure for Post-Acute Care (AMPAC) scores. Descriptive and inferential statistics were performed. Results: A total of 242 patients were found to have PRAs. Patients with PRAs were more likely to be female (57%, p = 0.002) and have a history of psychiatric disorders (0.9 ± 1.1 vs. 0.7 ± 1.0, p = 0.02). PRA patients exhibited greater improvements in PROMIS overall (11.5 ± 12.8 vs. 6.7 ± 10.2, p = 0.048) and mental health scores (13.5 ± 18.7 vs. 6.6 ± 14.6, p = 0.026), with no significant difference in ODI improvement. Increased fusion levels correlated with lower AMPAC scores (-1.096 per additional level fused, p < 0.05) but did not affect VAS. Preoperative opioid use had no effect on postoperative pain, mobility, or MCID achievement. ROC analysis demonstrated poor predictive value of PRAs for MCID (AUC < 0.600). Conclusion: Patient-reported allergies (PRAs) were not associated with worse outcomes following lumbar fusion procedures. Patients with PRAs exhibited greater improvement in PROMIS scores, particularly in mental health. The number of PRAs did not influence postoperative pain (VAS), mobility (AMPAC), or likelihood of achieving MCID in PROMIS or ODI outcome scores. These findings suggest the presence and quantity of PRAs should not be a deterrent in clinical decision-making for scheduling lumbar fusion surgery.

RF285: Interobserver concordance in lumbar vertebral Hounsfield Unit measurement on computed tomography: Validation across training levels

Maria Suarez 1 , Anderson Lopez 1 , Anayelis Lemos 2 , Maria Sanchez 2 , David Florez 1 , Victor Arrieta 1 , Javier Matta 1 , Sebastian Forero 1 , Hayde Fajardo 1

1 Hospital Militar Central, Bogota, Colombia, 2 Universidad Militar Nueva Granada, Bogota, Colombia

Introduction: Osteoporosis is a major public health issue associated with increased risk of fragility fractures, morbidity, and healthcare costs. Computed tomography (CT) Hounsfield Unit (HU) values have emerged as a promising tool for opportunistic bone quality assessment. However, the reproducibility of HU measurement across different levels of training - students, residents, and specialists - remains underexplored. Establishing interobserver agreement is crucial to validate HU as a reliable tool in clinical practice. Material and Methods: We conducted an observational, cross-sectional, analytical study to evaluate interobserver concordance in HU measurement of lumbar vertebrae (L1-L5) on CT scans. Thirty anonymized CT studies were randomly selected from institutional archives. Six observers were included: two medical students (with prior radiology rotation), two residents (orthopedics and radiology), and two specialists (spine surgery and radiology). Each observer independently measured HU values using a standardized region of interest (ROI) technique in axial slices from L1 to L5 and a sagittal slice of L1, avoiding cortical bone and basivertebral veins. Data were collected in a structured database. Interobserver agreement was calculated using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC, two-way random effects, single measures, consistency). Bland-Altman plots were used to assess systematic bias. Results: A total of 180 vertebral measurements were analyzed across the three training levels. The overall interobserver ICC for HU measurement was 0.86 (95% CI 0.78-0.92), indicating good agreement. Subgroup analysis revealed ICC values of 0.83 between students, 0.85 between residents, and 0.89 between specialists. Agreement across all levels of training was consistent, with no significant systematic bias detected in Bland-Altman plots. Repeat measurements in a subset of 10 cases confirmed intraobserver reliability, with ICC values > 0.80 for all participants. Conclusion: HU measurement of lumbar vertebrae on CT scans demonstrates good interobserver concordance across students, residents, and specialists when using a standardized protocol. These findings support the reproducibility and reliability of HU assessment, regardless of training level. Our results validate HU as a feasible tool for opportunistic osteoporosis screening and clinical decision-making in diverse clinical settings, including emergency and trauma care. Incorporating HU measurement into routine CT interpretation may enhance early detection of low bone density and improve surgical planning in spine and orthopedic practice.

RF286: PMMA-augmentation of the spinous process as an enhancing-protective measure against bone failure in “through the spinous process-vertebropexy”

1 Spine Biomechanics, Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Balgrist University Hospital, Zurich, Switzerland, 2 Institute of Biomechanics, ETH, Zurich, Switzerland

Introduction: Vertebropexy, a technique of semi-rigid stabilization of the spine, utilizes the spinous process as an anchor point for stabilizing elements such as tendons and flexible cerclages. In its primary form, it entailed drilling into the bone of two adjacent spinous processes and threading the stabilizing materials through the holes. Biomechanical studies have identified the spinous process as the weakest part of the vertebrae, while several cadaveric studies have demonstrated a significantly higher bone failure rate with osteoporosis. We investigated if cement augmentation of the cancellous bone of the spinous process could enhance the biomechanical strength of the bone and reduce the risk of fracture, in the setting of first-generation through the spinous process Vertebropexy. Material and Methods: Following quantitative computed tomography analysis and measurement of the bone mineral density of the corresponding spines, 12 lumbar segments are divided into two groups (Osteoporotic and Non-Osteoporotic) and then fixed in custom-made 3D-printed clamps. The spinous processes of 6 segments undergo cement augmentation (Augmented Group), and a CT scan is performed to confirm adequate augmentation. The other six segments remain uncemented. (Native Group). Posterior decompression, drilling of the spinous process, and instrumentation with bovine tendons are then conducted. Torque-to-failure stress tests of the spinous processes are performed on a biaxial static testing machine. Results: The cement-augmentation of the spinous process significantly increases the torque-to-failure in flexion (p = 0.00037/ Median & IQR: 13.0 & 5.25 in the Native Group vs 26.5 & 11.1 in the Augmented (PMMA) Group), regardless of the bone quality (p = 0.008). A statistically significant difference in torque-to-failure between Osteoporotic and Non-Osteoporotic groups inside the PMMA and Native groups was determined (p = 0.015 and p = 0.025respectively). However, no significant correlation between bone density and failure torque was observed (Spearman 0.276, p = 0.192). A comparison between the torque-to-failure of the Native Non-Osteoporotic spinous processes and that of the PMMA Osteoporotic showed no statistical significance (p = 0.240). Distinct models of failure were observed, but without any statistical correlation with any of our study groups. Bilateral pedicle fractures were observed only in the PMMA group. Conclusion: The cement-augmentation of the spinous processes can increase the torque-to-failure/fracture in both osteoporotic and non-osteoporotic conditions in the setting of through the spinous process-Vertebropexy.

RF287: Low-temperature spine-specific PMMA enhances bone regeneration via localized thermal necrosis in an osteoporotic rat model

Young-Yul Kim 1 , Jong-Beom Park 2

1 Catholic University of Korea, Daejeon St. Mary's Hospital, Daejeon, South Korea, 2 Catholic University of Korea, Uijeongbu St. Mary's Hospital, Uijeongbu, South Korea

Poly (methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) bone cement is widely used in percutaneous vertebroplasty to stabilize osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures. However, its clinical application is limited by its high compressive modulus, risk of thermal necrosis, and poor bone integration, unlike conventional PMMA formulations used in vertebrae or joint arthroplasty, which can reach polymerization temperatures exceeding 100 °C. Spine-specific PMMA is formulated to cure at a reduced polymerization temperature, thereby minimizing the rise in core temperature during the setting process. Consistent with our hypothesis, this moderate thermal output induces localized thermal injury that triggers osteogenic responses and extracellular matrix production, thereby enhancing osteoblast activity in the surrounding bone. This study aimed to evaluate bone remodeling following spine-specific PMMA injection in an osteoporotic Sprague-Dawley (SD) rat model. Twenty-four osteoporotic female SD rats were randomly assigned to three groups: Control (untreated), OVX + spine-specific PMMA (OVX + PMMA), and OVX (OVX + Defect). Bone regeneration was assessed using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), micro-computed tomography (Micro-CT), quantitative PCR (qPCR), immunohistochemistry (IHC), and Western blotting. At 12 weeks post-injection, the OVX + PMMA group exhibited significantly greater bone regeneration than the OVX group. Micro-CT analysis demonstrated a marked increase in trabecular thickness in the PMMA-treated group. Notably, bone formation was more pronounced in regions surrounding the cement compared to adjacent untreated areas. This suggests that spine-specific PMMA promotes osteogenesis via localized thermal necrosis and subsequent osteoblast recruitment. These findings highlight the dual role of spine-specific PMMA in both structural stabilization and biologically driven bone regeneration. Further research is warranted to optimize its clinical applications while minimizing potential adverse effects.

1 National Center for Spinal Disorders, Budapest, Hungary

Introduction: Imaging-based fusion assessment is a commonly used in everyday clinical practice and in clinical studies to assess the biological effectiveness of spinal fusion procedures. Currently there is no gold standard method for fusion assessment and existing technics can be characterized by variable reliability and accuracy. Moreover, imaging limitations compounded by imaging artefacts from cage and graft materials can influence the application of the assessment method especially in the intervertebral space. Previous methodological studies reported details about patients with mainly PEEK or composite cages, but data concerning the recently widespread 3D printed titanium implants is lacking. The goal of this study was to evaluate the reliability of radiological interbody fusion assessments in patients operated with lumbar 3D printed titanium TLIF cages. Material and Methods: 42 patients who underwent one- or two-level lumbar TLIF were included into the study. Lumbar X-ray and CT imaging studies from 6- and 12-month follow-up visits were evaluated by two independent raters (a radiologist and a consultant spine surgeon). Intervertebral fusion was assessed according to the Bridwell criteria. Interrater correlation coefficient (ICC) was calculated to determine the reliability (agreement) of the radiologic measurements. Results: 84 fusion level were evaluated. X-ray and CT-based grading moderately correlated to each other (rho = 0.449 in Rater 1 and 0.589 in Rater 2). Based on X-rays, 62 levels were classified as Grade 1, 20 levels as Grade 2 and 3 levels as Grade 3 fusions by Rater 1 and 49 as Grade 1, 34 as Grade 2, 1 as Grade 3 by Rater 2 (p = 0.009). Inter-rater agreement was weak in case of X-ray based fusion assessment (0.273-0.342) and also in case of CT-based assessment for the whole dataset (rho = 0.226). ICC was higher (moderate) in case of assessing 12-month CT images (0.476) and in L5 level (0.428). Conclusion: Our results underline the weak to moderate reliability of the Bridwell classification for intervertebral fusion assessment in case of 3D printed titanium TLIF cages supporting the previously reported results for other cage materials. Based on our results, the combination of X-ray and CT based assessment at 12-month is strongly advised for radiologic fusion evaluation. Further research and development of a more reliable method would be desirable.

RF290: Comparison of clinical efficacy and safety between endoscopic and microscopic anterior cervical discectomy and fusion

Chengyu Huang 1 , Kai Chen 2 , Honglin Liu 1 , zhilin ge 1 , Dingkun Lin 1,3 , Bolai Chen 1,3 , Guoyi Su 1,3 , Yongpeng Lin 1,3 , Yongjin Li 1,3

1 The Second Clinical School of Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou, China, 2 Huizhou Sixth People's Hospital, Huizhou, China, 3 Orthopaedic Hospital of Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou, China

Introduction: To compare and analyze the clinical outcomes and safety of endoscopic anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (Endo-ACDF) and microscope-assisted anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (Micro-ACDF) in the treatment of single-level cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM). Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was performed on the clinical data of 32 patients with single-level CSM who underwent either Endo-ACDF or Micro-ACDF in our hospital from February 2022 to January 2024. There were 17 males and 15 females, with an average age of (54.53 ± 12.52) years. According to the surgical method, the patients were divided into the Endo-ACDF group (n = 16) and the Micro-ACDF group (n = 16). The operation time, postoperative hospital stay, degree of soft tissue swelling, hidden blood loss, Cobb angle, and Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) scores were collected and compared between the two groups. Results: The JOA scores of both groups at 6 months after surgery were significantly improved compared with those before surgery (p < 0.05). The hidden blood loss in the Endo-ACDF group was significantly lower than that in the Micro-ACDF group (193.99 ± 163.17 ml vs 349.26 ± 213.75 ml, p < 0.05). The intraoperative blood loss in the Endo-ACDF group was lower than that in the Micro-ACDF group (20.94 ± 11.58 ml vs 22.50 ± 12.91 ml), but the difference was not statistically significant (p > 0.05). The operation time in the Endo-ACDF group was significantly longer than that in the Micro-ACDF group (143.19 ± 53.29 min vs 115.19 ± 34.50 min, p < 0.05). There were no statistically significant differences in postoperative hospital stay, drainage volume, or degree of soft tissue swelling between the two groups (p > 0.05). Additionally, no significant differences were observed in the Cobb angle or JOA scores between the two groups before surgery and at 6 months after surgery (p > 0.05). No complications such as postoperative infection, implant failure or displacement occurred in either group. Conclusion: Both Endo-ACDF and Micro-ACDF can achieve satisfactory surgical outcomes in the treatment of CSM. There were no statistically significant differences in degree of soft tissue swelling between the two groups. Although Endo-ACDF faces challenges such as longer operation time and a steep learning curve in the initial stage of application, it has the advantage of less hidden blood loss and equivalent safety to Micro-ACDF, thus providing a new option for the ACDF operation mode.

RF291: Percutaneous full endoscopic C1 laminectomy for developmental atlantal stenosis with myelopathy: a primary cases report and review of the literature

Yi-Hao Liang 1 , Yongpeng Lin 1 , Guoyi Su 1 , Yongjin Li 1 , Bolai Chen 1

1 Minimally Invasive Spine Center, Orthopaedic Hospital of Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou, China

Introduction: Developmental atlantal stenosis with myelopathy (DASM) in adults is a rare disease that only sporadic cases have been reported over the years. C1 laminectomy (C1L) is one of the most common operations for its treatment. However, as an open surgery, it has shortcomings such as large trauma and slow postoperative rehabilitation, and minimally invasive spine surgery (MISS) offers alternative treatment options with advantages. MISS instruments expand the technical capabilities of surgeons, which allows safer and more effective therapeutics for difficult and complicated diseases. This case report presents a new minimally invasive approach; percutaneous full endoscopic C1 laminectomy (PFEC1L), for the treatment of DASM, and to consolidate the current literature on the condition to summarize its etiologies, clinical manifestations, diagnostic criteria, surgical management, and prognoses. Material and Methods: The patient in Case 1 presented with neck pain and numbness and weakness in the limbs. The patient in Case 2 presented with numbness in the extremities and the patient in Case 3 presented with bilateral hand numbness and left lower limb weakness. They were all diagnosed with DASM and underwent PFEC1L treatment to maintain the enlargement and decompression of the atlantal canal, which achieved favorable outcomes without complications during the postoperative follow-up visit. Results: 68 patients were equally split into EA-ACDF and MA-ACDF groups. No statistical differences were found in age, gender, BMI, surgical segment and follow-up time between them. EA-ACDF had a significantly shorter hospital stay than MA-ACDF (p < 0.05). Its operation time and intraoperative blood loss showed no significant differences compared with the ACDF (p = 0.07, 0.72). The mJOA scores of both groups improved significantly after surgery (p < 0.05). There were no significant differences in Nurick scores and mJOA between the two groups. The EA-ACDF’s EAT-10 and DSQ was better than that of the ACDF at each post-surgery time point, yet not statistically significant. The EA-ACDF group’s PSTSR was significantly better than the MA-ACDF group’s from 3 days to 3 months after surgery (p<0.001). Conclusion: DASM is rare but potentially dangerous. Its diagnosis is made based on clinical manifestations combined with radiological imaging examinations, especially computed tomography (CT) scan and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). While C1L is the most common surgical method, PFEC1L is a new feasible and safe therapeutic option with comparable good outcomes and the advantage of being minimally-invasive. To our knowledge this is the first report that PFEC1L was applied for DASM treatment. Keywords: C1 laminectomy (C1L); Endoscopic spine surgery; case report; cervical myelopathy; spinal canal stenosis.

RF292: Biportal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion using the multi-layer bone grafting technique: an effective strategy in resource-limited institution

Tran Vu Hoang Duong 1 , Pham Anh Tuan 2,3 , Huynh Van Vu 1 , Chu Van Lam 1 , Le Tan Linh 1 , Phan Duy 4 , Wongthawat Liawrungrueang 5

1 Department of Neurosurgery, Xuyen A General Hospital, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, 2 Department of Neurosurgery, Nguyen Tri Phuong Hospital, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, 3 Faculty of Medicine, University of Medicine and Pharmacy at Ho Chi Minh City, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, 4 Department of Neurosurgery, Vinmec Central Park International Hospital, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, 5 Spine Division, Orthopaedics Department, School of Medicine, University of Phayao, Phayao, Thailand

Study Design: A retrospective cohort study. Purpose: This study aimed to describe the surgical technique of biportal endoscopic (BE) lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) using a multi-layer bone grafting method and to investigate its clinical effectiveness in treating patients with grade I or II lumbar spondylolisthesis (LS). Overview of Literature: Previous studies have described BE-LIF; however, these reports predominantly originate from advanced centers in developed countries, using sophisticated implants such as dual transforaminal LIF (TLIF), oblique LIF, or titanium cages. In contrast, the described method utilizes hydroxyapatite (HA) bone grafts and autologous bone obtained from the preserved inferior articular process (IAP), combined with a single conventional TLIF cage, which provides a cost-effective alternative. Methods: This study included 41 patients with single-level grades 1 or 2 LS from February 2023 to February 2024. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for back and leg pain and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Bridwell fusion grades were evaluated via lumbar spine computed tomography performed 6 months postoperatively. Results: Over a mean follow-up period of 10.6 months (range, 7-18 months), significant improvements were observed in VAS scores for low back pain (from 7.8 ± 0.8 to 2.1 ± 1.4) and leg pain (from 8.1 ± 1.3 to 1.9 ± 1.5) as well as ODI scores (from 50.4 ± 15.4 to 14.8 ± 10.5). The cohort consisted of patients with grades 1 (73.2%) and 2 LS (26.8%) at L4-L5 (58.6%), L5-S1 (34.1%), and L3-L4 (7.3%) levels. The mean operation time was 182.8 ± 36.4 minutes, with a mean intraoperative blood loss of 190.5 ± 81.3 mL and a mean hospital stay of 7.2±3.6 days. Successful fusion (Bridwell grades I/II) was achieved in 82.9% of the cases, with a 4.9% incidence of cage subsidence. Minor complications included durotomies in two patients (4.9%), whereas no major complications, such as nerve root injury, hardware-related issues, or postoperative infections, were reported. Conclusions: The described BE-LIF technique, using HA bone grafts, which are an autologous bone from the preserved IAP, and a TLIF cage, is a viable, safe, and effective option for treating low-grade LS. This approach achieves favorable clinical outcomes and high fusion rates, which provides a cost-effective alternative to advanced surgical implants. Keywords: Minimally invasive spine surgery; Biportal endoscopic lumbar interbody fusion; Lumbar spondylolisthesis; Bone grafting

RF293: Challenges of biportal endoscopic transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (BE-TLIF) in spondylolisthesis

Che Wei Liu 1,2

1 National Tsing Hua University, Taipei. School of Medicine, Taiwan, Hsinchu, Taiwan, 2 Department of Orthopedic Surgery, Cathy General Hospital Taipei, Taipei, Taiwan

Introduction: Spondylolisthesis is a common spinal disorder. Degenerative spondylolisthesis (DS) is progressive and often debilitating, representing one of the most frequent indications for lumbar surgery in older adults. In contrast, isthmic spondylolisthesis (IS) arises from a pars defect and typically affects younger patients with distinct biomechanical characteristics. DS develops through intervertebral disc degeneration and altered load-bearing dynamics, resulting in segmental hypermobility, facet arthropathy, and often symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS). Biportal endoscopic transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (BE-TLIF) with bilateral percutaneous pedicle screw fixation has emerged as a minimally invasive option for managing low-grade spondylolisthesis. This study compared the short- to mid-term outcomes of BE-TLIF mostly in grade II DS and IS patients, with emphasis on surgical techniques and postoperative outcomes. Materials and Methods: Between January 2021 and December 2023, 35 consecutive patients diagnosed with grade II DS or IS underwent BE-TLIF at our institution. All patients were followed for a minimum of 6 months. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for back and leg pain, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), intraoperative blood loss, length of hospitalization, radiographic reduction of olisthesis, and perioperative complications. Results: BE-TLIF demonstrated favorable perioperative outcomes in both DS and IS groups. Blood loss was low, postoperative VAS and ODI scores improved significantly, and hospital stays were short. Radiographic analysis showed greater reduction of olisthesis in DS patients, while correction was less pronounced in IS patients. Complications were slightly more frequent in the DS group, likely due to older age, female predominance, and higher prevalence of osteoporosis. Nevertheless, both groups experienced substantial improvement in pain and disability at short- to mid-term follow-up. Conclusions: BE-TLIF offers significant benefits in terms of early recovery and minimally invasive access for both DS and IS. However, the procedure remains technically demanding. When substantial reduction of olisthesis is required-particularly in IS-the correctional power of BE-TLIF may be limited. Surgeons should carefully consider pathology-specific goals when selecting BE-TLIF for spondylolisthesis. Longer follow-up and larger prospective studies are needed to clarify long-term efficacy and durability of outcomes. Keywords: spondylolisthesis, degenerative spondylolisthesis, isthmic spondylolisthesis, biportal endoscopic surgery, lumbar fusion

RF294: A clinical comparison between microscopic minimally invasive transforaminal interbody fusion (MIS-TLIF) with the enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocol and unilateral biportal transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (BE-TLIF)

Pang Hung Wu 1 , Yi-Hao Liang 2 , Rohit Kavishkar 3

1 Achieve Spine and Orthopaedic Centre, Mount Elizabeth Hospital, Singapore, Singapore, 2 Minimally Invasive Spine Center, Orthopaedic Hospital of Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine, Guangzhou, China, 3 Asha Nursing Home, Pune, India

Introduction: Unilateral biportal endoscopy has become a procedure of choice for lumbar discectomies and decompressions at our center replacing the microscopic techniques. Lumbar fusion is performed either by Unilateral biportal endoscopic transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (BE-TLIF) or Minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion by microscopic tubular technique(MT-TLIF). Our aim was to compare these two techniques. Material and Methods: This is a retrospective study involving 59 patients who underwent lumbar fusion between November 2022 and November 2023. 28 patients underwent BE-TLIF for 34 levels of fusion and 31 patients underwent MT-TLIF for 36 levels of fusion. All the patients were followed up for more than 12 months. Clinical outcome was measured by Visual Analogue Score (VAS) for back pain and leg pain, pre-operatively and at subsequent follow-up’s. Functional outcome was measured by Oswestery Disability Index (ODI) and McNab’s criteria. The Bridwell grading system was used for assessing fusion on Xrays at follow-up. Results: Both the cohorts (BE-TLIF and MT-TLIF) showed significant improvement of back pain and leg pain post-operatively and all the follow-ups. There was statistically significant improvement of VAS for back pain at immediate post-operative, 6 weeks post-operative, 6 months post-operative and final follow-up in BE-TLIF group as compared to MT-TLIF. At final follow-up BE-TLIF cohort had better ODI scores (p = 0.04). Fusion rates were better in BE-TLIF group at 6 months but eventually they were similar in both the groups at final follow-up but BE-TLIF cohort showed less subsidence than MT-TLIF group at final follow-up (p = 0.02). Conclusion: UBE fusion offers promising option of lumbar fusion with fusion rates similar to MIS-TLIF and added benefits of better clinical outcome scores, early ambulation, shorter hospital stay, less blood loss, faster time to fusion, less subsidence rate and very less incidence of surgical site infection.

RF295: A comparison of the long-term results of anterior lumbar interbody fusion and total disc arthroplasty: a prospective randomized controlled trial. Mean follow-up of 14 years

Jasmin Fussi 1 , Michael Putzier 2 , Thilo Khakzad 3 , Chris Lindemann 4 , Timo Zippelius 3 , Patrick Strube 4

1 IRCSS NEUROMED Istituto Neurologico Mediterraneo, Pozzilli, Italy, 2 Charité University Medicine, Berlin, Germany, 3 SRH-- Klinikum Karlsbad, Karlsbad-Langensteinbach, Germany, 4 Waldkliniken Eisenberg, Jena University Hospital, Eisenberg, Germany

Introduction: This prospective randomized study compares the clinical and radiological long-term outcomes of single-level anterior lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF) and total disc arthroplasty (TDA)

Material and Methods: Patients with symptomatic single-level degenerative disc disease (DDD) at L4/5 or L5/S1 were randomly assigned to groups ALIF or TDA. Clinical evaluations using the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and visual analogue scale (VAS) for pain were conducted preoperatively, at three, 12, and 24 months, and after a mean follow-up of 14 years (12.2 to 15.9). Radiological assessments included radiographs in two planes and flexion-extension views. Additionally, CT was performed in the ALIF group to evaluate fusion after 24 months. Complications and patient satisfaction were recorded. Outcomes were analyzed for the entire cohort and by spinal segment. Results: Of the 120 patients included (60 per group), 28 were lost to follow-up, including three excluded because of revision surgery. In the remaining patients, significant improvements in ODI and VAS were seen over time (all p < 0.001). Clinical scores had declined slightly by final follow-up but remained better than the preoperative levels. No significant overall differences were found between ALIF and TDA. However, subgroup analysis revealed that ALIF outperformed TDA at L5/S1 (ODI posthoc test at final follow-up p = 0.005): outcomes were comparable at L4/5. Conclusion: Both ALIF and TDA are safe and effective methods of treating single-level DDD. ALIF is preferable at L5/S1 due to biomechanical factors, such as variability in the centre of rotation and sagittal profile types, which have a negative impact on the outcomes of TDA at this level. Conversely, at L4/5, both procedures give comparable results. These findings emphasize the importance of considering segment-specific anatomical and biomechanical factors in surgical decision-making for DDD.

RF296: Comparison of clinical and radiological outcomes of percutaneous endoscopic decompression for stenosis associated with degenerative lumbar scoliosis between different scoliosis curve severity

Pornpavit Sripirom 1 , Chaiyaporn Siramanakul 2

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Phyathai Phaholyothin Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand, 2 Banphaeo General Hospital Sathon Vranch, Bangkok, Thailand

Introduction: There is ongoing controversy regarding the most appropriate surgical treatment for lumbar spinal stenosis with concurrent degenerative lumbar scoliosis: decompression alone, decompression with short-segment spinal fusion, or long-segment spinal fusion for deformity correction. According to evidence-based guidelines, the coexistence of degenerative stenosis and spinal deformity is a common scenario. Decompression alone is considered a less invasive procedure with comparable outcomes to fusion surgery and is recommended for patients with a small curve (Cobb angle of 10°-20°). For patients with a Cobb angle greater than 20°, decompression with fusion surgery is considered. In recent years, several authors have demonstrated that successful endoscopic decompression for lumbar spinal stenosis relies on preserving the posterior spinal elements. This technique may serve as an efficient alternative to traditional open decompression surgery for lumbar stenosis associated with degenerative lumbar scoliosis.

The aims of this study were:

1. To investigate the clinical outcomes of percutaneous endoscopic decompression surgery in patients with lumbar spinal stenosis and degenerative lumbar scoliosis.

2. To compare radiographic and clinical outcomes among patients with small curves (Cobb angle of 10°-20°), moderate curves (21°-40°), and curves greater than 40°. Material and Methods: Sixty-one consecutive patients were enrolled in this study. Inclusion criteria included evidence of lumbar spinal stenosis and degenerative scoliosis with a Cobb angle greater than 10°. The patients’ primary clinical symptom was radiculopathy rather than back pain. Percutaneous endoscopic decompression was performed via interlaminar, transforaminal, or posterior oblique lateral approaches, depending on the pathoanatomy of each patient. The visual analog scale (VAS) for leg pain, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and radiographic features were evaluated preoperatively and at more than two years postoperatively. For subgroup analysis, patients were classified into three groups: 1. Cobb angle 10°-20° 2. Cobb angle 21°-40° 3. Cobb angle > 40° to compare clinical and radiologic outcomes among the groups. Results: VAS and ODI scores significantly improved at the final follow-up. The recovery rates for VAS and ODI were 82.84% and 70.35%, respectively. The Cobb angle remained stable over the two-year postoperative period (p = 0.753). Regarding scoliosis severity, no significant differences were found in VAS and ODI improvement or scoliosis progression at final follow-up among the three groups. Conclusion: Clinical outcomes following percutaneous endoscopic decompression were generally favorable, with no progression of the scoliosis curve. Even in cases where the Cobb angle exceeded 40°, spinal fusion may not be necessary for all patients with spinal stenosis associated with degenerative lumbar scoliosis.

RF297: Uniportal endoscopic management in piriformis syndrome

Pornpavit Sripirom 1 , Chaiyaporn Siramanakul 2 , Kundol Tangruthaiwanich 3

1 Siriraj Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand, 2 Phyathai Phaholyothin Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand, 3 Ruamrudee International School, Bangkok, Thailand

Introduction: Piriformis syndrome (PS) is a neuromuscular disorder caused by compression and irritation of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis muscle. It is a non-discogenic cause of buttock pain radiating down the leg, with a reported prevalence of 0.3-6% among patients with sciatica or back pain. PS is classified into primary (due to anatomical variants) and secondary (due to trauma, overuse, or prolonged sitting). Conventional treatment includes physiotherapy, injections, or open surgery. We evaluated the outcomes of a novel minimally invasive approach-uniportal endoscopic sciatic-nerve decompression-for patients with refractory PS. Material and Methods: This retrospective case-series included 20 consecutive patients with clinically and radiologically diagnosed PS who underwent uniportal endoscopic sciatic-nerve decompression between 2018 and 2023. Diagnosis was based on clinical tests (FADIR, Freiberg, PACE, piriformis-tenderness sign), MRI and EMG findings, and exclusion of spinal causes. Surgery was performed via a single small incision under C-arm guidance with resection of the piriformis tendon, decompression of the sciatic nerve, and haemostasis. Outcomes included pain (Visual Analog Scale, VAS) and function (modified Harris Hip Score, mHHS), collected pre-operatively, immediately post-operatively, and at 1, 3, and 6 months. Statistical analysis used Friedman test and Durbin-Conover post hoc comparisons. Results: Of the 20 patients (9 male, 11 female; mean age 48.8 years), all completed at least 6-month follow-up. Pain scores improved significantly: mean VAS decreased from 6.4 pre-op to 3.6 immediate post-op, 2.3 at 1 month, 1.1 at 3 months, and 0 at last follow-up. Functional outcomes improved substantially: mean mHHS increased from 29.7 pre-op to 50.4 immediate post-op, 59.8 at 1 month, 80.6 at 3 months, and 90.0 at last follow-up. Friedman testing confirmed significant differences across timepoints (χ2 = 41.2, df = 3, p < 0.001), with all pairwise comparisons reaching statistical significance. No major intraoperative or postoperative complications were observed. Most patients ambulated on post-op day 1 and were discharged after a single overnight stay. Conclusion: Uniportal endoscopic sciatic-nerve decompression for piriformis syndrome is a safe and effective minimally invasive option, offering early mobilization, short hospital stay, and significant improvement in pain and function. In this series, outcomes showed durable benefits through 6 months with no reported complications. Larger prospective studies are warranted to validate these findings and further define the role of endoscopic decompression in managing PS.

RF298: Clinical outcomes, safety, and cost considerations of rhBMP-2 in infection-related spinal fusion: a systematic review

Humaid Al Farii 1

1 Sultan Qaboos University, Muscat, Oman

Introduction: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis remains a challenging clinical entity, particularly when surgical intervention is required. While recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) is well established in degenerative spine fusion, its role in the setting of active or treated spinal infection is controversial. This review aimed to evaluate the clinical outcomes, safety profile, and cost implications of rhBMP-2 in infection-related spinal fusion surgery. Material and Methods: A focused literature review was conducted to identify studies reporting on the use of rhBMP-2 in patients undergoing spinal fusion for pyogenic spondylodiscitis or vertebral osteomyelitis. Data were extracted on patient demographics, BMP dose, fusion rates, complication profiles, infection recurrence, neurological outcomes, and cost-related metrics. Results: Six studies encompassing 346 patients treated with rhBMP-2 were included. Fusion rates ranged from 96.5% to 100%, with a weighted average of 99.4%. The infection recurrence rate was low (2.63%), and no study attributed reinfection to BMP use. The complication rate averaged 15.86%, with only one transient BMP-related event (radiculitis) reported. Neurological improvement was observed in 62.98% of patients. Cost data, though limited, suggest reduced long-term healthcare utilization in BMP-treated patients, potentially offsetting initial implant costs. Conclusion: rhBMP-2 appears to be a safe and potentially effective adjunct in the surgical treatment of spinal infections, offering high fusion rates and a favourable complication profile when used selectively. These findings support further investigation in prospective, controlled trials to clarify optimal use, dosing, and cost-effectiveness in infection-related spinal fusion.

RF299: Efficacy and safety of ABM/P-15 in one- and two-level TLIF: a propensity score-matched comparison with rhBMP-2 or local autograft bone

Mitsuhiro Nishizawa 1 , Steven Glassman 1 , Mladen Djurasovic 1 , Charles Crawford, III 1 , Jeffrey Gum 1 , John Dimar 1 , Kirk Owens 1 , Anna Duncan 2 , Leah Carreon 1

1 Norton Leatherman Spine Center, Louisville, Kentucky, United States, 2 University of Louisville School of Medicine, Louisville, Kentucky, United States

Introduction: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (TLIF) has been widely performed since being introduced in 1982. Various alternative bone grafts have been adopted to enhance fusion. Recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) is potentially the current gold standard for supplemental bone grafting, but complications have been reported including postoperative radiculitis, inflammatory responses, and potential malignancy; and its high cost remains a concern, Anorganic bone matrix combined with a P-15 osteogenic cell-binding peptide (ABM/P-15) is a relatively new peptide-based graft substitute, classified as a bioactive molecule in the same category as BMP. Approved for anterior cervical fusion surgery in 2015, randomized trials have since demonstrated its safety and efficacy in anterior cervical procedures. However, research on its use in lumbar fusion remains limited, and its clinical outcomes have not been well described. This study aimed to assess the efficacy, safety, and cost of ABM/P-15 in TLIF, compared with rhBMP-2 or local autograft bone with no bioactive molecules. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 317 patients who underwent one- or two-level TLIF. Patients lacking complete patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) or 12-month radiographic evaluations were excluded. Patients were categorized into three groups based on graft material: ABM/P-15, rhBMP-2, or local autograft bone. Each ABM/P-15 patient was matched to a rhBMP-2 and local autograft patient based on demographics, number of levels fused, and graft dose/kit size. Postoperative complications, PROMs, and fusion rates were compared among the groups. Results: Each group consisted of 38 patients after matching. The mean ABM/P-15 volume was 4.4 ± 1.3 cc (cost: $2,432.3 ± 714.4), and the mean rhBMP-2 dose was 3.0 ± 1.1 mg (cost: $2,316.6 ± 843.0). At 12 months, PROMs improved significantly in all groups, with no significant differences among them. Fusion was achieved in 84% of the ABM/P-15 group, 79% in the rhBMP-2 group, and 82% in the autograft group (p = 0.265). Complication rates, including postoperative radiculopathy, were also comparable (p = 0.725). Conclusion: This is the first study to directly compare ABM/P-15 and rhBMP-2 in patients undergoing TLIF. ABM/P-15 demonstrated comparable fusion and complication rates to rhBMP-2 in one- or two-level TLIF procedures, at a similar cost.

RF300: Management and outcomes of fragility vertebral fractures: a single-centre descriptive cohort

André Beco 1 , Sérgio Pita 1 , Carlos João 1 , Inês Dias Monteiro 1 , Catia Machado 1 , Patricia Paredes 1 , João Souto 1 , Hugo Nogueira 1 , João Afonso 1

1 Unidade Local de Saúde da Região de Aveiro, Aveiro, Portugal

Introduction: Vertebral fragility fractures (VFF) are a frequent manifestation of osteoporosis, associated with significant morbidity and health service utilization. Management can be conservative or surgical, depending on fracture stability, patient comorbidity, and functional demands. Real-world descriptive reports are essential for service planning and hypothesis generation. However, cases are often incompletely recorded in hospital systems, and the exact fracture date is frequently uncertain. Material and Methods: We conducted a retrospective descriptive cohort (level IV) at a single district general hospital. Eligible patients were aged ≥ 45 years, presenting with a new low-energy thoracolumbar vertebral fracture, and managed between January 2019 and May 2025. To ensure ≥ 1-year follow-up, only cases diagnosed up to May 2024 were included. Data were extracted from the institutional registry using a predefined data dictionary. Results are presented as counts/proportions and medians with interquartile ranges (IQR), without hypothesis testing. Mortality and vertebral refracture were assessed across the entire cohort. In the surgical subgroup, postoperative infection, length of stay (LOS), 1-year mortality, and pain (VAS) were analyzed. Results: A total of 171 patients were included, with a median age of 69.5 years (IQR 61.5-74.3); 76.6% were female (131/171). A prior osteoporotic fracture within 2 years was documented in 8.2% (14/171). Management distribution was: conservative 50.9% (87/171), short-segment fixation with cement augmented screws 18.7% (32/171), four-level pedicle screw fixation 15.8% (27/171), standalone kyphoplasty 11.1% (19/171), and kyphoplasty plus short segment fixation (cement augmented screws) 3.5% (6/171). The median LOS was 10.0 days (IQR 6.0-13.0). Overall mortality occurred in 17.5% (30/171). In the surgical subgroup (n = 84), postoperative infection occurred in 3.6% (3/84), and a percutaneous approach was used in 72.6% (61/84). The 1-year mortality was 3.6% (3/84; 95% CI 1.2-10.0), with 13.0% (3/23) after open procedures and 0.0% (0/61; 95% CI upper 5.9) after percutaneous procedures. Pain improved across follow-up, with median VAS 2.0 (0.0-3.0) at 1 month (n = 75), 2.0 (0.0-2.0) at 6 months (n = 74), and 0.0 (0.0-2.0) at 12 months (n = 72). Conclusion: This descriptive institutional cohort provides a real-world overview of VFF management and outcomes. Conservative cases are frequently under-registered, and fracture dates are often unavailable, limiting time-to-event analyses. The findings, including complications and detailed VAS trajectories in the surgical subgroup, are relevant for clinical governance, serving as a baseline for future comparative studies.

RF301: Preclinical assessment of NVDX3 as a bone graft substitute in an posterolateral lumbar fusion model

Andres Bonilla 1 , Marie-Albane Minati 2 , Denis Dufrane 2 , Judy Ashworth 2 , Hara Episkopou 2 , Howard Seim 1 , Ben Gadomski 1 , Kevin Labus 1 , Drew Koch 1 , Katie Bisazza 1 , Jeremiah Easley 1

1 Colorado State University, Fort Collins, United States, 2 NOVADIP Biosciences S.A, Mont-Saint-Guibert, Belgium

Introduction: Spinal fusion is a standard treatment for degenerative spine conditions, but limitations of autologous iliac crest grafts drive the search for safer and more effective alternatives. NVDX3 (Novadip Biosciences, Belgium) is a novel, human-derived osteogenic implant composed of extracellular matrix, bioactive molecules, non-viable osteogenic cells, and hydroxyapatite/β-tricalcium phosphate particles. NVDX3 is designed to promote mineralization, angiogenesis, and osteogenesis. This study evaluated the xenogenic safety and preliminary efficacy of NVDX3 in an ovine posterolateral lumbar fusion (PLF) model. Material and Methods: Thirty-six skeletally mature sheep underwent bilevel PLF (L2-L3 and L4-L5) with pedicle screw and rod fixation, receiving either NVDX3 (treatment) or local autograft (control). Animals were assigned to two endpoints: 12 weeks (n = 18) and 26 weeks (n = 18). Approximately 3 g of graft material was bilaterally implanted at each level. All procedures were performed under an IACUC-approved protocol. Animals were monitored daily for general health, body weight, and systemic parameters, with scheduled bloodwork to assess safety. Imaging assessments (radiographs and CT scans) were conducted at 6, 12, and 26 weeks. At study endpoints, animals were euthanized for ex vivo analyses, including gross necropsy, manual palpation, nondestructive kinematic testing, micro-CT, histology, and histomorphometry. Results: All procedures were completed without complications, and all animals recovered uneventfully. Radiographs and CT confirmed correct hardware placement. Clinical monitoring revealed minimal weight fluctuations and unremarkable bloodwork. Ex vivo assessments indicated high functional fusion in both groups. At 12 weeks, autograft sites showed rapid bone formation with high rates of fusion and mechanical stability. NVDX3 promoted mineral bridging and remodeling, achieving moderate-to-complete fusion in 88% of cases. Mechanical stability was comparable, with minor differences in lateral bending. At 26 weeks, CT, palpation, and kinematic testing demonstrated high fusion rates and equivalent biomechanical stability in both groups. Micro-CT and histomorphometry showed higher bone volume and trabecular number in autograft, while NVDX3 exhibited higher mineral density but reduced bone area in some regions. Histology confirmed progressive NVDX3 remodeling with minimal local reactivity. No systemic toxicity was observed in either group. Conclusion: NVDX3 exhibited a slower but steady remodeling process, ultimately achieving comparable mechanical stability to autograft by 26 weeks. Unlike autograft, which demonstrated higher bone volume and trabecular organization, NVDX3 favored higher mineral density, suggesting the formation of a more mature and durable bone structure. Importantly, NVDX3 demonstrated consistent osteogenic potential without the need for donor-site harvesting, thereby eliminating the morbidity and variability associated with autograft. These findings underscore the translational advantages of NVDX3 as a safe, effective, and clinically practical osteogenic scaffold for spinal fusion.

RF302: Radiographic and patient reported outcomes following posterolateral lumbar fusion using P-15L: 12-month data inclusive of high-risk population

W. Bradley Jacobs 1 , Christopher Witiw 2 , Chris Bailey 3 , Perry Dhaliwal 4 , Carlo Santaguida 5 , Zhi Wang 6

1 University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, 2 University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada, 3 Western University, London, Canada, 4 University of Manitoba, Winnepeg, Canada, 5 McGill University, Montreal, Canada, 6 University of Montreal, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Posterolateral lumbar fusion (PLF) is a procedure used to treat degenerative conditions of the lumbar spine, aiming to restore stability, reduce pain, and improve quality of life. Comorbidities such as smoking, obesity, and diabetes, however, are known to have a negative impact on fusion and clinical success. A critical need remains for bone grafts backed by high-level clinical evidence to support their use in higher-risk patients undergoing PLF. P-15L is a composite bone graft consisting of an anorganic bone mineral and P-15, a 15 amino acid polypeptide mimicking the cell-binding domain of Type I collagen, enhancing attachment and differentiation of osteogenic precursor cells and new bone formation. The aim of the current study was to determine fusion rates and changes in clinical outcomes in a largely high-risk patient population undergoing PLF with P-15L (PearlMatrixTM, Cerapedics Inc, Westminster, CO, USA). Materials and Methods: A prospective study was conducted across six Canadian hospitals. Adult patients requiring PLF between L1-S1 were included. Higher-risk patient status was defined by active smoking, obesity (BMI ≥ 30), and/or diabetes. Baseline, 6-month, and 12-month patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) were collected including Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), 12-Item Short Form Survey (SF-12), and Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NRS). Fusion status was assessed using 1-mm thin-cut CT scans at 12-months by an independent laboratory (Medical Metrics Inc., Houston, TX, USA). Fusion status was reported at both the segmental and patient level, defined as: full fusion (presence of continuous bridging bone), partial fusion (early signs of fusion) and absence of fusion (no evidence of initial healing, consolidation or bridging bone). Adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) were documented. Results: Forty-four patients (60 operative levels) were included (mean age 67.7 ± 11.9 years; 14 male, 30 female). Fifteen were obese, seven were active smokers, and ten had diabetes. Overall, 54.5% of the population had ≥ 1 risk factor (58.3% of operative levels). The mean number of operative levels was 1.4 (range 1-3). At 12-months, a 100% (12/12) fusion rate was achieved in patients with multilevel PLF. In single level PLF, 86.2% (25/29) were fully fused and 13.8% (4/29) were partially fused. Among patients with ≥ 1 risk factor, 91.4% of segments (12/15 single level segments, 20/20 multilevel segments) achieved full fusion. Mean PROMs showed significant improvement during the 12-month follow-up period as compared to the pre-operative baseline: ODI, NRS back pain, NRS leg pain, SF-12 physical (all p < 0.001), and SF-12 mental (p < 0.01). No device-related AEs occurred within 12-months. Conclusion: Despite over half of the reported study population having more than one higher-risk factor, high fusion rates were demonstrated for P-15L at 12-months. The significant improvement in PROMs shows reduced disability and pain, and increased quality of life post-operatively in patients following PLF with P-15L. Further, no device-related AEs were reported. These findings suggest that P-15L is a safe and effective graft option for PLF, even in real-world higher-risk patients.

RF303: Radiographic and patient reported outcomes in posterior cervical fusion using P-15L: a cohort inclusive of long-segment constructs

W. Bradley Jacobs 1 , Christopher Witiw 2 , Chris Bailey 3 , Perry Dhaliwal 4 , Carlo Santaguida 5 , Zhi Wang 6

1 University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, 2 University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada, 3 Western University, London, Canada, 4 University of Manitoba, Winnepeg, Canada, 5 McGill University, Montreal, Canada, 6 University of Montreal, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: Long-segment posterior cervical fusion (PCF), defined as fusion involving 3 or more spinal levels, is often associated with higher incidence of pseudarthrosis and need for revision surgery. For the long-segment fusion, we focused on the fusion per number of segments. Fusion status was adjudicated by the following criteria: full fusion (presence of continuous bridging bone), partial fusion (early signs of fusion) or absence of fusion (no evidence of initial healing, consolidation or bridging bone). No device-related AEs occurred within 12-months. When focusing on the long-segments constructs, the mean number of levels treated per patient was 4.5 (range 3-7). When stratified by the number of treated levels in long-segment PCF, 96.3% (26/27) for three-level, 89.3% (50/56) for four-level, 95.6% (43/45) for five-level, 91.7% (33/36) for six-level, and 100% (14/14) for seven-level were fully fused. Conclusions: In the current prospective study, the use of P-15L has demonstrated high fusion rates and improved clinical outcomes in a cohort inclusive of long-segment PCF procedures. These findings suggest that P-15L is a safe and effective graft option for PCF in a cohort inclusive of multiple comorbidities and extensive multilevel pathology.

RF304: A two-stage YOLO-based deep learning system for automatic detection of Cobb angle from scoliosis radiographs

Recep Dincer 1 , Işın Selbeş 2 , Fahrettin Yıldız 3 , Cem İrençin 2 , Mehmet Ertuğrul 4 , Mehmet Yunus Kıhçer 5 , Hüseyin Sina Coşkun 6 , Özcan Kaya 7

1 Suleyman Demirel University Faculty of Medicine, Isparta, Turkey, 2 Suleyman Demirel University Electronics and Communications Engineer, Isparta, Turkey, 3 Suleyman Demirel University Computer Programming, Isparta, Turkey, 4 Suleyman Demirel University Electrical and Electronics Engineer, Isparta, Turkey, 5 Suleyman Demirel University Mechanical Engineer, Isparta, Turkey, 6 Ondokuz Mayıs University Faculty of Medicine, Samsun, Turkey, 7 Biruni University Faculty of Medicine Department of Orthopedics and Traumatology, Istanbul, Turkey

Introduction: Cobb angle is one of the most widely used measurement criteria in scoliosis treatment. In this study, we evaluated the outcomes of a two-stage YOLO-based deep learning system for the automatic detection of the Cobb angle. Material and Methods: The system provides an integrated workflow for vertebra detection and Cobb angle calculation. A total of 68 full-spine radiographs with scoliosis were introduced to the system. Radiographs were categorized as mild scoliosis (10°-25°), moderate scoliosis (25°-40°), and severe scoliosis (> 40°). Image preprocessing enhanced the delineation of vertebral borders in low-quality radiographs, thereby improving detection sensitivity. A YOLOv12-based object detection model was used to identify bounding boxes of the vertebrae, while a YOLOv11-based keypoint model predicted the central points of each vertebra. Comparative evaluation with two independent experts demonstrated excellent reliability (expert A vs. model: mean 0.97; expert B vs. model: mean 0.96). Repeated trials of the model yielded perfect consistency (1.0, deterministic). Conclusion: The results indicate that the model’s error margin remains well below the clinically significant progression threshold of 5°. This study introduces a two-stage YOLO-based deep learning architecture for the automatic detection of Cobb angle from scoliosis radiographs. The findings suggest that the system is clinically applicable in terms of both accuracy and reliability.

RF305: Isolated atypical pedicle stress fractures in patients on prolonged bisphosphonate therapy: report of two cases and a literature-based proposal for diagnostic criteria

Maria Auron 1 , Tamar Fisher-Negev 2,3 , Josh Schroeder 1

1 Spine Surgery Unit, Department of Orthopedics, Hadassah Medical Center, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel, 2 Department of Clinical Pharmacy, Faculty of Medicine, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel, 3 Department of Orthopedics, Hadassah Medical Center, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel

Introduction: Bisphosphonates (BPs) reduce osteoporotic fracture risk, but long-term use has been associated with atypical femoral fractures (AFFs). Emerging reports suggest that atypical insufficiency fractures may also occur in other skeletal regions, including the lumbar pedicles. We present two cases of isolated bilateral lumbar pedicle stress fractures in patients on prolonged BP therapy and review the literature to assess whether AFF-based diagnostic criteria may apply to these rare spinal fractures. Material and Methods: Two female patients with osteoporosis (ages 81 and 75) who sustained bilateral lumbar pedicle stress fractures after > 5 years of BP therapy were evaluated. Clinical presentation, imaging findings, and management were documented. A structured literature review identified previously reported cases of bilateral pedicle insufficiency fractures potentially linked to long-term BP use. All cases were compared to the 2014 American Society for Bone and Mineral Research (ASBMR) AFF case definition criteria. Results: Case 1: An 81-year-old woman (5 years zoledronate) presented with severe back and left leg pain without trauma. CT showed a left L2 pedicle fracture and incomplete right L2 fracture without vertebral body collapse. She was treated conservatively; at 3 months, MRI showed a persistent fracture line with incomplete healing. Case 2: A 75-year-old woman (4 years alendronate + 1 year risedronate) developed acute back and leg pain after sneezing. CT revealed bilateral L4 pedicle fractures without vertebral body involvement. She underwent robotic-assisted percutaneous fixation with bilateral L4 pedicle screws. BP therapy was discontinued and replaced with teriparatide. At 6 months, CT showed fracture healing. Literature review identified 7 prior patients with isolated pedicle insufficiency fractures and long-term BP use (3-10 years). Most were women in their 60s-70s, presenting with back or radicular pain and minimal/no trauma, with no other evident etiology. Imaging demonstrated characteristic stress fracture features analogous to AFFs. Treatments ranged from conservative management to surgical fixation. Based on these similarities, we propose preliminary diagnostic criteria for “atypical pedicular insufficiency fractures,” modeled on the ASBMR AFF definition. Conclusion: Isolated bilateral pedicle stress fractures are rare. Our two cases and the reviewed literature suggest a potential link between prolonged BP use and these atypical pedicle fractures, indicating a possible spinal analogue of AFFs. While a causal relationship with long-term bisphosphonate therapy remains unproven, heightened clinical awareness and use of AFF-based diagnostic criteria may aid in early recognition and standardized reporting of these rare spinal fractures. Larger studies are needed to define prevalence, risk factors, and optimal management.

RF306: Intraoperative 3D navigation for transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy at L5-S1: a technical note and video demonstration

Phanurut kaewpornmongkol 1 , Siravich Suvithayasiri 2,3 , Somyot Wunnasinthop 1,3 , Monchai Ruangchainikom 1

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Faculty of Medicine Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand, 2 Department of Orthopedics, Chulabhorn Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand, 3 Bone and Joint Excellent Center, Thonburi Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand

Introduction: Endoscopic spine surgery has rapidly evolved as a minimally invasive solution for managing a wide spectrum of degenerative lumbar spine conditions. The transforaminal endoscopic approach provides direct access to most lumbar disc pathologies and has been increasingly adopted due to its ability to minimize soft tissue disruption, preserve spinal stability, and reduce recovery time. However, the L5-S1 level presents unique anatomical challenges. The high iliac crest, narrow intervertebral foramen, and variable facet orientation often obstruct the surgical corridor, making traditional transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy (TELD) at this level technically demanding. In particular, foraminal disc herniations at L5-S1 remain difficult to address with standard techniques, frequently requiring modifications that risk iatrogenic instability. To overcome these barriers, intraoperative three-dimensional (3D) navigation has been proposed to optimize trajectory planning and execution. In this report, we describe the application of intraoperative 3D navigation in guiding a Wiltse-like approach for L5-S1 foraminal disc herniation, supported by detailed step-by-step surgical video demonstration. Material and Methods: A 43-year-old male presented with severe radicular leg pain secondary to a foraminal disc herniation at L5-S1. Preoperative evaluation included MRI imaging, confirming significant foraminal disc herniation with compression of the exiting L5 nerve root. The patient underwent navigated TELD using intraoperative 3D imaging for precise localization and trajectory planning. Navigation facilitated modification of the surgical approach to avoid obstruction by the iliac crest while maintaining minimal bone resection. Foraminoplasty was performed in a controlled manner to enlarge the working corridor, with particular attention to preserving more than 50% of the facet joint to prevent postoperative instability. Intraoperative navigation further enabled real-time confirmation of discectomy. Surgical steps were systematically recorded and edited into an educational video illustrating key technical nuance. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) for functional recovery. Results: Navigated TELD at L5-S1 was performed successfully without intraoperative complications. The use of intraoperative 3D navigation allowed accurate definition of the working trajectory, effective foraminoplasty, and complete removal of the foraminal disc fragment. Postoperative CT confirmed adequate decompression with minimal resection of the facet joint (<50%), thereby preserving spinal stability. Clinically, the patient experienced immediate improvement in radicular pain, with VAS decreasing from 9 preoperatively to 3 on the first postoperative day. At final follow-up, ODI had improved to 20%, indicating substantial functional recovery. The surgical video provided clear visualization of each operative step, highlighting the practical benefits of navigation in overcoming the challenges of L5-S1 TELD. Conclusion: Intraoperative 3D navigation significantly enhances the safety, precision, and reproducibility of TELD at the challenging L5-S1 level. By facilitating optimized trajectory planning and controlled foraminoplasty, this technique achieves complete decompression while minimizing facet joint resection and preserving spinal stability. Our case demonstrates that navigated TELD, combined with detailed surgical video documentation, offers both clinical efficacy and valuable educational insight. As navigation technology becomes more accessible, this approach has the potential to expand the indications for endoscopic spine surgery worldwide, particularly in anatomically complex lumbar cases.

RF307: Medical comorbidities and operative complexity are predictive of intensive care unit admission after three column osteotomy for surgical correction of adult spinal deformity

Christopher Lai 1 , Bradley Hammoor 1 , Joshua Coan 1 , Benjamin Varieur 1 , Jordan Gasho 1 , Theresa Chua 1 , Marcos Gonzalez 1 , Stuart Hershman 1

1 Massachusetts General Hospital Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Boston, United States

Introduction: Three column osteotomies (3CO) can be useful for correction of stiff or rigid deformities in adult spinal deformity surgery (ASD). However, they increase surgical complexity and risk, and patients often undergo postoperative intensive care unit monitoring. The factors associated with ICU admission after 3CO remain unclear, and indications for ICU placement are not well-defined. The purpose of this study was to identify predictors of ICU admission after 3CO. Material and Methods: Patients undergoing 3CO for ASD from November 2016 to 2023 in a large academic hospital system were included. Patient demographic and clinical characteristics were compared and stratified by postoperative ICU vs floor admission. Intraoperative complications included neurologic, respiratory, hematologic, or cardiovascular events. A multivariable logistic regression was performed with age, sex, number of vertebral levels fused, estimated blood loss (EBL), intraoperative packed red blood cells (PRBC), vasopressor use, operative time, intraoperative complication, and Elixhauser Comorbidity Index (ECI) as independent variables and ICU admission as the outcome variable. Descriptive statistics were calculated with point estimates. Wilcoxon rank-sum and Chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests were used to compare between groups, as appropriate. Regression statistics are reported as odds ratio (OR) and 95% confidence interval (CI). Results: A total of 198 patients met inclusion criteria for analysis. Two patients died during hospitalization and were excluded from length of stay (LOS) and discharge disposition analysis. Comparisons showed no difference in age [63 (15) vs. 64 (12) years], sex (57.6% vs. 58.3% female), body mass index [28.7 (8.5) vs. 29.3 (6.8) kg/m2], or ECI [0 (8) vs. 0 (3)] between ICU and no ICU groups (all p > 0.05). Number of levels fused [11.5 (6) vs. 9 (7)], EBL [2700 (2062) vs. 2000 (1700) mL], operative time [548 (180) vs. 414 (109) minutes], intraoperative PRBC [1201 (1332) vs. 840 (1400)], unsuccessful extubation at end of case (45.5 vs. 99.2%), LOS [9 (6.3) vs. 6 (4) days], and discharge to a facility [73.4% vs. 56.8%] were significantly greater in ICU patients (all p < 0.05). Individual baseline comorbidities did not significantly differ between ICU and floor groups. On multivariable logistic regression for postoperative ICU stay as the outcome variable, operative time > 448 minutes [OR 6.07 (2.87-13.6), p < 0.001] and comorbidity as measured by ECI [OR 1.08 (1.02-1.15), p = 0.015] were significant independent predictors of ICU admission. Conclusion: ICU admission following 3CO is associated with greater operative complexity and failure to extubate at end of case. Longer operative times and greater baseline medical comorbidity is predictive of ICU admission after 3CO. These risk factors should be used to help guide surgical planning, ICU placement, and perioperative management of patients undergoing 3CO.

RF308: The role of the thoracolumbar junction in proximal junctional complications in adult spinal deformity surgery

Atahan Durbas 1 , Francis Lovecchio 1 , Andrea Pezzi 1 , Farah Musharbash 1 , Robert Uzzo 1 , Tejas Subramanian 1 , Gabrielle Dykhouse 1 , Luis Felipe Colon 1 , Stephane Owusu-Sarpong 1 , Jung Kee Mok 1 , Mihir Dekhne 1 , Sereen Halayqeh 1 , Kasra Araghi 1 , Quante Singleton 1 , Matthew Cunningham 1 , Han Jo Kim 1

1 Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, United States

Introduction: Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and failure (PJF) are common complications after long-segment fusion in adult spinal deformity (ASD) surgery. While global sagittal parameters such as pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis (PI-LL) and T4-L1 pelvic angle (T4-L1PA) mismatch are established predictors, they may not fully capture the biomechanical complexity of proximal junctional pathology, especially at the thoracolumbar junction (TLJ), which is a transitional zone particularly vulnerable to stress concentration, and perioperative changes in TLJ-specific alignment may influence complication risk. This study aimed to evaluate the relationship between perioperative changes in TLJ parameters and proximal junctional complications following lower thoracic (LT) to pelvis fusions. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included ASD patients with preoperative supine and standing X-rays who underwent fusion from the upper instrumented vertebra (UIV) of T9-T12 to S1 or pelvis, with at least five levels fused. Patients with prior spinal fusion were excluded. Standing full-spine radiographs were analyzed preoperatively and postoperatively. TLJ-specific parameters included T10-L2 Cobb angle (CA), thoracolumbar slope (TLS), UIV slope (UIVS), and UIV-pelvic angle (UIVPA). Changes (Δ) in these metrics, along with T4-L1PA mismatch, T4-UIVPA mismatch, and UIV-L1PA mismatch, were assessed. Outcomes were PJK (PJA ≥ 10° and ΔPJA ≥ 10°), PJF (PJA ≥ 28° with ΔPJA ≥ 22° or UIV/UIV+1 fracture, hardware failure, or revision), and abnormal PJA (aPJA; > 2 SD above normative values). Multivariate logistic regression used significant univariate factors and TLJ-specific factors. CART and CHAID identified thoracolumbar thresholds linked to PJF. Results: A total of 135 ASD patients were included (mean age 66.3 ± 8.4 years, 27% male, mean BMI 26.5 ± 5.6, mean fused levels 7.0 ± 1.5). 45 (33%) developed radiographic PJK, 31 (23%) PJF, and 32 (24%) aPJA. PJK patients were older (68.6 ± 6.2 vs 65.1 ± 9.2 years, p = 0.03), had higher preoperative T4-L1PA mismatch (10.4° vs 7.7°, p = 0.03) and greater pelvic tilt (29.1° vs 24.2°, p = 0.04) compared to those without PJK/PJF. PJF patients were also older than controls (69.6 ± 6.1 vs 65.1 ± 9.2 years, p = 0.01) and showed smaller postoperative UIVPA-L1PA mismatch (2.7° vs 4.4°, p = 0.03). aPJA patients only had a higher postoperative UIVPA (14.7° vs 10.6°, p = 0.01). Multiple logistic regression identified that PJK was predicted by T4-L1PA mismatch (p = 0.03) and PT change (p = 0.02); PJF risk factors included older age (p = 0.023), larger L1PA correction (p = 0.03), and lordotic thoracolumbar slope change (p = 0.02). Decision-tree analyses found postoperative UIVS > 16.5°, limited L1PA correction (> 4.25°), and greater T10-L2CA change (≤ -6.95°) and TLS change ( > 20.3°) as discriminators of PJF risk. Conclusion: Perioperative TLJ alignment changes are strongly associated with proximal junctional complications after LT to pelvis fusions in ASD. Junctional failure mightn't only be due to a global sagittal imbalance but also to the biomechanical sensitivity of the thoracolumbar junction to correction. Age-related fragility and even small shifts suggest over-correction may destabilize this zone. Decision-tree thresholds show junctional integrity depends on more than global targets, and it requires maintaining the TLJ's local adaptability.

RF309: The role of multimodal intraoperative neuromonitoring in pron-transpsoas lateral lumbar interbody fusion

Dean Biddau 1 , Gregory Malham 2

1 Queensland University of Technology, Spine Surgery Research Foundation, Brisbane, Australia, 2 Spine Surgery Research Foundation, Melbourne, Australia

Introduction: The role of multimodal intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) in detecting early neural compromise during prone-transpsoas lateral lumbar interbody fusion (PTP-LLIF) is not well established. RF310: Revision rates and radiographic sagittal alignment after posterior lumbar fusions with adjacent laminectomies

Janet Hsu 1 , Rami AbuQubo 1 , Ahsan Ahmed 1 , Mitchell Fourman 2

1 Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, United States, 2 Montefiore Medical Center, Bronx, NY, United States

Introduction: Lumbar fusions can be done to help correct sagittal alignment. Laminectomies may be done at the same or an adjacent level to decompress the spine. This study aims to analyze how adjacent laminectomies may influence outcomes after posterior lumbar fusions, including revision rates, complications, and radiographic sagittal alignment and spinopelvic parameters. Material and Methods: A retrospective case-control study was conducted for patients who received a 1-3 level posterior lumbar fusion from seven spine surgeons from 2021 to 2024. Patients in the adjacent laminectomy group were propensity-score matched by age, BMI, level of spinal surgery, and open vs. minimally invasive surgery. The final cohort included 23 patients in the adjacent laminectomy group and 51 patients in the non-adjacent laminectomy group. Complications and rates of revision surgery were analyzed. Lumbar lordosis and pelvic tilt were measured by two independent and blinded raters from sagittal radiographs for patients with imaging. Results: Demographics (sex, age at surgery, BMI, and race) between the two groups were not significantly different between the two groups. Two patients (8.7%) in the adjacent laminectomy group had numbness post-operatively compared to 5 patients (9.8%) in the non-adjacent laminectomy group. The non-adjacent laminectomy group also had 1 patient with both sensory and motor deficits post-operatively (p = 0.8). Non-adjacent laminectomy patients had an average lumbar lordosis of 48.0 ± 15.2 pre-operatively and 48.5 ± 14.2 one-year post-operatively (p = 0.8). Adjacent laminectomy patients had an average pelvic tilt of 20.0 ± 3.2 pre-operatively and 23.2 ± 9.1 one-year post-operatively (p = 0.4). Non-adjacent laminectomy patients had an average pelvic tilt of 23.1 ± 11.0 pre-operatively and 23.6 ± 10.1 one-year post-operatively (p = 0.8). Conclusion: Patients with adjacent laminectomies had comparable complication rates but a significantly increased rate of revision surgery compared to non-adjacent laminectomy patients. The adjacent laminectomy group had an increased change in average pelvic tilt and lumbar lordosis post-operatively. While these differences were not significantly different, it is possible that clinically, there is increased compensation of the spine due to changes in alignment, increasing the rates of revision surgeries.
