RF311: Return to sport after spinal arthrodesis in adults: a literature review of functional recovery, biomechanical effects, and rehabilitation strategies

Marcos Parreira 1,2 , Marcelo Wajchenberg 1,2 , Delio E. Martins 1,2 , Felipe Monteiro 1,2 , Nelson Astur 1,2

1 Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein, São Paulo, Brazil, 2 Instituto Cohen, São Paulo, Brazil

Introduction: Spinal arthrodesis is widely used in adults to treat degenerative disease, deformity, and trauma-related instability. With increasing participation in recreational and competitive sports, return to sport (RTS) has emerged as a key outcome reflecting not only pain relief but also restoration of functional capacity and sport-specific performance. Biomechanical studies show that spinal fusion alters load transfer, increasing shear forces and intradiscal pressure at adjacent levels, highlighting the need for progressive rehabilitation and careful load management. Although low-impact sports are often resumed within months, high-impact or contact sports require longer recovery, especially after long-segment fusions. This literature review synthesized clinical, biomechanical, and rehabilitation evidence on RTS after spinal fusion in adults. Material and Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, and Scopus for studies published from January 2015 to July 2025. Inclusion criteria were open-access clinical studies reporting RTS outcomes after adult spinal fusion, biomechanical analyses of post-fusion mechanics, and rehabilitation studies addressing postoperative functional recovery. Reviews, abstracts, pediatric cohorts, and studies without relevant RTS outcomes were excluded. From 1,146 records, 20 studies met eligibility criteria. Data were extracted on study design, type and levels of fusion, RTS definitions and timing, functional and biomechanical outcomes, complications, and rehabilitation protocols. Results: Across studies, RTS after spinal fusion was common and achievable, though strongly dependent on sport type and surgical complexity. Recreational activities such as golf were typically resumed at 4.3 months in degenerative cases and 9.7 months in deformity fusions, with most patients maintaining or increasing participation postoperatively. Elective cervical procedures allowed return to golf, tennis, and swimming with stable or improved performance, while complex deformity fusions required 6-12 months before clearance, particularly for contact sports. Data from elite athletes indicated 74-80% successfully returned to competition after anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, with timelines of 9 weeks to 9 months. Clearance criteria consistently included pain-free status, preserved neurological function, range of motion, and strength symmetry. Case-specific evidence confirmed RTS feasibility in high-demand sports such as martial arts, usually within one year. Overall, low-impact sports were resumed within 3-6 months, and high-impact or contact sports within 6-12 months. Biomechanical studies consistently showed increased adjacent-segment loading after fusion, with longer constructs producing greater stress and mobility. Musculoskeletal models and finite-element analyses confirmed elevated shear and intradiscal pressures, influenced by cage height, bone density, and degeneration. Cadaveric studies supported these findings, while sacroiliac joint fusion showed minimal lumbar effects. These results justify cautious reintroduction of torque-intensive and multiplanar activities. Rehabilitation studies emphasized supervised, criterion-based protocols over time-based strategies. Interventions targeting trunk stability, hip endurance, balance, and sport-specific progression reduced pain and disability and facilitated safer RTS. Conclusion: This literature review demonstrates that RTS after spinal fusion in adults is feasible within predictable timelines when guided by functional recovery, biomechanical safety, and structured rehabilitation. Most patients resume low-impact sports within 3-6 months and high-impact sports within 6-12 months, depending on fusion complexity. Increased adjacent-segment loading underscores the need for progressive rehabilitation and individualized protocols. Although current evidence is limited by observational designs and heterogeneous definitions of RTS, the convergence of clinical, biomechanical, and rehabilitation data provides practical guidance for optimizing postoperative return to sport. Future multicenter trials with standardized RTS definitions are warranted.

RF312: Postoperative dexamethasone administration following posterior spinal fusion for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis a systematic review of worldwide data

Fahad Abduljabbar 1 , Raed Mohammedamin Sharaf 2 , Abdulrheem Almokhtar 3 , Rakan Farouk Y Bokhari 4

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, 2 Faculty of Medicine, King Abdulaziz University,, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, 3 Orthopaedic Surgery, King Abdullah Medical City, Makkah, Saudi Arabia, 4 Department of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, King Abdulaziz university, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia

Introduction: Posterior spinal fusion is the standard surgical treatment for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS), but it is associated with significant postoperative pain and opioid requirements. Dexamethasone, a synthetic glucocorticoid, has analgesic and antiemetic properties that may improve postoperative recovery, but its efficacy and safety in AIS fusion remain unclear. Material and Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for studies published between 2015 and 2024 evaluating postoperative dexamethasone in AIS posterior spinal fusion. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, prospective, and retrospective studies. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane ROB2 tool, Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and Joanna Briggs Institute tool for case series. Results: Out of 150 identified articles, 9 studies met inclusion criteria, including 866 patients. Most were retrospective (n = 4), with 2 prospective studies, 1 RCT, 1 prospective randomized study, and 1 case series. Dosing regimens varied (0.1-4 mg/kg IV, 0.15 mg/kg single IV, 0.66 mg/kg sub-myofascial, or up to 8 g per dose). Postoperative dexamethasone administration was associated with reduced opioid consumption, shorter length of stay, lower pain scores, and decreased postoperative nausea and vomiting. Infection rates did not significantly differ between dexamethasone and control groups across studies, though isolated cases were reported. Conclusion: Postoperative dexamethasone following AIS posterior spinal fusion improves pain control, reduces opioid requirements, and decreases postoperative nausea and vomiting without a consistent increase in infection risk. However, heterogeneity in dosing and limited high-quality evidence highlight the need for standardized dosing protocols and larger randomized trials.

RF313: Minimizing post-operative opioid use in common spine surgeries: a non-inferiority quality improvement study

Arianna Dalamaggas 1 , Catherine Olinger 1

1 University of Iowa, North Liberty, United States

Introduction: The goal of this study is to minimize opioid-related adverse effects in post-operative patients by reducing quantity and duration of opioid analgesia following surgery. The opioid epidemic continues necessitating thoughtful prescribing patterns following posterior thoracolumbar spinal fusions (PSF) and anterior cervical discectomies and fusions (ACDF). Material and Methods: This is a prospective quality improvement study with inclusion of patients > 18 years of age, who underwent primary PSF or ACDF, of any number of levels. Patients with a pre-operative diagnosis of infection, malignancy, trauma were excluded. Those with primary diagnoses of cervical or thoracolumbar spinal stenosis, myelopathy, radiculopathy, or degenerative spondylolisthesis were included. Pre intervention data showed an average of 60 pills prescribed for both procedures post-operatively. Post-operative narcotic prescriptions were adjusted to #40 for PSF and #30 for ACDF patients, with each refill doubling the dosing interval or halving the quantity. Patients are surveyed at 1-week and 1-month post operatively for their quantity and duration of opioid pills consumed, adverse opioid-related effects, and method of pill disposal using a validated questionnaire. Patient-reported outcomes including mJOA, ODI, and PROMIS Global Health and Pain Interference are also utilized pre- and post-operatively, as well as pre- and post-intervention to assess clinical function. Results: In our preliminary results from post-intervention data collection, we have surveyed 30 patients (PSF = 14, ACDF = 16). The primary adverse effect from narcotic medication was constipation, most severe at 1 week post operatively, reported by 30.8% of patients. The combined (PSF and ACDF) mean total patient-reported pill consumption at 1-month was 32 pills (range: 0-100). Average refill request was 1. All patients reported being provided education on taking non-narcotic analgesics and many report also being prescribed other medications including acetaminophen, gabapentin, or a muscle relaxer. Patients also reported high use of non-pharmacologic modalities including distraction/television, aromatherapy, ice/heat, stretching, prayer/meditation, and topicals. Patients were overall satisfied with their care on a scale of 1-10, mean 8.73 at 1 month post op (SD ± 1.68). A majority of patients reported finishing their prescription, but 18.2% report using a disposal bag, 9.1% report flushing down the toilet, 9.1% report keeping for later use. Following this intervention, ODI scores improved by an average 17.1 (pre-post: 47.8-30.7). PROMIS Global Health scores changed an average of 3.1 points (pre-post 38.6-41.7), and PROMIS pain interference scores changed an average of -7.1 points (pre-post: 65.6-58.5). Compared to our pre-intervention data, post-intervention data shows a trend towards increased improvement in ODI scores and similar change in mJOA. Conclusion: Limiting opioid utilization in the post-operative period shows non-inferior outcomes with respect to pain control, patient-reported, and functional outcome scores in our early survey results. We hypothesized from our pre-intervention analysis that smaller total dose of narcotic medication would lead to unchanged patient-reported outcomes and will result in similar scores for mJOA, ODI, and PROMIS data, with fewer adverse medication effects. While this study is ongoing to increase post-intervention survey responses, these early data show a positive direction of support for the noninferiority of smaller opioid prescription sizes.

RF314: Revision surgery for recurrence of cranio cervical junction chordoma: analysis of patient-specific surgical treatment strategies and outcomes

Chiara Cini 1 , Stefano Boriani 2 , riccardo ghermandi 1 , Stefano Bandiera 1 , Giuseppe Tedesco 1 , Valerio Pipola 1 , Marco Girolami 1 , Alessandro Gasbarrini 1,2

1 Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy, 2 Alma Mater Studiorum, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: The cranio-cervical junction (CCJ) is a preferred site of occurrence for chordoma. Surgical approach is technically demanding and tumor-free margin enbloc resection is not always feasible and associated with unacceptable loss of function and high rate of morbidity. Most previous studies focused more on the outcome after primary surgery for CCJ chordoma and limited data analyze the outcomes after revision surgery for CCJ chordoma local recurrences (LR). The aim of our study is to compare different surgical approaches to CCJ in relation to LR and extension of intralesional excision. Results: All primary surgeries were without exception intralesional excision. 2 patients were treated with endoscopical trans-sfenoidal approaches at the onset. In 7 patients anterior submandibular approach was performed with anterior strut graft reconstruction and CF/PEEK plate fixation while in 6 patients posterior decompression and fixation was performed. 15 LR were located at the CCJ and 5 at the subaxial cervical spine. C2 involvement was the most common, observed in 10 (55.5%) patients, followed by C3 involvement in 5 (27.7%) patients and Clivus-C1 involvement in 3 (16.6%) cases. In all cases 4 (22.2%) patients developed additional LRs after LR-post primary treatment, of these only 1 treated with Carbon Ion Radiotherapy (CIRT). All the other additional LRs were surgically treated. All chordomas were classified as conventional subtype at final histology, 1 of this showed progression to dedifferentiated at the third LR after our primary treatment. In 3 (16.6%) patients a lung metastatic wedge resection was performed. 2 (11.1%) patients were considered eligible for Imatinib therapy. The 5-year progression-free survival (PFS) rate is 89.8% while the 5-year recurrence rate was 45.3%. Conclusion: The approach with the widest operative field and the lowest rate of morbidity should be chosen. With profound preoperative planning and adjuvant post-operative radiotherapy, outcomes similar to those in primary surgery can be achieved.

RF315: Perception and clinical use of the NOMS framework in the management of spinal metastases: first national survey in Chile

Álvaro Silva 1,2 , Andrés Lisoni 1,2 , Joaquin Zuniga Soria 1,3 , Andrea Marre 3 , Vicente Jimenez 1

1 Clínica Alemana de Santiago, Santiago, Chile, 2 Hospital Clínico de la Fuerza Aérea de Chile, Santiago, Chile, 3 Facultad de Medicina Universidad del Desarrollo-Clínica Alemana, Santiago, Chile

Introduction: The Neurologic, Oncologic, Mechanical, and Systemic (NOMS) framework, formally introduced in 2013 at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, provides a structured multidisciplinary approach to the management of spinal metastases. Although it has gained recognition internationally, its real-world adoption outside of high-volume centers remains unclear. To date, no studies have evaluated its penetration in Latin America. This study aimed to assess knowledge, clinical use, and perceived barriers to NOMS implementation among specialists in Chile. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was distributed in September 2025 to spine surgeons, orthopedic traumatologists, neurosurgeons, medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, and residents. The questionnaire included demographics, awareness, familiarity, frequency of use, perceived utility, barriers to implementation, and opinions regarding official adoption in institutional protocols. Results: Forty-eight responses were collected. Awareness of NOMS was high (90%), yet only 23% reported high familiarity and regular use. Clinical application was heterogeneous: 31% never used it, 23% rarely, 25% sometimes, and 21% frequently. Among users, 70% rated NOMS as useful or very useful, with frequent users consistently reporting greater confidence in decision-making. In contrast, non-users primarily cited lack of dissemination among specialists (42%) and insufficient multidisciplinary collaboration (27%) as barriers. Despite these challenges, 54% supported official implementation of NOMS in Chilean institutions, while 35% remained undecided. Conclusion: This is the first national, multidisciplinary survey assessing NOMS adoption in Latin America. Although awareness is widespread, routine use remains limited. Importantly, those who apply NOMS report consistently positive experiences, reinforcing its clinical value. Barriers are driven by systemic factors-knowledge dissemination and multidisciplinary integration-rather than skepticism about the framework itself. These findings underscore the need for targeted educational initiatives and collaborative networks, paving the way for future research and the development of standardized protocols for the management of spinal metastases in the region.

RF316: Indication criteria for separation surgery and radiotherapy in thoracic spinal metastases (C41.2): radiological predictors of neurological deterioration

Artem Ilgeldiev 1 , Victoria Yushenko 1

1 Neurosurgery, Germany

Introduction: Thoracic spinal metastases frequently lead to canal narrowing and spinal cord compression. The aim of this study was to define evidence-based indication criteria for separation surgery followed by radiotherapy, based on clinical and radiological parameters-particularly ESCC grade, Tomita score, and residual canal diameter measured on MRI. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed data from 51 patients with thoracic spinal metastases (C41.2). Radiological evaluation included ESCC grade, Tomita score, and axial MRI measurements of residual spinal canal diameter. Clinical parameters such as ASIA grade, spinal ataxia, and CRP progression were assessed. The objective was to identify predictive thresholds to support decision-making for surgical decompression and subsequent radiotherapy. Results:

- ESCC grade 3 was found in 64.7% of cases and showed a significant correlation with neurological deficits (ρ = 0.79, p < 0.05). - The median residual canal diameter was 31% (mean 44%, p = 0.000397). A threshold of < 40% strongly correlated with symptomatic myelopathy.

- Neurological deficits (ASIA C, spinal ataxia) were present in 35% of cases (p = 0.0258), justifying surgical decompression prior to radiotherapy.

- The Tomita score (median 4-5) was relevant for oncological treatment planning but did not correlate with neurological decline. Conclusion: An ESCC grade of 3, an MRI-based residual canal diameter <40%, and the presence of neurological deficits are strong indicators for separation surgery. Surgical decompression should precede high-dose radiotherapy to reduce the risk of neurological deterioration and optimize functional outcomes.

Stefano Colonna 1 , Carla Paracampo 1 , Filippo Lacatena 1 , Luca Ceroni 2 , Stefano Marone 3 , Giuseppe Di Perna 4 , Salvatore Petrone 1 , Alessandro Fiumefreddo 1 , Nicola Marengo 1 , Marco Ajello 1 , Diego Garbossa 1 , fabio cofano 1

2 Department of Psychology, University of Turin, Turin, Italy,

4 Division of Neurosurgery, Policlinico “Riuniti”, University of Foggia, Foggia, Italy

Introduction: Carbon fiber (CF) implants are increasingly used in spinal oncology due to their significant radiological advantages compared to traditional titanium implants. RF322: Impact of tumor location on postoperative neurological function in spinal metastases surgery

Majdouline Barkache 1 , Affes Ameur 1 , Mahmoud Ben Messaoud 1 , Iadh Ksira 1

1 Neurosurgery Departement Sahloul Tunisia, Sousse, Tunisia

RF323: Socioeconomic status correlates with epidural spinal cord compression severity in patients treated for spine metastases

Leilani White 1 , Andrew Quinn 1 , Sabrina Crooks 1 , Haley Pang 1 , Keanu Chee 1 , Anand Hemmady 1 , Mahesh Karandikar 1 , Christoph Hofstetter 1 , Andrew Ko 1 , Fangyi Zhang 1 , Simon Lo 1 , Benjamin Grannan 1 , Anubhav Amin 1

1 University of Washington, Seattle, United States

Introduction: Spine metastases can cause severe neurologic deficits and functional decline, making them a major source of morbidity. Neurosurgical decompression plays a critical role in stabilizing the spine and alleviating neurological compromise. However, not all patients experience the same course of disease or outcomes. Prior studies suggest that socioeconomic status (SES) influences when and how patients present for care, but its relationship with postoperative outcomes remains unclear. This study investigates the association between SES and postoperative outcomes in patients undergoing surgery for metastatic spine disease. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of 114 patients who underwent surgery for spinal metastases at two institutions between 2018 and 2023. This may be attributable to separation surgery facilitating a reduction in ESCC score, thereby enabling safe stereotactic ablative spinal radiation. This suggests that neurosurgical intervention in metastatic spine disease is equitable without introducing disparities, underscoring the importance of equal access to surgical care.

Gabrielle Santangelo 1 , Thomas Pieters 2 , Zachary Pennington 3 , Aladine Elsamadicy 1 , Daniel Sciubba 1 , Larry Lo 1

1 Northwell Health, Manhasset, United States, 2 University of Massachusetts, Worcester, United States, 3 Mayo Clinic, Rochester, United States

RF325: Lactate: an epigenetic modulator in osteosarcoma

Shambhavi Bhagwat 1 , Matthew Goodwin 1

1 Washington University - School of Medicine, St. Louis, United States

Introduction: Osteosarcoma (OS) is a primary malignant tumor most found in long bones such as the femur, tibia or humerus. OS progression, like other cancers, can be influenced by metabolites present in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Clinically, OS is 18FDG-PET positive (based on glucose-uptake). However, recent in silico studies have shown that glucose has a very limited influence on growth of OS cells, while lactate can be utilized as a fuel source. In addition, OS tumors induce higher rates of glycolysis in the surrounding stromal cells, resulting in an excess in production and export of lactate via monocarboxylate transporters (MCTs). MCTs are responsible for shuttling lactate between producing and consuming cells throughout the body. Targeting this lactate shuttling in tumors has recently become a promising focus for anti-cancer therapy. However, the importance of lactate in OS is yet to be determined. Here, we show that extracellular lactate may promote OS progression via epigenetic regulation of histone as well as non-histone proteins. Material and Methods: Cell viability and proliferation was analyzed using the Incucyte live cell imaging system (Sartorius). Genes were knocked down by siRNA transfections, using RNAiMAX (Invitrogen) and gene expression was determined via qPCR analysis. Conditions included combinations of low (1mM) and high (10mM) [lactate] with normal (5.5mM) glucose. Immunoprecipitation/blotting technique was used to determine lactylation-deposits and protein expression. Lactate tracing was carried out by culturing cells in 13C-labelled lactate. Metabolites were extracted at various time points up to 30mins and analyzed via LC/MS. In addition, proteins with lactylation deposits were identified by immunoprecipitating whole cell protein lysates with anti-Lys Lactyl antibody (PTM Bio) and LC/MS. All data are presented as ​the means ± SD where appropriate. We performed statistical analysis using Student’s t-test or three-way ANOVA with post hoc analysis as appropriate; p value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: To confirm whether lactate is taken up by OS cells, we cultured cells in 13C-labeled lactate and extracted the metabolites in under 30 minutes. Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that lactate was not only taken up but also utilized via the TCA cycle. Further, we noted that not all of the lactate taken up was shunted to the TCA cycle, leading us to hypothesize that lactate may play another intracellular role. ‘Lactylation’ has been recently discovered to be a highly ubiquitous epigenetic phenomenon, observed in various physiologically and pathologically relevant pathways. We cultured cells in low vs high lactate conditions and observed that cells cultured in high lactate showed higher lactylation pattern in whole cell lysates, indicating that lactate taken up by these cells contributes to epigenetic regulation of not only histone proteins, but also non-histone cytosolic proteins. We then immunoprecipitated lactylated proteins from whole cell OS protein lysates and performed MS to determine which proteins are lactylated in OS pathology. Gene ontology analysis revealed that 937 proteins were enriched. Protein important in pathways such as nucleotide biosynthesis, ribosome biogenesis, mitochondrial translation and One-Carbon metabolism showed higher lactylation deposits. Importantly, Phosphoglycerate Dehydrogenase (PHGDH), a rate-limiting enzyme in serine-biosynthesis, was lactylated in OS cells. PHGDH expression has previously been correlated with worse prognosis of OS patients. Conclusion: In conclusion, our data suggests that lactate aids osteosarcoma progression by epigenetic regulation of important metabolic pathways, especially one-carbon metabolism. Therefore, targeting lactate transport along with lactylation writers may be a potential therapeutic strategy for OS. This study determines how lactate from the TME directly affects OS cell proliferation. The data acquired by the end of the study will be beneficial in developing novel therapies. Success in this study could lead to a clinical trial.

RF326: Planned versus emergent surgery for spinal metastases: short-term outcomes and implications

Sertac Kirnaz 1 , Ali Haider Bangash 1 , Rose Fluss 1 , Yaroslav Gelfand 1 , Saikiran Murthy 1 , Reza Yassari 1 , Rafael De La Garza Ramos 1

1 Montefiore Medical Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, United States

Introduction: Metastatic spine disease is a frequent complication of advanced malignancy, producing severe pain, neurological deficits, and pathologic fractures that substantially impair function and increase health-care utilization. Surgical management is selected based on prognosis, neurologic status, spinal stability, and tumor histology. Although many procedures are elective following multidisciplinary evaluation and preoperative optimization, a considerable subset are performed urgently for acute deterioration. Urgent interventions typically preclude correction of malnutrition, anemia, and cardiopulmonary derangements and limit coordinated perioperative planning, which may increase postoperative morbidity and mortality. The specific impact of surgical planning status on outcomes after metastatic spine surgery remains inadequately defined and merits further investigation. The purpose of this study was to compare short-term outcomes between patients undergoing planned versus emergent surgery for metastatic spinal lesions. Material and Methods: We performed a retrospective review of all patients who underwent surgery for spinal metastases at our institution from 2012 through 2025. Patients were allocated to two groups based on the timing of the surgery: emergency (< 24 hours) and planned (> 24 hours). Collected patient data included age at surgery, sex, preoperative functional status, body mass index (BMI), baseline albumin levels, as well as other comorbidities. The primary outcome was failure to rescue (FTR), defined as the occurrence of at least one major complication (Clavien-Dindo grade 3 or 4) in addition to death within 30 days of the index operation. Secondary outcomes were 30-day major complications, 30-day mortality, and hospital length of stay. Both univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to evaluate associations. Results: A total of 234 patients were identified and included in this study. 186 patients underwent planned surgery and 48 underwent emergent surgery. Overall, there were 17 deaths and 14 FTR events. In the emergency surgery group, both the FTR and 30-day mortality rates were 14.6% (7/48). In the planned surgery group, the FTR and 30-day mortality rates were 3.7% (7/186) and 5.4% (10/186), respectively. In multivariable analysis, emergent surgery was significantly associated with increased risk of FTR (OR 4.3 [95% CI 1.7 to 11.1]; p = 0.002). For our secondary endpoint, a crude analysis also showed a significant association between emergent surgery and 30-day mortality (OR 2.8 [95% CI 1.2 to 6.7]; p = 0.017). Conclusion: Patients undergoing emergent surgery for spinal metastases experienced significantly worse 30-day outcomes than those having planned procedures. This disparity is likely multifactorial, reflecting the acute and often more severe clinical status of patients requiring urgent intervention, more advanced disease or physiological compromise at presentation, and reduced opportunity for preoperative assessment and optimization. These findings highlight the need for early identification and expedited management pathways to reduce the necessity for emergency operations and to improve patient outcomes.

RF327: Neurological complication of stereotactic ablative radiotherapy for spinal metastases

Jinho Kim 1 , Soon Woo Hong 1

1 Seoul National University Hospital, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Neurological toxicity of stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) for the spine has been focused on radiation myelitis (RM). We investigated radiation-induced radiculo-plexopathy (RIRP) in patients who underwent SABR for spinal metastases. Material and Methods: Patients were included for the analysis who received SABR for metastatic spine tumors arising in C3 to T1 and T12 to S2 vertebrae from 2013 to 2023. Medical records and images were retrospectively reviewed. RIRP was defined as a motor power decrease by MRC grade 2 or greater in the myotome of the spinal level treated by SABR without evidence of local progression, RM or radiation-induced cauda equina syndrome. Each neural foramen that is covered by or adjacent to the treatment area was defined as an organ at risk for dosimetric analysis. While 407 neural foramina were contoured, only structures with a maximum EQD22 dose over 45Gy were included in the analysis. The Cox proportional hazard model was used to identify risk factors for RIRP. Results: From 2013 to 2023, 168 metastatic C1-T1 and T12 to S3 spine segments in 132 patients were treated with SABR. The median follow-up was 9.5 months. Twenty-four (14.3%) local recurrences occurred. No cases of radiation myelitis were observed, and a single case of radiation-induced cauda equina syndrome was identified (0.9%). Twelve cases of RIRP (9.1%) were observed. The planning target volume (PTV) of the treatment area and maximum dose for each neural foramen at risk were significantly associated with the occurrence of RIRP (p < 0.001). Conclusion: While RM or radiation-induced cauda equina syndrome rarely occurs, RIRP occurs more frequently after spinal SABR. Further studies are necessary to accurately characterize RIRP and sophisticatedly define more suitable organs at risk. Meanwhile, neural foramina may serve as surrogate organs at risk that are relevant to RIRP after spinal SABR.

RF328: Role of sodium fluorescein-guided resection in intradural spinal cord tumors: prospective observational study

Deepak Kumar 1 , Mayank Garg 1

1 ALL India Institution of Medical Sciences, Jodhpur, India

Introduction: Intradural spinal cord tumors present significant surgical challenges due to the limited intrathecal space, often with no distinct margin between normal and tumoral tissue in cases of intramedullary tumors. Sodium fluorescein has emerged as a valuable intraoperative tool for tumor visualization through its ability to accumulate in areas of blood-brain barrier disruption, guiding in maximal safe resection. Materials and Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted at AIIMS Jodhpur from July 2023 to June 2025. Thirty patients with intradural spinal cord tumors underwent surgery using sodium fluorescein (5 mg/kg) under yellow filter (560 nm) microscopy. Fluorescence patterns, surgical outcomes, and extent of resection were analyzed. Results: The cohort included 17 males and 13 females with a mean age of 37.27 ± 17.31 years. Intradural extramedullary tumors comprised 70% (21/30) and intramedullary tumors 30% (9/30). Gross total resection was achieved in 80% (24/30) of patients. Fluorescence was positive in 90% (27/30) of cases and deemed helpful by surgeons in 80% (24/30) of procedures. No fluorescein-related complications were observed. Conclusions: Sodium fluorescein-guided surgery is a safe and effective technique for intradural spinal tumor resection, particularly beneficial for extramedullary tumors. The technique enhances tumor visualization and contributes to higher rates of gross total resection while maintaining excellent safety profiles.

RF329: Surgical treatment of arachnoid cysts in the spinal canal - A systematic literature review and case series

Bojan Jelaca 1 , Milica Gledja 1 , Sara Azaric 1

1 University Clinical center of Vojvodina, Faculty of Medicine, Novi Sad, Serbia

Introduction: Arachnoid cysts are benign, intradural lesions continuous with the arachnoid membrane and filled with cerebrospinal fluid-like content. They are most often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally in adulthood, with symptoms arising due to compression of the spinal cord or nerve roots. Aim of this study Is to determine the effectiveness of surgical treatment of spinal canal arachnoid cysts in terms of symptom relief, functional recovery and morphological restoration. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis of our five clinical cases included demographic data, clinical presentation, cyst characteristics, complications, reoperations and functional and radiological outcomes. A systematic literature review was also conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and a pre-defined protocol. Inclusion criteria were defined based on the PICO model. Results: A total of 253 patients were identified across 13 retrospective studies (male to female ratio 1.19:1; mean age 50.56 years). The most common cyst locations were thoracic (73.5%), lumbar (9.9%), cervicothoracic (6.7%), cervical (5.1%), thoracolumbar (3.9%), and sacral (1 case). The most frequent symptoms included pain (72.3%), sensory disturbances (64.8%), motor weakness (62.2%), gait impairment (62.2%), and sphincter dysfunction (27.7%). Surgical treatments included microsurgical excision (49%), cyst fenestration (33%), marsupialization (16%), and cystoperitoneal shunting (4 cases). Postoperative improvement was observed in 50-70% of patients, with cyst reduction or resolution on follow-up MRI in 86-100% of cases. Conclusion: Surgical treatment is an effective method for managing symptomatic arachnoid cysts, resulting in symptom improvement and restoration of normal spinal canal anatomy, confirmed by MRI.

RF330: Impact of patient age on surgical decision-making and outcomes in spinal metastases

Meltem Ivren 1 , Dilber Yalman 1 , Basem Ishak 1,2 , Sebastian Ille 1 , Sandro Krieg 1 , Lenga Pavlina 1

1 Department of Neurosurgery, Heidelberg University, Im Neuenheimer Feld 400, 69120, Heidelberg, Germany, Heidelberg, Germany, 2 Department of Neurosurgery, ATOS Klinik Wiesbaden, Wiesbaden, Germany, Wiesbaden, Germany

Introduction: With rising survival in oncology, spinal metastases are increasingly common. The best surgical approach in elderly patients remains uncertain given higher risk profiles. We analyzed clinical profiles and outcomes, focusing on age-related differences and SINS 7-12 cases. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed all patients with spinal metastases undergoing surgery in our department between 2015 and 2024. Collected data included demographics, neurological status, surgical technique, complications, and 90-day mortality. Outcomes were compared between older (≥ 65 years) and younger (< 65 years) patients. Results: Data of 217 patients (median age 60 years, range 5-88) were analyzed. Primary malignancies were mostly lung (17.5%), breast (17.1%), and prostate (12.9%) cancer. Older patients presented with higher rates of severe neurological deficits (Frankel A/B: 35.8% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.01), although short-term mortality did not differ significantly between age groups (≥ 65 years: 14.5% vs. < 65 years: 13.4%, p = 0.837). Intraoperative blood loss was substantially lower in the older cohort (260 ± 373 mL vs. 758 ± 860 mL, p < 0.001). Surgical strategies were comparable across groups, with instrumentation performed in 32.3% and minimally invasive percutaneous methods in 18.6%. SINS-based evaluation revealed distinct trends: older patients were more frequently categorized as potentially unstable (65.2% vs. 26.7%, p < 0.001) but underwent decompression alone more often, despite similar SINS scores between laminectomy-only and fixation cases. By contrast, younger patients who received instrumentation typically had SINS scores ranging from 7 to 18. Conclusion: Age alone does not predict surgical success or survival in metastatic spine disease. Older patients achieved outcomes similar to younger ones. However, SINS 7-12 cases were managed differently, with less instrumentation in older patients, suggesting possible underuse. These findings underscore the need for guidelines that combine SINS, tumor biology, function and prognosis, ensuring age-inclusive, individualized surgical care.

RF331: Evaluation of separation surgery success rate and its impact on clinical and radiological outcomes in metastatic spinal cord compression: a postoperative MRI-based analysis

Seung Hyun Baek 1 , Sung Tan Cho 1 , Jae Hwan Cho 1 , Sehan Park 1 , Chang Ju Hwang 1 , Dong-Ho Lee 1

1 Asan Medical Center, University of Ulsan College of Medicine, Seoul, South Korea

Introduction: Separation surgery has become a pivotal intervention in the recent management of metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC). Despite its importance, data on the success rate of separation surgery and its impact on clinical and radiological outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the success rate of separation surgery confirmed by postoperative Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and investigate its association with clinical and radiological outcomes, including the role of radiotherapy (RTx) in improving outcomes. Material and Methods: Fifty-nine patients who underwent separation surgery for MSCC between 2020 and 2023 were included. All patients were evaluated 2-3 weeks after surgery using postoperative MRI with a metal artifact reduction protocol prior to radiotherapy initiation. According to MRI evaluation, patients were divided into separation (group S, n=26) and non-separation (group NS, n=33) groups. Demographic and radiological data were collected and compared. Clinical outcomes, including motor grade, ambulation status, hospital stay, duration of follow-up, and final status were assessed. A subgroup analysis of the NS group based on postoperative RTx was conducted. Results: More severe Bilsky grade was found in group NS (28/33) compared to group S (16/26, p = 0.041). Postoperative motor grade (4.54 ± 0.91 vs 3.67 ± 1.71, p = 0.015) and ambulation status (92.3% vs 69.7%, p = 0.032) were significantly better in group S. Group S also had a higher rate of postoperative RTx (76.9% vs 48.5%, p = 0.026) and shorter hospital stay (15.81 ± 9.46 vs 23.94 ± 19.65 days, p = 0.042). Follow-up duration was longer in group S (13.31 ± 9.55 vs. 6.02 ± 4.81 months, p = 0.001). In subgroup analysis of NS group, older patients did not receive RTx significantly (60.81 ± 9.50 vs 67.88 ± 8.60 yrs, p = 0.032). Regression of cord compression was observed in MRI during follow-up more frequently in RTx (+) patients within the NS group (43.8% vs 5.9%, p = 0.017), although clinical outcomes showed similar results between the two subgroups. The success of separation and the administration of RTx were both significantly associated with differences in survival rates (22.33 ± 2.94 vs 9.03 ± 1.37 months, p = 0.004 & 18.70 ± 2.37 vs 9.88 ± 2.38 months, p = 0.031). Conclusion: Successful separation surgery is strongly associated with immediate clinical improvements, particularly in motor recovery and ambulation. Our study demonstrates that separation success is linked to better survival outcomes, suggesting that rapid tumor progression within the early postoperative period is likely related to separation failure. Furthermore, MRI evaluations conducted 2-3 weeks postoperatively can serve as a predictive factor for survival, enhancing our understanding of the clinical significance of timely and accurate postoperative assessments. In patients with unsuccessful separation, radiotherapy may provide radiological improvement in cord compression despite limited clinical benefit.

RF332: Which patients have the best chances of improving their neurological status after pathological spine fractures presenting with neurological compromise?

Maroun Rizkallah 1 , Jesse Shen 2 , Ghassan Boubez 2 , Fidaa Al-Shakfa 2 , Daniel Shedid 2 , Sung-Joo Yuh 2 , Zhi Wang 2

1 Centre de formation medicale du nouveau Brunswick, Dr Georges L dumont university Hospital, Sherbrooke University, Moncton, Canada, 2 Centre Hospitalier de l'universite de Montreal, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: There is a lack of clear evidence regarding neurological outcomes in cancer patients presenting with pathological vertebral fracture and neurological compromise. This widens the gray zone in surgical indications in these patients and increases the room for surgeon’s subjective input. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included consecutive patients with pathological spine fractures and neurological compromise (ASIA scores D/C/B/A) who underwent posterior spinal decompression and fusion with transpedicular corpectomy and cement-based reconstruction. Patients’ charts were reviewed for demographic, medical, and surgical-related data as well as post-operative outcomes at 6 weeks of follow-up. The main outcome of this study is improvement in at least one grade on ASIA scale. A multivariate analysis was performed to look for predictive factors for this neurological improvement. Results: A total of 247 patients (43.7% females) were included with a mean age of 63.7 years. In this cohort, 195 patients had ASIA score D, 37 had ASIA score C, 10 had ASIA score B and 4 had ASIA score A. Neurological improvement occurred in 77 patients (31.2%). Of these patients, there were 45 ASIA D (23.1%); 25 ASIA C (67.6%), 6 ASIA B (60%) and 1 ASIA A (25%). Mean age in patients who improved postoperatively was 60.1 years compared to 65.5 in those who did not improve (p = 0.03). In patients with thoracic compression, 36.3% of patients improved compared to 24% of patients with lumbar compression (p = 0.02). Mean surgical time averaged 165 minutes in patients who improved post-operatively whereas it reached 189.4 minutes in patients who did not (p = 0.04). Multivariate analysis showed that healthier patients with lower ASA grade pre-operatively (p < 0.01); younger patients (p = 0.02), those with thoracic spine compression (p = 0.04) and those with lower initial ASIA score had significantly higher chances of post-operative neurological improvement. Time to surgery, patient’s sex, pre-operative sphincter function and duration of surgery did not affect the post-operative neurological outcome. Conclusion: Adding to already known favorable outcomes in patient with ASIA score D, post-operative neurological improvement could be expected in patients with vertebral pathological fractures and ASIA scale C/B scores, particularly if these patients were younger, healthy (ASA<3), and presented with a thoracic spinal cord level compression.

RF333: Could patients’ neurological status deteriorate after posterior decompression and fusion for unstable vertebral pathological fractures?

Maroun Rizkallah 1 , Ghassan Boubez 2 , Jesse Shen 2 , Fidaa Al-Shakfa 2 , Daniel Shedid 2 , Sung-Joo Yuh 2 , Zhi Wang 2

1 Centre de formation medicale du nouveau Brunswick, Dr Georges L dumont university Hospital, Sherbrooke University, Moncton, Canada, 2 Centre Hospitalier de l'universite de Montreal, Montreal, Canada

Introduction: In some instances, surgical candidates deteriorate neurologically post-operatively after unstable pathological vertebral fracture despite event-less surgery. Even though this complication is well known and dreaded by surgeons worldwide, predictive factors for this neurological compromise were never looked for. Material and Methods: This retrospective study included consecutive patients with pathological spine fractures and ASIA scale scores E/D/C/B who underwent posterior spinal decompression and fusion with transpedicular corpectomy and cement-based reconstruction, based on their neurological compromise or SINS score. Patients’ charts were reviewed for demographic, medical, and surgical-related data as well as post-operative outcomes at 6 weeks of follow-up. The main outcome of this study is a decline in at least one grade on ASIA scale. A multivariate analysis was performed to look for predictive factors for this neurological regression. Results: A total of 409 patients (46.0% females) were included with a mean age of 62.8 years. In this cohort, 164 patients (40.1%) had ASIA score E, 205 (50.1%) had ASIA score D, 37 (9.1%) had ASIA score C and 3 (0.7%) had ASIA score B. Neurological deterioration occurred in 54 patients (13.2%). Of these patients, there were 32 ASIA E (19.5%); 20 ASIA D (9.8%) and 2 ASIA C (5.4%). Mean age in patients who deteriorated postoperatively was 63.7 years compared to 62.6 in those who did not deteriorate (p = 0.40). In patients with thoracic compression, 16.4% of patients deteriorated compared to 11.7% of patients with lumbar level compression (p = 0.04). Mean surgical time averaged 233 minutes in patients who deteriorated post-operatively whereas it reached 192.3 minutes in patients who did not (p = 0.048). Multivariate analysis showed that diabetic patients (p = 0.04), those who underwent a longer surgery (p = 0.03), those with thoracic spine compression level (p = 0.029), and those with better scores on ASIA scale (p < 0.01) were at increased risk of post-operative neurological compromise. ASA score, smoking status and delay to surgery did not affect the post-operative neurological outcome. Conclusion: Risk of neurological compromise is significant and should be kept in mind while discussing outcomes and post-operative expectations in this particularly frail patients’ population. Particular attention should be drawn towards diabetic patients, those initially neurologically intact and those with thoracic compression.

RF334: Surgical practice patterns for metastatic spinal disease in Europe - A survey on spine surgeons

Leevi Toivonen 1 , Áron Lazáry 2 , Jorrit-Jan Verlaan 3 , Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad 4,5

1 Tampere University Hospital, Tampere, Finland, 2 National Center for Spinal Disorders, Semmelweis University, Budapest, Hungary, 3 University Medical Center Utrecht, Utrecht, Netherlands, 4 Spine Center, Helios Klinikum, Erfurt, Germany, 5 Assiut University, Assiut, Egypt

Introduction: Management of metastatic spinal disease (MSD) is rapidly evolving. We anticipate variability on current practices for MSD. The role of economic factors in this variability has not been studied. This regional survey on AO Spine European members sought to determine the current status of surgical practices for MSD in Europe. Material and Methods: An anonymous survey was distributed to the European AO Spine members. The first part of the survey explored basic characteristics of the respondents and their institutions. The second part consisted of clinical case scenarios geared to demonstrate the expected differences. Responses were compared between geographical regions (North, West, East, South) and economic tertiles after classifying the respondents’ countries per their gross national income (GNI) using the chi-squared test and logistic regression. Results: 199 surgeons completed the survey. Most were employed in academic institutions (57%) with an experience of over 5 years (89%). GNI was associated with the resources available but little with preoperative or surgical practices. Neurologic deficits were the most common surgical indication in the North (79%) and East (55%), whereas symptomatic or impending instability was most common in the West (53%) and South (52%), p = 0.007. Surgeons were more likely to use the separation surgery concept in the Eastern and Southern regions (51% and 53%) than in the Northern or Western regions (20% and 25%), p = 0.006. Conclusion: Geographical variability was observed in willingness to and timing of surgery in MSD. The economic status of countries had a little impact on practices, while it impacted the resources available. Results highlight the need for continued, evidence-based education and guidelines.

RF335: Carbon fiber-reinforced-pedicle screws for treatment of spinal tumors. Report of 54 patients

Hamdan Abdelrahman 1 , Seyed-Emadaldin Sadat 1 , Ahmed Shawky Abdelgawaad 1 , Ali Ezzati 1

1 Helios Clinic Erfurt- Germany, Asiut University Hospitals- Egypt, Erfurt, Germany

Introduction: Surgery for spinal metastases has gained a decisive role in modern oncological treatment. It regularly includes spinal instrumentation with pedicle screws. Recently, carbon-fiber-reinforced screws (CFR) became available for posterior instrumentation with the aim to reduce imaging artifacts by implants reducing artifacts on imaging and showing less perturbation effects on photon radiation. The study aims to report on the safety and efficacy of CFR pedicle screw systems for 54 patients with spinal tumors. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed prospectively the collected data of patients being operated on from April 2019 to 31 April 2023 using a CFR pedicle screw system for posterior stabilization alone or comined with corperectomy because of spinal tumors. Results: Fifty-four patients (38 males, 16 females) with mean nage 69,6 years (48-86). Spinal tumors were assessed (metastases in 41; lymphoma in 3, myeloma in 10. Implantation of CFR implants was feasible in all cases. Thoracic spine was operated in 25 patients, thoracolumbar junction in 16 and lumbar in 16. multiple regions were operated in 4 patients. On average, 4 levels were instrumented. Anterior reconstruction was performed in 20 (37%) patients. Intraoperative complications were documented in 3 (5,5%) patients. Revision surgery for postoperative complications was necessary in 5 (9%) patients; tumor growth in 3 patients (corperectomy was done), other segments with pathological fractures in 2 (got operated), screw loosening in one patient (1.8%) (extended the fixation percutaneously). Conclusion: The use of CFR screws is a safe and efficient alternative to titanium for oncological spinal instrumentation, with low complication and revision rates in routine use and with the advantage of its radiolucency. It reduces image artifacts on computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. Thereby, they are a valuable and feasible option for spinal instrumentations in patients harboring spinal tumors where postoperative imaging and radiation therapy planning are necessary and might be crucial for long-term outcome and overall survival.

RF336: Evaluating the outcomes of posterior-only, anterior-only and combined surgical approach in the management of cervical spine metastasis

Qinxiang Shant Sin 1 , Tan Jun Hao Tan 1 , Yi Zhang 2 , Qian Hui Rachel Lim 1 , Raymen Chandrasagran 1 , Cayden Leyu 3 , Adam Cheng 3 , Andre Loh 3 , Nishant Barua 4 , Naresh Kumar 1 , Jiong Hao Tan 1

1 National University Hospital Orthopaedic Spine Surgery, Singapore, Singapore, 2 Ministry of Health Holdings, Singapore, Singapore, 3 National University of Singapore, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, Singapore, Singapore, 4 Trinity College of Dublin, Dublin, Ireland

Introduction: Cervical spine metastasis accounts for 8-15% of all spinal metastasis and are associated with poorer outcomes then thoracolumbar metastases. Patients may present with mechanical pain, radicular or myelopathic symptoms, and progressive neurological deficits. Surgical treatment is aimed at restoring spinal stability and achieving surgical decompression thus improving quality of life and function. Unlike the thoracolumbar spine where surgical decompression and instrumentation is performed predominantly through a posterior approach, there is a considerable variation in surgical approaches used in treating cervical spinal metastases. These approaches include the posterior, anterior and combined anterior-posterior approaches. We aim to analyze and compare the outcomes of these surgical approaches to improve our understanding on their respective utility. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 78 patients with cervical and cervical-thoracic junction metastasis that underwent surgery in a single institution from 2006 to 2024. Baseline characteristics, including demographics, oncological characteristics and pre-operative function was collected. The Spinal Instability in Neoplasia (SINS) score and Bilsky Score were used to classify spinal instability and severity of cord compression. Surgical characteristics such as operative time, total blood loss(mls), need for transfusion, number of levels instrumented or decompressed, and pre-operative embolization were collected. Predicted survival was calculated based on the modified Tokuhashi score. Post-operative outcomes including neurological outcomes, presence of medical and surgical complications, disease recurrence and patient survival was also collected. Results: 78 patients were identified, 51 (65.4%) were treated with a posterior approach, 9 (11.5%) Anterior and 18 (23.1%) with a combined approach. There was no significant difference in baseline demographic, functional, neurological and oncological characteristics. A combined approach was significantly associated with increased duration of surgery when compared to posterior and anterior surgery (409 vs308 vs 252) minutes (p = 0.02) and an anterior only approach was associated with a significant decrease in number of levels instrumented when compared to posterior and combined approached surgery (4 vs 7 vs 7) levels. There was also no significant difference in neurological outcomes, post-operative outcome or overall survival in all 3 groups. A further analysis comparing posterior vs anterior + combined approach did not show any significant difference between the two groups (p < 0.05). Conclusion: In our cohort, there was no difference in outcome between patients treated with all 3 surgical outcomes. Selection of surgical approach should be based on patient factors such as location of tumor and severity of cord compression. However this study does suggest that a posterior only approach is a comparable alternative to an anterior or combined approached.

RF337: Five-year single-center experience with spinal tumors: tumour types and operative strategies

Ioannis Dravopoulos 1 , Kyriakos Papakonstantinou 1 , Ploutarchos Karydakis 1 , Christos Tsaggaris 1 , Nikolaos Georgakoulias 1 , Nikolaos Paidakakos 1

1 Athens General Hospital ‘G. Gennimatas’, Athens, Greece

Introduction: Spinal tumors are clinically heterogeneous, and operative strategy varies by compartment-extradural (ED), intradural-extramedullary (ID-EM), and intradural-intramedullary (IM). We describe the case mix and surgical patterns from a contemporary five-year, single tertiary center series. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed consecutive tumor operations performed between February 2020 and September 2025 (n = 164). Variables abstracted included date, age, anatomical region, tumor compartment (ED, ID-EM, IM), operation type and histology. Clinical outcomes and progression free survival (PFS) were evaluated. Descriptive statistics are presented as counts (%) and medians (IQR). Results: Median age was 63.5 years (IQR 50.9-72.5). Procedures by compartment were ED 94/164 (57.3%), ID-EM 56/164 (34.1%), and IM 14/164 (8.5%). Anatomical distribution favored the thoracic spine (67/164, 40.8%), followed by lumbar (53/164, 32.3%) and cervical (44/164, 26.8%) levels. Instrumentation was used in 67/94 ED cases (72.0%), 28/56 ID-EM (50.0%), and 8/14 IM (57.1%), yielding an overall rate of 62.8%. Among ID-EM cases meningioma accounted for 18/56 (32.1%) and schwannoma for 16/56 (28,5%). IM tumors were uncommon; histologies included ependymoma (7/14, 50%), astrocytoma (5/14, 35.7%) and hemangioblastoma (2/14, 14.3%). Within ED, 77/94 (82%) were documented as metastases with primary tumors accounting for 17/94 (18%) of whom 8/17 (47%) underwent en-bloc resection. Separation surgery and fixation was mostly used for metastatic epidural disease, except monometastatic disease were gross total resection and in one case en-bloc resection were considered. Of all cases approximately 63% improved, 6% worsened neurologically with 31% remaining stable at 3-month follow-up. 2- and 5-year PFS is analyzed per compartment. Annual procedural volume was 20 (2020), 25 (2021), 26 (2022), 41 (2023), 33 (2024), and 19 (through Sept, 2025). Conclusion: In this five-year experience, ED disease constituted the majority of spinal tumor operations, with predominant thoracic involvement and frequent need for stabilization. ID-EM cases were largely typical (meningioma, schwannoma), whereas IM tumors were rare. En bloc resection was selectively employed mainly in primary ED tumors. RF338: Impact of surgical planning status on survival, resource utilization, and functional outcomes of metastatic spine tumor surgery: systematic review

Ali Haider Bangash 1,2 , Jayden Boafo 1,2 , Michelle Lee 1,2 , Keyvan Ghadimi 2 , Sertac Kirnaz 1,2 , Rose Fluss 1,2 , Saikiran G. Murthy 1,2 , Yaroslav Gelfand 1,2 , Reza Yassari 1,2 , Rafael De la Garza Ramos 1,2

1 Spine Tumor Mechanics and Outcomes Research (TUMOR) Lab, Montefiore Medical Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, USA, 2 Department of Neurosurgery, Montefiore Medical Center, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, NY, USA

Introduction: Metastatic spine tumor surgery (MSTS) represents a critical intervention for patients with spinal metastases, often performed to preserve neurological function, achieve local tumor control, and improve quality of life. However, the influence of surgical planning status, whether procedures are conducted as planned, semi-elective interventions or as unplanned, emergent operations, on patient outcomes remains incompletely characterized. The distinction between planned and unplanned MSTS may have significant implications for perioperative risk stratification, resource allocation, and clinical decision-making. Therefore, we attempted to systematically synthesize the available evidence on the relationship between surgical planning status and comprehensive clinical outcomes in patients undergoing MSTS, addressing an important knowledge gap in the multidisciplinary management of spinal metastases. Material and Methods: PubMed, Cochrane, and Epistemonikos were searched for studies reporting outcomes in the context of surgical planning status for patients managed with MSTS from inception till May 14, 2025. Study quality was assessed using the Methodological index for non-randomized studies (MINORS) tool. We evaluated the impact of surgical planning status on survival, mortality, perioperative complications, resource utilization metrics, and functional outcomes. Meta-analysis feasibility was explored based on methodological and outcome reporting uniformity. Results: Out of a total of 1,278 studies, twenty-six studies reporting on 72,614 patients (Mean age 62 years; 43% female) met the inclusion criteria. 77% (n = 20 of 26) studies were found to have moderate methodological quality based on MINORS criteria, with none of the studies prospectively calculating the respective sample size for power analysis. A meta-analysis was precluded due to substantial variability in the definition of surgical planning status. Regarding survival, 44% of reporting studies (n = 7 of 16) found significantly lower survival with unplanned MSTS, while 50% (n = 8 of 16) found no significant difference. For perioperative complications, 44% of studies (n = 7 of 16) reported significantly higher rates with unplanned MSTS, while 56% (n = 9 of 16) found no significant difference. Resource utilization metrics consistently demonstrated disadvantages with unplanned procedures: 88% of studies (n = 7 of 8) reported significantly extended hospital stays, and all three studies examining discharge disposition reported significantly higher rates of non-routine discharge. Functional outcomes were worse with unplanned MSTS in 72% of reporting studies (n = 5 of 7). Blood loss was significantly lower in planned MSTS in 67% of studies (n = 2 of 3) examining this parameter. Patient-reported outcomes showed initial benefits with planned surgery that diminished by 6 months postoperatively. Surgical planning demonstrated no significant impact on perioperative transfusion requirements, reoperation rates, readmission, or recurrence outcomes. Conclusion: While evidence regarding survival and complications in MSTS shows variability, there is consistent evidence that unplanned MSTS are associated with increased resource utilization (extended hospital stays and higher non-routine discharge rates) and worse functional outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of timely surgical planning when clinically feasible. The substantial heterogeneity in defining “unplanned” surgery highlights a critical gap in standardized terminology. Future research should establish standardized terminology for surgical planning status and develop refined protocols to optimize intervention timing in this complex patient population by pursuing high-quality studies.

RF339: Evaluating the impact of UK GIRFT guidelines on cauda equina syndrome referrals and delays: a single-centre retrospective study

Youssef Sadek 1 , Shams Ali Baig 1 , Adrian Gardner 2

1 University of Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom, 2 Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, Birmingham, United Kingdom

Introduction: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a rare but serious spinal emergency involving lumbosacral nerve root compression, with an incidence of 0.3-0.5 per 100,000/year. Timely decompression may mitigate the risk of lasting bowel, bladder, and motor dysfunction. In February 2023, the UK Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) programme released updated national CES guidelines, setting prompt targets for the management of these patients, including MRI within 4 hours of assessment, to guide urgent surgical decision-making and reduce the risk of permanent neurological decline. The aim of this study was to evaluate referral quality, pathway performance, and delays in imaging before and after guideline implementation at a tertiary spinal referral centre. Material and Methods: This retrospective single-centre review included consecutive referrals for suspected CES between February 2022 and February 2024, stratified into pre- (Feb 2022-2023) and post-GIRFT (Feb 2023-2024) cohorts. Data were obtained from electronic referral systems. Key variables, benchmarked against GIRFT standards, included referral pathway use, time of presentation, assessment and referral, transfer rates, neurological and bladder assessments and time at which MRI was performed at referring hospitals. Outcomes are presented as proportions or medians with interquartile ranges. Results: A total of 137 CES referrals met inclusion criteria (pre-GIRFT n = 93; post-GIRFT n = 44). The median patient age was 49 years (IQR 38-60). The majority of patients presented with back pain or sciatica (96%). Bladder dysfunction occurred in 72%, most commonly incontinence (46.5%) or urinary retention (27.3%), with smaller proportions experiencing both retention and incontinence (2.0%) or other urinary abnormalities (24.2%). Bowel dysfunction was reported in 30 %, while abnormal perianal sensation in 42%, and reduced anal tone in 34%. Use of the dedicated CES referral pathway increased post-GIRFT (88% to 93%), while the level of urgency of referrals remained at a consistent level (emergency 66% vs 66%; urgent 34% vs 30%). Transfers to our centre rose (28% to 46%). Rates of bladder scanning (22% vs 23%), linked MRIs (22% vs 23%), and full neurological assessment (30% vs 25 %) remained largely unchanged, though MRI performed prior to referral increased (31 % to 44%). Among patients with documented MRI request and scan times, the median interval from order to completion decreased from 3.59 hours (0.74-23.8) pre-GIRFT to 1.92 hours (0.78-11.54) post-GIRFT. Conclusion: Following the release of the GIRFT guidelines, there were improvements in referral pathway adherence, higher rates of pre-transfer MRI, and a reduction in MRI request-to-scan times. However, documentation of many recommended variables including bladder scan assessment and full neurological examination remained suboptimal. Ongoing efforts to standardise assessment and optimise early imaging are required to fully realise the guideline’s aims of reducing delays and potentially mitigating long-term morbidity in CES.

RF340: Anterior column reconstruction with autologous vertebral bone graft after en bloc resection for primary tumors

Chiara Cini 1 , Marco Girolami 1,2 , Stefano Bandiera 1 , riccardo ghermandi 1 , Giovanni Barbanti Bròdano 1 , Silvia Terzi 1 , Giuseppe Tedesco 1 , Gisberto Evangelisti 1 , Valerio Pipola 1 , Cristiana Griffoni 1 , Stefano Pasini 1 , Luigi Falzetti 1 , Giovanni Tosini 1 , Alessandro Gasbarrini 1,3

1 Complex Spinal Surgery Unit, IRCCS Istituto Ortopedico Rizzoli, Bologna, Italy, 2 Spine Unit, Hospital Universitario Fundacion Jimenez Diaz, Madrid, Spain, 3 Department of Biomedical and Neuromotor Sciences, University of Bologna, Bologna, Italy

Introduction: Anterior reconstruction after en bloc resection for primary spine tumors is a challenging topic for which bone grafting is just one of several options available. Long bone or iliac crest bone grafts are most commonly used and make heterotopic structural graft the gold standard. In the reported cases an original technique of anterior column reconstruction using vertebral body allografts is described. Material and Methods: We included in our analysis 10 patients who underwent anterior column reconstruction with vertebral body graft (VBG) after en bloc resections. VBG, available from bone banks, are harvested on the surgical field and augmented with polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) to protect the graft from failure during creeping substitution phase of bone integration. VBG are manually placed to cover the anterior defect between the superior line of resection and the caudal line of resection. Connection of the anterior graft to the posterior instrumentation is realized by implanting a standard pedicle screw in the graft. Better is achieved applying a gentle posterior compression. VBG are modular by nature and closely resemble the resected specimen in terms of volume, decreasing the distance between host-bone and graft cortices that might have a positive impact on stress-distribution at the level of the end-plates. Results: All patients underwent en bloc resection for primary tumor of the spine. The most common histological diagnosis was Giant cell tumor with 4 patients (40%) and the most common location was of primary tumor was the thoracic spine (90%). 8 patients (80%) underwent a single-stage posterior procedure while 2 (20%) patients underwent surgery in two stages. The mean length of the graft was 5.01 ± 3.2 cm, and the mean construct spanned 8.3 ± 3.0 vertebral levels. Complete posterior graft fusion with superior and inferior endplates was achieved in 9 patients (90%) with a mean fusion time of 7 ± 2.1 months. One evidence of graft fracture was observed in one patient at 10 months of follow-up and required revision surgery for failure with loss of correction. Local recurrence of chordoma occurred in one patient at 12 months of follow-up and surgery was required with adjuvant Proton Beam Therapy with 54 Gy(RBE) in 25 fractions within 20 weeks from surgery. No patients complained axial pain at the final follow-up (52 ± 3.2 months)

Conclusion: Vertebral body allografts can be used to provide immediate and reliable anterior column support and restore weight-bearing capacity of the spine. Moreover grafts are radiolucent, thus suitable to be used in combination with CFR-PEEK posterior instrumentation in order not to interfere with heavy-particles radiation therapy protocols and to detect local recurrences.

RF341: Limitations of D-wave monitoring: nerve root injury despite preserved corticospinal tract function

Gabrielle Santangelo 1 , Daniel Sciubba 1 , Larry Lo 1 , Randy D'Amico 1 , Justin Silverstein 1

1 Northwell Health, Manhasset, United States

Introduction: D-wave monitoring is the gold standard for assessing corticospinal tract (CST) integrity during intramedullary tumor resections. Literature supports that when muscle motor evoked potentials (MMEPs) are lost but the D-wave remains stable, patients usually experience transient deficits. However, the risk of concomitant nerve root injury is less well described. This study reviews intradural intramedullary (IDIM) and intradural extramedullary (IDEM) surgeries using D-wave and MMEP monitoring involving the C8 or T1 nerve roots. Material and Methods: After IRB approval, a retrospective review was performed of patients undergoing IDIM or IDEM procedures (2021-2024). Nine consecutive cases were identified; seven met inclusion criteria. Two were excluded due to lack of D-wave monitoring. Results: Only one case demonstrated D-wave attenuation which recovered by closure with post-operative unilateral leg weakness. MMEP attenuation occurred in four procedures. One patient had full MMEP recovery at closure but awoke with sensory deficits and foot drop. In another, bilateral hand MMEPs transiently disappeared and partially recovered with increased MAP, resulting in postoperative hand weakness. A third case showed persistent lower extremity MMEP attenuation with corresponding post-operative weakness. The fourth demonstrated absent bilateral lower extremity and hand MMEPs who post-operatively had transient leg weakness and persistent hand weakness. Conclusion: Stable D-wave recordings are often interpreted as reassuring despite MMEP loss, under the assumption that weakness will be temporary. Our series suggests this approach may overlook nerve root or lower motor neuron injury, which D-wave monitoring does not capture. Larger studies are warranted, but intraoperative changes should be contextualized, particularly when critical nerve roots are involved.

Bipin Mishra 1 , Sivaraman Kumarasamy 1 , Sachin Borkar 1

1 AIIMS , New Delhi, Delhi, India

Introduction: Aneurysmal bone cysts (ABCs) are benign yet locally aggressive bone neoplasms. The data underscores the critical need for aggressive, multimodal management strategies, including extensive fixation, in cases with high instability and neurological compromise to optimize patient outcomes.

RF343: Disc signal-lordosis mismatch: the impact of cervical disc degeneration on supine MRI versus standing radiograph alignment

Yunus Emre Yilmaz 1

1 Ankara Etlik City Hospital, Ankara, Turkey

Introduction: Cervical sagittal alignment is commonly assessed using standing lateral radiographs, while supine MRI is the gold standard for evaluating disc quality. However, the discrepancy between posture-dependent radiographic parameters and supine MRI has not been fully elucidated. We hypothesized that decreased disc signal intensity on MRI is associated with greater mismatch in sagittal alignment parameters between modalities. Material and Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 60 patients (300 cervical segments) who underwent both standing lateral radiographs and cervical MRI within two weeks. For each segment (C2-3 through C6-7), disc signal intensity ratio (RSI) was calculated by normalizing disc T2 signal to spinal cord ROI. Segmental Cobb angles (C2-3 through C6-7) and global C2-7 Cobb, cervical sagittal vertical axis (cSVA), and T1 slope were measured on both modalities. Mismatch (Δ) was defined as radiograph - MRI. Correlations between RSI and ΔAngle were assessed using Pearson’s correlation. Paired t-tests compared global parameters. Results: RSI vs ΔAngle: Significant negative correlation (r = -0.22, p < 0.001). Lower disc signal was associated with greater mismatch between modalities. Global Cobb (C2-7): Standing radiographs showed greater lordosis than MRI (Δ = +4.6° ± 10.5°, p = 0.001). cSVA: Standing radiographs demonstrated anterior shift compared to MRI (Δ = +11.1 mm ± 7.4 mm, p < 0.001). T1 slope: Standing radiographs were significantly higher than MRI (Δ = +7.3° ± 5.8°, p < 0.001). Conclusion: Cervical disc degeneration, quantified by MRI signal intensity, is significantly associated with posture-dependent mismatch in segmental lordosis. Furthermore, standing radiographs consistently revealed greater lordosis, anterior sagittal translation, and higher T1 slope compared to supine MRI. These findings introduce the novel concept of Disc Signal-Lordosis Mismatch, highlighting the biomechanical interplay between disc quality and sagittal balance, and underscore the importance of considering posture when evaluating cervical alignment.

RF344: Miyazaki syndrome: diagnostic challenges and surgical outcomes - A systematic review

Filippos Chelmis 1 , Silvia Pecoraro 1 , Paraskevas Pakataridis 1 , Iliana Sorotou 1 , Mary Solou 2 , Philip Ho 2 , Athanasios Sivridis 3 , Athanasios Zisakis 2 , Alexandru Budu 2

1 Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski”, Sofia, Bulgaria, 2 Queen Elizabeth Hospital, Birmingham, United Kingdom, 3 Medical University of Sofia, Sofia, Bulgaria

Introduction: Miyazaki syndrome is a rare, important cause of cervical myelopathy, typically arising after cerebrospinal fluid shunting due to chronic overdrainage and venous engorgement. The literature consists of limited case reports, case series, no larger studies available. This condition is underrecognized/misdiagnosed, standardized management are lacking. Our study highlights key diagnostic features, effective treatment and early recognition to improve patient outcomes. Material and Methods: We performed a PRISMA-guided systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420251048122) of case reports/series on Miyazaki syndrome across PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Results: 31 studies (37 patients) met the criteria. Mean age was 43.9 years; ventriculoperitoneal shunts predominated. RF345: Cervical pedicle screws versus lateral mass screws: comparative analysis of efficacy and stability in cervical spine fusion

Anas Dyab 1 , Stefanos Apallas 2 , Muaaz AlAmeer 3

1 Medizentrum Limperstberg, Luxembourg, Luxembourg, 2 Chrisitan Doppler Clinic Salzburg, Paracelsus Private Medical University, Salzburg, Austria, 3 Centre Hospitalier de Luxembourg, Luxembourg, Luxembourg

Introduction: Spinal fusion procedures often require the use of screw fixation to provide stability and support for the healing process. When performing cervical spine fusion, surgeons have traditionally relied on lateral mass screws as a reliable method of fixation. (Yasuda & Takayasu, 2014) However, the use of cervical pedicle screws has emerged as an alternative approach that may offer greater stability and improved fusion outcomes. Literature Review

Methodology: This study retrospectively analyzed the outcomes of cervical fusion procedures performed at our institution between 2018 and 2023. Patients were divided into two groups: those who underwent fusion with lateral mass screws and those who received cervical pedicle screws. Demographic data, surgical details, and clinical outcomes were collected and compared between the two groups. Radiographic evaluation was performed to assess fusion rates, screw placement accuracy, and construct stability. Complications such as neurovascular injuries, screw loosening, and implant failure were also documented (Wang et al., 2021). Results: A total of 80 patients were included in the study, with undergoing lateral mass screw fixation and receiving cervical pedicle screws. Fusion rates were higher in the pedicle screw group at compared to the lateral mass screw group at . Screw placement accuracy, as measured by the pedicle perforation grading system, was excellent in the pedicle screw group with over of screws placed within the pedicle. (Wang et al., 2021) Construct stability, as indicated by the absence of screw loosening or implant failure, was also superior in the pedicle screw group compared to the lateral mass screw group. The pedicle screw group experienced a lower rate of complications, with neurovascular injuries occurring in only of patients compared to in the lateral mass screw group. (Tsirikos, 2019). Regarding screw accuracy, the pedicle screw group had a higher proportion of screws placed within the acceptable range, with of the screws graded as optimal or acceptable, compared to in the lateral mass screw group (Wang et al., 2021). Discussion: The findings of this study suggest that the use of cervical pedicle screws may offer several advantages over lateral mass screws for cervical spine fusion. The increased stability and improved fusion rates provided by pedicle screw fixation may lead to better long-term outcomes and a lower risk of complications (Kim et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021).

While the technical challenges and potential risks associated with pedicle screw placement must be carefully considered, the results of this study indicate that with proper surgical technique and intraoperative imaging guidance, cervical pedicle screws can be a safe and effective option for spinal stabilization. The literature supports these findings, with several studies demonstrating the superior biomechanical properties and clinical outcomes of cervical pedicle screws compared to lateral mass screws (Luo et al., 2019; Okuyama et al., 2001; Tsirikos, 2019; Wang et al., 2021). Conclusion: In conclusion, this retrospective analysis suggests that the use of cervical pedicle screws may be a more effective and stable construct for cervical spine fusion compared to lateral mass screws. The improved fusion rates, construct stability, and lower complication rates observed in the pedicle screw group support the consideration of this technique as a viable alternative to traditional lateral mass screw fixation.

Material and Methods: A total of 186 patients who underwent ACDF for degenerative cervical myelopathy and were followed up for over two years were retrospectively reviewed.
