Outcome measures included C2-C7 sagittal vertical axis, C2-C7 lordosis, neck pain visual analogue scale (VAS), arm pain VAS, and Japanese Orthopedic Association (JOA) score. Results: One hundred forty-seven patients (79.0%) were included in the no-SCCM group, while the remaining 39 patients were in the SCCM group (21.0%). Baseline characteristics and pre/postoperative radiographic results did not show significant intergroup differences. Both groups experienced significant improvements in neck pain VAS and arm pain VAS after the operation, with no significant differences between the two groups postoperatively. Additionally, JOA scores significantly improved in both groups postoperatively, with no significant intergroup differences in JOA score or JOA recovery rate (see Table 3). Canal-cord ratio was not significantly associated with JOA recovery rate at two years postoperative in linear regression analysis (beta, -0.014; 95% confidence interval, -204.416 - 169.889; p = 0.856). Conclusion: This study demonstrates that clinical outcomes, including neck pain, arm pain, and JOA score after ACDF, are not negatively affected by SCCM. Postoperative outcomes did not significantly differ between the no-SCCM and SCCM groups, and canal-cord ratio was not significantly associated with postoperative JOA score. Contrary to common belief that canal expansion surgery, such as laminoplasty or laminectomy, may benefit patients with SCCM, ACDF appears to provide favorable outcomes for cervical myelopathy complicated by SCCM. Further studies comparing anterior and posterior approaches for treating SCCM could provide clarity on this matter. In conclusion, ACDF can be safely and effectively applied for treating cervical myelopathy, regardless of the presence of SCCM, when the number of levels, sagittal alignment, and shape of compressive pathology favor the anterior approach.

RF350: Open-door cervical laminoplasty using repurposed titanium miniplates: favorable clinical and radiological outcomes with a cost-effective alternative

Mohammed Khaled M. Ahmed 1 , Hamdy Tammam 1 , Elsayed Said 1 , Mohammad El-Sharkawi 2

1 Department of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Qena Faculty of Medicine, South Valley University, Qena, Egypt, 2 Department of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, Assiut University, Assiut, Egypt

Introduction: Laminoplasty is a well-established, motion-preserving posterior decompression technique for multilevel degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM). Dedicated titanium laminoplasty plates improve stability and reduce hinge reclosure compared with suture-based fixation, but their high cost and limited availability restrict widespread use. Hand and maxillofacial titanium miniplates can be readily contoured to secure the opened lamina, offering a practical and cost-effective alternative. This prospective pilot study evaluated the clinical and radiological outcomes of open-door cervical laminoplasty using these repurposed plates. Material and Methods: Eighteen consecutive patients with symptomatic multilevel DCM underwent open-door laminoplasty stabilized with repurposed titanium miniplates. Operative time, intraoperative blood loss, hospital stay, and perioperative or implant-related complications were documented. Results: Eighteen patients (13 males, 5 females; mean age 54.7 ± 7.6 years) completed a minimum of 1 year follow-up. CT demonstrated significant spinal canal expansion from a median 10.3 mm (IQR 1.11) to 16.1 mm (IQR 2.30) (p < 0.01). Of 72 hinges created, 51 (70.8%) achieved ideal greenstick deformation, and 65 (90.3%) demonstrated solid healing at final follow-up. MRI confirmed adequate spinal cord decompression in all cases. Complications were limited to one superficial wound infection treated successfully with antibiotics and one transient C5 palsy that fully recovered. No implant loosening, failure, or laminar closure occurred. Conclusion: Open-door cervical laminoplasty using repurposed titanium miniplates is a simple, safe, and cost-effective posterior decompression technique that provides significant neurological recovery, pain and disability reduction, reliable canal expansion with high hinge-healing rates, and minimal implant-related complications, offering a practical alternative to dedicated laminoplasty plates in resource-limited settings.

Boston, United States

Introduction: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) arises from progressive spinal cord compression due to degenerative changes in the spinal column. Diagnosis is frequently delayed, often due to missed or incorrect initial identification. A lack of awareness and standardised screening criteria has been identified as a major contributor. Early identification of DCM is paramount; delayed diagnosis can have significant consequences such as worsening neurological impairment, suboptimal postoperative recovery and reduced independence. As part of the RECODE-DCM initiative to develop screening criteria for DCM, a three-step approach was proposed: (i) systematic literature reviews to ascertain the frequency and diagnostic accuracy of DCM-related symptoms and signs, (ii) a survey capturing expert perspectives, and (iii) a structured consensus process. This study represents the second stage. Objective: To conduct a survey of international experts and determine the value of various signs and symptoms in diagnosing patients with DCM. Aims: To identify a list of symptoms and signs with diagnostic significance for DCM that will ultimately inform a structured consensus process to develop pragmatic screening criteria for use by frontline clinicians. Materials and Methods: An open voluntary English-language Likert scale survey was created in accordance with CHERRIES guidance. The survey included thirty-nine symptoms and thirty-four signs related to DCM that were identified from previous systematic reviews. Respondents were asked to rank each sign and symptom on a scale of 0 (not important at all) to 10 (extremely important); a mean value of ≥ 6.5 was set a priori as the threshold to consider a sign or symptom as having significant diagnostic value. Basic sampling information with respect to participant discipline, country of practice, experience with DCM and demographic information was collected. Professional societies representing the key stakeholders involved in the diagnosis of DCM were approached to help disseminate the survey. Results: The survey was accessed by 860 international surgical and non-surgical experts; 390 participants started the survey (45.3% start rate). Complete responses for signs and symptoms were obtained from 355 respondents (91.0% completion rate). The survey cohort included 227 surgeons (58.2%), 23 neurologists (5.9%) and 101 allied healthcare professionals (25.9%). Respondents were from 57 countries across 6 continents. The mean clinical experience of responders was 15.9 years (SD 11.3 years; range 0-50 years), with 286 (73.3%) reporting at least 5 years. Experts ranked fifteen symptoms and twelve signs as having significant diagnostic value. Key symptoms included those related to upper limb and hand function, and gait disturbances. Important signs included reflex abnormalities, motor deficits, and impairments of gait and coordination. Conclusion: International experts ranked twenty-seven signs and symptoms of DCM as having high diagnostic value, comprising fifteen symptoms and twelve signs. The findings were relatively consistent across professional groups, experience levels and continental regions. These twenty-seven features will be carried forward to an international consensus meeting for consolidation to establish a standardised clinical screening toolkit for use by frontline healthcare professionals to support early recognition of DCM.

Matthew Kim 1 , Seungjun Lee 2 , Graham Goh 1 , K. Daniel Riew 3,4

1 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Boston University Medical Center, Boston, United States, 2 Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, United States, 3 Department of Neurological Surgery, Weill-Cornell Medical Center, New York, United States, 4 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Columbia University Medical Center, New York, United States

Introduction: GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are novel agents prescribed for obesity and type 2 diabetes. In addition to their metabolic effects, GLP-1RAs reduce inflammation, improve endothelial function, and potentially alter bone metabolism. This study aimed to compare the perioperative complications, resource utilization and revision rates in patients undergoing ACDF with or without perioperative GLP-1RA therapy. GLP-1RA users had prescriptions within 6 months before and 6 months after surgery. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed for age, sex, BMI, Charlson Comorbidity Index, smoking status, osteoporosis, and socioeconomic factors (education, employment, housing, occupational exposure). These findings suggest that perioperative GLP-1RA therapy could play a role in optimizing outcomes for high-risk spine surgery candidates, particularly those with obesity or diabetes.

RF353: Incidence of C5 palsy in anterior cervical decompression & fusion, posterior cervical decompression & fusion and laminoplasty for degenerative cervical myelopathy: systematic review and meta-analysis of 21,231 cases

Sathish Muthu 1,2 , Guna Pradeep 1,3 , Vibhu Krishnan Viswanathan 1,4

1 Department of Spine Surgery, Orthopaedic Research Group, Coimbatore, India, 2 Department of Orthopaedics, Government Medical College, Karur, India, 3 Department of Orthopaedics - Spine Division, Meenakshi Mission Hospital, Madurai, India, 4 Department of Spine Surgery, Devadoss Multispeciality Hospital, Madurai, India

Introduction: C5 palsy (C5P) is a common, yet poorly understood complication of cervical decompressive surgery, causing substantial disability and impacting postoperative quality of life. Despite extensive research, the actual incidence and distribution of C5P across different cervical surgical approaches over the past decade remain unclear. Materials and Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted on October 15, 2024, across Google Scholar, Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases. Studies reporting C5P incidence following surgery for degenerative cervical conditions, published until 2024, were included, excluding reviews, opinions, letters, and non-English manuscripts. Results: Ninety-seven articles were included, encompassing 21,231 patients undergoing decompressive cervical surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy. The overall incidence of postoperative C5P was 7% (95% confidence interval [CI], 4%-10%). The highest incidence was observed with circumferential fusion (combined anterior-posterior approach) at 16% (95% CI, 8%-24%), while the lowest was with anterior cervical decompression and fusion at 4% (95% CI, 3%-5%). Incidence rates following laminoplasty and laminectomy and fusion were 6% (95% CI, 5%-7%) and 10% (95% CI, 8%-12%), respectively. Recovery time ranged from 20.9 to 35 weeks, with 19.1%-33% of patients experiencing residual weakness. Significant risk factors included male sex, preoperative intervertebral foraminal stenosis, ossified posterior longitudinal ligament, open-door laminoplasty, laminectomy (with/without fusion), and excessive spinal cord shift. The role of C4-5 foraminotomy remains contested. Conclusions: Our meta-analysis identifies the posterior surgical approach as a significant risk factor for C5P. Circumferential fusion poses the highest risk, while laminoplasty can reduce the risk compared to laminectomy (alone or with instrumented fusion).

Mustafa Kavcar 1 , Baran Can Alpergin 1

Introduction: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM) is a leading cause of spinal cord dysfunction. This study compares posterior-only and combined anterior-posterior approaches in multilevel CSM with emphasis on alignment and functional recovery. RF355: Outcomes of posterior endoscopic decompression combined with anterior microsurgery in cervical myelomalacia and dynamic stenosis: a strategy for safe circumferential decompression and prevention of white cord syndrome

Hayati Aygun 1

1 Bursa Medicana Hospital, Istanbul, Turkey

Background: Cervical myelomalacia is often associated with advanced cervical spondylotic myelopathy and dynamic stenosis, where both anterior and posterior elements simultaneously compress the spinal cord. In these severe cases, direct anterior decompression alone may be hazardous:

1. Neck extension during surgery can transiently increase cord compression.

2. Sudden, single-stage decompression may cause ischemia-reperfusion injury, known as white cord syndrome (WCS). WCS is rare overall (< 2%) but reported to occur in up to 8-10% of patients with severe stenosis and T2 cord signal changes.

We developed a two-stage single-session strategy, beginning with posterior endoscopic decompression followed by anterior microsurgical stabilization, with three primary goals:

1. Prevent intraoperative positional cord compression during neck extension.

2. Create a posterior safety buffer, reducing the risk of iatrogenic cord injury when manipulating the cord anteriorly.

3. Achieve gradual, circumferential decompression to minimize abrupt hemodynamic changes and reperfusion injury, while providing more effective long-term neural release. Purpose: To evaluate neurological outcomes, white cord syndrome prevention, and complication rates following combined posterior endoscopic decompression and anterior microsurgery in cervical myelomalacia, particularly in dynamic stenosis cases. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 113 patients (mean age: 56 ± 9 years; 72 males, 41 females) treated between 2020 and 2024.

• Dynamic stenosis subgroup: 42 patients (37.2%) had combined anterior and posterior hypertrophic changes causing dynamic compression.

• All underwent single-session surgery, starting with posterior endoscopic decompression and then anterior microsurgical fusion.

• Follow-up: Mean 36 months (range, 24-60).

• Clinical assessments: Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, Neck Disability Index (NDI), and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for neck pain were recorded preoperatively and at final follow-up.

• Definition of WCS: New neurological deficit with T2-hyperintense cord signal on postoperative MRI.

• Statistics: Paired t-test and Fisher’s exact test; p < 0.05 considered significant. Results: JOA score: Improved from 8.4 ± 2.0 to 14.8 ± 1.9 (p < 0.001).

- VAS: Decreased from 8.0 ± 1.1 to 2.0 ± 0.9 (p < 0.001).

- NDI: Improved from 62 ± 11% to 18 ± 8% (p < 0.001).

- White Cord Syndrome: No cases of WCS occurred in the entire cohort, including all 42 high-risk dynamic stenosis patients.

This zero incidence was significantly lower than the 8-10% rate reported for severe stenosis in the literature (p = 0.04).

- Complications: Minor events occurred in 8 patients (7.0%), including transient C5 palsy (3 cases) and superficial wound irritation (5 cases). No permanent neurological deficits, postoperative kyphosis, or implant failures were observed. Overall complication rate was significantly lower than historical open posterior surgery data (p = 0.02). Conclusion: Dynamic stenosis with combined anterior and posterior compression poses a high risk for cord injury and WCS if decompression is abrupt. Our two-stage, single-session approach provides gradual decompression, allowing hemodynamic adaptation and reducing reperfusion injury:

- Step 1: Posterior endoscopic decompression relieves dorsal pressure and prevents intraoperative positional cord compression.

- Step 2: Anterior microsurgical fusion achieves definitive, safe manipulation of the cord and circumferential release.

This strategy resulted in excellent neurological recovery, zero WCS incidence, and a low complication profile, suggesting that gradual circumferential decompression is a key protective mechanism in high-risk cervical myelomalacia patients. Keywords: Cervical myelomalacia, dynamic stenosis, white cord syndrome, gradual decompression, posterior endoscopic decompression, anterior microsurgery, circumferential decompression

Laura Reynolds 1 , Kenneth Nguyen 2 , Aiyush Bansal 2 , Jerry Du 3 , Rafael Garcia de Oliveira 2 , Takeshi Fujii 2,4 , Patricia Lipson 2,5 , Maxey Cherel 2,5 , Michael Jeffko 2,5 , Jack Sedwick 2,5 , Eric Varley 3 , Venu Nemani 2 , Jean Christophe Leveque 2 , Philip Louie 2

Introduction: Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) has become more common in spine surgery and current guidelines recommend its use for high risk cases for its potential to prevent intraoperative neurological injury. The benefit of IONM in lower risk cases remains controversial, accompanied by concerns about its implication on procedural costs. This study aims to evaluate trends in the cost of IONM in cervical spine surgery, assess whether IONM contributes to higher surgical costs, and identify other clinical and sociodemographic drivers of cost in cervical spine surgery. Materials and Methods: Patients undergoing cervical disc replacements, anterior discectomy and fusion, and posterior decompression and fusion with and without IONM were isolated by ICD-10 procedural codes from the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database from 2017 to 2021. Regional trends in the cost of cervical spine surgery per million people were compared by IONM status. Stepwise linear regression models were employed to determine the impact of IONM on the cost of cervical spine surgery and identify additional cost-influencing factors. ACDF, PCDF, and CDR were associated with decreased costs by over $14,000. Clinically, discharge disposition of death increased cost by more than $30,000 and length of stay increased cost by $2,500 per additional day in the hospital. Geographically, when compared with New England, costs were higher in the Pacific region by over $10,000, while the East South Central region was associated with a marked reduction in cost by over $6,000. Conclusion: This study addresses a significant gap in the literature by evaluating the economic impact of IONM in cervical spine surgeries. Our analysis demonstrates that IONM is associated with increased hospital costs, primarily driven by procedural complexity and patient comorbidities. Regional variations in cost likely reflect differences in practice patterns and resource availability. Factors such as discharge disposition and length of stay further contribute to financial burden. Recognizing clinical and regional factors influencing cost is essential for optimizing resource utilization and guiding cost-effective practices in cervical spine surgery, ultimately informing healthcare policy and resource allocation.

However, these methods can cause devastating soft tissue injury by direct contact and are difficult to use in areas with an already compressed cord. We evaluated the use of an ultrasonic bone scalpel, for the patients operated for cervical myelopathy and compared the outcomes to those operated with HSB. Material and Methods: A retrospective analysis was done and patients operated for cervical laminectomy between January 2017 and October 2020 were included. They were divided into two groups based on the device used for laminectomy i.e, HSB and ultrasonic bone scalpel. We compared the demographic, clinical and functional outcomes for patients for one year post operatively. We used the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) and Visual Analogue score (VAS) for both arm and neck pain and Nurick Grading. Results: 177 patients were included of which 101 were operated with an HSB and 76 by ultrasonic bone aspirator. Demographic and baseline parameters were comparable. However, the duration of surgery (p < 0.001) and the rates of total complications (p = 0.041) were significantly higher in the HSB group. Of note, accidental durotomies were significantly lower in the ultrasonic bone scalpel group (p = 0.024). Other variables like blood loss, hospital stay and incision length were similar. Functional outcomes were comparable among the two groups. Conclusion: Ultrasonic bone scalpel has a higher safety margin and helps in achieving a shorter duration of surgery. Specially, the rates of accidental durotomies are significantly less with the use of ultrasonic bone scalpel.

ID: AGS26/3362

RF360: Preoperative hypoalbuminemia predicts increased 90-day complications following elective anterior cervical discectomy and fusion: a national propensity-matched analysis

Omar Diab 1 , Abdel Rahman Diab 2 , Pouya Alijanipour 3

1 University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, United States, 2 University of Michigan Medical Shcool, Ann Harbor, United States, 3 Department of Orthopedics, University of Texas Medical Branch, Galveston, United States

Study Design: Retrospective, propensity-matched cohort study. Objective: To evaluate the association between preoperative hypoalbuminemia and 90-day postoperative complications following elective anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). Summary of Background Data: Serum albumin is a well-established marker of nutritional and inflammatory status. While hypoalbuminemia has been linked to adverse outcomes after various spine procedures, its specific impact on 90-day complications following elective ACDF remains underexplored. Methods: Adult patients undergoing ACDF between 2003 and 2025 were identified in the TriNetX Research network. Patients with cervical trauma, neoplasm, or infection were excluded. Hypoalbuminemia was defined as serum albumin < 3.5 g/dL within 30 days preoperatively. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed based on demographics and comorbidities. Ninety-day postoperative complications were analyzed using z-tests for risk differences and Chi-square tests for categorical comparisons, with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) reported. Results: After matching (n = 2,684 per cohort), preoperative hypoalbuminemia was significantly associated with increased odds of several 90-day complications, including surgical site or spinal infection (OR 1.72; 95% CI 1.23-2.41), pneumonia (OR 1.60; 95% CI 1.19-2.16), acute renal failure (OR 1.44; 95% CI 1.12-1.86), and hospital readmission (OR 1.49; 95% CI 1.19-1.87). No significant differences were observed for thromboembolic events, wound disruption, seroma, hematoma, or hoarseness. Conclusions: Preoperative hypoalbuminemia is an independent predictor of increased 90-day medical and infectious complications following elective ACDF. Because albumin is a potentially modifiable risk factor, these findings support routine preoperative nutritional assessment and optimization to reduce postoperative morbidity.
